context: Estimate the external electric field magnitude required to pull an electron out of a hydrogen-like atom in a time comparable to half an orbital period. Let Z be the nuclear charge number, e the magnitude of the electron charge, E the magnitude of the external electric field, a the average orbital radius, and a_0 the Bohr radius. Use the data: the ionization energy is 13.6 Z^2 in units of electronvolts, the average orbital radius is a=a_0/Z, and the Bohr radius is a_0=0.53×10^{-8} in units of centimeters.
solution:
The average orbital radius is
$$
a=\frac{a_0}{Z}
$$
The Bohr radius is
$$
a_0=0.53\times 10^{-8} \unit{cm}
$$
Requiring that the energy gained in about half a cycle in field E exceed the ionization energy gives
$$
e E a \gtrsim 13.6 Z^2 \unit{eV}
$$
Using a=a_0/Z, this implies
$$
E \gtrsim \frac{13.6 Z^3}{0.53\times 10^{-8}} \unit{V/cm}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\frac{13.6 Z^3}{0.53\times 10^{-8}} \unit{V/cm} \approx 2\times 10^9 Z^3 \unit{V/cm}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as an inequality of the form E >= ... , expressed in units of V/cm. Write the expression using only the symbols E and Z (numerical constants are allowed). Do not include any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: The spread in measurement of the \pi^0 mass, given that the \pi^0 lifetime is \tau. Define \Delta E as the energy spread associated with the measured mass
subquestions.solution: The spread in the measured mass (in energy units) is related to the lifetime \tau through the uncertainty principle $$\Delta E\tau\gtrsim\hbar$$ which gives $$\Delta E\gtrsim\frac{\hbar}{\tau}$$

subquestions.subproblem: The magnetic field B at which there is a 10^{-4} excess of free protons in one spin direction at a temperature T
subquestions.solution: Consider the free protons as an ideal gas in which the proton spins have two quantized directions: parallel to B with energy E_p=-\mu_p B and antiparallel to B with energy E_p=\mu_p B, where \mu_p=\frac{\hbar e}{2m_p} is the magnetic moment of the proton. As the number density n\propto\exp\left(-\frac{E_p}{kT}\right), we have $$\frac{\exp\left(\frac{\mu_p B}{kT}\right)-\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_p B}{kT}\right)}{\exp\left(\frac{\mu_p B}{kT}\right)+\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_p B}{kT}\right)}=10^{-4}$$ or $$\exp\left(\frac{2\mu_p B}{kT}\right)=\frac{1+10^{-4}}{1-10^{-4}}$$ giving $$\frac{2\mu_p B}{kT}\approx2\times10^{-4}$$ i.e. $$B=\frac{kT}{\mu_p}\times10^{-4}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B = ..., and your response should be written with k, T, \mu_p only.

subquestions.subproblem: Fine structure splitting in the n_q=2 state of hydrogen, where the quantum numbers are n_q=2, l=1, j_1=\frac{3}{2}, j_2=\frac{1}{2}. Define \Delta E as the energy splitting between these fine-structure levels
subquestions.solution: From the expression for the fine-structure energy levels of hydrogen, we get $$\Delta E=-\frac{2\pi R h c\alpha^2}{n_q^3}\left(\frac{1}{j_1+\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{j_2+\frac{1}{2}}\right)$$ $$\Delta E=\frac{\pi R h c\alpha^2}{8}$$ where $$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c}$$ and $$R=\left(\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\right)^2\frac{m_e}{4\pi\hbar^3 c}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta E = ..., and your response should be written with R, h, c, \alpha only.

context: As shown in Fig. 1.2, consider an ensemble of identical atoms with two energy levels: a lower level 1 and an upper level 2. Let E_1 and E_2 be the energies of levels 1 and 2, respectively, with degeneracies g_1 and g_2. Let ω be the angular frequency of the transition, defined by E_2 - E_1 = ħ ω, where ħ is the reduced Planck constant. The upper level decays spontaneously with Einstein A coefficient A_{21} and lifetime τ, so that A_{21} = 1/τ. The natural linewidth of level 2 is Γ, with Γ ≈ ħ/τ. The radiation field is characterized by the spectral intensity I_ω, defined as the incident energy per unit area per unit time per angular-frequency interval, and by the spectral energy density N_ω, related by N_ω = I_ω / c, where c is the speed of light in vacuum. For absorption from level 1 to level 2, the Einstein B coefficient is B_{12}. Define the absorption cross-section at angular frequency ω by σ_A = P_ω / I_ω, where P_ω dω is the absorbed power per atom in the interval [ω, ω + dω]. Assume the absorption line shape is described by the Lorentzian form factor g(ω) = ħ/(2π) · Γ / [(E_2 - E_1 - ħ ω)^2 + Γ^2/4]. The wave number is defined as \tilde{ν} = 1/λ, where λ is the wavelength. Tasks: 1) Using the Einstein relations and the Lorentzian form factor, find σ_A at resonance (ω such that E_2 - E_1 = ħ ω). 2) For the sodium D line (yellow), take g_1 = 2, g_2 = 6, λ = 5890 \unit{Å}, and compute σ_A at resonance. 3) For the same line with τ ≈ 10^{-8} \unit{s}, estimate the natural linewidth Γ and the linewidth in wave numbers Δ\tilde{ν}.
solution:
The absorption cross-section is defined by
$$
\sigma_A = \frac{P_\omega}{I_\omega}
$$
The total absorbed power per atom is related to the Einstein B coefficient by
$$
\int P_\omega d\omega = B_{12} \hbar \omega N_\omega
$$
The Einstein relation between B_{12} and A_{21} is
$$
B_{12} = \frac{\pi^2 c^3}{\hbar \omega^3} \frac{g_1}{g_2} A_{21}
$$
The spontaneous emission coefficient is
$$
A_{21} = \frac{1}{\tau}
$$
The natural linewidth is
$$
\Gamma \approx \frac{\hbar}{\tau}
$$
Combining the above gives
$$
B_{12} = \frac{\pi^2 c^3}{\hbar^2 \omega^3} \frac{g_1}{g_2} \Gamma
$$
The spectral energy density and spectral intensity are related by
$$
N_\omega = \frac{I_\omega}{c}
$$
Thus the absorbed power per unit angular frequency can be written as
$$
P_\omega = \frac{\pi^2 c^2}{\hbar \omega^2} \frac{g_1}{g_2} \Gamma I_\omega
$$
Introducing the line shape g(\omega), we take
$$
P_\omega = \frac{\pi^2 c^2}{\hbar \omega^2} \frac{g_1}{g_2} \Gamma I_\omega g(\omega)
$$
The Lorentzian form factor is
$$
g(\omega) = \frac{\hbar}{2 \pi} \frac{\Gamma}{\left(E_2 - E_1 - \hbar \omega\right)^2 + \frac{\Gamma^2}{4}}
$$
At resonance,
$$
E_2 - E_1 = \hbar \omega
$$
Therefore,
$$
g\left(\omega = \frac{E_2 - E_1}{\hbar}\right) = \frac{2 \hbar}{\pi \Gamma}
$$
Hence the resonant absorption cross-section is
$$
\sigma_A = \frac{2 \pi c^2}{\omega^2} \frac{g_1}{g_2}
$$
For the sodium D line with g_1 = 2, g_2 = 6, and λ = 5890 \unit{Å}, use ω = 2 \pi c / \lambda to obtain
$$
\sigma_A = \frac{1}{3} \frac{\lambda^2}{2 \pi}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\sigma_A = 1.84 \times 10^{-10} \unit{cm^2}
$$
For the lifetime τ ≈ 10^{-8} \unit{s}, the natural linewidth is
$$
\Gamma \approx \frac{\hbar}{\tau}
$$
With the given values,
$$
\Gamma \approx 6.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{eV}
$$
Relating the energy width to the wavenumber width,
$$
\Gamma = \Delta E
$$
$$
\Delta E = \hbar \Delta \omega
$$
$$
\Delta \omega = \Delta \left(\frac{2 \pi c}{\lambda}\right)
$$
$$
\Gamma = 2 \pi \hbar c \Delta \tilde{\nu}
$$
Thus,
$$
\Delta \tilde{\nu} = \frac{\Gamma}{2 \pi \hbar c}
$$
Using \Gamma \approx \hbar/\tau gives
$$
\Delta \tilde{\nu} \approx \frac{1}{2 \pi c \tau}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Delta \tilde{\nu} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-4} \unit{cm^{-1}}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form 'σ_A = ...' at resonance, and should use only the variables c, ω, g_1, and g_2. Do not introduce any other variables. Numerical constants (e.g., π) are allowed.
Your final answer should express the resonant absorption cross-section σ_A as a numerical value in cm^2, in the form 'σ_A = [value] cm^2'. Report the value with 3 significant figures.

Your final answer should express both the natural linewidth Γ (in eV) and the linewidth in wave numbers Δ\tilde{ν} (in cm^{-1}) as numerical values, in the form 'Γ = [value] eV, Δ\tilde{ν} = [value] cm^{-1}'. Report each quantity with 2 significant figures.

context: The cross section for electron-impact excitation of atomic level A is σ_A = 1.4 × 10^{-20} \unit{cm^2}. The level has lifetime τ = 2 × 10^{-8} \unit{s} and decays with branching fractions f_{AB} = 1/10 to level B and f_{AC} = 9/10 to level C (see Fig. 1.3). The wavelength of the A → B transition is λ_B = 500 \unit{nm}. Definitions used in the solutions: J is the electron beam current density, e is the elementary charge, n_0 = J/e is the electron number flux (number of electrons crossing unit area per unit time), N_A is the number of atoms in level A, N_{BC} is the number of atoms in levels B and C combined, N is the total number of atoms, V is the volume, n = N_A/V is the number density in level A, p is the gas pressure, T is the absolute temperature, k is Boltzmann’s constant, h is Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light in vacuum. The production rate dN_{BC→A}/dt denotes the number of transitions from B or C to A per unit time, and the loss rate dN_{A→BC}/dt denotes the number of decays from A to B or C per unit time. Define λ_1 as the decay probability for A → B per unit time, so λ_1 = f_{AB}/τ. I is the emitted light intensity per unit solid angle attributed to a unit volume for the A → B transition. Fig. 1.3

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the equilibrium population per cm^3 in level A when an electron beam of J = 5 \unit{mA/cm^2} is passed through a vapor of these atoms at a pressure of p = 0.05 \unit{torr}. Take the room temperature to be T = 300 \unit{K}.
subquestions.solution:
According to Einstein's relation, the rate of production of A is
$$\frac{dN_{BC\rightarrow A}}{dt} = n_0 \sigma_A N_{BC}$$
and the total loss rate from A is
$$\frac{dN_{A\rightarrow BC}}{dt} = \left(\frac{1}{\tau} + n_0 \sigma_A\right) N_A$$
At equilibrium,
$$\frac{dN_{BC\rightarrow A}}{dt} = \frac{dN_{A\rightarrow BC}}{dt}$$
so
$$N_A = \frac{n_0 \sigma_A N}{\frac{1}{\tau} + 2 n_0 \sigma_A}$$
with
$$N = N_A + N_{BC}$$
The electron current density is
$$J = 5\unit{mA/cm^2}$$
The elementary charge is
$$e = 1.6\times 10^{-19}\unit{C}$$
The electron number flux is
$$n_0 = \frac{J}{e}$$
Numerically,
$$n_0 = 3.1\times 10^{16}\unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{1}{\tau} \gg 2 n_0 \sigma_A$$
which gives the approximation
$$N_A \approx n_0 \sigma_A N \tau$$
The number density in level A is
$$n = \frac{N_A}{V}$$
Using the ideal gas relation,
$$\frac{N}{V} = \frac{p}{k T}$$
Pressure conversion is
$$1\unit{torr} = 1.333\times 10^{3}\unit{dyn/cm^2}$$
Therefore,
$$p = 0.05\times 1.333\times 10^{3}\unit{dyn/cm^2}$$
Boltzmann’s constant is
$$k = 1.38\times 10^{-16}\unit{erg/K}$$
The given parameters are
$$\sigma_A = 1.4\times 10^{-20}\unit{cm^2}$$
$$\tau = 2\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}$$
$$T = 300\unit{K}$$
Hence,
$$n = \tau n_0 \sigma_A \frac{p}{k T}$$
Substituting numbers,
$$n = 2\times 10^{-8} \times 3.1\times 10^{16} \times 1.4\times 10^{-20} \times \frac{0.05\times 1.333\times 10^{3}}{1.38\times 10^{-16} \times 300}$$
Therefore,
$$n = 1.4\times 10^{4}\unit{cm^{-3}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the equilibrium number density n (population per cm^3 in level A) as a numerical value in cm^-3, rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the light intensity emitted per cm^3 in the transition A → B, expressed in watts/steradian.
subquestions.solution:
The decay probability for A → B is
$$\lambda_1 = \frac{1}{10\tau}$$
The intensity per unit solid angle attributed to a unit volume satisfies
$$4\pi I = n \lambda_1 \frac{h c}{\lambda_B}$$
Hence,
$$I = \frac{n h c}{40\pi\tau\lambda_B}$$
Using
$$n = 1.4\times 10^{4}\unit{cm^{-3}}$$
Planck’s constant is
$$h = 6.63\times 10^{-27}\unit{erg s}$$
The speed of light is
$$c = 3\times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s}$$
The lifetime is
$$\tau = 2\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}$$
The wavelength is
$$\lambda_B = 500\times 10^{-7}\unit{cm}$$
Thus,
$$I = \frac{1.4\times 10^{4} \times 6.63\times 10^{-27} \times 3\times 10^{10}}{40\pi \times 2\times 10^{-8} \times 500\times 10^{-7}}$$
Therefore,
$$I = 2.2\times 10^{-2}\unit{erg s^{-1} sr^{-1}}$$
In SI units,
$$I = 2.2\times 10^{-9}\unit{W sr^{-1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the emitted light intensity I for the A → B transition as a numerical value in W sr^-1, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context:
The electric field that an atom experiences from its surroundings within a molecule or crystal can noticeably affect properties of low-lying atomic levels. Consider an atom containing one valence electron moving in a central atomic potential. The electron is in an l=1 level and spin is ignored. Work to lowest order in degenerate perturbation theory within the threefold-degenerate hydrogenic n=2, l=1 subspace of unperturbed energy E_{2}. Use Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) with the atomic nucleus at the origin and spherical coordinates (r,theta,phi). The external static perturbation potential due to the surroundings is
$$
V_{pert}=Ax^{2}+By^{2}-(A+B)z^{2}
$$
The spherical and Cartesian variables satisfy
$$
r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}
$$
Each perturbed eigenstate in the n=2, l=1 subspace can be written in the form
$$
\Psi=(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)f'(r)
$$
where f'(r) is a common real central radial function and (alpha,beta,gamma) are real constants specific to each level. Define the Bohr radius parameter
$$
a=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{\mu e^{2}}
$$
where \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, e is the elementary charge, and mu is the reduced mass of the valence electron. The imaginary unit i satisfies
$$
i^{2}=-1
$$
Use the standard hydrogenic basis states Psi_{nlm}(r,theta,phi) for the unperturbed problem, with the following explicit forms for the n=2, l=1 manifold
$$
\Psi_{210}=\left(\frac{1}{32\pi a^{3}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{r}{a}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{2a}\right)\cos\theta
$$
$$
\Psi_{21\pm1}=\mp\left(\frac{1}{64\pi a^{3}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{r}{a}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{2a}\right)\exp(\pm i\phi)\sin\theta
$$
A general state in this degenerate subspace can be written as
$$
\Psi=a_{1}\Psi_{211}+a_{2}\Psi_{21-1}+a_{3}\Psi_{210}
$$
For first-order degenerate perturbation theory, let E' denote the first-order energy correction obtained from the secular equation. Define the secular matrix elements
$$
C=\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{1}{2}(A+B)r^{2}|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
$$
A'=-\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{3}{2}(A+B)z^{2}|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
$$
B'=\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{1}{2}(A-B)(x^{2}-y^{2})|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
Let L_{z} denote the z component of the orbital angular momentum operator. For later reference, define the Cartesian-form basis states
$$
\Psi_{x}=-x f'(r)
$$
$$
\Psi_{y}=y f'(r)
$$
$$
\Psi_{z}=z f'(r)
$$
and let E_{x}, E_{y}, E_{z} denote the corresponding perturbed energies. Define the energy shifts relative to the unperturbed value by
$$
\Delta E_{x}=E_{x}-E_{2}
$$
$$
\Delta E_{y}=E_{y}-E_{2}
$$
$$
\Delta E_{z}=E_{z}-E_{2}
$$

subquestions.subproblem:
The l=1 level now splits into three distinct levels. As you can confirm, each has a wave function of the form shown below. Determine the three eigenstates and sketch the energy level diagram, specifying the relative shifts \Delta E in terms of the parameters A and B (i.e., compute the three shifts up to a common factor). The wave function form is
$$
\Psi=(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)f'(r)
$$
subquestions.solution:
Rewrite the perturbation as
$$
V_{pert}=\frac{1}{2}(A+B)r^{2}-\frac{3}{2}(A+B)z^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(A-B)(x^{2}-y^{2})
$$
The secular equation in the basis {\Psi_{211}, \Psi_{21-1}, \Psi_{210}} is
$$
\begin{pmatrix}C+A'-E'&B'&0\\B'&C+A'-E'&0\\0&0&C+3A'-E'\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}\\a_{2}\\a_{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}
$$
with matrix elements
$$
C=\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{1}{2}(A+B)r^{2}|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
$$
A'=-\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{3}{2}(A+B)z^{2}|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
$$
B'=\langle\Psi_{211}|\frac{1}{2}(A-B)(x^{2}-y^{2})|\Psi_{211}\rangle
$$
The first-order energy corrections obtained from the secular equation are
$$
E'=C+3A'
$$
$$
E'=C+A'+B'
$$
$$
E'=C+A'-B'
$$
Evaluating the matrix elements for the n=2, l=1 hydrogenic states yields the three perturbed energies
$$
E_{z}=E_{2}-12(A+B)a^{2}
$$
$$
E_{x}=E_{2}+\frac{3}{2}(5A+3B)a^{2}
$$
$$
E_{y}=E_{2}+\frac{3}{2}(3A+5B)a^{2}
$$
A convenient real Cartesian set of eigenfunctions is
$$
\Psi_{z}=z f'(r)
$$
$$
\Psi_{x}=-x f'(r)
$$
$$
\Psi_{y}=y f'(r)
$$
The common radial factor can be chosen to match the hydrogenic form via
$$
z f'(r)=\Psi_{210}
$$
An explicit choice is
$$
f'(r)=\left(\frac{1}{32\pi a^{5}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{2a}\right)
$$
The three shifts relative to E_{2} are
$$
\Delta E_{z}=-12(A+B)a^{2}
$$
$$
\Delta E_{x}=\frac{3}{2}(5A+3B)a^{2}
$$
$$
\Delta E_{y}=\frac{3}{2}(3A+5B)a^{2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include both: (1) the three eigenstates specified as coefficient triplets for the Cartesian-form states, written explicitly as (alpha, beta, gamma)_Psi_x, (alpha, beta, gamma)_Psi_y, and (alpha, beta, gamma)_Psi_z for Psi = (alpha x + beta y + gamma z) f'(r); and (2) the three relative energy shifts written as Delta E_x = ..., Delta E_y = ..., Delta E_z = ..., each expressed only in terms of A, B, and a.

subquestions.subproblem:
Here f'(r) is the common central function. Identify one Cartesian-form eigenfunction explicitly by giving its coefficients (alpha, beta, gamma). The general Cartesian-form eigenfunction is
$$
\Psi=(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)f'(r)
$$
subquestions.solution:
An explicit choice is
$$
\Psi_{x}=-x f'(r)
$$
which corresponds to
$$
\alpha=-1
$$
$$
\beta=0
$$
$$
\gamma=0
$$
The corresponding energy is
$$
E_{x}=E_{2}+\frac{3}{2}(5A+3B)a^{2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should state the coefficients as exact numerical values in the form: alpha = ..., beta = ..., gamma = ....
Your final answer should present the three shifts in the form Delta E_x = ..., Delta E_y = ..., Delta E_z = ..., expressed only in terms of A, B, and a.

subquestions.subproblem: More interesting: Compute the expectation value of L_{z}, the z component of angular momentum, for each of the three levels.
subquestions.solution:
The corrected wave functions give
$$
\langle\Psi_{x}|L_{z}|\Psi_{x}\rangle=0
$$
$$
\langle\Psi_{y}|L_{z}|\Psi_{y}\rangle=0
$$
$$
\langle\Psi_{z}|L_{z}|\Psi_{z}\rangle=0
$$
Hence, the expectation value of the z component of angular momentum is zero for all three energy levels
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should state the expectation values as numerical values in the form: <L_z>_x = ..., <L_z>_y = ..., <L_z>_z = ....

context: In a crude picture, a metal is modeled as a system of free electrons confined by an energy barrier of height V_0 at the surface. The outward normal to the surface is taken as the z axis. Electrons whose normal kinetic energy exceeds V_0 escape. Let m be the electron mass, e>0 the elementary charge, h Planck's constant, k Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature, μ the chemical potential (Fermi level), ε the single-electron energy inside the metal, and A the surface area. Let p_x, p_y, p_z be the momentum components, with v_z = p_z/m the normal velocity component. The occupation factor of a state of energy ε in the high-energy tail is f(ε) = exp(-(ε-μ)/(kT)). Define R as the emission rate of electrons per unit area per unit time (number flux) and J as the emission current density with the sign convention J = - e R. Find and discuss J for this model (SUNY, Buffalo).
solution:
The number of quantum states per unit real-space volume in the momentum-space volume element dp_x dp_y dp_z is
$$
dN = 
\frac{2}{h^3} dp_x dp_y dp_z
$$
The occupation factor in the high-energy tail is
$$
f(\epsilon) = \exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon - \mu}{kT}\right)
$$
Electrons can escape only if the normal momentum satisfies
$$
p_z > (2 m V_0)^{1/2}
$$
Equivalently, the normal velocity condition is
$$
m v_z > (2 m V_0)^{1/2}
$$
The number of electrons escaping from area A in time dt from the momentum-space element is
$$
dN' = A v_z dt \frac{2}{h^3} dp_x dp_y dp_z f(\epsilon)
$$
The emission rate per unit area per unit time is
$$
R = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \int_{(2 m V_0)^{1/2}}^{+\infty} \frac{2 v_z}{h^3} \exp\left(-\frac{\epsilon - \mu}{kT}\right) dp_x dp_y dp_z
$$
With
$$
v_z = \frac{p_z}{m}
$$
and
$$
\epsilon = \frac{p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2}{2 m}
$$
we obtain
$$
R = \frac{2}{m h^3} \exp\left(\frac{\mu}{kT}\right) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp\left(-\frac{p_x^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_x \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp\left(-\frac{p_y^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_y \int_{(2 m V_0)^{1/2}}^{+\infty} p_z \exp\left(-\frac{p_z^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_z
$$
The Gaussian integrals evaluate to
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp\left(-\frac{p_x^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_x = (2 \pi m k T)^{1/2}
$$
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \exp\left(-\frac{p_y^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_y = (2 \pi m k T)^{1/2}
$$
For the normal component, letting a = (2 m V_0)^{1/2},
$$
\int_{a}^{+\infty} p_z \exp\left(-\frac{p_z^2}{2 m k T}\right) dp_z = m k T \exp\left(-\frac{a^2}{2 m k T}\right)
$$
Since
$$
\frac{a^2}{2 m k T} = \frac{V_0}{kT}
$$
we find
$$
R = \frac{4 \pi m k^2 T^2}{h^3} \exp\left(\frac{\mu - V_0}{kT}\right)
$$
The emission current density is
$$
J = - e R
$$
Thus
$$
J = - \frac{4 \pi m e k^2 T^2}{h^3} \exp\left(\frac{\mu - V_0}{kT}\right)
$$
This result is the Richardson–Dushman equation for thermionic emission in this simplified model

context: Rutherford scattering of a proton beam by an aluminum window. The accelerator supplies a proton beam with particle rate n = 10^{12} \unit{s^{-1}} and momentum p = 200 \unit{MeV/c}. The aluminum window has thickness t_len = 0.01 \unit{cm}, density \rho = 2.7 \unit{g/cm^3}, radiation length x_0 = 24 \unit{g/cm^2}, atomic number Z = 13, and mass number A = 27. Use z = 1 for the projectile charge number of the proton. Define the elementary charge e, the proton mass m with m c^2 = 938 \unit{MeV}, the electron mass m_e, and the speed of light c. The proton speed is v, with \beta = v/c, and kinetic energy E = \frac{1}{2} m v^2. The classical electron radius is r_0 = e^2/(m_e c^2) = 2.82 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}. Let \theta be the scattering angle. The differential cross section is d\sigma/d\Omega in \unit{cm^2/sr}, and the integrated cross section for \theta \ge 5^\circ is \sigma_I in \unit{cm^2}. The rate of scattered protons is \delta n in \unit{s^{-1}}. Avogadro's number is A_v = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}, and the molar mass is approximated as A \unit{g/mol}. The areal mass thickness of the window is T = \rho t_len in \unit{g/cm^2}. A circular counter of radius R = 1 \unit{cm} is placed a distance L = 2 \unit{m} from the window at polar angle 30^\circ relative to the beam direction. subquestions.subproblem: If you remember it, write down the differential cross section for Rutherford scattering in $\mathrm{cm^{2} / s r}$ . If you do not remember it, say so, and write down your best guess. Make sure that the $Z$ dependence, energy dependence, angular dependence and dimensions are "reasonable". Use the expression you have just given, whether correct or your best guess, to evaluate parts (b-e) below. An accelerator supplies a proton beam of $10^{12}$ particles per second and 200 MeV/c momentum. This beam passes through a 0.01- cm aluminum window. (Al density $\rho = 2.7 \mathrm{gm / cm^3}$, Al radiation length $x_0 = 24 \mathrm{gm / cm^2}$, $Z = 13$, $A = 27$).
subquestions.solution: The differential cross section for Rutherford scattering is $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \left(\frac{z Z e^2}{2 m v^2}\right)^2 \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-4}$$ This can be obtained, to a dimensionless constant, if we remember $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \sim \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-4}$$ and assume that it depends also on z e, Z e and E = \frac{1}{2} m v^2. Let $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = K (z Z e^2)^x E^y \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-4}$$ where K is a dimensionless constant. Dimensional analysis then gives $$[L]^2 = (e^2)^x E^y$$ As $$\left[\frac{e^2}{r}\right] = [E]$$ the above gives $$x = 2$$ $$y = -x$$ $$y = -2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of d\sigma/d\Omega = [expression], and your response should be written using only z, Z, e, m, v, and \theta.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the differential Rutherford scattering cross section in $\mathrm{cm^2 / sr}$ at $30^{\circ}$ for the above beam in Al.
subquestions.solution: For the protons, $$\beta = \frac{v}{c}$$ $$\beta = \frac{p c}{\sqrt{m^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2}}$$ $$\beta = \frac{200}{\sqrt{938^2 + 200^2}}$$ $$\beta = 0.2085$$ We also have $$\frac{e^2}{m v^2} = r_0 \left(\frac{m_e}{m}\right) \left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{-2}$$ where $$r_0 = \frac{e^2}{m_e c^2}$$ $$r_0 = 2.82 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}$$ Hence at $$\theta = 30^\circ$$ $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \left(\frac{13}{2}\right)^2 r_0^2 \left(\frac{m_e}{m}\right)^2 \left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{-4} \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-4}$$ $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \left(\frac{6.5 \times 2.82 \times 10^{-13}}{1836 \times 0.2085^2}\right)^2 \left(\sin 15^\circ\right)^{-4}$$ $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = 5.27 \times 10^{-28} \left(\sin 15^\circ\right)^{-4}$$ $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = 1.18 \times 10^{-25} \unit{cm^2/sr}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the differential cross section at \theta = 30^\circ as a numerical value in \unit{cm^2/sr}, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: How many protons per second will enter a 1-cm radius circular counter at a distance of 2 meters and at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the beam direction?
subquestions.solution: The counter subtends a solid angle $$\delta \Omega = \frac{\pi (0.01)^2}{2^2}$$ $$\delta \Omega = 7.85 \times 10^{-5} \unit{sr}$$ The number of protons scattered into it in unit time is $$\delta n = n \left(\frac{\rho t_{len}}{A}\right) A_v \left(\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\right) \delta \Omega$$ $$\delta n = 10^{12} \left(\frac{2.7 \times 0.01}{27}\right) 6.02 \times 10^{23} 1.18 \times 10^{-25} 7.85 \times 10^{-5}$$ $$\delta n = 5.58 \times 10^3 \unit{s^{-1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the proton count rate \delta n entering the counter as a numerical value in \unit{s^{-1}}, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the integrated Rutherford scattering cross section for angles greater than $5^{\circ}$. (Hint: $\sin \theta d\theta = 4 \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} d\frac{\theta}{2}$)
subquestions.solution: $$\sigma_I = \int \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} d\Omega$$ $$\sigma_I = 2 \pi \int_{5^\circ}^{180^\circ} \left(\frac{Z e^2}{2 m v^2}\right)^2 \frac{\sin \theta}{\sin^4 \frac{\theta}{2}} d\theta$$ $$\sigma_I = 8 \pi \left(\frac{Z e^2}{2 m v^2}\right)^2 \int_{5^\circ}^{180^\circ} \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-3} d \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2}\right)$$ $$\sigma_I = 4 \pi \left(\frac{Z e^2}{2 m v^2}\right)^2 \left[\frac{1}{\left(\sin 2.5^\circ\right)^2} - 1\right]$$ $$\sigma_I = 4 \pi \times 5.27 \times 10^{-28} \left[\frac{1}{\left(\sin 2.5^\circ\right)^2} - 1\right]$$ $$\sigma_I = 3.47 \times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the integrated cross section \sigma_I for \theta \ge 5^\circ as a numerical value in \unit{cm^2}, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: How many protons per second are scattered out of the beam into angles $> 5^{\circ}$?
subquestions.solution: The number of protons scattered into $$\theta \ge 5^\circ$$ is $$\delta n = n \left(\frac{\rho t_{len}}{A}\right) A_v \sigma_I$$ $$\delta n = 2.09 \times 10^9 \unit{s^{-1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the scattered proton rate \delta n into angles greater than 5^\circ as a numerical value in \unit{s^{-1}}, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the projected rms multiple Coulomb scattering angle for the proton beam through the above window. Take the constant in the expression for multiple Coulomb scattering as 15 MeV/c.
subquestions.solution: The projected rms multiple Coulomb scattering angle for the proton beam through the Al window is given by $$\theta_{rms} = \frac{k Z}{\sqrt{2} \beta p} \sqrt{\frac{T}{x_0}} \left[1 + \frac{1}{9} \ln \left(\frac{T}{x_0}\right)\right]$$ where $$k = 15 \unit{MeV/c}$$ As $$Z = 13$$ $$p = 200 \unit{MeV/c}$$ $$\beta = 0.2085$$ $$T = 0.01 \times 2.7 \unit{g/cm^2}$$ $$x_0 = 24 \unit{g/cm^2}$$ $$\frac{T}{x_0} = 1.125 \times 10^{-3}$$ we have $$\theta_{rms} = \frac{15 \times 13}{\sqrt{2} \times 0.2085 \times 200} \sqrt{1.125 \times 10^{-3}} \left[1 + \frac{1}{9} \ln \left(1.125 \times 10^{-3}\right)\right]$$ $$\theta_{rms} = 2.72 \times 10^{-2} \unit{rad}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the projected rms multiple-scattering angle \theta_{rms} as a numerical value in \unit{rad}, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: An atom can exist in two states: a ground state with rest mass M and an excited state with rest mass M + Δ. In the laboratory frame where the atom is initially at rest, a photon is absorbed to induce the transition to the excited state. Let ν be the required photon frequency, p be the momentum of the atom after absorption, c be the speed of light in vacuum, and h be Planck's constant. Find ν.
solution:
By conservation of energy and momentum for photon absorption from an initially stationary atom, we have

$$
Mc^2 + h\nu = \sqrt{(M+\Delta)^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2}
$$

$$
\frac{h\nu}{c} = p
$$

Solving for the required photon frequency gives

$$
\nu = \frac{\Delta c^2}{h} \left(1 + \frac{\Delta}{2M}\right)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ν = [expression], and your response should use only the variables M, Δ, c, and h.

context: Estimate (order of magnitude) the full Doppler width Δλ of an emission line with wavelength λ = 5000 \unit{Å} emitted by argon at temperature T = 300 \unit{K}. Use A = 40 for the mass number and Z = 18 for the atomic number. Let m be the mass of the argon atom, c the speed of light, k the Boltzmann constant, v the thermal speed, and \overline{v^{2}} the mean square thermal speed. Define β = v/c and let Δλ denote the full Doppler width. You may approximate the atomic rest energy by m c^{2} ≈ A × 938 \unit{MeV}. Report the final answer as Δλ.
solution:
Using equipartition of energy
$$
\frac{1}{2} m \overline{v^{2}} = \frac{3}{2} k T
$$
From this
$$
\overline{v^{2}} = \frac{3 k T}{m}
$$
Estimate the thermal speed
$$
v \approx \sqrt{\overline{v^{2}}}
$$
Express v in terms of c
$$
v = c \sqrt{\frac{3 k T}{m c^{2}}}
$$
Use the argon rest energy approximation
$$
m c^{2} = 40 \times 938 \unit{MeV}
$$
Evaluate kT
$$
k T = 8.6 \times 10^{-5} \unit{eV/K} \times 300 \unit{K}
$$
Thus
$$
k T = 2.58 \times 10^{-2} \unit{eV}
$$
Define
$$
\beta = \frac{v}{c}
$$
Hence
$$
\beta = \sqrt{\frac{3 k T}{m c^{2}}}
$$
Numerically
$$
\beta = 1.44 \times 10^{-6}
$$
Given
$$
\lambda = 5000 \unit{\AA}
$$
The full Doppler width is
$$
\Delta \lambda \approx 2 \beta \lambda
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta \lambda \approx 1.44 \times 10^{-2} \unit{\AA}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the full Doppler width Δλ as a numerical value in Ångström (Å) with 3 significant figures.

context: An electron of mass m is confined to the interior of a hollow spherical cavity of radius R with impenetrable walls. In its ground state (zero angular momentum), find P(R), the pressure exerted by the electron on the cavity walls. Use the following definitions: E is the electron's energy, P is the pressure on the wall, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, r is the radial coordinate, \Psi is the wave function, \chi(r) is the radial function defined by \Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\frac{\chi(r)}{r}, k is the wave number, and A is a constant. The impenetrable wall imposes the boundary condition that the wave function vanishes at r=R.
solution:
For an infinitesimal increase of the cavity radius by dR, the change in the electron's energy satisfies
$$
dE=-4\pi R^2 P dR
$$
Hence
$$
P=-\frac{1}{4\pi R^2}\frac{dE}{dR}
$$
In the ground state, the wave function has the form
$$
\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\frac{\chi(r)}{r}
$$
The radial function satisfies
$$
\frac{d^2\chi}{dr^2}+k^2\chi=0
$$
with
$$
k^2=\frac{2mE}{\hbar^2}
$$
and the regularity condition
$$
\chi(0)=0
$$
Thus
$$
\chi(r)=A\sin(kr)
$$
The impenetrable wall imposes
$$
\chi(R)=0
$$
which gives
$$
k=\frac{\pi}{R}
$$
Therefore the ground-state energy is
$$
E=\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mR^2}
$$
Differentiating with respect to R gives
$$
\frac{dE}{dR}=-\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{mR^3}
$$
Substituting into the pressure relation yields
$$
P=\frac{\pi\hbar^2}{4mR^5}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P(R) = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables m, R, and \hbar.

context: A spin-1/2 particle with magnetic moment mu = mu_0 s is placed in a uniform magnetic field B pointing along the x axis. Work in the (s^2, s_x) representation, i.e., the eigenbasis of s_x. Let s = (s_x, s_y, s_z) denote the spin operators, with s_k = (1/2) sigma_k where sigma_k are the Pauli matrices in this basis. Let the time-dependent spinor be psi(t) = (a(t), b(t))^T in this basis. At t = 0 the particle is found to have s_z = +1/2. Here mu_0 is a constant, hbar is the reduced Planck constant, and i is the imaginary unit. Find the probabilities at time t of measuring s_y = ±1/2.
solution:
In the (s^2, s_x) representation the Pauli matrices are
$$
\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}
$$
The spin operators satisfy
$$
s_k=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_k
$$
Normalized eigenvectors with eigenvalue +\frac{1}{2} are
$$
\nu_{x+}=\binom{1}{0}$$
$$
\nu_{y+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{1}
$$
$$
\nu_{z+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{i}
$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$
H=-\pmb{\mu}\cdot B
$$
Since B points along x and \pmb{\mu}=\mu_0 s, we have
$$
H=-\mu_0 B s_x
$$
In matrix form
$$
H=-\frac{\mu_0 B}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
$$
Let
$$
\psi(t)=\binom{a(t)}{b(t)}
$$
The Schr\"odinger equation is
$$
i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H\psi(t)
$$
The initial condition from s_z=+\frac{1}{2} is
$$
\psi(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\binom{1}{i}
$$
Solving the decoupled equations gives
$$
a(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\exp\left(i\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}\right)
$$
$$
b(t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\exp\left(-i\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}\right)
$$
Define
$$
\alpha=\frac{\mu_0 B t}{2\hbar}
$$
The amplitude for s_y=+\frac{1}{2} is
$$
c_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}\binom{a(t)}{b(t)}
$$
Using the expressions for a(t), b(t) we obtain
$$
c_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\exp(i\alpha)+i\exp(-i\alpha)\right)
$$
The probability is
$$
P_{+}(t)=|c_{+}(t)|^2
$$
Using
$$
\left|\exp(i\alpha)+i\exp(-i\alpha)\right|^2=2\left(1+\sin(2\alpha)\right)
$$
we find
$$
P_{+}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sin\frac{\mu_0 B t}{\hbar}\right)
$$
Similarly
$$
P_{-}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\sin\frac{\mu_0 B t}{\hbar}\right)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P_{+}(t) = ... and P_{-}(t) = ..., and your response should be written with the variables mu_0, B, t, and hbar only.

context: The ground state of the realistic helium atom is nondegenerate. However, consider a hypothetical helium atom in which the two electrons are replaced by two identical spin-1 particles of negative charge. Neglect spin-dependent forces. For this hypothetical atom, what is the degeneracy of the ground state? Give your reasoning. Definitions for clarity: Let S denote the total spin quantum number of the two-particle system. For a given S, let g_S denote the spin multiplicity, where g_S = 2S + 1. Let g_{gs} denote the total degeneracy of the ground state to be found.
solution:
Spin-1 particles are bosons, so the total wave function of two identical particles must be symmetric under particle exchange. In the ground state, the spatial wave function is symmetric; therefore, the spin part must also be symmetric. For two spin-1 particles, the possible total spins are S = 2, 1, 0. Among these, the spin wave functions for S = 2 and S = 0 are symmetric, while that for S = 1 is antisymmetric and thus excluded for the ground state. Using g_S = 2S + 1, we compute the contributions from the allowed S values:

$$g_2 = 2\cdot 2 + 1$$

$$g_2 = 5$$

$$g_0 = 2\cdot 0 + 1$$

$$g_0 = 1$$

$$g_{gs} = g_2 + g_0$$

$$g_{gs} = 6$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express g_{gs} as an integer numerical value.

context: A beam of neutrons (mass m) traveling with nonrelativistic speed v impinges on a rectangular two-path interferometer ABCD shown in Fig. 1.7. The two paths BAD (upper arm AD) and BCD (lower arm BC) recombine at point D, and a detector labeled E placed immediately after D records the intensity. The vertical segments are BA and CD. The two horizontal arms AD and BC have equal length L and are separated vertically by a height H. When the apparatus is in a vertical plane, gravity with acceleration g acts downward parallel to BA and CD. The reduced Planck constant is denoted by \hbar. The total neutron energy is E, and t is the time. A static, path-independent phase offset \delta accounts for mirrors and beam splitters. The complex wave amplitude at D is denoted by \Psi, and the detected intensity is given by |\Psi|^{2}. With the entire system in a horizontal plane, the reference detector intensity is I_0. Define I_g as the detector intensity when the system is in a vertical plane. In part (a), let v be the neutron speed along BC and v_1 the neutron speed along AD. In part (b), the system lies in a horizontal plane. A uniform magnetic field, pointing out of the plane, acts only over a dotted region along BC. The incident neutrons are polarized with spin pointing along BA, which defines the z-axis. Neutrons that pass through the magnetic field have their spin expectation values precessed by an angle \theta before recombination. Work in the spin basis of simultaneous eigenstates of s^{2} and s_{z}; two-component spinors \chi are written in that basis. Let I(\theta) denote the detector intensity as a function of \theta, with I(0)=I_0.

subquestions.subproblem: Assume the system lies in a vertical plane (so gravity points down parallel to AB and CD). Given that the detector intensity is I_0 when the system lies in a horizontal plane, derive the intensity I_g recorded after recombination at D for the vertical configuration.
subquestions.solution: When the system lies in a horizontal plane, the two split beams have equal intensity at D, so each path contributes a wave amplitude of sqrt(I_0)/2. In the vertical configuration, BA and CD are dynamically equivalent and need not be considered for the phase difference between the horizontal arms. Energy conservation between the two horizontal arms gives $$\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{1}^{2} + m g H$$ Solving for v_1 gives $$v_{1} = \sqrt{v^{2} - 2 g H}$$ The recombined wave at D is $$\Psi = \frac{\sqrt{I_{0}}}{2} \exp\left(i \frac{m v_{1} L}{\hbar}\right) \exp\left(-i \frac{E t}{\hbar}\right) \exp(i \delta) + \frac{\sqrt{I_{0}}}{2} \exp\left(i \frac{m v L}{\hbar}\right) \exp\left(-i \frac{E t}{\hbar}\right) \exp(i \delta)$$ The detector intensity is $$I_{g} = |\Psi|^{2}$$ Using the standard two-beam interference result gives $$I_{g} = \frac{I_{0}}{2} + \frac{I_{0}}{2} \cos\left(\frac{m L (v - v_{1})}{\hbar}\right)$$ Equivalently, $$I_{g} = I_{0} \cos^{2}\left(\frac{m L (v - v_{1})}{2 \hbar}\right)$$ In the limit where the kinetic energy greatly exceeds the potential difference, $$\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} \gg m g H$$ the speed along AD can be approximated as $$v_{1} \approx v - \frac{g H}{v}$$ and the intensity reduces to $$I_{g} \approx I_{0} \cos^{2}\left(\frac{m g H L}{2 \hbar v}\right)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of I_g = ..., and your response should be written using only the symbols I_0, m, L, v, g, H, and \hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: Now suppose the system lies in a horizontal plane. A uniform magnetic field, pointing out of the plane, acts only in the dotted region along BC. The incident neutrons are polarized with spin pointing along BA (define this as the z-axis). Neutrons that pass through the magnetic field have their spin expectation values precessed by an angle \theta. Let I(\theta) be the intensity at the detector E. Derive I(\theta) as a function of \theta, given that I(\theta = 0) = I_0.
subquestions.solution: Work in the (s^{2}, s_{z}) representation with the z-axis along BA. At D, the spinor for neutrons along BAD is $$\chi_{BAD} = \binom{1}{0}$$ For neutrons along BCD after precession by \theta, the spinor is $$\chi_{BCD} = \binom{\cos \frac{\theta}{2}}{\sin \frac{\theta}{2}}$$ The recombined state at D is $$\Psi = \frac{\sqrt{I_{0}}}{2} \exp\left(-i \frac{E t}{\hbar}\right) \exp(i \delta) \left( \chi_{BAD} + \chi_{BCD} \right)$$ The detector intensity is $$I(\theta) = |\Psi|^{2}$$ Evaluating the norm gives $$I(\theta) = \frac{I_{0}}{4} \left[ \left(1 + \cos \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2} + \sin^{2} \frac{\theta}{2} \right]$$ Hence, $$I(\theta) = I_{0} \cos^{2} \frac{\theta}{4}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of I(\theta) = ..., and your response should be written using only the symbols I_0 and \theta.

context: Choose the closest option for the spin–orbit splitting energy of the hydrogen 2p state from {10^{-6}, 10^{-4}, 10^{-2}, 10^{0}} eV. Let n be the principal quantum number, l the orbital angular momentum quantum number, s the electron spin quantum number, and j the total electronic angular momentum. For the hydrogen 2p state use n=2, l=1, s=1/2, with fine-structure levels labeled by j_1=3/2 and j_2=1/2. Let R be the Rydberg constant, h Planck's constant, c the speed of light, and alpha the fine-structure constant. Use h c R = 13.6 eV and alpha = 1/137. Let E_split denote the spin–orbit splitting energy between the j_1 and j_2 levels to be computed, and let E_option denote the selected option that best matches E_split.
solution:
For the hydrogen 2p state, the quantum numbers are
$$
n=2
$$
$$
l=1
$$
$$
s=\frac{1}{2}
$$
with fine-structure levels
$$
j_1=\frac{3}{2}
$$
$$
j_2=\frac{1}{2}
$$
The spin–orbit splitting energy is
$$
E_{split}=\frac{h c R\alpha^{2}}{n^{3} l (l+\frac{1}{2})(l+1)}\frac{j_1(j_1+1)-j_2(j_2+1)}{2}
$$
Constants and values used are
$$
h c R=13.6\unit{eV}
$$
$$
\alpha=\frac{1}{137}
$$
The angular factors are
$$
j_1(j_1+1)=\frac{15}{4}
$$
$$
j_2(j_2+1)=\frac{3}{4}
$$
Substituting values gives
$$
E_{split}=13.6\unit{eV}\times\frac{1}{137^{2}}\times\frac{1}{2^{3}\times 1\times \frac{3}{2}\times 2}\times\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{15}{4}-\frac{3}{4}\right)
$$
Simplifying the numerical factors
$$
E_{split}=13.6\unit{eV}\times\frac{1}{137^{2}}\times\frac{1}{24}\times\frac{3}{2}
$$
Therefore
$$
E_{split}=4.5\times 10^{-5}\unit{eV}
$$
Identifying the closest option
$$
E_{option}=10^{-4}\unit{eV}
$$

context: We may generalize the semiclassical Bohr–Sommerfeld relation for a closed real-space orbit C by replacing p with p - eA/c in the integrand. In zero field the rule is $$ \oint p\cdot dr = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)2\pi\hbar $$ In an electromagnetic field we use $$ \oint \left(p-\frac{e}{c}A\right)\cdot dr = \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)2\pi\hbar $$ Use this and the equation of motion for the linear momentum p in a uniform magnetic field B to derive a quantized condition on the magnetic flux Φ through any surface Σ bounded by C. For electrons in a solid this condition can be restated in terms of the k-space orbit area S. Let A_r denote the real-space area enclosed by C in a plane perpendicular to B, and let S denote the area enclosed by the corresponding k-space orbit. You may use the relations Δp = ħ Δk and Δp = (e/c) B Δr for small in-plane displacements of magnitudes Δr and Δk. Ignore spin effects. Symbols: p is the electron linear momentum, r is the position vector, A is the vector potential, B is the magnetic field, C is the closed real-space orbit, Σ is any surface bounded by C, dS is the oriented area element on Σ with vector form dS, Φ is the magnetic flux through Σ, A_r is the real-space area enclosed by C, k is the crystal wavevector, S is the k-space orbit area, n is a nonnegative integer, e is the magnitude of the electron charge, c is the speed of light, and ħ is the reduced Planck constant.
solution:
Assume B is uniform. Newton's second law for p in a magnetic field gives
$$
\frac{dp}{dt}=-\frac{e}{c}\frac{dr}{dt}\times B
$$
Integrating around C yields
$$
\oint_C p\cdot dr=-\frac{e}{c}\oint_C (r\times B)\cdot dr
$$
Using the scalar triple product identity gives
$$
\oint_C (r\times B)\cdot dr=-\oint_C B\cdot r\times dr
$$
Using the geometric identity for a closed planar loop gives
$$
\oint_C B\cdot r\times dr=2\int_\Sigma B\cdot dS
$$
Define the magnetic flux by
$$
\Phi=\int_\Sigma B\cdot dS
$$
Therefore
$$
\oint_C p\cdot dr=\frac{2e}{c}\Phi
$$
By Stokes' theorem
$$
\oint_C A\cdot dr=\int_\Sigma (\nabla\times A)\cdot dS
$$
Since
$$
\nabla\times A=B
$$
it follows that
$$
\oint_C A\cdot dr=\int_\Sigma B\cdot dS
$$
Hence
$$
-\frac{e}{c}\oint_C A\cdot dr=-\frac{e}{c}\Phi
$$
Combining the two line integrals gives
$$
\oint_C \left(p-\frac{e}{c}A\right)\cdot dr=\frac{e}{c}\Phi
$$
The generalized Bohr–Sommerfeld condition implies
$$
\oint_C \left(p-\frac{e}{c}A\right)\cdot dr=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)2\pi\hbar
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{e}{c}\Phi=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)2\pi\hbar
$$
Thus the flux quantization is
$$
\Phi=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{e}
$$
On a plane perpendicular to B we use
$$
\Delta p=\hbar\Delta k
$$
and
$$
\Delta p=\frac{e}{c}B\Delta r
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta r=\frac{\hbar c}{eB}\Delta k
$$
The areas A_r in real space and S in k space are related by
$$
A_r=\left(\frac{\hbar c}{eB}\right)^2 S
$$
For uniform B the flux is
$$
A_r=\frac{\Phi}{B}
$$
Using the flux quantization gives
$$
A_r=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{eB}
$$
Equating the two expressions for A_r yields
$$
\left(\frac{\hbar c}{eB}\right)^2 S=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{eB}
$$
Therefore the quantization condition on the k-space orbit area is
$$
S=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{2\pi e}{\hbar c}B
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic equations as your final answer. 1) Give the magnetic-flux quantization in the form 'Φ = ...' expressed solely in terms of n, ħ, c, and e. 2) Give the k-space orbit area quantization in the form 'S = ...' expressed solely in terms of n, B, e, ħ, and c. Do not include any additional variables or intermediate steps; present only these two equations.

context: Consider a very small uniform-density sphere of charge in an electrostatic potential V(r). To leading order in its very small radius r_0, its potential energy is given by the truncation of the multipole expansion below. Use this to treat the finite-size correction as a small perturbation to the Coulomb potential of the hydrogen atom and compute the resulting Lamb shifts for the 1s and 2p levels. Let ΔE_{1s} and ΔE_{2p} denote the first-order energy shifts of the 1s and 2p levels, respectively. Use the unperturbed hydrogenic wave functions provided and express your results in terms of r_0 and fundamental constants. The unperturbed potential energy of the electron in the hydrogen atom is V(r) = - e^2 / r with e > 0 the magnitude of the electron charge. The unperturbed wave functions are normalized with spherical harmonics Y_l^m chosen so that Y_0^0 = 1, and m ∈ {-1,0,1} for l = 1. The Bohr radius is a_B = ħ^2 / (m_e e^2), where m_e is the electron mass and ħ is the reduced Planck constant.
solution:
The potential energy to leading order in r_0 is
$$
U(r) = V(r) + \frac{r_0^2}{6} \nabla^2 V(r)
$$
The Coulomb potential is
$$
V(r) = -\frac{e^2}{r}
$$
The unperturbed wave functions are
$$
\psi_{1s}(r) = 2 a_B^{-3/2} \exp\left(-\frac{r}{a_B}\right) Y_0^0
$$
$$
\psi_{2pm}(r) = a_B^{-5/2} r \exp\left(-\frac{r}{2 a_B}\right) \frac{Y_1^m}{\sqrt{24}}
$$
The Bohr radius is
$$
a_B = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_e e^2}
$$
First-order perturbation theory gives
$$
\Delta E = \frac{r_0^2}{6} \int \psi^*(r) \nabla^2 V(r) \psi(r) d^3 r
$$
Using the identity
$$
\nabla^2 \frac{1}{r} = -4 \pi \delta(r)
$$
we obtain
$$
\nabla^2 V(r) = 4 \pi e^2 \delta(r)
$$
Hence
$$
\int \psi^*(r) \nabla^2 V(r) \psi(r) d^3 r = 4 \pi e^2 \psi^*(0) \psi(0)
$$
For the 1s state
$$
\psi_{1s}(0) = 2 a_B^{-3/2} Y_0^0
$$
With Y_0^0 = 1, this gives
$$
|\psi_{1s}(0)|^2 = 4 a_B^{-3}
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta E_{1s} = \frac{r_0^2}{6} \cdot 4 \pi e^2 \cdot 4 a_B^{-3}
$$
$$
\Delta E_{1s} = \frac{8 \pi e^2 r_0^2}{3 a_B^3}
$$
For the 2p states, the radial factor r makes the wave function vanish at the origin, so
$$
\psi_{2pm}(0) = 0
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta E_{2p} = 0
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions in the exact forms: 'ΔE_{1s} = ...' and 'ΔE_{2p} = ...'. Each expression should be written solely using r_0, e, a_B, and numerical constants (e.g., π). Do not introduce any other variables or constants.

subquestions.subproblem: In Bohr's original theory of the hydrogen atom (circular orbits) what postulate led to the choice of the allowed energy levels?
subquestions.solution:
Bohr proposed the quantization condition
$$m v r = n\hbar$$
This condition gives discrete values of the electron momentum
$$p = m v$$
which in turn leads to discrete energy levels
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of m v r = ..., and your response should use only the variables m, v, r, n, and ħ.

subquestions.subproblem: Later de Broglie pointed out a most interesting relationship between the Bohr postulate and the de Broglie wavelength of the electron. State and derive this relationship.
subquestions.solution:
Bohr's circular orbits can hold an integral number of electron de Broglie wavelengths. Starting from the Bohr quantization
$$p r = n\hbar$$
and using
$$\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi}$$
we obtain
$$2\pi r = \frac{n h}{p}$$
Using the de Broglie relation
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$
we conclude
$$2\pi r = n\lambda$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of 2π r = ..., and your response should use only the variables r, n, and λ.

context: A tritium atom in its ground electronic state beta- decays to He^{+}. Immediately after the decay, in the sudden approximation, the electronic spatial wavefunction remains the hydrogenic 1s state of Z=1, while the bound eigenstates of the new Hamiltonian are those of He^{+} with Z=2. Let a_0 denote the Bohr radius. Use spherical harmonics Y_{lm} normalized so that ∫ Y_{lm}^{*} Y_{l'm'} dΩ = δ_{l l'} δ_{m m'}. The hydrogenic radial functions needed are: R_{10}^{(Z=1)}(r) = 2 a_0^{-3/2} e^{-r/a_0}, R_{10}^{(Z=2)}(r) = 2 (2/a_0)^{3/2} e^{-2 r/a_0}, R_{20}^{(Z=2)}(r) = 1/√2 (2/a_0)^{3/2} (1 - r/a_0) e^{-r/a_0}, R_{21}^{(Z=2)}(r) = 1/(2√6) (2/a_0)^{3/2} (2 r/a_0) e^{-r/a_0}. Define the overlap amplitudes a_1 = ⟨1s_{He^{+}}|1s_{H}⟩, a_2 = ⟨2s_{He^{+}}|1s_{H}⟩, a_3 = ⟨2p_{He^{+}}|1s_{H}⟩. The corresponding probabilities are W⟨nl⟩ = |a|^{2}. Ignore spin in this problem.

subquestions.subproblem: Immediately after the decay, what is the probability that the helium ion is in its ground state?
subquestions.solution:
$$a_1=\langle 1s_{He^{+}}|1s_{H}\rangle$$
$$a_1=\int_0^{\infty}\left[2\left(\frac{2}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}e^{-\frac{2r}{a_0}}\right]\left[\frac{2}{a_0^{3/2}}e^{-\frac{r}{a_0}}\right]r^2 dr\int Y_{00}^2 d\Omega$$
$$\int Y_{00}^2 d\Omega=1$$
$$\int_0^{\infty}r^2 e^{-\frac{3r}{a_0}} dr=\frac{2 a_0^3}{27}$$
$$a_1=\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{27}$$
$$W\langle 1s\rangle=|a_1|^2$$
$$W\langle 1s\rangle=\frac{512}{729}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the probability W⟨1s⟩ that the helium ion is in the 1s state immediately after the decay as a numerical value.

$$\int Y_{00}^2 d\Omega=1$$
$$a_2=-\frac{1}{2}$$

context: Using the Bohr model of the atom. Let m be the electron mass, e be the magnitude of the electron charge, epsilon_0 be the vacuum permittivity, and \hbar be the reduced Planck constant. For the He^+ ion the nuclear charge number is Z=2. Let n be the principal quantum number (a positive integer), r be the orbital radius, v be the orbital speed, and L_\phi be the orbital angular momentum. Let l be the orbital angular momentum quantum number. In part (b), let A be the orbit area, \omega be the angular velocity, T be the orbital period, I be the current due to the electron’s orbital motion, \mu be the magnetic moment, and B be the magnitude of a uniform external magnetic field. Let \phi denote the azimuthal angle used in the area integral. Define E_n as the energy of the nth Bohr level and \Delta E as the interaction energy (energy shift) in the magnetic field. Neglect the electron spin throughout.

subquestions.subproblem: derive an expression for the energy levels of the He^{+} ion.
subquestions.solution:
Bohr quantization of the orbital angular momentum gives
$$L_\phi=m v r$$
$$L_\phi=n \hbar$$
The centripetal force is provided by the Coulomb attraction for Z=2
$$m \frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{2 e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}$$
The total energy is
$$E_n=\frac{1}{2} m v^2-\frac{2 e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r}$$
Using the relations above, this becomes
$$E_n=-\frac{1}{2} m v^2$$
and finally
$$E_n=-\frac{2 m e^4}{(4 \pi \epsilon_0)^2 n^2 \hbar^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_n = ..., and your response should be written with m, e, epsilon_0, n, \hbar.

subquestions.subproblem: calculate the energies of the l = 1 state in a magnetic field, neglecting the electron spin.
subquestions.solution:
The area of the electron orbit is
$$A=\int_0^{2 \pi} \frac{1}{2} r^2 d\phi$$
Using d\phi=\omega dt, this becomes
$$A=\frac{1}{2} \int_0^T r^2 \omega dt$$
With
$$L_\phi=m r^2 \omega$$
one finds
$$A=\frac{L_\phi}{2 m} T$$
For l=1,
$$L_\phi=\hbar$$
The magnetic moment due to the orbital motion is
$$\mu=I A$$
with
$$I=-\frac{e}{T}$$
which gives
$$\mu=-\frac{e \hbar}{2 m}$$
The interaction energies for the three allowed orientations relative to the field of magnitude B are
$$\Delta E=\frac{e \hbar}{2 m} B$$
$$\Delta E=0$$
$$\Delta E=-\frac{e \hbar}{2 m} B$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the three distinct interaction energies as ΔE = ..., ΔE = ..., and ΔE = ..., and your response should be written with e, m, \hbar, B.

context: An atom has a nucleus of charge Z and one electron. The nucleus has radius R, inside which the positive charge is uniformly distributed. We want to study the effect of the finite nuclear size on the electron energy levels using the electron potential energy V(r) due to the nucleus. Symbols and constants: Z is the atomic number, e is the elementary charge, epsilon_0 is the vacuum permittivity, R is the nuclear radius, r is the electron-nucleus distance, a_0 is the Bohr radius, h is Planck's constant, c is the speed of light, r_0 is a nuclear radius parameter, A is the mass number, E_0 is the ground-state energy of a hydrogen-like atom, and Delta E and Delta \tilde{\nu} denote the energy and wavenumber shifts, respectively. For {}^{208}Pb use Z = 82 and A = 208. When needed, use R = r_0 A^{1/3} with r_0 = 1.2 fermi, where 1 fermi = 1 \unit{fm} = 10^{-15} \unit{m}. Provide numerical results in \unit{eV} and \unit{cm^{-1}} as appropriate.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the electron potential energy V(r) taking into account the finite size of the nucleus, assuming a uniformly charged spherical nucleus of radius R.
subquestions.solution:
For r \geq R
$$
V(r) = -\frac{Z e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r}
$$
For r < R
$$
V(r) = -\frac{Z e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 R} \left( \frac{3}{2} - \frac{r^2}{2 R^2} \right)
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide V(r) piecewise for r \geq R and r < R in terms of Z, e, \epsilon_0, r, and R. Use the format: 'For r \geq R: V(r) = ...; For r < R: V(r) = ...'.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the level shift due to the finite size of the nucleus for the 1s state of {}^{208}Pb using perturbation theory, assuming that R is much smaller than the Bohr radius and approximating the wave function accordingly.
subquestions.solution:
For r < R, take the departure of the Hamiltonian from that of a point nucleus as the perturbation H'
$$
H' = \frac{Z e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 r} - \frac{Z e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 R} \left( \frac{3}{2} - \frac{r^2}{2 R^2} \right)
$$
For r \geq R
$$
H' = 0
$$
The 1s position-space wave function of {}^{208}Pb is
$$
\psi_{1s}(r) = 2 \left( \frac{Z}{a_0} \right)^{3/2} \exp \left( -\frac{2 r}{a_0} \right) \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}
$$
With the approximation r \ll a_0 so that \exp \left( -\frac{2 r}{a_0} \right) \approx 1, the first-order energy shift is
$$
\Delta E = \langle 1s | H' | 1s \rangle
$$
$$
\Delta E = -\frac{4 Z^4 e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 a_0^3} \int_0^R \left( \frac{3}{2 R} - \frac{r^2}{2 R^3} - \frac{1}{r} \right) r^2 dr
$$
$$
\Delta E = \frac{4}{5} Z^2 |E_0| \left( \frac{R}{a_0} \right)^2
$$
where
$$
E_0 = -\frac{Z^2 e^2}{(4\pi \epsilon_0) 2 a_0^3}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of 'ΔE = ...' and your response should be written using only Z, e, \epsilon_0, a_0, and R (do not use E_0).

subquestions.subproblem: Give a numerical answer to the energy shift and the corresponding wavenumber shift.
subquestions.solution:
$$
\Delta E = \frac{4}{5} \times 82^2 \times \left( 82^2 \times 13.6 \unit{eV} \right) \times \left( \frac{1.2 \times 10^{-19} \times 208^{1/3}}{5.29 \times 10^{-9}} \right)^2
$$
$$
\Delta E = 8.89 \unit{eV}
$$
$$
\Delta \tilde{\nu} = \frac{\Delta E}{h c}
$$
$$
\Delta \tilde{\nu} \approx 7.2 \times 10^4 \unit{cm^{-1}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the 1s-state energy shift ΔE in eV and the wavenumber shift Δ\tilde{\nu} in cm^{-1} as numerical values. Report ΔE to 3 significant figures and Δ\tilde{\nu} to 2 significant figures.

With the approximation r \ll a_0 so that \exp \left( -\frac{2 r}{a_0} \right) \approx 1, the first-order energy shift is

$$

\Delta E = -\frac{4 Z^4 e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0 a_0^3} \int_0^R \left( \frac{3}{2 R} - \frac{r^2}{2 R^3} - \frac{1}{r} \right) r^2 dr

solution:
Perturbation due to the finite proton size, defined as the difference between the finite-size potential and the point-Coulomb potential, is for r<R $$
H'=\frac{e^{2}}{r}-\frac{e^{2}}{R}\bigg(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\bigg)
$$ and for r\ge R $$
H'=0
$$ The unperturbed s-state hydrogenic wave function can be written as $$
\Psi_{ns}=N_{n0} \exp\bigg(-\frac{r}{n a_{0}}\bigg) F\Big(-n+1,2,\frac{2r}{n a_{0}}\Big) Y_{00}
$$ with $$
N_{n0}=\frac{2}{(n a_{0})^{3/2}}\sqrt{\frac{n!}{(n-1)!}}
$$ and the power-series expansion $$
F\Big(-n+1,2,\frac{2r}{n a_{0}}\Big)=1-\frac{n-1}{2}\cdot\frac{2r}{n a_{0}}+\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2\cdot 3}\cdot\frac{1}{2!}\bigg(\frac{2r}{n a_{0}}\bigg)^{2}+\dots
$$ For r\ll a_{0} one has $$
F\Big(-n+1,2,\frac{2r}{n a_{0}}\Big)\approx 1
$$ and $$
\exp\bigg(-\frac{r}{n a_{0}}\bigg)\approx 1
$$ so near the origin $$
\Psi_{ns}\approx N_{n0} Y_{00}
$$ Using first-order perturbation theory, $$
\Delta E_{ns}=\langle\Psi_{ns}|H'|\Psi_{ns}\rangle
$$ and with R\ll a_{0}, one may replace the wave function inside the nucleus by its value at the origin to obtain $$
\Delta E_{ns}=|\Psi_{ns}(0)|^{2}\int d\Omega\int_{0}^{R}\bigg[\frac{e^{2}}{r}-\frac{e^{2}}{R}\bigg(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\bigg)\bigg] r^{2} dr
$$ The angular integral gives $$
\int d\Omega=4\pi
$$ The radial pieces are $$
\int_{0}^{R} e^{2} r\, dr=\frac{e^{2} R^{2}}{2}
$$ and $$
-\frac{e^{2}}{R}\int_{0}^{R}\bigg(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\bigg) r^{2} dr=-\frac{2}{5} e^{2} R^{2}
$$ so that $$
\int_{0}^{R}\bigg[\frac{e^{2}}{r}-\frac{e^{2}}{R}\bigg(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{r^{2}}{2R^{2}}\bigg)\bigg] r^{2} dr=\frac{e^{2} R^{2}}{10}
$$ Therefore $$
\Delta E_{ns}=\frac{2\pi}{5} e^{2} |\Psi_{ns}(0)|^{2} R^{2}
$$ The shift is much smaller for non-s states because for l\ge 1 one has $$
\Psi_{nlm}(0)=0
$$ so the leading contribution proportional to |\Psi(0)|^{2} vanishes and only higher-order terms in the small-r expansion contribute. For the 2s state, from the given wave function, $$
\Psi_{2s}(0)=(2a_{0})^{-3/2} \pi^{-1/2}
$$ Hence $$
\Delta E_{2s}=\frac{2\pi}{5} e^{2} |\Psi_{2s}(0)|^{2} R^{2}
$$ and, since \Psi_{2p}(0)=0, $$
\Delta E_{\text{split}}=\Delta E_{2s}-\Delta E_{2p}\approx\Delta E_{2s}
$$ Using a_{0}\approx 5\times 10^{-9} \unit{cm} and R\approx 10^{-13} \unit{cm}, it is convenient to rewrite $$
\frac{e^{2} R^{2}}{20 a_{0}^{3}}=\bigg(\frac{e^{2}}{\hbar c}\bigg)^{2}\cdot\frac{R^{2} m c^{2}}{20 a_{0}^{2}}
$$ Therefore $$
\Delta E_{\text{split}}\approx\bigg(\frac{1}{137}\bigg)^{2}\times\frac{10^{-26}}{20\times(5\times 10^{-9})^{2}}\times 0.511\times 10^{6} \unit{eV}
$$ which gives the numerical estimate $$
\Delta E_{\text{split}}\approx 5.4\times 10^{-10} \unit{eV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔE_split = E_{2s} − E_{2p} as a numerical value in eV. Round your final result to 2 significant figures.

context: Problem. Derive an expression for the hyperfine energy splitting of an atomic level produced by the magnetic dipole hyperfine interaction between the nuclear magnetic moment and the magnetic field of a single electron. Work to first order in perturbation theory for a hydrogenic one-electron atom with nuclear charge Z. Use the unperturbed atomic state |l s j I F M_F>, where l is the electron orbital angular momentum quantum number, s is the electron spin quantum number, j is the total electronic angular momentum quantum number, I is the nuclear spin quantum number, F is the total atomic angular momentum quantum number, and M_F is its z-component. Define all quantities as follows: r is the electron position vector relative to the nucleus, v is the electron velocity, r' is the displacement from the electron to a generic field point, A is the vector potential, B_e is the magnetic field from the electron’s orbital motion, B_s is the magnetic field from the electron’s spin magnetic moment, H_{lI} and H_{sI} are the corresponding interaction Hamiltonians, and H_{hf} is the total hyperfine Hamiltonian. The electron mass is m, the vacuum permeability is mu_0, the elementary charge is e, and the reduced Planck constant is hbar. The Bohr magneton is mu_B = e hbar/(2 m). The nuclear magnetic moment is m_N = g_N mu_N I/hbar, where mu_N is the nuclear magneton and g_N is the nuclear Landé g-factor. The Bohr radius is a_0 and n is the principal quantum number. The operators l, s, I, and j are vector operators for orbital, spin, nuclear, and total electronic angular momenta, respectively, and F is the total atomic angular momentum operator with F = I + j. The Dirac delta is denoted by delta(r). The gradient with respect to r is denoted by nabla, and that with respect to r' is denoted by nabla'. Use the identity nabla^2(1/r) = -4 pi delta(r). Express your final answers for the hyperfine energy corrections Delta E in terms of the angular momentum quantum numbers and, where needed, the hydrogenic expectation values.
solution:
The magnetic field at the nucleus due to the electron’s orbital motion is
$$
B_e(0) = \frac{\mu_0 e}{4\pi} \frac{v \times r}{r^3}
$$
Using l = m r \times v and mu_B = \frac{e hbar}{2 m}, this becomes
$$
B_e(0) = - \frac{2 \mu_0 \mu_B}{4\pi hbar} \frac{l}{r^3}
$$
The interaction Hamiltonian between the nuclear magnetic moment m_N and B_e(0) is
$$
H_{lI} = - m_N \cdot B_e(0)
$$
With m_N = \frac{g_N \mu_N I}{hbar}, this gives
$$
H_{lI} = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2 r^3} l \cdot I
$$
The electron spin magnetic moment is
$$
m_s = - \frac{2 \mu_B s}{hbar}
$$
The corresponding vector potential at r + r' is
$$
A = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} m_s \times \frac{r'}{r'^3}
$$
The magnetic field from m_s is
$$
B_s = \nabla \times A
$$
Substituting A gives
$$
B_s = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \times \left( m_s \times \frac{r'}{r'^3} \right)
$$
Using r'/r'^3 = - \nabla' \left( \frac{1}{r'} \right) and m_s = - \frac{2 \mu_B s}{hbar}, we obtain
$$
B_s = \frac{2 \mu_0 \mu_B}{4\pi hbar} \nabla' \times \left( s \times \nabla' \frac{1}{r'} \right)
$$
Evaluating the curl gives
$$
B_s = \frac{2 \mu_0 \mu_B}{4\pi hbar} \left[ s \nabla'^2 \left( \frac{1}{r'} \right) - (s \cdot \nabla') \nabla' \left( \frac{1}{r'} \right) \right]
$$
Using \nabla'^2 (1/r') = - 4 \pi \delta(r'), we get
$$
B_s = - \frac{2 \mu_0 \mu_B}{4\pi hbar} \left[ 4 \pi s \delta(r') + (s \cdot \nabla') \nabla' \left( \frac{1}{r'} \right) \right]
$$
Setting r' = - r, the field at the origin is
$$
B_s(0) = - \frac{2 \mu_0 \mu_B}{4\pi hbar} \left[ 4 \pi s \delta(r) + (s \cdot \nabla) \nabla \left( \frac{1}{r} \right) \right]
$$
The corresponding interaction Hamiltonian is
$$
H_{sI} = - m_N \cdot B_s(0)
$$
With m_N = \frac{g_N \mu_N I}{hbar}, this becomes
$$
H_{sI} = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \left[ 4 \pi I \cdot s \delta(r) + (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right]
$$
The total hyperfine Hamiltonian is
$$
H_{hf} = H_{lI} + H_{sI}
$$
Hence
$$
H_{hf} = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \left[ \frac{l \cdot I}{r^3} + 4 \pi s \cdot I \delta(r) + (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right]
$$
In first-order perturbation theory, for the state |l s j I F M_F>, the energy correction is
$$
\Delta E = \langle l s j I F M_F | H_{hf} | l s j I F M_F \rangle
$$
Case l \neq 0. The wavefunction vanishes at the origin, so only the r \neq 0 part contributes. Then
$$
H_{hf} = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \left[ \frac{I \cdot l}{r^3} + (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right]
$$
This can be written as
$$
H_{hf} = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2 r^3} G \cdot I
$$
where
$$
G = l + 3 \frac{(s \cdot r) r}{r^2}
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta E = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \left\langle \frac{1}{r^3} G \cdot I \right\rangle
$$
Using angular momentum algebra,
$$
\Delta E = \frac{\mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi} \cdot \frac{l(l+1)}{j(j+1)} \cdot \left[ F(F+1) - I(I+1) - j(j+1) \right] \left\langle \frac{1}{r^3} \right\rangle
$$
For hydrogenic states,
$$
\left\langle \frac{1}{r^3} \right\rangle = \frac{Z^3}{a_0 n^3 \left( l + \frac{1}{2} \right)}
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta E = \frac{\mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi} \cdot \frac{Z^3}{a_0 n^3 \left( l + \frac{1}{2} \right) j(j+1)} \cdot \left[ F(F+1) - I(I+1) - j(j+1) \right]
$$
Case l = 0. The wavefunction is spherically symmetric and
$$
\Delta E = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \left[ 4 \pi \langle s \cdot I \delta(r) \rangle + \left\langle (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle \right]
$$
Evaluate the second expectation value as
$$
\left\langle (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle = \left\langle \sum_{i,j=1}^3 s_i I_j \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} \left( \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle
$$
By spherical symmetry,
$$
\left\langle (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle = \frac{1}{3} \left\langle s \cdot I \nabla^2 \left( \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle
$$
Using \nabla^2 (1/r) = - 4 \pi \delta(r), we obtain
$$
\left\langle (s \cdot \nabla) \left( I \cdot \nabla \frac{1}{r} \right) \right\rangle = - \frac{4 \pi}{3} \langle s \cdot I \delta(r) \rangle
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta E = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi hbar^2} \cdot \frac{8 \pi}{3} \langle s \cdot I \delta(r) \rangle
$$
Using s \cdot I = \frac{1}{2} \left[ F(F+1) - I(I+1) - s(s+1) \right] in expectation values, we get
$$
\Delta E = \frac{\mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{4\pi} \left[ F(F+1) - I(I+1) - s(s+1) \right] \cdot \frac{8 \pi}{3} \langle \delta(r) \rangle
$$
For hydrogenic s states,
$$
\langle \delta(r) \rangle = \frac{Z^3}{\pi a_0^3 n^3}
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta E = \frac{2 \mu_0 g_N \mu_N \mu_B}{3 \pi} \cdot \frac{Z^3}{a_0^3 n^3} \cdot \left[ F(F+1) - I(I+1) - s(s+1) \right]
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions for the first-order hyperfine energy correction. Your final answers should be written as: (1) Delta E(l ≠ 0) = ... using only the symbols mu_0, g_N, mu_N, mu_B, Z, a_0, n, l, j, I, F, and numerical constants; and (2) Delta E(l = 0) = ... using only the symbols mu_0, g_N, mu_N, mu_B, Z, a_0, n, F, I, s, and numerical constants. Do not introduce any other variables or expectation-value notation; express the results in hydrogenic form.

subquestions.subproblem: the natural line width. (Hint: the lifetime of the 2p state of hydrogen is 10^{-9} sec)
subquestions.solution:
The lifetime of the 2p state of the muonic atom scales as
$$
\tau_{\mu}=\frac{1}{Z^{4}}\frac{m_{e}}{m_{\mu}}\tau_{H}
$$
Using Z=38 and the given tau_H, this gives
$$
\tau_{\mu}=2.4\times 10^{-18}\unit{s}
$$
By the uncertainty principle, the natural width is
$$
\Gamma\approx \frac{\hbar}{\tau_{\mu}}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Gamma=2.7\times 10^{2}\unit{eV}
$$

context: What is the energy of the photon emitted in the transition from the n=3 to n=2 level of the μ− mesic atom of carbon? Express the answer in terms of the γ energy for the electronic transition from n=2 to n=1 of hydrogen. Use the following definitions: Z is the atomic number of carbon with Z=6, m_μ is the muon mass, m_e is the electron mass with m_μ/m_e=210, E_n(H) is the energy of the nth bound state of the hydrogen atom (electronic, Z=1), E_n(μC) is the energy of the nth bound state of the μ− mesic carbon atom, E_γ^{(μC,3→2)} is the photon energy for the μ− mesic carbon transition n=3→2, and E_γ^{(H,2→1)} is the photon energy for the hydrogen electronic transition n=2→1.
solution:
For hydrogen-like systems, the bound-state energies scale as
$$
E_n(μC)=Z^2 \frac{m_μ}{m_e} E_n(H)
$$
The photon energy for the μ− mesic carbon transition n=3→2 is
$$
ΔE=Z^2 \frac{m_μ}{m_e} \bigl(E_3(H)-E_2(H)\bigr)
$$
For hydrogen levels, the magnitude scales as
$$
-E_n(H)\propto \frac{1}{n^2}
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{36}{5} \bigl(E_3(H)-E_2(H)\bigr)=\frac{4}{3} \bigl(E_2(H)-E_1(H)\bigr)
$$
Hence
$$
ΔE=\frac{5 Z^2 m_μ}{27 m_e} \bigl(E_2(H)-E_1(H)\bigr)
$$
With Z=6 and \(m_μ/m_e=210\)
$$
ΔE=1400 \bigl(E_2(H)-E_1(H)\bigr)
$$
Identifying \(ΔE=E_γ^{(μC,3→2)}\) and \(E_2(H)-E_1(H)=E_γ^{(H,2→1)}\)
$$
E_γ^{(μC,3→2)}=1400 E_γ^{(H,2→1)}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_γ^{(μC,3→2)} = ... E_γ^{(H,2→1)}, and your response should be written with E_γ^{(H,2→1)} only.

context: Consider the situation which arises when a negative muon is captured by an aluminum atom with atomic number Z=13. After the muon gets inside the electron cloud it forms a hydrogen-like muonic atom with the aluminum nucleus. The muon mass satisfies m_μ/m_e = 105.7/0.511. subquestions.subproblem: Compute the wavelength (in \(\mathrm{\AA}\)) of the photon emitted when this muonic atom decays from the 3d state. Sliderule accuracy; neglect nuclear motion
subquestions.solution:
The hydrogen-like muonic atom has energies
$$E=E_0\left[\frac{1}{n^2}+\frac{\alpha^2 Z^2}{n^3}\left(\frac{1}{j+\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{3}{4n}\right)\right]$$
with
$$E_0=-\frac{2\pi^2 m_\mu e^4 Z^2}{(4\pi \epsilon_0)^2 h^2}$$
$$E_0=-13.6\times\frac{105.7}{0.511}\times 13^2\unit{eV}$$
$$E_0=-4.754\times 10^5\unit{eV}$$
$$\alpha=\frac{1}{137}$$
The relevant transition energies are
