subquestions.subproblem: Compute the mean life of the above muonic atom in the 3d state, taking into account the fact that the mean life of a hydrogen atom in the 3d state is 1.6 \times 10^{-8} sec
subquestions.solution:
The probability of a spontaneous transition is
$$P\propto \frac{e^2 \omega^3}{\hbar c^3} R^2$$
with
$$\omega\propto \frac{m_\mu (Z e^2)^2}{\hbar^3}$$
$$R\propto \frac{\hbar^2}{m_\mu Z e^2}$$
Thus
$$P\propto m_\mu (Z e^2)^4$$
As the mean life of the initial state is
$$\tau=\frac{1}{P}$$
the mean life of the 3d state of the muonic atom is
$$\tau=\frac{m_e \tau_0}{m_\mu Z^4}$$
$$\tau=2.7\times 10^{-15}\unit{s}$$
where the hydrogen 3d mean life is
$$\tau_0=1.6\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the mean life τ (in seconds) as a numerical value. Report the value to 2 significant figures.

context: A proposal has been made to study the properties of an atom composed of a positive pion and a negative muon in order to measure the charge radius of the positive pion. The positive pion has mass m_{\pi^+}=273.2 m_e and its charge is assumed to be spread uniformly on a spherical shell of radius r_0=10^{-13} \unit{cm}. The negative muon has mass m_{\mu^-}=206.77 m_e and is treated as a point charge. Let r be the radial coordinate. Use the reduced mass m of the two-body system defined by m=m_{\mu^-} m_{\pi^+}/(m_{\mu^-}+m_{\pi^+}). Use e for the elementary charge magnitude and \hbar for Planck's constant divided by 2\pi. Let a_0 denote the Bohr radius for this reduced mass. The unperturbed point-Coulomb potential is V_{\text{point}}(r)=-e^2/r. The perturbation due to the finite-size spherical shell is denoted by \delta V(r), which equals e^2(1/r-1/r_0) for 0\le r<r_0 and 0 for r\ge r_0. Neglect spin-orbit effects and the Lamb shift. The unperturbed hydrogenic energies are E_n=-m e^4/(2\hbar^2 n^2). Let \Delta denote the unperturbed energy difference \Delta=E_{2p}-E_{1s}. Let \Delta E_{1s} and \Delta E_{2p} denote the first-order shifts due to \delta V(r). Define the percentage shift P by P=100\times(\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p})/\Delta and report the numerical value of P in \unit{%}.

subquestions.subproblem: $$R_{10}(r)=2\left(\frac{1}{a_0}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{a_0}\right)$$
$$R_{21}(r)=\left(\frac{1}{2 a_0}\right)^{3/2}\frac{r}{a_0}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{a_0}\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

solution:
The point-Coulomb potential is
$$V_{\text{point}}(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
For 0\le r<r_0, the perturbation is
$$\delta V(r)=e^2\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{r_0}\right)$$
For r\ge r_0, the perturbation is
$$\delta V(r)=0$$
The first-order shifts are
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\int_0^{r_0} R_{10}(r)^2\,\delta V(r)\,r^2\,dr$$
$$\Delta E_{2p}=\int_0^{r_0} R_{21}(r)^2\,\delta V(r)\,r^2\,dr$$
Using r_0\ll a_0 and the given R_{10} and R_{21}, we obtain
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\frac{2 e^2 r_0^2}{3 a_0^3}$$
$$\Delta E_{2p}\approx\frac{e^2 r_0^4}{480 a_0^3}$$
Thus the shift of the 1s-2p separation is
$$\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p}\approx\Delta E_{1s}$$
The unperturbed energies satisfy
$$E_n=-\frac{m e^4}{2\hbar^2 n^2}$$
The unperturbed 1s-2p energy difference is
$$\Delta=E_{2p}-E_{1s}$$
Using n=2 and n=1 gives
$$\Delta=-\frac{m e^4}{2\hbar^2}\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-1\right)$$
Which simplifies to
$$\Delta=\frac{3 m e^4}{8\hbar^2}$$
Using a_0=\hbar^2/(m e^2), this can be written as
$$\Delta=\frac{3 e^2}{8 a_0}$$
Therefore, the fractional shift is
$$\frac{\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p}}{\Delta}\approx\frac{16}{9}\left(\frac{r_0}{a_0}\right)^2$$
The reduced mass is
$$m=\frac{m_{\mu^-} m_{\pi^+}}{m_{\mu^-}+m_{\pi^+}}$$
Numerically,
$$m=117.7\,m_e$$
The Bohr radius for this reduced mass is
$$a_0=\frac{\hbar^2}{m e^2}$$
It can be expressed using the electron Bohr radius as
$$a_0=\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{m_e e^2}\right)\frac{m_e}{m}$$
Using \left(\hbar^2/(m_e e^2)\right)=0.53\times 10^{-8} \unit{cm}, we find
$$a_0=\frac{0.53\times 10^{-8}}{117.7} \unit{cm}$$
Which gives
$$a_0=4.5\times 10^{-11} \unit{cm}$$
The pion charge radius is
$$r_0=1\times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}$$
Hence the fractional shift is
$$\frac{\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p}}{\Delta}=\frac{16}{9}\left(\frac{1\times 10^{-13}}{4.5\times 10^{-11}}\right)^2$$
Which evaluates to
$$\frac{\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p}}{\Delta}=8.8\times 10^{-6}$$
Defining the percentage shift by P=100\times(\Delta E_{1s}-\Delta E_{2p})/\Delta, the result is
$$P=8.8\times 10^{-4} \unit{%}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the percentage shift P as a numerical value in percent (%), rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A mu- meson (negatively charged muon) of mass M = 210 m_e, where m_e is the electron mass, is captured into a circular orbit around a proton. Its initial orbital radius R is approximately the Bohr radius of an electron bound to a proton. Using classical arguments, including the Larmor formula for the power radiated by a nonrelativistic accelerating charge, estimate the time t it takes the mu- meson to radiate enough energy to reach its ground state. Use Gaussian electromagnetic units for intermediate formulas. Definitions: e is the elementary charge magnitude, c is the speed of light, ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, r is the instantaneous orbital radius of the mu- around the proton, K(r) is the kinetic energy, E(r) is the total mechanical energy, F_Coul is the magnitude of the Coulomb force, a is the centripetal acceleration magnitude, P is the radiated power, t is time, R is the initial orbital radius, and r_0 is the ground-state orbital radius of the muonic hydrogen atom. In intermediate steps, m denotes m_e.
solution:
The total energy as a function of orbital radius r is
$$
E(r) = K(r) - \frac{e^2}{r}
$$
$$
E(r) = -\frac{e^2}{2 r}
$$
The radiated power for a nonrelativistic accelerating charge is
$$
P = \frac{2 e^2 a^2}{3 c^3}
$$
The Coulomb force magnitude is
$$
F_{Coul} = \frac{e^2}{r^2}
$$
The centripetal acceleration is
$$
a = \frac{F_{Coul}}{M}
$$
$$
a = \frac{e^2}{r^2 M}
$$
Energy conservation gives
$$
\frac{dE}{dt} = -P
$$
Using
$$
\frac{dE}{dr} = \frac{e^2}{2 r^2}
$$
and the expression for a, we obtain
$$
\frac{e^2}{2 r^2} \frac{dr}{dt} = -\frac{2 e^2}{3 c^3} \frac{e^4}{r^4 M^2}
$$
With the initial condition
$$
r(0) = R
$$
integration gives
$$
R^3 - r^3 = \frac{4}{c^3} \frac{e^4}{M^2} t
$$
The initial orbital radius is approximately the electronic Bohr radius
$$
R \approx \frac{\hbar^2}{m e^2}
$$
The ground-state orbital radius for the muonic atom is
$$
r_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{M e^2}
$$
Therefore, the time to spiral down from R to r_0 satisfies
$$
\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{e^2}\right)^3 \left(\frac{1}{m^3} - \frac{1}{M^3}\right) = \frac{4 e^4}{c^3 M^2} t
$$
For
$$
M \gg m
$$
we have the approximation
$$
t \approx \frac{M^2 c^3 R^3}{4 e^4}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
t \approx \left(\frac{M}{m}\right)^2 \left(\frac{m c^2}{e^2}\right)^2 \frac{R^3}{4 c}
$$
Numerically, using M/m = 210, R \approx 5.3\times 10^{-11} \unit{m}, 2.82\times 10^{-15} \unit{m}, and c = 3\times 10^{8} \unit{m/s},
$$
t \approx 210^2 \left(\frac{5.3\times 10^{-11} \unit{m}}{2.82\times 10^{-15} \unit{m}}\right)^2 \frac{5.3\times 10^{-11} \unit{m}}{4\times 3\times 10^{8} \unit{m/s}}
$$
$$
t \approx 6.9\times 10^{-7} \unit{s}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express t, the time for the mu- meson to radiate enough energy to reach its ground state, as a numerical value in seconds. Report your result to 2 significant figures.

context: Use a variational method, a perturbation method, sum rules, and/or other method to obtain crude estimates of the following properties of the helium atom. Definitions and notation: The helium atom has two electrons and a nucleus of charge +2e. The Bohr radius is a0. The electron mass is me and the reduced Planck constant is ħ. The principal quantum number is n. The single-electron orbital angular momentum quantum number is l, and the total orbital angular momentum for the atom is L. The static electric dipole polarizability is α. The ionization energy is EI, defined as the minimum energy required to remove one electron from the atom. In part (b), let E denote the bound-state energy of the effective hydrogenic outer electron so that EI = −E. In part (b), the lowest F state corresponds to L = 3; the outer electron with l = 3 is far from the nucleus, and the nucleus plus the inner 1s electron acts as an effective core of charge +e, so the outer electron sees an effective nuclear charge Z = 1 and has n = 4. Unperturbed eigenfunctions are Ψ0 and Ψn with eigenvalues E0 and En. The perturbing potential is u, with matrix elements u_{n0} = ⟨0|u|n⟩ and u_{00} = ⟨0|u|0⟩. The variational parameter is λ. The kinetic-energy operator is \hat{T}, with momenta p1 and p2 and gradients ∇i acting on electron i. The total Hamiltonian is \hat{H} with unperturbed part \hat{H}_0. Surface integrals use a boundary S with element dS. The symbol E′ denotes a representative average of E0 − En. Angle brackets ⟨⋯⟩ denote expectation values. Atomic units are used where stated, defined by a0 = ħ = e = 1. The lowest singlet P state lies approximately 21 \unit{eV} above the ground state. Note: For grading consistency, the provided source solution for part (a) reports the static polarizability α; we retain that reported quantity as-is.

In the lowest F state the electron in the l = 3 orbit is so far from the nucleus that the latter together with the 1s electron can be treated as a core of charge +e. Thus the excited atom can be considered as a hydrogen atom in the state n = 4. The ionization energy EI, i.e. the energy required to remove one electron from the atom, is

$$

$$

subquestions.subproblem: the electric polarizability of the atom in its ground state. (The lowest singlet $P$ state lies $\sim 21 \unit{eV}$ above the ground state.)
subquestions.solution:
Consider a perturbation u. The wave function and energy for the ground state, correct to first order, are
$$
\Psi = \Psi_{0} + \sum_{n \neq 0} \frac{u_{n0}}{E_{0} - E_{n}} \Psi_{n}
$$
$$
E = E_{0} + u_{00} + \sum_{n \neq 0} \frac{(u_{n0})^{2}}{E_{0} - E_{n}}
$$
where
$$
\nu_{n0} = \langle 0|u|n \rangle
$$
Write
$$
\sum_{n \neq 0} u_{n0} \Psi_{n} = \sum_{n = 0} u_{n0} \Psi_{n} - u_{00} \Psi_{0}
$$
with
$$
\nu \Psi_{0} = \sum_{n = 0} u_{n0} \Psi_{n}
$$
Then
$$
\Psi = \Psi_{0} \left(1 + \frac{u - u_{00}}{E'}\right)
$$
The average total kinetic energy of the electrons is calculated using a variational method with \Psi = (1 + \lambda u) \Psi_{0} as the trial function
$$
\langle T \rangle = \frac{\int \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \hat{T} \Psi_{0} (1 + \lambda u) dr}{\int \Psi_{0}^{*} \Psi_{0} (1 + \lambda u)^{2} dr}
$$
where
$$
\hat{T} = \frac{1}{2 m_{e}} (p_{1}^{2} + p_{2}^{2})
$$
$$
\hat{T} = -\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m_{e}} (\nabla_{1}^{2} + \nabla_{2}^{2})
$$
In atomic units
$$
\hat{T} = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{2} \nabla_{i}^{2}
$$
Consider
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{2} \int \nabla_{i} \cdot [\Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i} u] dr = \oint_{S} \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \sum_{i=1}^{2} \nabla_{i} u \cdot dS
$$
Using Gauss' theorem and the vanishing surface term,
$$
\oint_{S} \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \sum_{i=1}^{2} \nabla_{i} u \cdot dS = 0
$$
Also
$$
\nabla_{i} \cdot [\Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i} u] = \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i}^{2} u + (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i} (\Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*}) \cdot \nabla_{i} u + \lambda \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} \nabla_{i} u \cdot \nabla_{i} u
$$
so that
$$
\int [\Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i}^{2} u + (1 + \lambda u) \nabla_{i} (\Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*}) \cdot \nabla_{i} u] dr = -\lambda \int \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} \nabla_{i} u \cdot \nabla_{i} u dr
$$
Hence
$$
\langle T \rangle = -\frac{1}{4} \sum_{i=1}^{2} \int [\Psi_{0}^{*} (1 + \lambda u)^{2} \nabla_{i}^{2} \Psi_{0} + \Psi_{0} (1 + \lambda u)^{2} \nabla_{i}^{2} \Psi_{0}^{*}] dr + \frac{\lambda^{2}}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{2} \int \Psi_{0} \Psi_{0}^{*} \nabla_{i} u \cdot \nabla_{i} u dr
$$
The total Hamiltonian is
$$
\hat{H} = \hat{H}_{0} + \hat{T} + u
$$
Therefore
$$
E = E_{0} + \frac{\frac{1}{2} \int \Psi_{0}^{*} u (1 + \lambda u)^{2} \Psi_{0} dr + \frac{\lambda^{2}}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{2} \int \Psi_{0}^{*} \Psi_{0} \nabla_{i} u \cdot \nabla_{i} u dr}{\int \Psi_{0}^{*} \Psi_{0} (1 + \lambda u)^{2} dr}
$$

context: A furnace contains atomic sodium at low pressure and temperature T=2000\unit{K}. Consider only three energy levels of sodium, with energies measured relative to the ground state: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s: ^2S at E_0=0\unit{eV} (ground state), 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3p: ^2P at E_1=2.10\unit{eV}, and 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 4s: ^2S at E_2=3.18\unit{eV}. Define E_0, E_1, E_2 as the level energies of the 3s, 3p, and 4s states, respectively. Let T be the temperature, k the Boltzmann constant, e the elementary charge, c the speed of light in vacuum, and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. For a radiative transition k→i, define the angular frequency \omega_{ki}=(E_k−E_i)/\hbar, the Einstein A coefficient for spontaneous emission A_{ik}, the Einstein B coefficient for absorption B_{ik}, the level population N_i, and the spectral line intensity I_{ik}. Let g_i denote the degeneracy of level i. Magnetic quantum numbers are denoted m_k and m_i. The electric-dipole operator is r. For fine-structure sublevels with total angular momentum J, the degeneracy factor is g_J=2J+1; for the ^2P term there are J=3/2 and J=1/2 sublevels. Assume Boltzmann equilibrium populations N_i proportional to g_i exp(−E_i/(kT)). For absorption, the incident radiation has spectral energy density \rho(\omega); in part (b) it is flat so \rho(\omega) is constant over the relevant frequencies.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the photon energies of the emission lines present in the spectrum? What are their relative intensities? (Give appropriate expressions and evaluate them approximately as time permits).
subquestions.solution:
There are two electric-dipole emission transitions: 3p→3s and 4s→3p. Their photon energies are
$$E_{10}=E_1-E_0$$
$$E_{10}=2.10\unit{eV}$$
$$E_{21}=E_2-E_1$$
$$E_{21}=1.08\unit{eV}$$
The spontaneous-emission probability for k\to i is
$$A_{ik}=\frac{e^2\omega_{ki}^3}{3\hbar^2 c^3}\frac{1}{g_k}\sum_{m_k,m_i}|\langle i m_i| r | k m_k\rangle|^2$$
with
$$\omega_{ki}=\frac{E_k-E_i}{\hbar}$$
The emission line intensity scales as
$$I_{ik}\propto N_k\hbar\omega_{ki}A_{ik}$$
with level populations
$$N_i\propto g_i\exp\left(-\frac{E_i}{kT}\right)$$
For the ^2P term there are J=\frac{3}{2} and J=\frac{1}{2} sublevels. Suppose the dipole matrix elements and sublevel statistical weights for the two emission lines are approximately equal. Then the intensity ratio is
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}=\left(\frac{\omega_{10}}{\omega_{21}}\right)^4\exp\left(\frac{E_{21}}{kT}\right)$$
Numerically,
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}\approx\left(\frac{2.10}{1.08}\right)^4\exp\left(\frac{1.08\unit{eV}}{8.6\times10^{-5}\unit{eV/K}\times2000\unit{K}}\right)$$
$$\frac{I_{01}}{I_{12}}\approx8\times10^3$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express (1) the photon energies of each allowed electric-dipole emission line between the given levels as numerical values in eV, and (2) the relative intensity ratio as a single numerical value. Report the intensity ratio as I(high-frequency emission line)/I(low-frequency emission line).

subquestions.subproblem: Continuous radiation with a flat spectrum is now passed through the furnace and the absorption spectrum observed. What spectral lines are observed? Find their relative intensities.(UC, Berkeley)
subquestions.solution:
With a flat incident spectrum, \rho(\omega) is constant. The absorption lines observed are 3s→3p and 3p→4s. The absorption-line intensity is
$$I_{ik}\propto B_{ik}N_k\rho(\omega_{ik})\hbar\omega_{ik}$$
where
$$B_{ik}=\frac{4\pi^2 e^2}{3\hbar^2}\frac{1}{g_k}\sum_{m_k,m_i}|\langle i m_i| r | k m_k\rangle|^2$$
The intensity ratio is
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}=\frac{B_{10}N_0\omega_{10}}{B_{21}N_1\omega_{21}}$$
Assuming comparable matrix elements and statistical weights,
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx\left(\frac{\omega_{10}}{\omega_{21}}\right)\exp\left(\frac{E_{10}}{kT}\right)$$
Numerically,
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx\left(\frac{2.10}{1.08}\right)\exp\left(\frac{2.10\unit{eV}}{8.62\times10^{-5}\unit{eV/K}\times2000\unit{K}}\right)$$
$$\frac{I_{10}}{I_{21}}\approx4\times10^5$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list all allowed absorption transitions between the given levels in the form X→Y with X,Y ∈ {3s, 3p, 4s}, and provide the relative intensity ratio as a single numerical value. Report the intensity ratio as I(higher-photon-energy absorption line)/I(lower-photon-energy absorption line).

context: Sodium chloride forms cubic crystals with four Na and four Cl atoms per cubic unit cell. The molar masses of Na and Cl are M_{Na} = 23.0 \unit{g/mol} and M_{Cl} = 35.5 \unit{g/mol}. The density of NaCl is 2.16 \unit{g/cm^3}. Use Avogadro's number N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}. Notation: V is the volume of the cubic unit cell, a is the side length of the cubic unit cell, d is the interplanar spacing used in Bragg's law, d_{100} is the spacing of the (100) planes, ρ is the mass density, n is the Bragg order (a positive integer), λ is the X-ray wavelength, θ is the Bragg angle in degrees, θ_n is the Bragg angle for order n, and λ_{max} is the longest wavelength that still satisfies Bragg reflection for the (100) planes. For the longest-wavelength Bragg reflection, use the (100) planes so that d = d_{100} = a

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the longest wavelength for which X-rays can be Bragg reflected.
subquestions.solution:
Let V be the volume of the unit cell, N_A Avogadro's number, and ρ the density of NaCl.
$$V ρ N_A = 4(M_{Na} + M_{Cl})$$
$$V = \frac{4(M_{Na} + M_{Cl})}{ρ N_A}$$
$$V = \frac{4 \times 58.5}{2.16 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}}$$
$$V = 1.80 \times 10^{-22} \unit{cm^3}$$
$$a = V^{1/3}$$
$$a = 5.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{cm}$$
$$a = 5.6 \unit{\AA}$$
$$2 d \sin \theta = n \lambda$$
$$d = d_{100}$$
$$d_{100} = a$$

context: Given are the 2p binding energies for two elements. For niobium with atomic number Z = 41, the measured 2p binding energies are 2370 \unit{eV} for the 2P_{1/2} level and 2465 \unit{eV} for the 2P_{3/2} level. For lead with atomic number Z = 82, the measured 2p binding energies are 13035 \unit{eV} for the 2P_{1/2} level and 15200 \unit{eV} for the 2P_{3/2} level. The observed trends are that the average 2p binding energy is roughly proportional to (Z - a)^2, and the fine-structure splitting between the 2P_{1/2} and 2P_{3/2} levels is roughly proportional to (Z - a)^4. Explain these scalings using a central-potential model with effective screening and spin-orbit coupling, and determine reasonable screening constants. Use the following definitions and conventions: E is the energy of the 2p electron, B is the binding energy with B = -E, R h c is the Rydberg energy in electron-volts, \alpha is the fine-structure constant, j is the total angular momentum quantum number for the 2p levels (j = 1/2 or j = 3/2), a_1 is the effective screening constant entering the central-field term that controls the average binding energy, and a_2 is the effective screening constant entering the fine-structure term that controls the splitting. State clearly how the data for niobium and lead determine a_1 and a_2, and report numerical values for a_1 and a_2 for each element. Note that according to Hund's rule the 2P_{3/2} level lies lower in energy than the 2P_{1/2} level, so it has the larger binding energy. In your final numerical expressions, use \unit{} for units. The final answers should be written in the explicit forms a_1^{\mathrm{Nb}} = \dots, a_2^{\mathrm{Nb}} = \dots, a_1^{\mathrm{Pb}} = \dots, a_2^{\mathrm{Pb}} = \dots
solution:
A 2p electron in a multi-electron atom experiences a central potential due to the nucleus and inner-shell screening, plus fine-structure corrections from relativistic and spin-orbit effects. This explains the observed scalings: the central-field energy scales as Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^2 with Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = Z - a_1, while the spin-orbit splitting scales as \alpha^2 Z_{\mathrm{eff}}^4 with Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = Z - a_2.

We model the 2p energy including fine structure by
$$
E = -\frac{1}{4} R h c (Z - a_1)^2 + \frac{1}{8} R h c \alpha^2 (Z - a_2)^4 \left( \frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{j + \frac{1}{2}} \right)
$$
with
$$
R h c = 13.6 \unit{eV}
$$
$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{137}
$$
Numerically,
$$
E = -3.4 (Z - a_1)^2 + 9.06 \times 10^{-5} (Z - a_2)^4 \left( \frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{j + \frac{1}{2}} \right)
$$
The binding energy is
$$
B = -E
$$
According to Hund's rule, the 2P_{3/2} level has lower energy E and therefore larger binding energy B than the 2P_{1/2} level.

For niobium (Z = 41), the measured splitting is
$$
\Delta B_{\mathrm{Nb}} = 2465 \unit{eV} - 2370 \unit{eV}
$$
The model gives
$$
\Delta B_{\mathrm{Nb}} = 9.06 \times 10^{-5} (41 - a_2)^4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}
$$
Solving yields
$$
a_2 = 2.9
$$
Using the 2P_{3/2} binding energy to fix a_1,
$$
B_{3/2}^{\mathrm{Nb}} = 2465 \unit{eV}
$$
$$
B_{3/2}^{\mathrm{Nb}} = 3.4 (41 - a_1)^2 - 9.06 \times 10^{-5} (41 - 2.9)^4 \left( \frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{2} \right)
$$
which gives
$$
a_1 = 14.7
$$
For lead (Z = 82), the measured splitting is
$$
\Delta B_{\mathrm{Pb}} = 15200 \unit{eV} - 13035 \unit{eV}
$$
The model gives
$$
\Delta B_{\mathrm{Pb}} = 9.06 \times 10^{-5} (82 - a_2)^4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}
$$
Solving yields
$$
a_2 = -1.2
$$
Using the 2P_{3/2} binding energy to fix a_1,
$$
B_{3/2}^{\mathrm{Pb}} = 15200 \unit{eV}
$$
$$
B_{3/2}^{\mathrm{Pb}} = 3.4 (82 - a_1)^2 - 9.06 \times 10^{-5} (82 + 1.2)^4 \left( \frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{2} \right)
$$
which gives
$$
 a_1 = 21.4
$$
Thus the effective screening constants inferred from the data are
$$
 a_2^{\mathrm{Nb}} = 2.9
$$
$$
 a_1^{\mathrm{Nb}} = 14.7
$$
$$
 a_2^{\mathrm{Pb}} = -1.2
$$
$$
 a_1^{\mathrm{Pb}} = 21.4
$$
These values quantify the observed scalings: the average 2p binding energy varies approximately as (Z - a_1)^2, and the fine-structure splitting varies approximately as (Z - a_2)^4
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express a_1^{\mathrm{Nb}}, a_2^{\mathrm{Nb}}, a_1^{\mathrm{Pb}}, and a_2^{\mathrm{Pb}} as numerical values, written explicitly as a_1^{\mathrm{Nb}} = ..., a_2^{\mathrm{Nb}} = ..., a_1^{\mathrm{Pb}} = ..., a_2^{\mathrm{Pb}} = .... Report each value to three significant figures.

$$

context: Sketch a derivation of the Landé g-factor g, i.e., the factor determining the effective magnetic moment of an atom in weak magnetic fields. Let P_L, P_S, and P_J denote the total orbital, total spin, and total angular momentum operators of the electrons, respectively, all expressed in units of ħ, so that their squared magnitudes have eigenvalues L(L+1), S(S+1), and J(J+1). The corresponding magnetic moments are defined by mu_L = - mu_B P_L and mu_S = - 2 mu_B P_S, where mu_B is the Bohr magneton. The total magnetic moment is taken to be mu_J = - g mu_B P_J, which defines the Landé g-factor g. Derive g in terms of the quantum numbers L, S, and J.
solution:
$$P_J = P_L + P_S$$
$$\mu_L = - \mu_B P_L$$
$$\mu_S = - 2 \mu_B P_S$$
$$\mu_J = \mu_L + \mu_S$$
$$\mu_J = - \mu_B \left(P_L + 2 P_S\right)$$
$$P_L = P_J - P_S$$
$$\mu_J = - \mu_B \left(P_J + P_S\right)$$
$$\mu_J = - g \mu_B P_J$$
$$\mu_J = \frac{\mu_J \cdot P_J}{P_J^2} P_J$$
$$\mu_J = - \mu_B \frac{\left(P_J + P_S\right) \cdot P_J}{P_J^2} P_J$$
$$g = \frac{P_J^2 + P_S \cdot P_J}{P_J^2}$$
$$g = 1 + \frac{P_S \cdot P_J}{P_J^2}$$
$$P_L \cdot P_L = \left(P_J - P_S\right) \cdot \left(P_J - P_S\right)$$
$$P_L^2 = P_J^2 + P_S^2 - 2 P_J \cdot P_S$$
$$P_J \cdot P_S = \frac{1}{2} \left(P_J^2 + P_S^2 - P_L^2\right)$$
$$g = 1 + \frac{P_J^2 + P_S^2 - P_L^2}{2 P_J^2}$$
$$P_J^2 = J(J+1)$$
$$P_L^2 = L(L+1)$$
$$P_S^2 = S(S+1)$$
$$g = 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2 J(J+1)}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of g = ... and must be an algebraic expression written solely in terms of the variables L, S, and J. Do not include any other variables or numerical values.

context: In a Stern-Gerlach experiment using hydrogen atoms, a narrow atomic beam travels along the x axis through a region of inhomogeneous magnetic field of length L_1. The magnetic field points along the z axis and has a spatial gradient \frac{\partial B}{\partial z} along z, which is perpendicular to the beam direction. After the field region, the atoms drift freely over a flight path of length L_2 to a detection screen. The atomic mass is m, the longitudinal beam speed is v, and gravitational deflection is neglected. The Bohr magneton is denoted by \mu_B and the electron g factor in the ground state is denoted by g. The total electronic angular momentum is J with magnetic quantum number M_J. The magnetic moment is denoted by \mu, and the force component along z experienced by a magnetic moment in the field gradient is denoted F_z. The transverse velocity acquired while in the field is v_z. The transverse displacements inside the field and in the drift region are \Delta z_1 and \Delta z_2, respectively. The observed separation between the two lines on the screen is d. Figure reference: Fig. 1.51.

subquestions.subproblem: What determines the number of lines one sees? What features of the apparatus determine the magnitude of the separation between the lines?
subquestions.solution: A narrow beam of hydrogen atoms passes through an inhomogeneous magnetic field with gradient \frac{\partial B}{\partial z} along the z axis, perpendicular to the beam. Let N_{lines} denote the number of resolved lines on the screen. The number of lines equals the number of allowed M_J values, which is 2J+1, so for hydrogen in the ground state with J=\frac{1}{2} there are two lines. The magnitude of the separation depends on the field gradient \frac{\partial B}{\partial z}, the field length L_1, the drift length L_2, the atomic mass m, and the longitudinal speed v. The magnetic moment is given by $$\mu=g\mu_B J$$ with $$g=2$$ In the inhomogeneous field, the force along z is $$F_z=2\mu_B M_J \frac{\partial B}{\partial z}$$ With $$J=\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$M_J=\pm\frac{1}{2}$$ the beam splits into two components. The transverse velocity acquired while in the field is $$v_z=\frac{F_z}{m}\frac{L_1}{v}$$ The transverse displacement accrued inside the field region is $$\Delta z_1=\frac{1}{2}\frac{F_z}{m}\left(\frac{L_1}{v}\right)^2$$ The additional transverse displacement in the drift region is $$\Delta z_2=v_z\frac{L_2}{v}$$ Let d be the total separation between the two spots on the screen. Then $$N_{lines}=2J+1$$ and $$d=\frac{\mu_B L_1}{m v^2}\left(L_1+2L_2\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\partial B}{\partial z}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should contain two algebraic expressions: (1) Provide the number of lines in the form N_{lines} = ... using only the variable J. (2) Provide the line separation in the form d = ... using only the variables \mu_B, L_1, L_2, m, v, and \frac{\partial B}{\partial z}.

subquestions.subproblem: Make an estimate of the separation between the two lines if the Stern-Gerlach experiment is carried out with H atoms. Make any reasonable assumptions about the experimental setup. For constants which you do not know by heart, state where you would look them up and what units they should be substituted in your formula.
subquestions.solution: Assume the following typical values in SI units: $$L_1=0.03\unit{m}$$ $$L_2=0.10\unit{m}$$ $$\frac{\partial B}{\partial z}=1.0\times10^{3}\unit{T/m}$$ $$v=1.0\times10^{3}\unit{m/s}$$ $$m=1.67\times10^{-27}\unit{kg}$$ $$\mu_B=9.27\times10^{-24}\unit{J/T}$$ Values for m and \mu_B can be looked up in standard references such as NIST or the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics and should be used in SI units as written. Using the result from part (a), the separation is $$d=\frac{\mu_B L_1}{m v^2}\left(L_1+2L_2\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{\partial B}{\partial z}$$ Substituting the assumed values gives $$d=\frac{\left(9.27\times10^{-24}\unit{J/T}\right)\left(0.03\unit{m}\right)}{\left(1.67\times10^{-27}\unit{kg}\right)\left(1.0\times10^{3}\unit{m/s}\right)^2}\left(0.03\unit{m}+2\times0.10\unit{m}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(1.0\times10^{3}\unit{T/m}\right)$$ Numerically, $$d=3.8\times10^{-2}\unit{m}$$ In centimeters, $$d=3.8\unit{cm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express d as a numerical value in meters (SI units), rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A heated gas of neutral lithium atoms with atomic number Z=3 is placed in a uniform external magnetic field of magnitude B directed along the z axis. Spectroscopic term symbols are written as n^{2S+1}L_J, where n is the principal quantum number, S is the total electron spin, L is the orbital angular momentum with L=0 denoted by S and L=1 denoted by P, and J is the total electronic angular momentum. Magnetic sublevels are labeled by M_J, the projection of J along the field. Let E(n^{2S+1}L_J,M_J) denote the energy of a specific magnetic substate in the field and E(n^{2S+1}L_J) denote the center-of-gravity energy of that fine-structure level. Let M_J^{min}(n^{2S+1}L_J) be the value of M_J that minimizes E for that level in the given field. Let \Delta E_Z denote the Zeeman splitting scale induced by the field and \Delta E_{LS} the fine-structure (LS-coupling) splitting between J levels. Within a given J manifold for these doublet S and P states, the lowest Zeeman sublevel is the one with the most negative M_J. For each pair or set below, determine which state lies lowest in energy in the presence of the field and briefly justify your choice. When energy differences are quoted with \sim, they are order-of-magnitude estimates and are given in electronvolts using \unit{eV}.

subquestions.solution:
$$E(3^{2}P_{1/2})>E(2^{2}S_{1/2})$$
$$E(3^{2}P_{1/2})-E(2^{2}S_{1/2})\sim 1\unit{eV}$$
$$E(2^{2}S_{1/2},-\frac{1}{2})<E(2^{2}S_{1/2},+\frac{1}{2})$$
Because the principal quantum number is larger for $3^{2}P_{1/2}$, its center-of-gravity energy is higher than that of $2^{2}S_{1/2}$ by roughly an electronvolt for lithium. Within the $2^{2}S_{1/2}$ manifold, the Zeeman effect makes the most negative $M_J$ sublevel lowest.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should contain exactly two inequalities: (1) E(3^{2}P_{1/2}) [< or >] E(2^{2}S_{1/2}); (2) E(2^{2}S_{1/2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}) [< or >] E(2^{2}S_{1/2}, +\tfrac{1}{2}). Use only the symbols E(...), the specified term symbols, and the explicit M_J values \pm\tfrac{1}{2}.

subquestions.solution:
$$E(5^{2}S_{1/2})<E(5^{2}P_{1/2})$$
$$E(5^{2}P_{1/2})-E(5^{2}S_{1/2})\sim 1\unit{eV}$$
$$E(5^{2}S_{1/2},-\frac{1}{2})<E(5^{2}S_{1/2},+\frac{1}{2})$$
The $^{2}S$ term lies below the $^{2}P$ term at the same $n$ mainly due to orbital penetration and core screening in alkali atoms, giving an energy separation of order $\sim 1\unit{eV}$. Within $5^{2}S_{1/2}$, the lowest Zeeman sublevel has $M_J=-\frac{1}{2}$.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should contain exactly two inequalities: (1) E(5^{2}S_{1/2}) [< or >] E(5^{2}P_{1/2}); (2) E(5^{2}S_{1/2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}) [< or >] E(5^{2}S_{1/2}, +\tfrac{1}{2}). $$\Delta E_Z>\Delta E_{LS}$$
$$E(5^{2}P_{3/2},-\frac{3}{2})<E(5^{2}P_{1/2},-\frac{1}{2})$$
In the high-field regime where the Zeeman splitting exceeds the LS-coupling splitting, the state with $M_J=-\frac{3}{2}$ from $5^{2}P_{3/2}$ lies lowest among these.

context: Compare the weak-field Zeeman effect for the helium transitions (1s3s) ^1S_0 -> (1s2p) ^1P_1 and (1s3s) ^3S_1 -> (1s2p) ^3P_1 in LS coupling. Be qualitative but make the important features evident. Use the following definitions and notation so all symbols are clear. J is the total electronic angular momentum quantum number, L is the total orbital angular momentum quantum number, and S is the total spin quantum number. M_J is the magnetic quantum number associated with J. B is the external magnetic field measured in \unit{T}. μ_B is the Bohr magneton. g is the Landé g factor. The spectroscopic term ^{2S+1}L_J specifies S, L, and J. When needed, a level may also be denoted by the ordered triple (J,L,S). For the specific helium levels in this problem, the assignments are: (1s3s) ^1S_0 corresponds to (J,L,S)=(0,0,0), (1s2p) ^1P_1 corresponds to (1,1,0), (1s3s) ^3S_1 corresponds to (1,0,1), and (1s2p) ^3P_1 corresponds to (1,1,1). The Zeeman energy shift of a sublevel with given M_J is denoted by ΔE. The total number of resolved spectral components for a transition is denoted by N_lines.
solution:
In the weak-field Zeeman regime, a level with J=1 splits into the three sublevels M_J=-1,0,1, while a level with J=0 remains unsplit. The relevant selection rules are
$$
\Delta J=0,\pm 1
$$
$$
\Delta M_J=0,\pm 1
$$
For the transition (1s3s) ^1S_0 -> (1s2p) ^1P_1, the lower level has J=0 with only M_J=0, so the allowed final sublevels are M_J=-1,0,1, yielding three Zeeman components
$$
N_{lines}^{(1s3s)^{1}S_{0}\rightarrow(1s2p)^{1}P_{1}}=3
$$
For the transition (1s3s) ^3S_1 -> (1s2p) ^3P_1, both levels have J=1 with M_J=-1,0,1. The allowed transitions with \Delta M_J=0,\pm 1 produce six distinct Zeeman components in frequency
$$
N_{lines}^{(1s3s)^{3}S_{1}\rightarrow(1s2p)^{3}P_{1}}=6
$$
The Zeeman energy shift of a sublevel in a magnetic field B is
$$
\Delta E=g M_J \mu_B B
$$
The Landé factor in LS coupling is
$$
g=1+\frac{J(J+1)-L(L+1)+S(S+1)}{2J(J+1)}
$$
For the four levels involved, using their (J,L,S) values, the g factors are
$$
g_{(1s3s)^{1}S_{0}}=0
$$
$$
g_{(1s2p)^{1}P_{1}}=1
$$
$$
g_{(1s3s)^{3}S_{1}}=2
$$
$$
g_{(1s2p)^{3}P_{1}}=\frac{3}{2}
$$
Equivalently, the corresponding Zeeman shifts of the sublevels are
$$
\Delta E_{(1s3s)^{1}S_{0}}=0
$$
$$
\Delta E_{(1s2p)^{1}P_{1}}=M_J \mu_B B
$$
$$
\Delta E_{(1s3s)^{3}S_{1}}=2 M_J \mu_B B
$$
$$
\Delta E_{(1s2p)^{3}P_{1}}=\frac{3}{2} M_J \mu_B B
$$
Transition photon energies follow from differences between the upper and lower Zeeman shifts for each allowed pair of sublevels, producing the three-line pattern for ^1S_0 -> ^1P_1 and the six-line pattern for ^3S_1 -> ^3P_1 as depicted in Fig. 1.54.
final_answer_instructions: Provide the final results in algebraic form only, with no derivations. Include all of the following items exactly in these formats: (1) The total number of resolved spectral components for each transition, written as 'N_lines^{(1s3s)^1S_0->(1s2p)^1P_1} = ...' and 'N_lines^{(1s3s)^3S_1->(1s2p)^3P_1} = ...'. (2) The Landé g factors for each involved level, written as 'g_{(1s3s)^1S_0} = ...', 'g_{(1s2p)^1P_1} = ...', 'g_{(1s3s)^3S_1} = ...', and 'g_{(1s2p)^3P_1} = ...'. (3) The Zeeman energy shift for each involved level, written as 'ΔE_{(1s3s)^1S_0} = ...', 'ΔE_{(1s2p)^1P_1} = ...', 'ΔE_{(1s3s)^3S_1} = ...', and 'ΔE_{(1s2p)^3P_1} = ...', using only the symbols M_J, μ_B, and B (and numerical constants as needed). Do not introduce any variables other than M_J, μ_B, and B in the ΔE expressions.

context: Discuss qualitatively the Stark shift due to a constant external electric field of the n = 2 energy levels of hydrogen. Neglect spin. Include the observed zero-field splitting W between the 2s and 2p states, where E_{2s} and E_{2p} are the unperturbed 2s and 2p energies. Let e denote the positive elementary charge magnitude, a_0 the Bohr radius, r the electron position operator, and E the constant external electric field vector with magnitude E_0 = |E|. Use the hydrogenic basis kets |n l m>, and focus on the four n = 2 states |200>, |210>, |211>, |21 -1>. Define H' as the perturbation Hamiltonian due to the electric field. Define u as the dipole matrix element u = <210|H'|200>. Let E_+ and E_- denote the two perturbed energies within the subspace spanned by |200> and |210>. Use the following datum for the zero-field splitting:
solution:
The zero-field splitting is
$$W = E_{2s} - E_{2p}$$
$$W \approx 10^{-5} \unit{eV}$$
Treat the external field as a perturbation
$$H' = e E \cdot r$$
Among the four n = 2 states |200>, |210>, |211>, |21 -1>, only the dipole coupling between |200> and |210> is nonzero. Define

The first-order shifts vanish and the leading corrections are second order

context: A beam of hydrogen molecules H2 travels in the z direction with kinetic energy E0=1 \unit{eV}. The molecules are in an excited state and dissociate into two hydrogen atoms H. In events where one product atom emerges with final velocity perpendicular to the z direction, that atom's kinetic energy is E1=\frac{4}{5} \unit{eV}. Let m(H) denote the mass of a hydrogen atom and m(H2)=2 m(H). Let c denote the speed of light in vacuum. Use the nonrelativistic relation p=\sqrt{2 m E}, with masses expressed in \unit{eV/c^2} and momenta in \unit{eV/c}. Let p0 be the magnitude of the initial H2 momentum, p1 the magnitude of the perpendicular product atom's momentum, and p2 the magnitude of the second atom's momentum. Let E2 be the kinetic energy of the second atom. Define the energy released (reaction Q-value) as Q=E1+E2−E0. Calculate Q.
solution:
Using the nonrelativistic relation between kinetic energy and momentum for each particle:

$$
p_0=\sqrt{2 m(H_2) E_0}
$$

$$
m(H_2)=2 m(H)
$$

$$
m(H)=938\times10^6 \unit{eV/c^2}
$$

$$
E_0=1 \unit{eV}
$$

Numerically for the initial molecule:

$$
p_0\approx6.13\times10^4 \unit{eV/c}
$$

For the product atom emitted perpendicular to z:

$$
E_1=\frac{4}{5} \unit{eV}
$$

$$
p_1=\sqrt{2 m(H) E_1}
$$

$$
p_1\approx3.87\times10^4 \unit{eV/c}
$$

Momentum conservation with p1 perpendicular to p0 gives a right triangle in momentum space:

$$
p_2=\sqrt{p_0^2+p_1^2}
$$

$$
p_2\approx7.25\times10^4 \unit{eV/c}
$$

The second atom's kinetic energy is:

$$
E_2=\frac{p_2^2}{2 m(H)}
$$

$$
E_2\approx2.80 \unit{eV}
$$

The reaction energy released is:

$$
Q=E_1+E_2-E_0
$$

$$
Q\approx2.6 \unit{eV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the reaction Q-value as a numerical value in eV. Round your final result to 2 significant figures.

context: Approximate the molecule 1H35Cl as a rigid dumbbell with internuclear separation r = 1.29×10^{-10} \unit{m}. Use m_H = 1 amu and m_Cl = 35 amu with 1 amu = 1.67×10^{-27} \unit{kg}, and Planck's constant h = 6.6×10^{-34} \unit{J s}. Let I be the moment of inertia, \mu the reduced mass, c the speed of light, J the rotational quantum number, \nu the frequency of the J → J − 1 transition, and \Delta \nu the frequency separation between adjacent rotational lines to be reported as the final answer. Let \hbar denote the reduced Planck constant, defined as h divided by 2\pi. The rotational constant B is defined by B = \hbar^2/(2 I h c).
solution:
The moment of inertia of the molecule is
$$
I = \mu r^2
$$
The reduced mass is
$$
\mu = \frac{m_{Cl} m_H}{m_{Cl} + m_H}
$$
The chlorine mass is
$$
m_{Cl} = 35 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \unit{kg}
$$
The hydrogen mass is
$$
m_H = 1 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \unit{kg}
$$
The bond length is
$$
r = 1.29 \times 10^{-10} \unit{m}
$$
Hence
$$
I = \frac{35}{36} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times \left(1.29 \times 10^{-10}\right)^2 \unit{kg m^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
I = 2.7 \times 10^{-47} \unit{kg m^2}
$$
The line frequency for the J \to J - 1 transition is
$$
\nu = \frac{h c B J(J + 1) - h c B J(J - 1)}{h}
$$
Thus
$$
\nu = 2 c B J
$$
With
$$
B = \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I h c}
$$
It follows that
$$
\nu = \frac{\hbar^2}{I h} J
$$
Therefore the separation between adjacent rotational lines is
$$
\Delta \nu = 2 c B
$$
Equivalently
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{\hbar^2}{h I}
$$
And
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{h}{4 \pi^2 I}
$$
Substituting the values gives
$$
\Delta \nu = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \unit{J s}}{4 \pi^2 \times 2.7 \times 10^{-47} \unit{kg m^2}}
$$
Hence
$$
\Delta \nu = 6.2 \times 10^{11} \unit{Hz}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \Delta \nu as a numerical value in Hz, rounded to 2 significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$\nu = \frac{h c B J(J + 1) - h c B J(J - 1)}{h}$$

context: Consider the homonuclear diatomic molecule {}^{14}N_{2}. Each nitrogen nucleus has nuclear spin I=1, so the two nuclei are identical bosons and the total molecular wave function must be symmetric under exchange of the nuclei. Let J denote the rotational quantum number. Under exchange of the nuclei, the rotational wave function acquires the parity factor P_J. Define P_J by the equation below, and note that even J corresponds to a symmetric rotational state while odd J corresponds to an antisymmetric rotational state. For two identical nuclei of spin I, let g_S and g_A denote, respectively, the numbers of nuclear spin states that are symmetric and antisymmetric under exchange. For rotational Raman scattering in a homonuclear diatomic, the selection rule is stated below, and the nuclear spin symmetry does not change during the transition. Define I_even and I_odd as the intensities of spectral lines arising from even-J and odd-J rotational manifolds, respectively. Define the ratio of intensities of adjacent rotational lines as R_int, where R_int=I_even/I_odd. Report the final answer as R_int
solution:
Because the nuclei are identical bosons with I=1, the total molecular wave function is symmetric under exchange. The rotational part transforms with the exchange parity factor
$$
P_J=(-1)^J
$$
Even J rotational states are symmetric and odd J rotational states are antisymmetric, so even J must be combined with symmetric nuclear spin states and odd J with antisymmetric nuclear spin states. For two identical nuclei of spin I, the numbers of symmetric and antisymmetric nuclear spin states are
$$
g_S=(I+1)(2I+1)
$$
$$
g_A=I(2I+1)
$$
In rotational Raman transitions with
$$
\Delta J=0,\pm 2
$$
the nuclear spin symmetry is preserved, so the line intensities alternate in proportion to the corresponding spin statistical weights. Therefore the ratio of intensities of adjacent lines is
$$
R_{int}=\frac{I_{even}}{I_{odd}}
$$
which equals the spin statistical weight ratio
$$
R_{int}=\frac{g_S}{g_A}
$$
Substituting g_S and g_A gives
$$
R_{int}=\frac{(I+1)(2I+1)}{I(2I+1)}
$$
which simplifies to
$$
R_{int}=\frac{I+1}{I}
$$
For I=1 we obtain
$$
R_{int}=2
$$
This corresponds to a 2:1 ratio for successive even-J and odd-J lines
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express R_int as a numerical value.

context: Estimate the lowest neutron kinetic energy at which a free neutron, in an inelastic collision with a molecule of gaseous oxygen (O2), can lose energy by exciting molecular rotation. Use the rigid-rotor model with the following definitions and data: - Let r denote the O–O bond length. - Let m denote the mass of a single oxygen atom and let μ = m/2 be the reduced mass of the molecule. - Let I = μ r^2 be the moment of inertia of the molecule about its center of mass. - The rotational energy eigenvalues are E_J = h^2/(8π^2 I) J(J+1) with J = 0, 1, 2, .... - Let E_min be the minimum rotational excitation energy required for the transition J = 0 → 1. - Let E_{n,min} be the minimum neutron kinetic energy in the lab frame; neglect molecular recoil so that E_{n,min} = E_min to lowest order. Use the numerical data r = 1.2 \unit{Å}, m ≈ 16 u with u the atomic mass unit and u c^2 = 931.5 \unit{MeV}, and \hbar c = 197.327 \unit{eV nm}. Express the final numerical answer for E_{n,min} in \unit{eV}.
solution:
For a rigid diatomic rotor, the moment of inertia is
$$
I = 
\\mu r^2
$$
$$
\\mu = \\frac{m}{2}
$$
The rotational energy levels are
$$
E_J = \\frac{h^2}{8\\pi^2 I} J(J+1)
$$
The minimum energy that must be absorbed to excite the molecule from J = 0 to J = 1 is
$$
E_{\\min} = E_1 - E_0
$$
$$
E_{\\min} = \\frac{h^2}{4\\pi^2 I}
$$
Using I = \\mu r^2 with \\mu = m/2 gives
$$
E_{\\min} = \\frac{h^2}{2\\pi^2 m r^2}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
E_{\\min} = \\frac{2(\\hbar c)^2}{m c^2 r^2}
$$
Numerical data for evaluation:
$$
\\hbar c = 197.327 \\unit{eV\\,nm}
$$
$$
mc^2 = 16 \\times 931.5 \\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
mc^2 = 1.4904 \\times 10^{10} \\unit{eV}
$$
$$
r = 0.12 \\unit{nm}
$$
Substituting,
$$
E_{\\min} = \\frac{2\\times (197.327 \\unit{eV\\,nm})^2}{(1.4904\\times 10^{10} \\unit{eV})\\, (0.12 \\unit{nm})^2}
$$
$$
E_{\\min} \\approx 3.6 \\times 10^{-4} \\unit{eV}
$$
Since the neutron mass is much smaller than the mass of the O2 molecule, the minimum neutron kinetic energy required equals this excitation energy to lowest order:
$$
E_{n,\\min} = E_{\\min}
$$
$$
E_{n,\\min} \\approx 3.6 \\times 10^{-4} \\unit{eV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_{n,min} as a numerical value in eV. Include the unit eV. Report the value to 2 significant figures.

context: A {}^{14}N nucleus has nuclear spin I=1. Consider a diatomic nitrogen molecule N_{2} that can rotate but does not vibrate at ordinary temperatures, and ignore electronic motion. Ortho denotes the symmetric nuclear-spin state, and para denotes the antisymmetric nuclear-spin state. Let N_{ortho} and N_{para} denote the equilibrium populations of ortho- and para-N_{2}, respectively. Define the relative abundance ratio R_{p/o}=N_{para}/N_{ortho}. To present the final abundance as an a:b form, define A_{p:o} to denote the para:ortho abundance in a:b notation. The rotational quantum number is J, the moment of inertia is H, the reduced Planck constant is \hbar, the Boltzmann constant is k, and the absolute temperature is T. The rotational energies are E_J and the rigid-rotor approximation is used. Define Z_{even} and Z_{odd} as the rotational partition-function contributions from even-J and odd-J rotational levels, respectively. In the approximations below, introduce continuous variables x and y to replace discrete indices when sums are approximated by integrals. Determine R_{p/o} and A_{p:o} at ordinary temperatures, and describe the behavior of R_{p/o} as T is lowered towards 0 \unit{K}
solution:
Because the {}^{14}N nucleus has integer spin I=1, it is a boson, so the total molecular wave function must be symmetric under exchange of the two nuclei. For ortho-N_{2} (symmetric nuclear spin), the allowed rotational quantum numbers are even. For para-N_{2} (antisymmetric nuclear spin), the allowed rotational quantum numbers are odd.

$$
E_J=\frac{\hbar^2}{2H}J(J+1)
$$

$$
J=0,1,2,\ldots
$$

Define the abundance ratio

$$
R_{p/o}=\frac{N_{para}}{N_{ortho}}
$$

Define the even- and odd-J rotational sums

$$
Z_{even}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(4m+1)\exp\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2H k T}2m(2m+1)\right]
$$

$$
Z_{odd}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(4m+3)\exp\left[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2H k T}(2m+1)(2m+2)\right]
$$

Ignoring spin multiplicities initially, the rotational contribution to the ratio is

$$
R_0=\frac{Z_{even}}{Z_{odd}}
$$

Including nuclear-spin multiplicities gives

$$
R_{p/o}=\frac{I+1}{I}R_0
$$

High-temperature limit with \hbar^2/(H k T)\ll 1. For even J set J=2m and introduce

$$
x=2m(2m+1)
$$

Then

$$
Z_{even}\approx\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2H k T}x\right)dx
$$

$$
Z_{even}\approx\frac{H k T}{\hbar^2}
$$

For odd J set J=2m+1 and introduce

$$
y=(2m+1)(2m+2)
$$

Then

$$
Z_{odd}\approx\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2H k T}y\right)dy
$$

$$
Z_{odd}\approx\frac{H k T}{\hbar^2}\exp\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{H k T}\right)
$$

Therefore

$$
R_0=\exp\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{H k T}\right)
$$

$$
R_{p/o}=\frac{I+1}{I}\exp\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{H k T}\right)
$$

For \hbar^2/(H k T)\ll 1 this reduces to

$$
R_{p/o}\approx\frac{I+1}{I}
$$

With I=1 one obtains

$$
I=1
$$

$$
R_{p/o}=2
$$

To present the result in a:b form for para:ortho, use A_{p:o}

$$
A_{p:o}=2:1
$$

Low-temperature limit with \hbar^2/(H k T)\gg 1. Retaining only the lowest terms in each set

$$
Z_{even}\approx 1
$$

$$
Z_{odd}\approx 3\exp\left(-\frac{\hbar^2}{H k T}\right)
$$

Therefore

$$
R_{p/o}\approx\frac{I+1}{3I}\exp\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{H k T}\right)
$$

As T\to 0 one has

$$
R_{p/o}\to\infty
$$

Thus, as the temperature approaches 0 \unit{K}, the N_{2} molecules become entirely para
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the ordinary-temperature para-to-ortho ratios numerically in two parts: (1) R_{p/o} = [number] with no variables; (2) A_{p:o} = a:b using the smallest integers. Provide exactly these two lines and no additional text or derivations.
