context: In a recent issue of Science Magazine, G. Zweig discussed the idea of using free quarks (if they should exist) to catalyze fusion of deuterium. In an ordinary negative deuterium molecule (ded) the two deuterons are held together by an electron, which spends most of its time between the two nuclei. In principle a neutron can tunnel from one proton to the other, making a tritium plus p + energy, but the separation is so large that the rate is negligible. If the electron is replaced with a massive quark Q of charge -\frac{4e}{3}, the separation is reduced and the tunneling rate considerably increased. After the reaction, the quark generally escapes and captures another deuteron to make a dQ atom, net charge -\frac{e}{3}. The atom decays radiatively to the ground state, then captures another deuteron in a large-n orbit. This again decays down to the ground state. Fusion follows rapidly and the quark is released again. Assume the quark mass M_Q is much larger than the deuteron mass m, so the deuterons move in the field of a fixed Q. Let r_1 and r_2 be the position vectors of the two deuterons measured from Q, with magnitudes r_1 and r_2, and separation r_{12}=|r_1-r_2|. Let p_1 and p_2 be the canonical momenta conjugate to r_1 and r_2 for the two deuterons in the dQd molecule. Define the effective Bohr length for a single deuteron bound to Q of charge -\frac{4e}{3} as a_Q=\frac{3\hbar^2}{4me^2}, and also define a_Q'=\frac{3\hbar^2}{me^2}. For the nuclear part, model the neutron-proton interaction by a finite square well of depth V_0>0 and radius a_N, and let the deuteron binding energy be W>0 so that the deuteron energy is -W. Let M be the reduced mass of the neutron-proton system, M=\frac{m_p m_n}{m_p+m_n}. Let r_0\ge 10^{-13} \unit{cm} be a capture radius. Let p denote the magnitude of the neutron radial momentum inside the nuclear well. Use standard constants e, \hbar, and c as the elementary charge, reduced Planck constant, and speed of light, respectively. Fig. 1.67 sketches the nuclear potential.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose the quark is much more massive than the deuteron. What is the order of magnitude of the separation of the deuterons in the ground state of the d Q d molecule?
subquestions.solution:
The dQd molecule can be considered as an H_2^+ ion with the replacements electron mass \to m (the deuteron mass) and nuclear charge e \to quark charge -\frac{4e}{3}. The Hamiltonian is
$$H=\frac{p_1^2}{2m}+\frac{p_2^2}{2m}-\frac{4e^2}{3r_1}-\frac{4e^2}{3r_2}+\frac{e^2}{r_{12}}$$
Assume the ground state wavefunction factorizes as
$$\Psi(r_1,r_2)=\Psi_{100}(r_1)\Psi_{100}(r_2)$$
with the 1s orbital
$$\Psi_{100}(r)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}a_Q^{-3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{a_Q}\right)$$
where
$$a_Q=\frac{3\hbar^2}{4me^2}$$
The average separation is
$$\bar r_{12}=\frac{1}{\pi^2 a_Q^6}\iint r_{12}\exp\left[-\frac{2(r_1+r_2)}{a_Q}\right]d^3r_1 d^3r_2$$
Using the hydrogenic integral, one finds
$$\bar r_{12}=\frac{8}{5}a_Q$$
Equivalently
$$\bar r_{12}=\frac{6\hbar^2}{5me^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \bar r_{12} = ... , and your response should be written using only a_Q (with a_Q = 3\hbar^2/(4 m e^2) as defined).

subquestions.subproblem: Write down an expression for the order of magnitude of the time for a deuteron captured at large radius (large n) in dQ to radiatively settle to the ground state. Introduce symbols like mass, charge, etc. as needed; do not evaluate the expression.
subquestions.solution:
A hydrogen-like atom of nuclear charge Ze and orbiting mass m has energy
$$E_n=-\frac{Z^2 e^4 m}{2\hbar^2 n^2}$$
For the dQd molecule, by the H_2^+ analogy, the ground state energy can be written as
$$E=-2\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2\frac{m e^4}{2\hbar^2}+\frac{e^2}{r_{12}}$$
Using the expectation values in the 1s product state expressed through a_Q, this gives
$$E=-\frac{4}{3}\frac{e^2}{a_Q}+\frac{5}{8}\frac{e^2}{a_Q}$$
Hence
$$E_0=-\frac{17}{24}\frac{e^2}{a_Q}$$
For large n, treat the system as hydrogenic with dQ as the nucleus of charge -\frac{e}{3} and the orbiting deuteron of charge +e and mass m. Then
$$E_n=-\frac{4}{6}\frac{e^2}{a_Q}-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2\frac{m e^4}{2\hbar^2 n^2}$$
Equivalently,
$$E_n=-\frac{4}{6}\frac{e^2}{a_Q}-\frac{1}{6}\frac{e^2}{a_Q'}\frac{1}{n^2}$$
where
$$a_Q'=\frac{3\hbar^2}{me^2}$$
The emitted energy in the cascade to the ground state is
$$\Delta E=E_n-E_0$$
In terms of a_Q and a_Q',
$$\Delta E=-\frac{4e^2}{6a_Q}+\frac{17e^2}{24a_Q}-\frac{e^2}{6a_Q'}\frac{1}{n^2}$$
To order of magnitude for large n,
$$\Delta E\approx\frac{e^2}{24a_Q}$$
The photon frequency is
$$\omega=\frac{\Delta E}{\hbar}$$
To order of magnitude,
$$\omega\approx\frac{e^2}{24\hbar a_Q}$$
The dipole transition rate is
$$A_{n1}=\frac{4e^2\omega^3}{3\hbar c^3}|r_{1n}|^2$$
The corresponding time scale is
$$\tau=\frac{1}{A_{n1}}$$
Hence
$$\tau=\frac{3\hbar c^3}{4e^2\omega^3|r_{1n}|^2}$$
With the two-deuteron symmetrized state
$$\Psi_\pm=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big[\Psi_{100}(r_1)\Psi_{nlm}(r_2)\pm\Psi_{100}(r_2)\Psi_{nlm}(r_1)\big]$$
and the 1s dipole matrix element vanishing,
$$\langle\Psi_{100}|r|\Psi_{100}\rangle=0$$
so
$$r_{1n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle\Psi_{nlm}|r|\Psi_{100}\rangle$$
Therefore,
$$\tau=\frac{3\hbar c^3}{2e^2\omega^3|\langle\Psi_{nlm}|r|\Psi_{100}\rangle|^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \tau = ... , and your response should be written using only \hbar, c, e, \omega, and the dipole matrix element \langle\Psi_{nlm}|r|\Psi_{100}\rangle.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the expression for the probability of finding the neutron-proton separation in a deuteron being r \ge r_0, with r_0 \ge 10^{-13} \unit{cm}. Again, introduce symbols like deuteron binding energy as needed, and do not evaluate the expression.
subquestions.solution:
Model the n–p interaction by a finite square well of depth V_0 and radius a_N, with bound-state energy -W. For an s-wave, define \\kappa=\\sqrt{\\frac{2MW}{\\hbar^2}} for r\\ge a_N. The radial wavefunction outside the well can be written as
$$R(r)=\\frac{C\\exp(-\\kappa r)}{r}$$
The probability to find the separation r\\ge r_0 is
$$P(r\\ge r_0)=4\\pi\\int_{r_0}^{\\infty}|R(r)|^2 r^2 dr$$
Equivalently, using the outside form,
$$P(r\\ge r_0)=4\\pi C^2\\int_{r_0}^{\\infty}\\exp(-2\\kappa r)dr$$
The constant C is fixed by matching R and R' at r=a_N and by overall normalization
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P(r \ge r_0) = ... , and your response should be written using only r_0, \kappa, and C (you may also state \kappa = \sqrt{2 M W / \hbar^2} if you choose to define \kappa).

subquestions.subproblem: As a simple model for the tunneling rate suppose that if the neutron reaches a distance r \ge r_0 from the proton it certainly is captured by the other deuteron. Write down an order of magnitude expression for the halflife of dQd (but do not evaluate it).
subquestions.solution:
Inside the nuclear well of radius a_N and depth V_0, the neutron radial speed is
$$v=\frac{p}{M}$$
with
$$p=\sqrt{2M(V_0-W)}$$
so
$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2(V_0-W)}{M}}$$
If P is the probability to find r\ge r_0 from part (c), the escape attempt frequency is of order v/a_N, so the transition rate is
$$\lambda=\frac{vP}{a_N}$$
The halflife is
$$\tau_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$
Using the exponential tail P\sim\exp(-2\kappa r_0) with \kappa=\sqrt{\frac{2MW}{\hbar^2}}, one obtains the order of magnitude
$$\tau_{1/2}\approx a_N\ln 2\sqrt{\frac{M}{2(V_0-W)}}\exp(2\kappa r_0)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \tau_{1/2} = ... , and your response should be written using only a_N, M, V_0, W, r_0, and \hbar (you may also use \kappa and state \kappa = \sqrt{2 M W / \hbar^2}).

context: The size R of a nucleus can be determined by three types of measurements: (a) electron scattering, (b) energy levels of muonic atoms, and (c) ground state energies within an isotopic spin multiplet. Definitions used throughout: F(q^2) is the elastic nuclear form factor defined from the ratio of differential cross sections dσ_exp and dσ_point for experimental data and a pointlike nucleus, respectively; q is the momentum transfer and r is the position vector relative to the nuclear center; ρ(r) is the spherically symmetric nuclear charge density normalized to 1 with ⟨r^2⟩ = ∫ρ(r) r^2 d^3r the mean square charge radius; θ is the angle between q and r. In the muonic-atom method, m_μ is the muon mass, m_e is the electron mass, a_μ is the muonic Bohr radius, and a_0 is the electronic Bohr radius; H is the Hamiltonian, V(r) is the electrostatic potential, V_0(r) is the point-nucleus Coulomb potential, H′ = V − V_0 is the perturbation due to finite nuclear size, e is the elementary charge, Φ_0 is the 1s wavefunction for a point nucleus, ΔE is the ground-state energy shift, E_0 and E_1 are point-nucleus energy levels of the ground and first excited states, and E_X is the X-ray transition energy between these states. In the isotopic-multiplet method, M(Z,A) is the mass of a nucleus with proton number Z and mass number A, ΔE_e is the electromagnetic contribution to the mass difference, m_n and m_p are the neutron and proton masses, c is the speed of light, and R_0 is an empirical constant. All units, when shown, use \unit{}, e.g. \unit{fm} and \unit{cm}.

subquestions.subproblem: electron scattering,
subquestions.solution:
The measured quantity is the elastic nuclear form factor obtained from the ratio of differential cross sections
$$F(q^2)=\frac{(d\sigma)_{exp}}{(d\sigma)_{point}}$$
In the first Born approximation
$$F(q^2)=\int \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r} d^3 r$$
Assuming spherical symmetry ρ(r)=ρ(r) and small momentum transfer q\cdot r \ll 1, expand the exponential and keep terms to order q^2
$$F(q^2)\approx\int \rho(r)\bigl[1-\tfrac{1}{2}(q\cdot r)^2\bigr] d^3 r$$
Carrying out the angular average gives
$$F(q^2)=1-\frac{1}{6} q^2\langle r^2\rangle$$
with the mean square radius defined by
$$\langle r^2\rangle=\int \rho(r) r^2 d^3 r$$
By measuring the angular distribution of elastically scattered electrons one determines F(q^2), and by inversion obtains ρ(r) and hence the nuclear size.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of F(q^2) = ..., and your response should use only the symbols q and ⟨r^2⟩ on the right-hand side.

subquestions.subproblem: energy levels of muonic atoms, or
subquestions.solution:
The measured quantities are the transition energies between muonic-atom levels, which are highly sensitive to the finite nuclear radius because m_\mu \approx 210 m_ e and a_\mu \approx \frac{1}{210} a_0. For an s state the Hamiltonian is
$$H=-\frac{1}{2 m_\mu} \nabla^2+V(r)$$
For a pointlike nucleus
$$V_0(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
For a uniformly charged sphere of radius R, inside the nucleus one has
$$V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{2 R^3}\bigl(3 R^2-r^2\bigr)$$
for 0<r\le R, and outside the nucleus
$$V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
for r>R. The perturbation due to finite size is H′=V−V_0. Inside the nucleus
$$H'= -\frac{e^2}{2 R^3}\bigl(3 R^2-r^2\bigr)+\frac{e^2}{r}$$
for 0<r\le R, and outside the nucleus
$$H'=0$$
for r>R. The ground-state energy shift is
$$\Delta E=\langle \Phi_0\vert H'\vert \Phi_0\rangle$$
which gives
$$\Delta E=4\pi \int_0^R |\Phi_0|^2 H' r^2 dr$$
with the 1s wavefunction
$$\Phi_0=\bigl(\frac{1}{\pi a_\mu^3}\bigr)^{1/2} e^{-r/a_\mu}$$
Since R\sim 10^{-12} \unit{cm} and a_\mu\sim 10^{-10} \unit{cm}, we have
$$\frac{R}{a_\mu}\ll 1$$
and therefore
$$e^{-2 r/a_\mu}\approx 1-\frac{2 r}{a_\mu}$$
Keeping terms up to order (R/a_\mu)^2 yields
$$\Delta E=\frac{2}{5}\bigl(\frac{e^2}{2 a_\mu}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{R}{a_\mu}\bigr)^2$$
The X-ray energy for the transition from the first excited state to the ground state is then
$$E_X=(E_1-E_0)-\frac{2}{5}\bigl(\frac{e^2}{a_\mu}\bigr)\bigl(\frac{R}{a_\mu}\bigr)^2$$
where E_1 and E_0 are the point-nucleus energy levels of the first excited and ground states. Given E_X and E_1-E_0, the radius R can be deduced.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_X = ..., and your response should use only the symbols E_1, E_0, e, a_μ, and R on the right-hand side.

subquestions.subproblem: ground state energies of the isotopic spin multiplet . Discuss what physical quantities are measured in two and only two of these three experiments and how these quantities are related to the radius of the nucleus.
subquestions.solution:
For nuclei within the same isotopic spin multiplet, the strong-interaction structure is the same, so mass differences arise from electromagnetic interactions and the proton–neutron mass difference. Define the measured mass-energy difference
$$\Delta E=[M(Z,A)-M(Z-1,A)] c^2$$
This can be written as
$$\Delta E=\Delta E_e-(m_n-m_p) c^2$$
The electromagnetic contribution for a uniformly charged sphere of radius R is
$$\Delta E_e=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R}\bigl[Z^2-(Z-1)^2\bigr]$$
From these relations R is deduced. Empirically one finds
$$R\approx R_0 A^{1/3}$$
with
$$R_0=1.2-1.4 \unit{fm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present two equations: (1) ΔE = ΔE_e − (m_n − m_p) c^2, using only the symbols ΔE, ΔE_e, m_n, m_p, and c; and (2) ΔE_e = (3 e^2 / 5R)[Z^2 − (Z − 1)^2], using only the symbols ΔE_e, e, R, and Z.

context: Consider a deformed nucleus modeled as a uniformly charged, axially symmetric ellipsoid with semimajor axis a and semiminor axis b, where the long axis is 10\% longer than the short axis. Let the total nuclear charge be Q. Let the nuclear radius scale as R = r_0 A^{1/3} with r_0 = \frac{6}{5}\unit{fm}, and choose a representative mass number A \approx 125. Let the first Bohr radius be a_0 = 0.53 \times 10^{-8}\unit{cm}. Estimate the relative error in the electric potential V at distance r = a_0 if the nucleus is treated as a point charge. You may set a = (1 + \varepsilon) R and b = (1 - \varepsilon/2) R with small deformation parameter \varepsilon, and use the quadrupole correction V_q = M Q / r^3 with M = \frac{2}{5}(a^2 - b^2). Provide your final answer as the relative error \Delta V = V_q / V_p.
solution:
Assume the charge distribution in the nucleus is uniform, ellipsoidal, and axially symmetric, so the electric dipole moment vanishes and the potential can be written as

$$
V = V_p + V_q
$$

with the point-charge term

$$
V_p = \frac{Q}{r}
$$

and the quadrupole correction

$$
V_q = \frac{M Q}{r^3}
$$

Parameterize the semiaxes by

$$
a = (1 + \varepsilon) R
$$

$$
b = \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right) R
$$

The 10\% elongation implies, to first order in \varepsilon,

$$
\frac{3 \varepsilon}{2} = \frac{1}{10}
$$

so

$$
\varepsilon = \frac{1}{15}
$$

For a uniform ellipsoid, take the quadrupole parameter as

$$
M = \frac{2}{5} \left(a^2 - b^2\right)
$$

Substituting a and b and using \varepsilon = \frac{1}{15} gives

$$
M = \frac{61}{750} R^2
$$

For a representative medium nucleus, use

$$
R = r_0 A^{1/3}
$$

with

$$
r_0 = \frac{6}{5} \unit{fm}
$$

and

$$
A \approx 125
$$

so

$$
R = 6 \unit{fm}
$$

Converting to centimeters,

$$
1 \unit{fm} = 10^{-13} \unit{cm}
$$

$$
R = 6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}
$$

At the first Bohr radius,

$$
r = a_0
$$

$$
a_0 = 0.53 \times 10^{-8} \unit{cm}
$$

Define the relative correction

$$
\Delta V = \frac{V_q}{V_p}
$$

Then

$$
\Delta V = \frac{M}{r^2}
$$

and hence

$$
\Delta V = \frac{61}{750} \frac{R^2}{r^2}
$$

Numerically,

$$
\Delta V \approx \frac{61}{750} \left( \frac{6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}}{0.53 \times 10^{-8} \unit{cm}} \right)^2
$$

$$
\Delta V \approx 1 \times 10^{-9}
$$

Thus, the relative error in the potential if the nucleus is treated as a point charge is about 10^{-9} at the first Bohr orbit.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the relative error \Delta V = V_q / V_p at r = a_0 as a numerical value in scientific notation, computed using the given parameters (r_0, A, a_0, and the 10\% deformation). Report \Delta V to 1 significant figure.

context: A nucleus with nuclear g-factor g and mass m_N undergoes Larmor precession in the Earth's magnetic field B. In Gaussian-cgs units, the precession angular frequency is given by omega = g e B / (2 m_N c), where e is the elementary charge and c is the speed of light. Use the order-of-magnitude values g = 1, e = 4.8 × 10^{-10} esu, c = 3 × 10^{10} cm/s, B ≈ 0.5 Gs, and m_N ≈ 10^{-23} g for a light nucleus. Estimate omega and select the closest option among 10^{-1}, 10^{1}, 10^{3}, 10^{5} s^{-1}. State the final answer as omega in s^{-1}.
solution:
The precession angular frequency is
$$
\omega = \frac{g e B}{2 m_N c}
$$
Given
$$
g = 1
$$
$$
e = 4.8 \times 10^{-10} \unit{esu}
$$
$$
c = 3 \times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s}
$$
$$
B = 0.5 \unit{Gs}
$$
$$
m_N = 10^{-23} \unit{g}
$$
Substituting values gives
$$
\omega = \frac{4.8 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 10^{-23} \times 3 \times 10^{10}} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Evaluating the powers and numerical factors yields
$$
\omega = 0.4 \times 10^{3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Thus, the closest option is
$$
\omega = 10^{3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express omega as a numerical value in s^{-1}. Use 1 significant figure.

context: Assume Gaussian (cgs) units with 1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)=1, so the electric-field energy density is E^2/(8\pi). Let Q be the total charge uniformly distributed throughout a solid sphere of radius R. Let r be the distance from the center, E(r) the magnitude of the electric field at radius r, and W the electrostatic self-energy obtained by integrating the field energy density over all space with volume element d\tau. In part (b), treat the mirror nuclei {}^{27}_{14}Si and {}^{27}_{13}Al as uniformly charged spheres of the same radius R; let Z_1=14 and Z_2=13 be their proton numbers, \Delta W the difference of their ground-state masses expressed as energy, e the elementary charge, \hbar the reduced Planck constant, c the speed of light, and \alpha=e^2/(\hbar c) the fine-structure constant. Give the final numerical radius R in femtometers (\unit{fm}).

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the electrostatic energy of a charge Q distributed uniformly throughout a sphere of radius R.
subquestions.solution:
For 0 \le r < R, the electric field is
$$E(r)=\frac{Q r}{R^3}$$

For r \ge R, the electric field is
$$E(r)=\frac{Q}{r^2}$$

The electrostatic energy is
$$W=\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{8\pi} E^2 d\tau$$

With spherical symmetry, the volume element is
$$d\tau=4\pi r^2 dr$$

Substituting the field and volume element gives
$$W=\frac{1}{8\pi} \Big[ \int_0^R \frac{Q^2 r^2}{R^6} 4\pi r^2 dr + \int_R^\infty \frac{Q^2}{r^4} 4\pi r^2 dr \Big]$$

Factoring constants yields
$$W=\frac{Q^2}{2} \Big[ \int_0^R \frac{r^4}{R^6} dr + \int_R^\infty \frac{dr}{r^2} \Big]$$

The first integral evaluates to
$$\int_0^R \frac{r^4}{R^6} dr=\frac{1}{5R}$$

The second integral evaluates to
$$\int_R^\infty \frac{dr}{r^2}=\frac{1}{R}$$

Therefore
$$W=\frac{Q^2}{2} \Big[ \frac{1}{5R}+\frac{1}{R} \Big]$$

Hence
$$W=\frac{3 Q^2}{5 R}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of W = ... and your response should be written using only the variables Q and R.

subquestions.subproblem: Since {}^{27}_{14}Si and {}^{27}_{13}Al are mirror nuclei, their ground states are identical except for charge. If their mass difference is 6 MeV, estimate their radius (neglecting the proton–neutron mass difference).
subquestions.solution:
The mass–energy difference equals the difference in Coulomb self-energies
$$\Delta W=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R} \big( Z_1^2 - Z_2^2 \big)$$

Solving for the radius gives
$$R=\frac{3 e^2 \big( Z_1^2 - Z_2^2 \big)}{5 \Delta W}$$

Using
$$e^2=\alpha \hbar c$$

We obtain
$$R=\frac{3 \alpha \hbar c \big( Z_1^2 - Z_2^2 \big)}{5 \Delta W}$$

With Z_1=14, Z_2=13, \alpha=\frac{1}{137}, \hbar c\approx 197 \unit{MeV\,fm}, and \Delta W=6 \unit{MeV},
$$R\approx \frac{3 \times 197 \times \big(14^2-13^2\big)}{5 \times 6 \times 137} \unit{fm}$$

Since 14^2-13^2=27,
$$R\approx \frac{3 \times 197 \times 27}{5 \times 6 \times 137} \unit{fm}$$

Numerically,
$$R\approx 3.88 \unit{fm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the nuclear radius R as a numerical value in femtometers (fm). Report your result to 3 significant figures.

context: The nucleus ^{27}_{14}Si decays to its mirror nucleus ^{27}_{13}Al by positron emission. The decay is ^{27}_{14}Si -> ^{27}_{13}Al + beta^+ + nu, where beta^+ denotes the positron and nu denotes the neutrino. The maximum total positron energy E_{pos,max}, defined as kinetic energy plus m_e c^2, is 3.48 MeV. Neglect the recoil energy of the daughter nucleus. Assume that the mass-energy difference between the initial and final nuclei is entirely due to the Coulomb energy. Model each nucleus as a uniformly charged sphere with total charge Z e and radius R, where Z is the atomic number and e is the elementary charge. Assume the nuclear radius satisfies R = r_0 A^{1/3}, where A is the mass number and r_0 is a constant to be estimated. Let m_e be the electron mass, c the speed of light, and hbar the reduced Planck constant. Define E_e as the Coulomb energy difference between the two nuclei, computed from the uniform-sphere model. For numerical evaluation, use e^2 = hbar c / 137 and hbar c = 197 \unit{MeV fm}.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express r_0, in units of fm, as a numerical value rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: Given the binding energies B(^{90}Zr)=783.916\unit{MeV} and B(^{90}Y)=782.410\unit{MeV}, estimate the excitation energy E_{exc} of the lowest T'=6 isospin state in ^{90}Zr. Use the Coulomb displacement energy between isobaric analog states and the neutron–proton mass difference. Take A=90 for both nuclei, Z=39 for ^{90}Y, and the nuclear radius R=1.2 A^{1/3}\unit{fm}. Constants and symbols: e is the elementary charge, \alpha is the fine-structure constant, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, c is the speed of light, m_n and m_p are the neutron and proton masses, and B denotes nuclear binding energy.
solution:
For isobaric analog states, define the displacement energy

$$
\Delta E = E(A,Z+1) - E(A,Z)
$$

The displacement energy is given by the Coulomb contribution minus the neutron–proton mass term

$$
\Delta E = \Delta E_e - (m_n - m_p) c^2
$$

The Coulomb term for a uniformly charged sphere is

$$
\Delta E_e = \frac{3 e^2}{5 R} (2 Z + 1)
$$

Using e^2 = \alpha \hbar c, this becomes

$$
\Delta E = \frac{3 (2 Z + 1) \alpha \hbar c}{5 R} - 0.78\unit{MeV}
$$

Substitute the numerical inputs

$$
A = 90
$$

$$
Z = 39
$$

$$
R = 1.2 A^{1/3} \unit{fm}
$$

$$
\hbar c = 197 \unit{MeV.fm}
$$

$$
\alpha = \frac{1}{137}
$$

Evaluate the displacement energy

$$
\Delta E = 11.89 \unit{MeV}
$$

The excitation energy of the T'=6 state in ^{90}Zr is

$$
E_{exc} = - B(^{90}Y) + \Delta E + B(^{90}Zr)
$$

Insert the given binding energies

$$
E_{exc} = -782.410 \unit{MeV} + 11.89 \unit{MeV} + 783.916 \unit{MeV}
$$

Compute the result

$$
E_{exc} = 13.40 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the excitation energy E_{exc} as a numerical value in MeV, formatted as 'E_{exc} = ... MeV'. Use the specified number of significant figures.

context: The masses of a set of isobars (nuclei with the same mass number) that are members of the same isospin multiplet can be written as the expectation value of a mass operator of the form $$M=a+b T_z+c T_z^2$$ where a, b, c are constants and T_z is the operator for the z component of the total isospin T. Let A be the mass number, Z the proton number, N the neutron number, e the elementary charge, R the nuclear charge radius, m_p the proton mass, m_n the neutron mass, and M_0 the isospin-symmetric contribution common to the multiplet. The spin-parity quantum number is denoted by J^p. In part (b), let n denote the number of members in a given isospin multiplet, and let T_min denote the minimal isospin required to test the mass formula experimentally.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive this formula.
subquestions.solution: Members of the same isospin multiplet have the same spin-parity J^p due to their similar structure. Their mass differences are determined by the Coulomb energy and the neutron-proton mass difference. Define the standard isospin relations $$A=Z+N$$ $$T_z=\frac{Z-N}{2}$$ which imply $$Z=\frac{A}{2}+T_z$$ For a uniformly charged sphere, the Coulomb self-energy is $$E_C=\frac{3 e^2 Z^2}{5 R}$$ Including the neutron-proton mass difference and an isospin-symmetric term M_0, the nuclear mass can be written as $$M=\frac{3 e^2 Z^2}{5 R}+(m_p-m_n) T_z+M_0$$ Introduce the constants $$B=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R}$$ $$C=m_p-m_n$$ and substitute Z= A/2+T_z to obtain $$M=B \left(\frac{A}{2}+T_z\right)^2+C T_z+M_0$$ Expanding gives $$M=\frac{B A^2}{4}+B A T_z+B T_z^2+C T_z+M_0$$ Grouping terms yields $$M=a+b T_z+c T_z^2$$ where $$a=M_0+\frac{B A^2}{4}$$ $$b=C+B A$$ $$c=B$$ The linear terms arise from the neutron-proton mass difference and the Coulomb energy, while the quadratic term is mainly due to the Coulomb energy
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form M = a + b T_z + c T_z^2, and you must also state a, b, and c explicitly in terms of the variables A, e, R, m_p, m_n, and M_0 only. Do not introduce any new symbols.

subquestions.subproblem: How large must the isospin be in order to test it experimentally?
subquestions.solution: There are three constants a, b, c in the formula, so three independent mass values within the same isospin multiplet are required. The number of members in a multiplet is $$n=2 T+1$$ To determine a, b, c we need $$n\ge 3$$ which implies $$T\ge 1$$ Therefore, the minimal isospin required is $$T_{min}=1$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T_min as a numerical value.

context:
Both nuclei ^{14}_7 N and ^{12}_6 C have ground-state isospin T=0. The lowest T=1 state has an excitation energy E_exc(^{14}N)=2.3 \unit{MeV} in ^{14}_7 N and E_exc(^{12}C)\approx 15.0 \unit{MeV} in ^{12}_6 C. Explain why there is such a marked difference. Also indicate the basis on which an isospin value T is ascribed to such nuclear states by considering the other members of the T=1 isospin triplets and explaining their relationships via systematic nuclear properties. Definitions and conventions used below (all symbols appear in the solution): - T is the total isospin and T_3 is its third component with T_3=(Z-N)/2 for a nucleus with proton number Z and neutron number N - For a fixed mass number A, an isospin T=1 triplet has members with T_3=+1, 0, -1, corresponding to three isobars differing by one unit in Z - M(Z,A) denotes the nuclear mass of the nuclide with proton number Z and mass number A - The mass excess is \Delta=M-A, tabulated in \unit{MeV/c^2} for the nuclides used below - The excitation energy of the lowest T=1 state in nucleus X is defined as E_exc(X)=[M(X,T=1)-M(X,T=0)] c^2 and should be reported in \unit{MeV} - The Coulomb displacement energy between neighboring isobars is defined as \Delta E=[M(Z,A)-M(Z-1,A)] c^2 and is estimated in \unit{MeV} - The nuclear radius is R=R_0 A^{1/3}, with R_0 the radius parameter - e is the elementary charge, h is Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light, m_n and m_p are the neutron and proton masses, and \alpha=\frac{e^2}{h c}=\frac{1}{137} - h c=197 \unit{MeV fm} - J^p denotes the spin-parity quantum numbers of the state - An asterisk, as in ^{A}Z^*, denotes an excited isobaric analog state of the same A Final answers should be written as E_exc(^{14}N) and E_exc(^{12}C), in \unit{MeV}. The following mass-excess values \Delta=M-A (in \unit{MeV/c^2}) are used:
Nuclide\Delta = M - A (MeV/c^2)
^{12}_5 B13.370
^{14}_7 N2.864
^{12}_6 C3.020
solution:
The T=1 excited states in the A=12 isobars form an isospin triplet consisting of ^{12}_5 B, ^{12}_6 C, and ^{12}_7 N. The members ^{12}_5 B and ^{12}_7 N have |T_3|=1 and are ground states of the triplet, while the T=1 state in ^{12}_6 C appears as an excited state. Likewise, for A=14, the T=1 triplet consists of ^{14}_6 C, ^{14}_7 N, and ^{14}_8 O, with ^{14}_6 C and ^{14}_8 O the ground states and the T=1 state appearing as an excited state in ^{14}_7 N.

The Coulomb displacement energy between neighboring members of an isospin multiplet is estimated by

$$\Delta E=[M(Z,A)-M(Z-1,A)] c^2$$

Using a uniform-charge-sphere Coulomb energy and the neutron-proton mass difference, this is approximated by

$$\Delta E=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R} (2 Z-1)-(m_n-m_p) c^2$$

With R=R_0 A^{1/3}, this becomes

$$\Delta E=\frac{3 e^2}{5 R_0 A^{1/3}} (2 Z-1)-0.78 \unit{MeV}$$

Introducing h c and the fine-structure constant \alpha=\frac{e^2}{h c}, we obtain

$$\Delta E=\frac{3 h c}{5 R_0 A^{1/3}} \frac{e^2}{h c} (2 Z-1)-0.78 \unit{MeV}$$

Using h c=197 \unit{MeV fm} and \alpha=\frac{1}{137}, this yields

$$\Delta E=\frac{3 \times 197}{5 \times 137 R_0 A^{1/3}} (2 Z-1) \unit{MeV}-0.78 \unit{MeV}$$

Taking

$$R_0 \approx 1.4 \unit{fm}$$

we estimate the mass differences between neighboring members in the triplets as

$$M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}C,T=1)=2.5 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

$$M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}B,T=1)=2.2 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

For A=14, the excitation energy of the T=1 state in ^{14}_7 N relative to its T=0 ground state is obtained by adding and subtracting analog masses within the triplet:

$$M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}N,T=0)=M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}C,T=1)+M(^{14}C,T=1)-M(^{14}N,T=0)$$

$$M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}N,T=0)=2.5 \unit{MeV/c^2}+3.02 \unit{MeV/c^2}-2.86 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

$$M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}N,T=0)=2.66 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

Therefore

$$E_{exc}(^{14}N)=[M(^{14}N,T=1)-M(^{14}N,T=0)] c^2$$

$$E_{exc}(^{14}N)=2.66 \unit{MeV}$$

For A=12, the excitation energy of the T=1 state in ^{12}_6 C is similarly

$$M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}C,T=0)=M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}B,T=1)+M(^{12}B,T=1)-M(^{12}C,T=0)$$

$$M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}C,T=0)=2.2 \unit{MeV/c^2}+13.37 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

$$M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}C,T=0)=15.5 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

Therefore

$$E_{exc}(^{12}C)=[M(^{12}C,T=1)-M(^{12}C,T=0)] c^2$$

$$E_{exc}(^{12}C)=15.5 \unit{MeV}$$

These are in agreement with the experimental excitation energies E_{exc}(^{14}N)=2.3 \unit{MeV} and E_{exc}(^{12}C)=15.0 \unit{MeV}. The large difference between the excitation energies in ^{12}C and ^{14}N is attributed to the pronounced alpha-cluster structure in the ^{12}C ground state, which lowers its T=0 ground-state energy relative to the isobaric analog.

Basis for isospin assignment: Members of an isospin multiplet have similar intrinsic structure and identical J^p. The mass differences within a multiplet are governed by Coulomb energies and the neutron-proton mass difference. Agreement of observed excitation energies and J^p with the systematic Coulomb displacement energies across the isobars provides the basis for assigning T. For example, ^{14}O, ^{14}N^*, and ^{14}C form a T=1 triplet with J^p=0^+, where ^{14}C and ^{14}O are ground states and ^{14}N^* is the excited isobaric analog state. Similarly, ^{12}C^*, ^{12}C, and ^{12}B form a T=1 multiplet with J^p=1^+, where ^{12}B and ^{12}N are ground-state analogs and ^{12}C^* is the excited analog in the central isobar.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two parts: (1) Express E_exc(^{14}N) and E_exc(^{12}C) as numerical values in MeV, reported exactly in the format: E_exc(^{14}N)=..., E_exc(^{12}C)=.... Use 3 significant figures; (2) After the numbers, provide exactly two sentences: one briefly explaining the reason for the marked difference between these excitation energies, and one stating the basis for assigning the isospin value T by referring to the structure of the T=1 isospin triplets and their systematic nuclear properties.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta E=\frac{3 h c}{5 R_0 A^{1/3}} \frac{e^2}{h c} (2 Z-1)-0.78 \unit{MeV}$$

context: Isospin structure of magnetic dipole moment. The magnetic dipole moments of the free neutron and free proton are -1.913 \unit{\mu_N} and +2.793 \unit{\mu_N} respectively. Define \mu_n and \mu_p as the magnetic moments of the free neutron and free proton in units of \unit{\mu_N}. Consider a nucleus with nucleon number A, treated as a collection of neutrons and protons having their free moments. Throughout, all magnetic moments and operators are expressed in units of \unit{\mu_N}. For the i-th nucleon, let g_l^{(i)} and g_s^{(i)} denote the orbital and spin g-factors, l_i and S_i the orbital and spin angular momentum operators, and \sigma_i the Pauli spin operator with S_i = \frac{1}{2} \sigma_i. The total nuclear angular momentum operator is J = \sum_{i=1}^{A} ( l^{i} + S^{i} ), with projection J_z. For mirror nuclei, denote the operators in nucleus 1 by l_1^{i}, S_1^{i} and in nucleus 2 by l_2^{i}, S_2^{i}, with corresponding z components l_{1z}^{i}, S_{1z}^{i}, l_{2z}^{i}, S_{2z}^{i}. The magnetic moment operator is \mu, and for nucleus k we denote it by \mu_k. Expectation values are taken in the relevant nuclear states, with \mu = \langle \mu_z \rangle. Introduce isospin T with third component T_z. Let \tau_j be the Pauli matrices in isospin space, define T_j = \frac{1}{2} \tau_j, and \tau_\pm = \tau_1 \pm i \tau_2. The proton and neutron isospin wavefunctions are \psi_p and \psi_n, respectively, with T_3 \psi_p = \frac{1}{2} \psi_p and T_3 \psi_n = -\frac{1}{2} \psi_n, and T_+ \psi_n = \psi_p, T_- \psi_p = \psi_n. Mirror nuclei have the same T but opposite T_z. Let \sigma_z^{(i)} denote the z component of the Pauli spin operator for nucleon i.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the magnetic moment operator for a nucleus of A nucleons.
subquestions.solution:
The magnetic moment operator for a nucleus of A nucleons is
$$\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( g_l^{(i)} l_i + g_s^{(i)} S_i \big)$$
For neutrons
$$g_l = 0$$
$$g_s = 2 \mu_n$$
For protons
$$g_l = 1$$
$$g_s = 2 \mu_p$$
The spin operator is related to the Pauli matrices by
$$S_i = \frac{1}{2} \sigma_i$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form μ = ∑_{i=1}^{A} ( g_l^{(i)} l_i + g_s^{(i)} S_i ). Your response should be written using only the symbols μ, A, g_l^{(i)}, g_s^{(i)}, l_i, S_i.

subquestions.subproblem: Introduce the concept of isospin and determine the isoscalar and isovector operators. What are their relative sizes?
subquestions.solution:
If Coulomb forces are ignored, charge independence implies that the p-p, p-n, and n-n forces are identical when the pair of nucleons are in the same spin and orbital states. Introduce isospin T with third component
$$T_z(p) = \frac{1}{2}$$
$$T_z(n) = -\frac{1}{2}$$
Let the proton and neutron isospin wavefunctions be
$$\psi_p = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\psi_n = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$
Define
$$T_j = \frac{1}{2} \tau_j$$
$$\tau_\pm = \tau_1 \pm i \tau_2$$
Their actions are
$$T_3 \psi_p = \frac{1}{2} \psi_p$$
$$T_3 \psi_n = -\frac{1}{2} \psi_n$$
$$T_+ \psi_n = \psi_p$$
$$T_- \psi_p = \psi_n$$
The isoscalar and isovector one-body operators in isospin space are
$$O_S = I$$
$$O_{V,j} = \tau_j$$
For the magnetic moment operator the isospin decomposition of the g-factors is
$$g_l = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \tau_3$$
$$g_s = ( \mu_p + \mu_n ) + ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) \tau_3$$
Thus the magnetic moment operator decomposes as
$$\mu = \mu^{(S)} + \mu^{(V)}$$
with
$$\mu^{(S)} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( l_i + S_i \big) + \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \sum_{i=1}^{A} S_i$$
$$\mu^{(V)} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)} \big[ l_i + 2 ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) S_i \big]$$
The relative sizes are governed by
$$| \mu_p - \mu_n | \approx 4.706$$
$$| \mu_p + \mu_n | \approx 0.880$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide: (i) the isoscalar one-body operator O_S = I and the isovector one-body operator O_{V,j} = τ_j in isospin space; and (ii) the isospin decomposition of the magnetic-moment g-factors written as g_l = 1/2 + 1/2 τ_3 and g_s = ( μ_p + μ_n ) + ( μ_p − μ_n ) τ_3. Additionally, express the relative sizes symbolically by giving the two magnitudes |μ_p − μ_n| and |μ_p + μ_n| without numerical evaluation. Use only the symbols O_S, O_{V,j}, I, τ_j, τ_3, μ_p, μ_n, g_l, g_s.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that the sum of magnetic moments in nuclear magnetons of two T = 1/2 mirror nuclei is J + ( \mu_p + \mu_n - 1/2 ) \langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} \sigma_z^{(i)} \rangle, where J is the total nuclear spin and \sigma_z^{(i)} is the Pauli spin operator for a nucleon.
subquestions.solution:
Mirror nuclei are obtained by interchanging protons and neutrons, so they have the same T but opposite T_z. For nucleus 1, the magnetic moment operator is
$$\mu_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( g_l^{(i)} l_1^{i} + g_s^{(i)} S_1^{i} \big)$$
Using
$$g_l = \frac{1}{2} ( 1 + \tau_3 )$$
$$g_s = ( 1 + \tau_3 ) \mu_p + ( 1 - \tau_3 ) \mu_n$$
we obtain
$$\mu_1 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( l_1^{i} + S_1^{i} \big) + \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \sum_{i=1}^{A} S_1^{i} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)} \big[ l_1^{i} + 2 ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) S_1^{i} \big]$$
Similarly for the mirror nucleus 2
$$\mu_2 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( l_2^{i} + S_2^{i} \big) + \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \sum_{i=1}^{A} S_2^{i} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)} \big[ l_2^{i} + 2 ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) S_2^{i} \big]$$
Define
$$J = \sum_{i=1}^{A} \big( l^{i} + S^{i} \big)$$
$$T_3 = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)}$$
$$S_i = \frac{1}{2} \sigma_i$$
The observed magnetic moment is
$$\mu = \langle \mu_z \rangle$$
For nucleus 1 this gives
$$\mu_1 = \frac{J_z}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} ( \sigma_1^{i} )_z \big\rangle + \frac{1}{2} \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)} \big[ l_{1z}^{i} + 2 ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) S_{1z}^{i} \big] \big\rangle$$
For nucleus 2 this gives
$$\mu_2 = \frac{J_z}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} ( \sigma_2^{i} )_z \big\rangle + \frac{1}{2} \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} \tau_3^{(i)} \big[ l_{2z}^{i} + 2 ( \mu_p - \mu_n ) S_{2z}^{i} \big] \big\rangle$$
Adding the two mirror nuclei and using that J is the same while T_3 changes sign, the last terms cancel and
$$\mu_1 + \mu_2 = J_z + \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} \sigma_z^{(i)} \big\rangle$$
For stretched states with J_z = J this becomes
$$\mu_1 + \mu_2 = J + \big( \mu_p + \mu_n - \frac{1}{2} \big) \big\langle \sum_{i=1}^{A} \sigma_z^{(i)} \big\rangle$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form μ_1 + μ_2 = J + ( μ_p + μ_n − 1/2 ) ⟨ ∑_{i=1}^{A} σ_z^{(i)} ⟩. Your response should be written using only the symbols μ_1, μ_2, J, μ_p, μ_n, σ_z^{(i)}, A.

context: Hard sphere scattering. Consider classical elastic scattering of point particles from an infinitely massive, fixed sphere of radius R. Particles approach along the -z direction. Let theta be the polar angle of the surface point of contact (measured from the +z axis). Let alpha be the scattering (deflection) angle between the incident and emergent directions. Let b be the impact parameter, defined as the perpendicular distance from the incident trajectory to the sphere's center. Let dσ/dΩ denote the differential scattering cross section, with dσ = 2 pi b db the area element in impact-parameter space and dΩ = 2 pi sin alpha d alpha the azimuthally averaged solid-angle element. Show that dσ/dΩ is independent of alpha, i.e., the scattering is isotropic.
solution:
In classical specular reflection from a hard, fixed surface, the emergent angle equals the incident angle, so the deflection angle satisfies
$$
\alpha = 2\theta
$$
The impact parameter is related to the surface polar angle by
$$
 b = R \sin \theta
$$
The azimuthally averaged elements are
$$
 d\sigma = 2 \pi b db
$$
$$
 d\Omega = 2 \pi \sin \alpha d\alpha
$$
Using b = R \sin \theta, we have
$$
 db = R \cos \theta d\theta
$$
From \alpha = 2\theta, we have
$$
 d\alpha = 2 d\theta
$$
Also
$$
 \sin \alpha = 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta
$$
Therefore
$$
 \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \frac{2 \pi b db}{2 \pi \sin \alpha d\alpha}
$$
Substituting the relations above yields
$$
 \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \frac{R^2}{4}
$$
which is independent of \alpha (and \theta), so the scattering is isotropic.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of dσ/dΩ = ..., and your response should be written with R only, where R is the sphere's radius.

context: Neutron–nucleus elastic scattering at center-of-mass kinetic energy E = 5 MeV is considered. The partial-wave phase shifts are denoted by δ_l, with δ_0 = 30° and δ_1 = 10°, and all higher shifts δ_2, δ_3, … are negligible. The scattering angle is θ. The Legendre polynomials are P_l(cos θ). The incident neutron wave number in the center-of-mass frame is k, with k^2 ≈ 2 m_n E / ℏ^2 under the assumption that the target nucleus mass is much larger than the neutron mass m_n, so that the center-of-mass and laboratory frames coincide for k. We take m_n c^2 ≈ 938 MeV and ℏ c ≈ 197 MeV fm. The differential cross section is dσ/dΩ and the total cross section is σ. In part b, the potential is V(r), J_l denotes the spherical Bessel function of order l, and R is the effective range of the potential. Units are written with \unit{ } and angles are in degrees. When reporting final numerical cross sections, use \unit{cm^2} and \unit{b}, where 1 b = 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}.

subquestions.subproblem: At a center-of-mass energy of 5 MeV, the phase describing the elastic scattering of a neutron by a certain nucleus has the following values: δ_0 = 30°, δ_1 = 10°. Assuming all other phase shifts to be negligible, plot dσ/dΩ as a function of scattering angle θ. Explicitly calculate dσ/dΩ at θ = 30°, 45°, and 90°. What is the total cross section σ?
subquestions.solution:
The differential cross section is
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = \frac{1}{k^2} \bigg\vert \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (2l+1) e^{i\delta_l} \sin \delta_l P_l(\cos \theta) \bigg\vert^2$$
Keeping only l = 0 and l = 1 gives
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \approx \frac{1}{k^2} \big\vert e^{i\delta_0} \sin \delta_0 + 3 e^{i\delta_1} \sin \delta_1 \cos \theta \big\vert^2$$
Expanding the magnitude yields
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \approx \frac{1}{k^2} \big[ \sin^2 \delta_0 + 9 \sin^2 \delta_1 \cos^2 \theta + 6 \sin \delta_0 \sin \delta_1 \cos(\delta_1 - \delta_0) \cos \theta \big]$$
Using δ_0 = 30° and δ_1 = 10° gives the numerical form
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \approx \frac{1}{k^2} \big[ \tfrac{1}{4} + 0.27 \cos^2 \theta + 0.49 \cos \theta \big]$$
The wave number k is
$$k^2 \approx \frac{2 m_n E}{\hbar^2}$$
Equivalently
$$k^2 \approx \frac{2 m_n c^2 E}{(\hbar c)^2}$$
Numerically
$$k^2 \approx 2.4 \times 10^{25} \unit{cm^{-2}}$$
Define the dimensionless quantity D(\theta) by D(\theta) = k^2 \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}. Then
$$D(\theta) \approx \tfrac{1}{4} + 0.27 \cos^2 \theta + 0.49 \cos \theta$$
At θ = 30°
$$D(30^\circ) \approx 0.88$$
Thus
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=30^\circ} \approx \frac{0.88}{k^2}$$
Numerically
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=30^\circ} \approx 3.7 \times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^2}$$
At θ = 45°
$$D(45^\circ) \approx 0.73$$
Thus
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=45^\circ} \approx \frac{0.73}{k^2}$$
Numerically
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=45^\circ} \approx 3.0 \times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^2}$$
At θ = 90°
$$D(90^\circ) \approx \tfrac{1}{4}$$
Thus
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=90^\circ} \approx \frac{\tfrac{1}{4}}{k^2}$$
Numerically
$$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\bigg\rvert_{\theta=90^\circ} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^2}$$
The angular distribution can be plotted from the expression for dσ/dΩ as a function of θ above. The total cross section is
$$\sigma = \int \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} d\Omega$$
Using the truncated form gives
$$\sigma = \frac{2\pi}{k^2} \int_0^{\pi} \big[ \tfrac{1}{4} + 0.49 \cos \theta + 0.27 \cos^2 \theta \big] \sin \theta d\theta$$
Evaluating the integral yields
$$\sigma = \frac{4\pi}{k^2} \bigg( \tfrac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3} \cdot 0.27 \bigg)$$
Numerically
$$\sigma \approx 1.78 \times 10^{-25} \unit{cm^2}$$
In barns
$$\sigma \approx 0.18 \unit{b}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (1) a plot of dσ/dΩ versus θ for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 180°, with θ in degrees on the horizontal axis and dσ/dΩ in cm^2/sr on the vertical axis; (2) numerical values of dσ/dΩ at θ = 30°, 45°, and 90°, each expressed in cm^2/sr; and (3) the total cross section σ expressed as numerical values in both cm^2 and barns (b). Round each dσ/dΩ value to 2 significant figures, round σ (in cm^2) to 3 significant figures, and round σ (in b) to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: What does the fact that all of the phase shifts δ_2, δ_3, … are negligible imply about the range R of the potential V(r)? Be as quantitative as you can.
subquestions.solution:
For weak or short-range potentials, the phase shift can be estimated by
$$\delta_l \approx - \frac{2 m_n k}{\hbar^2} \int_0^{\infty} V(r) J_l^2(kr) r^2 dr$$
Here J_l is the spherical Bessel function of order l. Since J_l(x) is appreciable mainly near x \approx l, higher-l contributions are suppressed unless the potential extends to radii where kr \gtrsim l. Negligible δ_2, δ_3, … thus imply a range on the order of
$$R \approx \frac{1}{k}$$
Using the k from part (a)
$$R \approx (2.4 \times 10^{25})^{-1/2} \unit{cm}$$
Numerically
$$R \approx 2 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}$$
In femtometers
$$R \approx 2 \unit{fm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the potential range R as a numerical value in femtometers (fm). Round to 1 significant figure.

grading_standard.formula: $$\delta_l \approx - \frac{2 m_n k}{\hbar^2} \int_0^{\infty} V(r) J_l^2(kr) r^2 dr$$

context: Neutrons with kinetic energy E = 1000 eV are incident on a carbon target. The inelastic scattering cross section is σ_in = 400 × 10^{-24} cm^2. At this energy, assume only s-wave scattering contributes. Define the s-wave phase shift δ and the s-wave S-matrix element S = e^{2 i δ}. Let m_n be the neutron mass, m_c the carbon nucleus mass, and μ = m_n m_c / (m_c + m_n) the reduced mass. Let k be the center-of-mass wave number and λ = 1/k the corresponding reduced wavelength. Use ħ for the reduced Planck constant and c for the speed of light. Take m_c ≈ 12 m_n, ħ c = 197 MeV fm, and m_n c^2 = 940 MeV. Find upper and lower limits on the elastic scattering cross section σ_e.
solution:
At E = 1000 \unit{eV}, only s-wave scattering is involved, and an inelastic process requires Im δ > 0

$$
\sigma_e = \pi \lambda^2 | e^{2 i \delta} - 1 |^2
$$

$$
\sigma_{in} = \pi \lambda^2 \bigl(1 - | e^{2 i \delta} |^2 \bigr)
$$

$$
\mu = \frac{m_n m_c}{m_c + m_n}
$$

$$
\mu \approx \frac{12}{13} m_n
$$

$$
\lambda = \frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2 \mu E}}
$$

$$
\lambda = \frac{\hbar c}{\sqrt{2 \mu c^2 E}}
$$

$$
\hbar c = 197 \unit{MeV\,fm}
$$

$$
 m_n c^2 = 940 \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
E = 10^{-3} \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
\lambda = \frac{197}{\sqrt{2 \times \frac{12}{13} \times 940 \times 10^{-3}}} \unit{fm}
$$

$$
\lambda = 150 \unit{fm}
$$

$$
\pi \lambda^2 = 707 \times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
\sigma_{in} = 400 \times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
1 - | e^{2 i \delta} |^2 = \frac{\sigma_{in}}{\pi \lambda^2}
$$

$$
1 - | e^{2 i \delta} |^2 = \frac{400}{707}
$$

$$
| e^{2 i \delta} | = \sqrt{1 - 0.566}
$$

$$
| e^{2 i \delta} | = 0.659
$$

To obtain bounds on | e^{2 i \delta} - 1 | at fixed | e^{2 i \delta} |, take e^{2 i \delta} = \pm 0.659

$$
\sigma_e = \pi \lambda^2 | e^{2 i \delta} - 1 |^2
$$

$$
\sigma_{e,\max} = 707 \times 10^{-24} \bigl(-0.659 - 1\bigr)^2 \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
\sigma_{e,\max} = 1946 \times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
\sigma_{e,\min} = 707 \times 10^{-24} \bigl(0.659 - 1\bigr)^2 \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
\sigma_{e,\min} = 82 \times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express σ_{e,max} and σ_{e,min} as numerical values in cm^2. Report both values to three significant figures.

context: The study of the scattering of high energy electrons from nuclei has yielded much interesting information about the charge distributions in nuclei and nucleons. We shall here consider a simple version in which the electrons are supposed to have zero spin. We also assume that the nucleus, of charge Z e, remains fixed in space (i.e., its mass is assumed infinite). Let rho(x) denote the spherically symmetric, normalized charge distribution in the nucleus, so that ∫ rho(x) d^3 x = 1 and the physical charge density is Ze rho(x). Let f_c(p_i, p_f), where p_i is the initial and p_f the final momentum, be the scattering amplitude in the first Born approximation for the scattering of an electron from a point-nucleus of charge Z e. Let f(p_i, p_f) be the scattering amplitude of an electron from a real nucleus of the same charge. Let q = p_i - p_f denote the momentum transfer. The quantity F defined by f(p_i, p_f) = F(q^2) f_c(p_i, p_f) is called the form factor. It is easily seen that F, in fact, depends on p_i and p_f only through the quantity q^2. Symbols and definitions used below: m is the electron mass, e is the elementary charge, ħ is the reduced Planck constant, x and r are position vectors with r = |r| the radial coordinate, and θ is the angle between q and r.

subquestions.subproblem: The form factor F(q^2) and the Fourier transform of the charge density rho(x) are related in a very simple manner. State and derive this relationship within the framework of the nonrelativistic Schrödinger theory. The assumption that the electrons are nonrelativistic is here made so that the problem will be simplified. However, on careful consideration it will probably be clear that the assumption is irrelevant: the same result applies in the relativistic case of the actual experiment. It is also the case that the neglect of the electron spin does not affect the essence of what we are here concerned with.
subquestions.solution:
In the first Born approximation, the scattering amplitude of a high energy electron from a nucleus is
$$f(p_i,p_f)=-\frac{m}{2\pi \hbar^2}\int V(x)e^{i q\cdot x/\hbar} d^3 x$$
For a nucleus of spherically symmetric charge distribution, the potential at position x is
$$V(x)=\int \frac{\rho(r) Z e}{|x-r|} d^3 r$$
Thus
$$f(p_i,p_f)=-\frac{m}{2\pi \hbar^2}\int d^3 x\, e^{i q\cdot x/\hbar}\int d^3 r\, \frac{\rho(r) Z e}{|x-r|}$$
Reordering the integrations gives
$$f(p_i,p_f)=-\frac{m}{2\pi \hbar^2}\int d^3 r\, \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r/\hbar}\int d^3 x\, \frac{Z e}{|x-r|} e^{i q\cdot (x-r)/\hbar}$$
With the substitution x' = x - r, we obtain
$$f(p_i,p_f)=-\frac{m}{2\pi \hbar^2}\int d^3 r\, \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r/\hbar}\int d^3 x'\, \frac{Z e}{x'} e^{i q\cdot x'/\hbar}$$
For a point nucleus
$$V(x)=\frac{Z e}{x}$$
so that
$$f_c(p_i,p_f)=-\frac{m}{2\pi \hbar^2}\int \frac{Z e}{x} e^{i q\cdot x/\hbar} d^3 x$$
Comparing the two expressions yields
$$f(p_i,p_f)=f_c(p_i,p_f)\int d^3 r\, \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r/\hbar}$$
Hence the form factor is
$$F(q^2)=\int d^3 r\, \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r/\hbar}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be written in the form F(q^2) = ..., where the right-hand side is expressed as an explicit integral over d^3 r. Use only the symbols F, q, r, ρ, and ħ in your final expression.

subquestions.subproblem: Figure 2.3 shows some experimental results pertaining to the form factor for the proton, and we shall regard our theory as applicable to these data. On the basis of the data shown, compute the root-mean-square (charge) radius of the proton. Let r_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle r^2 \rangle} denote the root-mean-square charge radius. Hint: Note that there is a simple relationship between the root-mean-square radius and the derivative of F(q^2) with respect to q^2, at q^2 = 0. Find this relationship, and then compute. (UC, Berkeley)
subquestions.solution:
When q \approx 0,
$$F(q^2)=\int \rho(r) e^{i q\cdot r/\hbar} d^3 r$$
Using the small-q expansion,
$$F(q^2)\approx \int \rho(r)\left[1+\frac{i}{\hbar} q\cdot r-\frac{1}{2\hbar^2}(q\cdot r)^2\right] d^3 r$$
The linear term vanishes because
$$\frac{i}{\hbar}\int \rho(r) q\cdot r d^3 r=0$$
and
$$\int_0^{\pi} \cos\theta\sin\theta d\theta=0$$
Carrying out the angular integration gives
$$F(q^2)-F(0)=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\frac{q^2}{\hbar^2}\int r^4 \rho(r) dr$$
The mean-square radius is defined by
$$\langle r^2 \rangle=\int d^3 r\, \rho(r) r^2$$
and equivalently
$$\langle r^2 \rangle=4\pi\int \rho(r) r^4 dr$$
Hence
$$\langle r^2 \rangle=-6\hbar^2\frac{F(q^2)-F(0)}{q^2}$$
and
$$\langle r^2 \rangle=-6\hbar^2\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial q^2}\right)_{q^2=0}$$
From Fig. 2.3,
$$-\hbar^2\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial q^2}\right)_{q^2=0}\approx -\frac{0.8-1.0}{2-0}\times 10^{-26}\unit{cm^2}$$
Thus
$$-\hbar^2\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial q^2}\right)_{q^2=0}\approx 0.1\times 10^{-26}\unit{cm^2}$$
Hence
$$\langle r^2 \rangle=0.6\times 10^{-26}\unit{cm^2}$$
Define
$$r_{rms}=\sqrt{\langle r^2 \rangle}$$
Therefore
$$r_{rms}=0.77\times 10^{-13}\unit{cm}$$
and
$$r_{rms}=0.77\unit{fm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express r_rms as a numerical value in femtometers (fm), rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: When a proton beam with momentum p such that p c = 300 \unit{GeV} strikes a hydrogen target (see Fig. 2.4), model elastic scattering as diffraction from a circular object of radius r. Define h as Planck's constant, \hbar = h/(2\pi), c as the speed of light, and the de Broglie wavelength \lambda = h/p = 2\pi \hbar c/(p c). Let \theta_{min} denote the scattering angle of the first diffraction minimum in the small-angle approximation, defined by r \theta_{min} = \lambda/2. Use \hbar c \approx 0.197 \unit{GeV fm}. For a proton target, take r = 1.0 \unit{fm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}. For a lead (chemical symbol Pb) target with mass number A, use r = 1.1 A^{1/3} \unit{fm}. Tasks: (a) Compute \lambda and \theta_{min} for the hydrogen target at p c = 300 \unit{GeV}. (b) If the beam momentum is increased to p c = 600 \unit{GeV}, compute the new \theta_{min}. (c) For a lead target with A = 208 at p c = 300 \unit{GeV}, compute \theta_{min}. (d) For the same lead target and beam as in (c), compute the angle of the second minimum, defined by r \theta_{2,min} = 3\lambda/2. Define \theta_{2,min} as the scattering angle of the second diffraction minimum.
solution:
(a) The minimum in the elastic cross section arises from destructive interference of waves scattered at different impact parameters, which can be modeled as diffraction from an object of radius r. The de Broglie wavelength is
$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{p}
$$
$$
\lambda = \frac{2\pi \hbar c}{p c}
$$
Using \hbar c \approx 0.197 \unit{GeV fm} and p c = 300 \unit{GeV},
$$
\lambda = \frac{2\pi \times 0.197}{300} \unit{fm}
$$
With 1 \unit{fm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm},
$$
\lambda = 4.1 \times 10^{-16} \unit{cm}
$$
The first minimum condition is
$$
r \theta_{min} = \frac{\lambda}{2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\frac{\lambda}{2} = 2.1 \times 10^{-16} \unit{cm}
$$
With r = 1.0 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm},
$$
\theta_{min} = 2.1 \times 10^{-3} \unit{rad}
$$
(b) For p c = 600 \unit{GeV}, the wavelength halves, so the first minimum angle halves:
$$
\theta_{min} = 1.05 \times 10^{-3} \unit{rad}
$$
(c) For lead with A = 208,
$$
r = 1.1 A^{1/3} \unit{fm}
$$
Numerically,
$$
r \approx 6.5 \unit{fm}
$$
Using the same \lambda as in part (a) at p c = 300 \unit{GeV},
$$
\theta_{min} = \frac{\lambda/2}{r}
$$
$$
\theta_{min} = 3.2 \times 10^{-4} \unit{rad}
$$
(d) The second minimum occurs when the path difference is 3\lambda/2, so
$$
r \theta_{2,min} = \frac{3\lambda}{2}
$$
Thus,
$$
\theta_{2,min} = 3 \theta_{min}
$$
For the lead target of part (c),
$$
\theta_{2,min} = 9.6 \times 10^{-4} \unit{rad}
$$

context: Draw the qualitative curve of mean binding energy per nucleon as a function of nuclear mass number. Use values in \unit{MeV} as accurately as possible, and indicate the location of the maximum. From the form of this curve, explain why nuclear fission of a heavy nucleus releases energy and estimate the energy released per fission of uranium-235. Finally, state which force is principally responsible for the behavior of the curve in the upper mass region. Definitions and notation: Let A be the nuclear mass number, B the total nuclear binding energy, and b=B/A the mean binding energy per nucleon (measured in \unit{MeV/nucleon}). Let A_{max} denote the value of A at which b is maximal along the valley of stability. For the fission estimate, let A_U=235 for ^{235}U, let b_{parent} be the mean binding energy per nucleon of ^{235}U, and let b_{prod} be the mean binding energy per nucleon of the typical fission products (take two fragments near A\approx 117 as a representative case). Let E_{release} be the energy released per fission event, to be reported as E_{release}=\dots\unit{MeV}. The final answers should be written in the forms A_{max}=\dots and E_{release}=\dots\unit{MeV}.
solution:
Qualitative features of the curve b versus A: starting from light nuclei, b rises sharply for small A with noticeable fluctuations due to pairing and symmetry effects; once A exceeds a few tens, b exceeds about 8 \unit{MeV/nucleon} and then decreases slowly for heavier nuclei due to increasing Coulomb repulsion among protons. The maximum occurs in the iron–nickel region. The maximum location is reported as follows:

$$A_{max}=50$$

For medium and heavy nuclei the mean binding energy per nucleon exceeds approximately 8 \unit{MeV/nucleon} when A>30:

$$b>8\unit{MeV/nucleon}$$

Explanation of fission energy release: in fission, a heavy nucleus splits into two medium-mass fragments whose mean binding energy per nucleon is higher than that of the parent, so the difference in binding energy is released. Estimating for ^{235}U with two fragments near A\approx 117, take the following values:

$$A_U=235$$

$$b_{parent}=7.6\unit{MeV/nucleon}$$

$$b_{prod}=8.5\unit{MeV/nucleon}$$

The energy released per fission is modeled by

$$E_{release}=A_U(b_{prod}-b_{parent})\unit{MeV}$$

Substituting the numbers gives

$$E_{release}=235(8.5-7.6)\unit{MeV}$$

$$E_{release}=210\unit{MeV}$$

Physical origin in the upper mass region: as A increases, nuclear forces saturate while the long-range Coulomb repulsion between protons grows, reducing b and producing the gradual downward trend for heavy nuclei. The principal force responsible for the fall of the curve at large A is the Coulomb repulsion among protons.
final_answer_instructions: Provide two numerical final answers in the exact formats: (1) A_{max} = ... ; (2) E_{release} = ... MeV.

context:
Figure 2.5 shows a plot of the average binding energy per nucleon as a function of the mass number A. Let epsilon(A) denote the average binding energy per nucleon for a nucleus with mass number A, so E is defined by the relation
$$
E = \varepsilon(A)
$$
Consider the fission of a parent nucleus characterized by mass number A_0, proton number Z_0, mass M_0, and total binding energy B_0 into two fragments characterized by mass numbers A_1 and A_2, proton numbers Z_1 and Z_2, masses M_1 and M_2, and total binding energies B_1 and B_2, respectively. Let c denote the speed of light, m_p the proton mass, and m_n the neutron mass. The energy released Q is defined by
$$
Q = M_0 c^2 - M_1 c^2 - M_2 c^2
$$
Express Q in terms of \varepsilon(A) and A. Then estimate Q for symmetric fission with A_0 = 240, where symmetric means A_1 = A_2 = 120. Use values read from Figure 2.5: \varepsilon(120) \approx 8.5 \unit{MeV} and \varepsilon(240) \approx 7.6 \unit{MeV}.
solution:
The mass of a nucleus with mass number A and proton number Z is
$$
M = Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n - \frac{B}{c^2}
$$
Conservation of proton number gives
$$
Z_0 = Z_1 + Z_2
$$
Conservation of nucleon number gives
$$
A_0 = A_1 + A_2
$$
Combining these with the mass expression yields
$$
M_0 = M_1 + M_2 + \frac{B_1 + B_2 - B_0}{c^2}
$$
Therefore
$$
Q = M_0 c^2 - M_1 c^2 - M_2 c^2
$$
which implies
$$
Q = B_1 + B_2 - B_0
$$
The total binding energy relates to the average per-nucleon value by
$$
B = A \varepsilon(A)
$$
Hence
$$
Q = A_1 \varepsilon(A_1) + A_2 \varepsilon(A_2) - A_0 \varepsilon(A_0)
$$
For symmetric fission we take
$$
A_0 = 240
$$
$$
A_1 = 120
$$
$$
A_2 = 120
$$
From Figure 2.5 we use
$$
\varepsilon(120) \approx 8.5 \unit{MeV}
$$
$$
\varepsilon(240) \approx 7.6 \unit{MeV}
$$
Substituting gives
$$
Q \approx 120\,(8.5 \unit{MeV}) + 120\,(8.5 \unit{MeV}) - 240\,(7.6 \unit{MeV})
$$
Therefore
$$
Q \approx 216 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Although you should first express Q in terms of ε(A) and A, the final graded answer is the numerical estimate. Your final answer should be written as 'Q = [value] MeV', rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: Assume a uranium nucleus breaks up spontaneously into two roughly equal parts. Estimate the reduction in electrostatic energy of the nuclei, and state how this relates to the total change in energy. Use the uniform charge distribution model with nuclear radius R(A)=1.2×10^{-13} A^{1/3} cm. Define Z_0=92, A_0=236 for the initial uranium nucleus, with initial radius R_0=R(A_0). After fission into two equal fragments, each fragment has Z=Z_0/2 and A=A_0/2, with radius R=R(A). Let Q=Ze be the charge of a fragment, where e is the magnitude of the elementary charge. Use Gaussian units for electrostatics so that the electrostatic self-energy of a uniformly charged sphere is E_self=(3/5) Q^2/R. For numerical evaluation, take the fine-structure constant α=e^2/(ħ c)≈1/137 and ħ c≈1.97×10^{-11} MeV cm. Let ΔE denote the reduction in electrostatic energy, defined as initial minus final.
solution:
Given Z_0=92 and A_0=236, the initial nuclear radius is
$$R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-13} A_0^{1/3} \unit{cm}$$
Each fragment has
$$Z = \frac{1}{2} Z_0$$
$$A = \frac{1}{2} A_0$$
$$R = 1.2 \times 10^{-13} A^{1/3} \unit{cm}$$
The electrostatic self-energy of a uniformly charged sphere is
$$E_{\text{self}} = \frac{3}{5} \frac{Q^2}{R}$$
The reduction in electrostatic energy is
$$\Delta E = \frac{3}{5} \left( \frac{(Z_0 e)^2}{R_0} - 2 \frac{(Z e)^2}{R} \right)$$
Using Z=Z_0/2 and R=R_0 2^{-1/3}, this becomes
$$\Delta E = \frac{3 Z_0^2 e^2}{5 R_0} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{2^{2/3}} \right)$$
Numerically, this can be written as
$$\Delta E = 0.222 \frac{Z_0^2}{R_0} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right) \hbar c$$
With R_0=1.2 \times 10^{-13} \times 236^{1/3} \unit{cm}, Z_0=92, e^2/(\hbar c)=1/137, and \hbar c=1.97 \times 10^{-11} \unit{MeV cm}, we obtain
$$\Delta E \approx 0.222 \times \frac{92^2}{1.2 \times 10^{-13} \times 236^{1/3} \unit{cm}} \times \frac{1}{137} \times 1.97 \times 10^{-11} \unit{MeV cm}$$
$$\Delta E \approx 364 \unit{MeV}$$
Interpretation: This reduction in electrostatic energy is the primary source of the energy released in uranium fission. The actual total energy release also includes other contributions, such as an increase in nuclear surface energy and changes in nuclear binding of the fragments.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should contain two parts in the exact format: 'ΔE = [value] MeV; [statement]'. The first part must express the reduction in electrostatic energy ΔE as a numerical value in MeV, reported to 3 significant figures. The second part must be exactly one of the following sentences: 'It is the dominant contributor to the total energy release.' or 'It is not the dominant contributor to the total energy release.'

context: Estimate (order of magnitude) the ratio of the energy released when 1\unit{g} of uranium undergoes fission to the energy released when 1\unit{g} of TNT explodes. Define E_TNT as the energy released by the explosion of 1\unit{g} of TNT, E_fiss as the energy released by the fission of 1\unit{g} of uranium, and let the final answer be reported as r=E_fiss/E_TNT. Use U-238 with mass number A=238 for the uranium sample. Let N_A be Avogadro's number and epsilon_fiss be the energy released per fission event of a uranium nucleus. Let N_U denote the number of uranium nuclei in 1\unit{g} of U-238. Energies may be expressed in \unit{eV} or \unit{MeV}, written with \unit{} units.
solution:
Order-of-magnitude reasoning: nuclear interaction energies are about 1\unit{MeV} per nucleon, while typical chemical bond energies are about 1\unit{eV} per molecule. Since the number of nucleons in 1\unit{g} of uranium is of the same order as the number of molecules in 1\unit{g} of TNT, the ratio is of order one million.

$$r \approx 10^6$$

More precise estimate:

$$E_{TNT} \approx 2.6\times 10^{22} \unit{eV}$$

$$\epsilon_{fiss} \approx 210 \unit{MeV}$$

$$N_A = 6.023\times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}$$

$$A = 238$$

$$N_U = \frac{N_A}{A}$$

$$E_{fiss} = N_U \epsilon_{fiss}$$

$$E_{fiss} \approx \frac{6.023\times 10^{23}}{238} \times 210 \unit{MeV}$$

$$E_{fiss} \approx 5.3\times 10^{23} \unit{MeV}$$

$$E_{fiss} \approx 5.3\times 10^{29} \unit{eV}$$

$$r = \frac{E_{fiss}}{E_{TNT}}$$

$$r \approx 2\times 10^{7}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the dimensionless ratio r as a numerical value with 1 significant figure.

context:
A nuclear reactor operates at constant thermal power P=100\unit{MW}. Let N denote the number of fission events per second in the core, and let E_f be the energy released per fission. Assume E_f=200\unit{MeV}.

Select the correct order of magnitude for N from the set {10^6, 10^{12}, 10^{18}, 10^{24}, 10^{30}}.
solution:
Energy released per fission:
$$
E_f=200\unit{MeV}
$$
Converted to joules:
$$
E_f=320\times 10^{-13}\unit{J}
$$
Reactor power:
$$
P=100\unit{MW}
$$
In SI base units:
$$
P=100\times 10^{6}\unit{J/s}
$$
Number of fissions per second:
$$
N=\frac{P}{E_f}
$$
Substitution:
$$
N=\frac{100\times 10^{6}}{320\times 10^{-13}}\unit{1/s}
$$
Evaluation:
$$
N\approx 3\times 10^{18}\unit{1/s}
$$
Final choice:
$$
ans=10^{18}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the selected order of magnitude as a numerical value in the exact form ans=10^k, where k is chosen from {6, 12, 18, 24, 30}. Use only the variable ans and do not include units.

context: Discuss thermonuclear reactions. Provide concrete examples of reactions important in the Sun, in the H bomb (uncontrolled thermonuclear reaction), and in controlled fusion attempts. Estimate, in electron volts per reaction, the energy release for each example. Also describe the most important characteristic of the nuclear force relevant to these reactions. Notation and definitions to be used in the solution: p denotes a proton, d denotes a deuteron (2H), t denotes a triton (3H), n denotes a neutron, 3He and 4He denote helium-3 and helium-4, respectively, 6Li denotes lithium-6, e^{+} denotes a positron, ν_e denotes an electron neutrino, and γ denotes a gamma ray. The quantity Q denotes the energy released per reaction. M(X) denotes the atomic mass of nuclide X, and c denotes the speed of light. Energies are expressed in eV (specifically MeV) and masses in amu, with units written using \unit{}.
solution:
In the Sun, the dominant thermonuclear process is the proton–proton chain:

$$
p + p \to d + e^{+} + \nu_e
$$

$$
d + p \to {}^{3}He + \gamma
$$

$$
{}^{3}He + {}^{3}He \to {}^{4}He + 2 p
$$

The net reaction is

$$
4 p \to {}^{4}He + 2 e^{+} + 2 \nu_e
$$

The energy release for the net reaction is

$$
Q = [4 M({}^{1}H) - M({}^{4}He)] c^{2}
$$

$$
4 \times 1.008142 - 4.003860
$$

$$
0.02871 \unit{amu}
$$

$$
26.9 \unit{MeV}
$$

In an H bomb, an uncontrolled thermonuclear reaction uses a condensed mixture typically containing deuterium, tritium, and lithium. A representative reaction chain is

$$
{}^{6}Li + n \to {}^{4}He + t
$$

$$
d + t \to {}^{4}He + n

The most important characteristic of the nuclear force in these reactions is saturation: a nucleon interacts strongly only with nearby nucleons. As a result, nucleons in the interior of a nucleus have their interactions saturated, whereas those on the surface do not. context: A deuteron of rest mass M and binding energy B is disintegrated into a neutron of rest mass m_n and a proton of rest mass m_p by a gamma ray of energy E_{\gamma}. Let c denote the speed of light. Assume B \ll M c^2. The binding energy satisfies B = ( m_n + m_p - M ) c^2. Define \Delta = E_{\gamma} - B and let \Delta_{min} be the minimum value of \Delta for which the reaction can occur, i.e., the threshold at which the final nucleons are at rest in their center-of-mass frame. Find \Delta_{min} to lowest order in B / ( M c^2 ).
solution:
At threshold the final nucleons are at rest in their center-of-mass frame, so the total center-of-mass energy is
$$
E^* = ( m_n + m_p ) c^2
$$
Using the Lorentz-invariant of the total four-momentum, in the deuteron rest frame we have
$$
( E_{\gamma} + M c^2 )^2 - E_{\gamma}^2 = ( m_n + m_p )^2 c^4
$$
This gives
$$
M^2 c^4 + 2 E_{\gamma} M c^2 = ( m_n + m_p )^2 c^4
$$
Equivalently
$$
2 E_{\gamma} M c^2 = \, [ \, ( m_n + m_p )^2 - M^2 \, ] \, c^4
$$
Using B = ( m_n + m_p - M ) c^2, we write
$$
m_n + m_p = M + \frac{B}{c^2}
$$
Hence
$$
[ \, ( m_n + m_p )^2 - M^2 \, ] \, c^4 = 2 M B c^2 + B^2
$$
Therefore
$$
2 E_{\gamma} M c^2 = 2 M B c^2 + B^2
$$
Solving for E_{\gamma} - B yields
$$
E_{\gamma} - B = \frac{B^2}{2 M c^2}
$$
Thus the threshold value is
$$
\Delta_{min} = \frac{B^2}{2 M c^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \Delta_{min} = ..., and the expression on the right-hand side should involve only B, M, and c (no other symbols).

grading_standard.formula: $$2 E_{\gamma} M c^2 = 2 M B c^2 + B^2$$

context: According to a simple square-well model, the neutron and proton in a deuteron interact through a spherical square-well potential of width b and depth V_0 in an l = 0 state. Assume equal nucleon masses m_n = m_p = M, and let the bound-state energy be E = -ε, where ε > 0 is the deuteron binding energy. Define the interior wave number k and exterior decay constant k_1 by k = sqrt(M (V_0 - ε)) / ħ and k_1 = sqrt(M c^2 ε) / (ħ c). Use the approximation k b = π/2. For the s-wave, take the spatial wavefunction to be ψ(r) = A sin(k r) / r for 0 < r < b and ψ(r) = A sin(k b) e^{-k_1 (r - b)} / r for r ≥ b, where A is a normalization constant. Use the numerical values b = 1.9 × 10^{-15} m, V_0 = 40 MeV, M c^2 = 940 MeV, and ħ c = 197 MeV fm, with 1 fm = 10^{-15} m. Here c is the speed of light and ħ is the reduced Planck constant.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the probability P that the proton is within the range of the neutron, i.e., within r < b. Use the approximation m_n = m_p = M and k b = π/2, where k = sqrt(M (V_0 - ε)) / ħ and ε is the deuteron binding energy.
subquestions.solution:
The probability inside the well is
$$P = 4 \pi A^2 \int_0^b \sin^2(k r) dr$$
Using normalization across both regions yields
$$P = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{k_1 b} \right)^{-1}$$
With k defined by
$$k = \frac{\sqrt{M (V_0 - \varepsilon)}}{\hbar}$$
and the approximation
$$k b = \frac{\pi}{2}$$
we have
$$k \approx \frac{\pi}{2 b}$$
Thus
$$\varepsilon \approx V_0 - \frac{1}{M c^2} \left( \frac{\pi \hbar c}{2 b} \right)^2$$
Numerically,
$$\varepsilon \approx 40 \unit{MeV} - \frac{1}{940 \unit{MeV}} \left( \frac{\pi \times 1.97 \times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV m}}{2 \times 1.9 \times 10^{-15} \unit{m}} \right)^2$$
$$\varepsilon \approx 11.8 \unit{MeV}$$
The exterior decay constant is
$$k_1 = \frac{\sqrt{M c^2 \varepsilon}}{\hbar c}$$
Numerically,
$$k_1 = \frac{\sqrt{940 \unit{MeV} \times 11.8 \unit{MeV}}}{1.97 \times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV m}}$$
$$k_1 \approx 5.3 \times 10^{14} \unit{m^{-1}}$$
Therefore,
$$P = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{k_1 b} \right)^{-1}$$
$$P = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{5.3 \times 10^{14} \times 1.9 \times 10^{-15}} \right)^{-1}$$
$$P \approx 0.50$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the probability P (dimensionless) as a numerical value rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the mean-square radius of the deuteron. Define the mean-square radius as overline{r^2} = ⟨Ψ| r^2 |Ψ⟩ and the root-mean-square radius r_{rms} = (overline{r^2})^{1/2}.
subquestions.solution:
The mean-square radius is
$$\overline{r^2} = \langle \Psi | r^2 | \Psi \rangle_{r<b} + \langle \Psi | r^2 | \Psi \rangle_{r>b}$$
With the given wavefunction,
$$\overline{r^2} = 4 \pi A^2 \left[ \int_0^b \sin^2(k r) r^2 dr + \int_b^\infty e^{-2 k_1 (r-b)} r^2 dr \right]$$
This evaluates to
$$\overline{r^2} = \frac{b^2}{1 + \frac{1}{k_1 b}} \left[ \left( \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4}{\pi^2} \right) + \frac{1}{k_1 b} + \frac{1}{(k_1 b)^2} + \frac{1}{2 (k_1 b)^3} \right]$$
Using k_1 b \approx 1, we approximate
$$\overline{r^2} \approx \frac{b^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4}{\pi^2} + 2.5 \right)$$
Substituting b numerically,
$$\overline{r^2} \approx \frac{(1.9 \times 10^{-15} \unit{m})^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4}{\pi^2} + 2.5 \right)$$
$$\overline{r^2} \approx 5.8 \times 10^{-30} \unit{m^2}$$
Define the root-mean-square radius r_{rms} by
$$r_{rms} = \left( \overline{r^2} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$
Numerically,
$$r_{rms} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{-15} \unit{m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express both the mean-square radius overline{r^2} (in m^2) and the root-mean-square radius r_{rms} (in m) as numerical values, each rounded to 2 significant figures.
