context:
Consider the radiative capture reaction of a proton and a neutron forming a deuteron and emitting a photon
$$p + n \to d + \gamma$$
Use m_p, m_n, m_d for the proton, neutron, and deuteron masses, respectively. Let c be the speed of light. Define the released energy (Q-value) as Q. Let E_\gamma denote the photon energy, and let E_{recoil} denote the kinetic energy of the recoiling deuteron. Let p_\gamma be the magnitude of the photon momentum; the deuteron recoil momentum has the same magnitude and opposite direction. For part (b), let r_1 and r_2 be the position vectors of the neutron and proton, respectively, R be the center-of-mass position vector, and r = r_1 - r_2 be the relative position vector. Define the reduced mass
$$\mu = \frac{m_p m_n}{m_p + m_n}$$
Define the relative momentum and laboratory momentum
$$p_{rel} = \mu \frac{dr}{dt}$$
$$p_{lab} = m_n \frac{dr_1}{dt}$$
Define the relative kinetic energy and total kinetic energy
$$T' = \frac{p_{rel}^2}{2 \mu}$$
$$T = T' + \frac{1}{2} (m_p + m_n) \left( \frac{dR}{dt} \right)^2$$
Let \Gamma denote the kinetic energy of the incident neutron in the laboratory frame
$$\Gamma = \frac{p_{lab}^2}{2 m_n}$$
For orbital angular momentum, let l be the orbital quantum number and L the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum
$$L = \sqrt{l(l+1)} \hbar$$
Let a be the deuteron radius. Use the following numerical data where needed
$$m_p = 1.00783 \unit{amu}$$
$$m_n = 1.00867 \unit{amu}$$
$$m_d = 2.01410 \unit{amu}$$
$$1 \unit{amu} = 931 \unit{MeV}$$
$$\hbar c = 1.97 \times 10^{-11} \unit{MeV\ cm}$$
$$m_n c^2 \approx 940 \unit{MeV}$$

subquestions.subproblem: A neutron and a proton can undergo radiative capture at rest: p + n -> d + gamma. Find the photon energy E_\gamma emitted in this capture. Is the recoil of the deuteron important?
subquestions.solution:
The Q-value is
$$Q = (m_p + m_n - m_d) c^2$$
The mass difference is
$$(m_p + m_n - m_d) = 1.00783 \unit{amu} + 1.00867 \unit{amu} - 2.01410 \unit{amu}$$
Therefore
$$(m_p + m_n - m_d) = 0.00240 \unit{amu}$$
Converting to energy units gives
$$Q = 0.00240 \unit{amu} \times 931 \unit{MeV/amu}$$
Hence
$$Q = 2.234 \unit{MeV}$$
Energy conservation with nonrelativistic deuteron recoil gives
$$Q = p_\gamma c + \frac{p_\gamma^2}{2 m_d}$$
This implies
$$(p_\gamma c)^2 + 2 m_d c^2 (p_\gamma c) - 2 m_d c^2 Q = 0$$
Solving for p_\gamma c gives
$$p_\gamma c = m_d c^2 \left( -1 + \sqrt{1 + \frac{2 Q}{m_d c^2}} \right)$$
Since
$$\frac{Q}{m_d c^2} \ll 1$$
we approximate
$$p_\gamma \approx \frac{Q}{c}$$
Thus the deuteron recoil energy is
$$E_{recoil} = \frac{p_\gamma^2}{2 m_d}$$
Using p_\gamma \approx Q/c gives
$$E_{recoil} \approx \frac{Q^2}{2 m_d c^2}$$
Using
$$m_d c^2 = 2.01410 \unit{amu} \times 931 \unit{MeV/amu}$$
we obtain
$$E_{recoil} \approx \frac{(2.234 \unit{MeV})^2}{2 \times 2.01410 \times 931 \unit{MeV}}$$
Hence
$$E_{recoil} \approx 1.33 \times 10^{-3} \unit{MeV}$$
The fractional effect on the photon energy is
$$\frac{E_{recoil}}{E_\gamma} \approx 6.0 \times 10^{-4}$$
Therefore the recoil of the deuteron is negligible at the level of about 10^{-4}
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_\gamma as a numerical value in MeV, reported to 4 significant figures. Additionally, include exactly one sentence assessing recoil importance, using either 'Recoil of the deuteron is negligible.' or 'Recoil of the deuteron is significant.'

subquestions.subproblem: Estimate the energy \Gamma that a neutron incident on a proton at rest must have if the radiative capture is to take place with reasonable probability from a p-state with l = 1. The deuteron radius is a \approx 4 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}. Use m_p = 1.00783 \unit{amu}, m_n = 1.00867 \unit{amu}, m_d = 2.01410 \unit{amu}, 1 \unit{amu} = 1.66 \times 10^{-24} \unit{g}, 1 \unit{amu} = 931 \unit{MeV}, 1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{J}, 1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-6} \unit{erg}, and \hbar = 1.05 \times 10^{-25} \unit{erg\ s}.
subquestions.solution:
The total kinetic energy in terms of relative and center-of-mass motion is
$$T = T' + \frac{1}{2} (m_p + m_n) \left( \frac{dR}{dt} \right)^2$$
with
$$T' = \frac{p_{rel}^2}{2 \mu}$$
The center-of-mass velocity is
$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{m_n \frac{dr_1}{dt} + m_p \frac{dr_2}{dt}}{m_n + m_p}$$
Initially the proton is at rest, so \frac{dr_2}{dt} = 0, and taking m_p \approx m_n gives
$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{dr_1}{dt}$$
The neutron laboratory kinetic energy is
$$\Gamma = \frac{p_{lab}^2}{2 m_n}$$
with
$$p_{lab} = m_n \frac{dr_1}{dt}$$
Substituting into the energy relation yields
$$\frac{p_{lab}^2}{2 m_n} = \frac{p_{rel}^2}{m_n} + \frac{p_{lab}^2}{4 m_n}$$
Therefore
$$p_{lab}^2 = 4 p_{rel}^2$$
For capture into the p-state with l = 1, the orbital angular momentum magnitude is
$$L = \sqrt{l(l+1)} \hbar$$
Thus for l = 1
$$L = \sqrt{2} \hbar$$
Using the deuteron radius a as an orbital radius gives the estimate
$$p_{rel} a \approx L$$
Hence
$$p_{rel} a \approx \sqrt{2} \hbar$$
The incident neutron energy is
$$\Gamma = \frac{p_{lab}^2}{2 m_n}$$
Using p_{lab}^2 = 4 p_{rel}^2 gives
$$\Gamma = \frac{2 p_{rel}^2}{m_n}$$
Expressing in terms of a and \hbar gives
$$\Gamma = \frac{4}{m_n c^2} \left( \frac{\hbar c}{a} \right)^2$$
Using
$$m_n c^2 \approx 940 \unit{MeV}$$
$$\hbar c = 1.97 \times 10^{-11} \unit{MeV\ cm}$$
$$a \approx 4 \times 10^{-13} \unit{cm}$$
we obtain
$$\Gamma \approx \frac{4}{940} \left( \frac{1.97 \times 10^{-11}}{4 \times 10^{-13}} \right)^2 \unit{MeV}$$
Hence
$$\Gamma \approx 10.32 \unit{MeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \Gamma as a numerical value in MeV, reported to 4 significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$(p_\gamma c)^2 + 2 m_d c^2 (p_\gamma c) - 2 m_d c^2 Q = 0$$

context: Consider two nucleons with position vectors x_1 and x_2 in ordinary space, intrinsic spin operators J^(1) and J^(2), and isospin operators I^(1) and I^(2). Neglect all velocity- or momentum-dependent terms. Define the relative coordinate x = x_1 - x_2 and r = |x|. The two-body potential is V(x_1, x_2, J^(1), J^(2), I^(1), I^(2)). Derive the most general form of V that is consistent with the following symmetries and conservation laws: spatial translations, spatial rotations, spatial parity, isospin rotations, hermiticity (probability conservation), and time reversal. For each symmetry, state the transformation law and the corresponding restriction on V. Use the spatial rotation operator R, the isospin rotation operator R_I, and the time-reversal operator U. Treat x as a polar vector and J^(i) and I^(i) as axial vectors in their respective spaces. Use the Kronecker delta δ_ij and the Levi-Civita symbol ε_ijk as needed. Conclude with the final structured form of V in terms of rotational and isospin invariants and scalar coefficient functions of r. The final answer should be written as V(x_1, x_2, J^(1), J^(2), I^(1), I^(2)) equals a sum of terms built from the allowed invariants
solution:
(a) Momentum conservation — invariance under spatial translations. The potential depends only on the relative coordinate

$$
x = x_1 - x_2
$$

Therefore the potential can be written as

$$
V = V(x, J^{(1)}, J^{(2)}, I^{(1)}, I^{(2)})
$$

(b) Angular momentum conservation — invariance under continuous spatial rotations. Under a rotation R,

$$
x' = R x
$$

$$
J^{(i)'} = R J^{(i)}
$$

for i = 1, 2. Rotationally invariant scalar building blocks include

$$
1
$$

$$
x^2
$$

$$
J^{(i)} \cdot x
$$

$$
J^{(1)} \cdot J^{(2)}
$$

$$
\bigl[J^{(1)} \times J^{(2)}\bigr] \cdot x
$$

Higher than first order spin products can be reduced using

$$
J_i J_j = \delta_{ij} + i \varepsilon_{ijk} J_k
$$

and the identity

$$
\bigl(J^{(1)} \times x\bigr) \cdot \bigl(J^{(2)} \times x\bigr) = \bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot J^{(2)}\bigr) x^2 - \bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot x\bigr) \bigl(J^{(2)} \cdot x\bigr)
$$

(c) Parity conservation — invariance under spatial inversion. Under parity,

$$
x' = -x
$$

$$
J^{(i)'} = J^{(i)}
$$

for i = 1, 2. Since x is the only polar vector, only even powers of x may appear in V. Allowed parity-even invariants are

$$
1
$$

$$
x^2
$$

$$
J^{(1)} \cdot J^{(2)}
$$

$$
\bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot x\bigr) \bigl(J^{(2)} \cdot x\bigr)
$$

The pseudoscalar \bigl[J^{(1)} \times J^{(2)}\bigr] \cdot x is excluded by parity

(d) Isotopic spin conservation — invariance under isospin rotations. Under an isospin rotation R_I,

$$
I^{(i)'} = R_I I^{(i)}
$$

for i = 1, 2. Isospin invariants are

$$
1
$$

$$
I^{(1)} \cdot I^{(2)}
$$

(e) Conservation of probability — hermiticity of the Hamiltonian. The potential satisfies

$$
V^+ = V
$$

Hence all scalar coefficient functions that multiply invariants are real functions of r, where

$$
r = |x|
$$

(f) Time reversal invariance. Under time reversal,

$$
V = U^{-1} V^* U
$$

$$
U^{-1} J^* U = -J
$$

This imposes no additional restriction on V for a potential without velocity-dependent terms

Combining these results, a general two-nucleon potential consistent with the listed symmetries can be written as

$$
V(x_1, x_2, J^{(1)}, J^{(2)}, I^{(1)}, I^{(2)}) = V_a + \bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot J^{(2)}\bigr) V_b
$$

where V_a and V_b each have the general rotationally and parity invariant form

$$
V_s = V_{0}(r) + V_{1}(r) \bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot J^{(2)}\bigr) + V_{2}(r) \frac{\bigl(J^{(1)} \cdot x\bigr) \bigl(J^{(2)} \cdot x\bigr)}{x^2}
$$

for s in {a, b}. Hermiticity requires that the coefficient functions V_{sk}(r) for s in {a, b} and k in {0, 1, 2} are real. Finally, the potential is symmetric under the interchange of the two nucleons 1 and 2

Do not introduce any additional variables or parameters. Present the expression explicitly as a sum of invariant scalar operators multiplying those coefficient functions.

$$

context: To some approximation, a medium-weight nucleus can be regarded as a flat-bottomed potential with rigid walls. To simplify this picture still further, model the nucleus as a cubical box of side length a equal to the nuclear diameter. Consider a nucleus of iron-56, which has 28 protons and 28 neutrons. Assume the nonrelativistic single-particle Schrödinger equation in a three-dimensional infinite square well, with zero potential inside the box and infinite potential outside, and neglect interactions beyond the Pauli principle. Use a nuclear diameter a=10^{-12}\unit{cm}. Let m be the nucleon mass, \hbar the reduced Planck constant, and c the speed of light. Let E denote the single-particle total energy eigenvalue, which equals the kinetic energy inside the box because V=0 there. Let E_{\max} denote the kinetic energy of the highest-energy (most energetic) nucleon in the filled ground-state configuration of the nucleus. Estimate E_{\max}.
solution:
Inside the box (|x|<a/2, |y|<a/2, |z|<a/2)
$$V(x,y,z)=0$$
Outside the box (otherwise)
$$V(x,y,z)=\infty$$
The time-independent Schrödinger equation is
$$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}\nabla^2 \Psi(x,y,z)+V(x,y,z)\Psi(x,y,z)=E\Psi(x,y,z)$$
Use separation of variables
$$\Psi(x,y,z)=\Psi(x)\Psi(y)\Psi(z)$$
For each coordinate i=1,2,3 with x_1=x, x_2=y, x_3=z, we obtain
$$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}\frac{d^2}{dx_i^2}\Psi(x_i)+V(x_i)\Psi(x_i)=E_i\Psi(x_i)$$
with
$$E=E_1+E_2+E_3$$
The general solution in the interior is
$$\Psi(x_i)=A_i\sin(k_i x_i)+B_i\cos(k_i x_i)$$
with
$$k_i=\frac{\sqrt{2 m E_i}}{\hbar}$$
Imposing the boundary conditions \Psi(\pm a/2)=0 yields the allowed forms
$$\Psi(x_i)=A_i\sin\left(\frac{n\pi}{a}x_i\right)$$
$$\Psi(x_i)=B_i\cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{a}x_i\right)$$
with n even for the sine solutions and n odd for the cosine solutions. The corresponding one-dimensional energy contributions are
$$E_i=\frac{k_i^2\hbar^2}{2 m}$$
Quantization gives
$$E_i=\frac{\pi^2 n_i^2 \hbar^2}{2 m a^2}$$
with
$$n_x=1,2,3,\ldots$$
The three-dimensional energies are
$$E=E_0(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)$$
where
$$E_0=\frac{\pi^2 \hbar^2}{2 m a^2}$$
Using relativistic-unit substitutions,
$$E_0=\frac{\pi^2 (c\hbar)^2}{2 m c^2 a^2}$$
with
$$c\hbar=1.97\times 10^{-11}\unit{MeV\,cm}$$
$$m c^2=939\unit{MeV}$$
$$a=10^{-12}\unit{cm}$$
we find
$$E_0=2.04\unit{MeV}$$
According to the Pauli principle, each spatial state can accommodate one pair of neutrons and one pair of protons (4 nucleons total). Fill states in order of increasing n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2:
- (1,1,1): number of distinct states 1, accommodates 4 nucleons, energy 3E_0
- (2,1,1) and permutations: number of distinct states 3, accommodates 12 nucleons, energy 6E_0
- (2,2,1) and permutations: number of distinct states 3, accommodates 12 nucleons, energy 9E_0
- (3,1,1) and permutations: number of distinct states 3, accommodates 12 nucleons, energy 11E_0
- (2,2,2): number of distinct states 1, accommodates 4 nucleons, energy 12E_0
- (1,2,3) and permutations: number of distinct states 6, accommodates 24 nucleons, energy 14E_0
For ^{56}Fe, 56 nucleons fill up through 44 nucleons at 12E_0 and then partially occupy the 14E_0 group, so the highest occupied single-particle energy is 14E_0. Therefore,
$$E_{\max}=14 E_0$$
Using the numerical value of E_0,
$$E_{\max}=2.04\times 14\unit{MeV}$$
$$E_{\max}=28.6\unit{MeV}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_max as a numerical value in MeV with 3 significant figures.

context: The simplest single-particle model for low-lying states of nuclei with neutron number N and proton number Z between 20 and 28 assumes that valence nucleons occupy the f_{7/2} shell. Symbols and definitions used throughout: A is the mass number, Z is the proton number, N is the neutron number, l is the single-particle orbital angular momentum, s is the single-nucleon spin with s = 1/2, j is the total single-particle angular momentum, J is the total nuclear spin, and K is the projection of J on the symmetry axis. The nuclear magnetic dipole moment is denoted by mu, with mu_N the nuclear magneton used as a unit. The orbital and spin g-factors of a nucleon are g_l and g_s, and we use g_p and g_n as the proton and neutron spin g-factors derived from single-nucleon magnetic moments mu_p and mu_n. Experimental single-nucleon magnetic moments are taken as mu_p = 2.79 mu_N and mu_n = -1.91 mu_N. The electric quadrupole moment is Q, and the intrinsic quadrupole moment is Q_0. The mean-square nuclear radius is denoted by \langle r^2 \rangle, with the crude size estimate R \approx 1.2 A^{1/3} \unit{fm} and \langle r^2 \rangle \approx R^2. The reduced transition probability for an electric quadrupole transition is B(E2), quoted in \unit{e^2 fm^4}, where e is the elementary charge magnitude and e = 1 may be used in nuclear units when explicitly stated. Electromagnetic transition multipolarity is denoted by L, photon energy by E_\gamma in \unit{MeV}, transition rates by \lambda_{M1} and \lambda_{E2} in \unit{s^{-1}}, and half-life by T_{1/2} in \unit{s}. In Weisskopf-type single-particle estimates we use dimensionless parameters \tilde L and |\tilde \Psi|^2 of order unity, the nuclear radius scale R_W \approx 1.4 A^{1/3} \unit{fm}, and \hbar c \approx 197 \unit{MeV fm}, so that E_\gamma/197 is dimensionless when E_\gamma is in \unit{MeV}. Where needed, take E_\gamma = 0.37 \unit{MeV} for the first excited state shown in Fig. 2.14.

subquestions.subproblem: Using the f_{7/2} single-particle model, predict the magnetic dipole moments of ^{41}_{20}Ca_{21} and ^{41}_{21}Sc_{20}. Estimate crudely the electric quadrupole moments for these two cases as well. Use mu_p = 2.79 mu_N, mu_n = -1.91 mu_N, s = 1/2, j for total single-particle angular momentum, l for orbital angular momentum, g_l and g_s for orbital and spin g-factors, and mu_N for the nuclear magneton. Use A for the mass number and Z for the proton number. Take e = 1 when explicitly stated for quadrupole moments.
subquestions.solution:
^{41}Ca has a neutron and ^{41}Sc has a proton outside closed shells in the 1f_{7/2} state. Closed shells do not contribute to the magnetic moment, so the moment is determined by the valence nucleon.

The single-particle magnetic moment is
$$
\mu = g j \mu_N
$$
For j = l + \frac{1}{2} the effective g-factor is
$$
g = \frac{(2j - 1) g_l + g_s}{2j}
$$
For j = l - \frac{1}{2} the effective g-factor is
$$
g = \frac{(2j + 3) g_l - g_s}{2(j + 1)}
$$
Neutron case for ^{41}Ca:
$$
g_l = 0
$$
$$
g_s = g_n
$$
$$
g_s = \frac{\mu_n}{s \mu_N}
$$
$$
g_s = \frac{-1.91}{\frac{1}{2}}
$$
$$
g_s = -3.82
$$
$$
l = 3
$$
$$
j = \frac{7}{2}
$$
For j = l + \frac{1}{2} the g-factor is
$$
g = \frac{g_s}{2j}
$$
The magnetic moment is
$$
\mu(^{41}Ca) = g j \mu_N
$$
$$
\mu(^{41}Ca) = \frac{g_s}{2} \unit{\mu_N}
$$
$$
\mu(^{41}Ca) = -1.91 \unit{\mu_N}
$$
Proton case for ^{41}Sc:
$$
g_l = 1
$$
$$
g_s = g_p
$$
$$
g_s = \frac{\mu_p}{s \mu_N}
$$
$$
g_s = \frac{2.79}{\frac{1}{2}}
$$
$$
g_s = 5.58
$$
$$
j = \frac{7}{2}
$$
The effective g-factor is
$$
g = \frac{(2j - 1) g_l + g_s}{2j}
$$
Numerically
$$
g = \frac{6 + 5.58}{7}
$$
The magnetic moment is
$$
\mu(^{41}Sc) = g j \mu_N
$$
$$
\mu(^{41}Sc) = 5.79 \unit{\mu_N}
$$
The electric quadrupole moment of ^{41}Sc is
$$
Q(^{41}Sc) = - e^2 \langle r^2 \rangle \frac{2j - 1}{2(j + 1)}
$$
With the proton charge taken as unity this is
$$
Q(^{41}Sc) = - \langle r^2 \rangle \frac{2j - 1}{2(j + 1)}
$$
Use the estimate
$$
\langle r^2 \rangle = \bigl(1.2 A^{1/3}\bigr)^2 \unit{fm^2}
$$
For A = 41 and j = \frac{7}{2}
$$
Q(^{41}Sc) = - \frac{2}{3} \bigl(1.2 \times 41^{1/3}\bigr)^2 \unit{fm^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
Q(^{41}Sc) = -11.4 \unit{fm^2}
$$
In cgs units
$$
Q(^{41}Sc) = -1.14 \times 10^{-25} \unit{cm^2}
$$
For ^{41}Ca the quadrupole moment arises from polarization and is estimated by
$$
Q(^{41}Ca) \approx \frac{Z}{(A - 1)^2} \bigl|Q(^{41}Sc)\bigr|
$$
Numerically
$$
Q(^{41}Ca) = 1.43 \times 10^{-27} \unit{cm^2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the following as numerical values with units: (i) the magnetic dipole moment mu(41Ca) in mu_N; (ii) the magnetic dipole moment mu(41Sc) in mu_N; (iii) the electric quadrupole moment Q(41Sc) in fm^2; and (iv) the electric quadrupole moment Q(41Ca) in cm^2. Report each quantity to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: What states are expected in ^{42}_{20}Ca according to the f_{7/2} model? Calculate the magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments for these states. Sketch the complete decay sequence expected experimentally for the highest spin state. Use mu_N for the nuclear magneton and B(E2) in \unit{e^2 fm^4}.
subquestions.solution:
For ^{42}Ca there are two identical valence neutrons in the f_{7/2} shell, so the allowed coupled spins are J = 0, 2, 4, 6.

The two-particle magnetic moment can be written as
$$
\mu = g J \mu_N
$$
With single-particle contributions g_1 and g_2 and angular momenta j_1 and j_2 one has
$$
g J(J + 1) = \frac{g_1}{2} \bigl[J(J + 1) + j_1(j_1 + 1) - j_2(j_2 + 1)\bigr] + \frac{g_2}{2} \bigl[J(J + 1) + j_2(j_2 + 1) - j_1(j_1 + 1)\bigr]
$$
Hence
$$
g = \frac{g_1 + g_2}{2} + \frac{g_1 - g_2}{2} \frac{j_1(j_1 + 1) - j_2(j_2 + 1)}{J(J + 1)}
$$
For ^{42}Ca the two valence particles are neutrons with j_1 = j_2 = \frac{7}{2}
$$
g_1 = g_2 = \frac{-3.82}{j_1}
$$
$$
j_1 = \frac{7}{2}
$$
Thus
$$
\mu(^{42}Ca) = g_1 J \unit{\mu_N}
$$
$$
\mu(^{42}Ca) = -1.09 J \unit{\mu_N}
$$
with
$$
J = 0, 2, 4, 6
$$
The ground-state quadrupole moment is
$$
Q = 0
$$
Relate the intrinsic quadrupole moment to the reduced transition probability by
$$
B(E2, 2^+ \to 0^+) = \frac{e^2 Q_0^2}{16 \pi}
$$
For the first excited 2^+ state of ^{42}Ca with excitation energy 1.524 \unit{MeV}
$$
B(E2: 2^+ \to 0^+) = 81.5 \unit{e^2 fm^4}
$$
Hence
$$
Q_0 = \sqrt{16 \pi \times 81.5} \unit{fm^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
Q_0 = 64 \unit{fm^2}
$$
For a K = 0 band the spectroscopic quadrupole moments are
$$
Q = \frac{K^2 - J(J + 1)}{(J + 1)(2J + 3)} Q_0
$$
With K = 0 this gives
$$
Q = - \frac{J}{2J + 3} Q_0
$$
For J = 2
$$
Q = 18.3 \unit{fm^2}
$$
For J = 4
$$
Q = 23.3 \unit{fm^2}
$$
For J = 6
$$
Q = 25.6 \unit{fm^2}
$$
The highest spin state is expected to decay via an E2 cascade along the K = 0 band down to the 0^+ ground state
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide: (i) the list of allowed total spins J predicted by the f7/2 two-neutron configuration in 42Ca; (ii) the magnetic dipole moments mu(J) for each allowed J state in units of mu_N as numerical values; (iii) the electric quadrupole moments Q(J) for the excited states with J > 0 in fm^2 as numerical values; and (iv) a single-sentence description of the expected decay sequence for the highest-spin state. Report all numerical values to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: The first excited state in ^{43}_{21}Ca_{23} is shown in Fig. 2.14. Use E_\gamma = 0.37 \unit{MeV} in Weisskopf estimates. Reference values: mu_n = -1.91 mu_N, mu(^{41}Ca) = -1.59 mu_N, mu_p = 2.79 mu_N, mu(^{41}Sc) = 5.43 mu_N.
subquestions.solution:
For the \gamma transition (\tfrac{5}{2})^- \to (\tfrac{7}{2})^- the angular momentum selection rule gives
$$
L \geq 1
$$
$$
L \leq 6
$$
Thus the allowed multipoles are
$$
L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6
$$
Parity conservation favors the lowest orders M1 and E2. The Weisskopf-type single-particle estimates give
$$
\lambda_{M1} = \frac{1.9 (\tilde L + 1)}{L \bigl(2 (2 \tilde L + 1) |\tilde \Psi|^2\bigr)} \biggl( \frac{3}{L + 3} \biggr)^2 \biggl( \frac{E_\gamma}{197} \biggr)^{2L + 1} \bigl(1.4 \times A^{1/3}\bigr)^{2L - 2} \times 10^{21}
$$
For L = 1, A = 43, and E_\gamma = 0.37 \unit{MeV}
$$
\lambda_{M1} = \frac{1.9 \times 2}{3^2} \biggl( \frac{3}{4} \biggr)^2 \biggl( \frac{0.37}{197} \biggr)^3 \bigl(1.4 \times 43^{1/3}\bigr)^0 \times 10^{21}
$$
Numerically
$$
\lambda_{M1} = 1.57 \times 10^{12} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Similarly
$$
\lambda_{E2} = \frac{4.4 (\tilde L + 1)}{L (2 2 L + 1) |\tilde \Psi|^2} \biggl( \frac{3}{L + 3} \biggr)^2 \biggl( \frac{E_\gamma}{197} \biggr)^{2L + 1} \bigl(1.4 \times A^{1/3}\bigr)^{2L} \times 10^{21}
$$
For L = 2 with the same A and E_\gamma
$$
\lambda_{E2} = \frac{4.4 \times 3}{2 \times (5 \times 3)^2} \biggl( \frac{3}{L + 3} \biggr)^2 \biggl( \frac{0.37}{197} \biggr)^5 \bigl(1.4 \times 43^{1/3}\bigr)^4 \times 10^{21}
$$
Numerically
$$
\lambda_{E2} = 1.4 \times 10^{3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Since
$$
\lambda_{E2} \ll \lambda_{M1}
$$
we estimate the half-life by
$$
T_{1/2} \approx \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_{M1}}
$$
Numerically
$$
T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{1.57 \times 10^{12}}
$$
Thus
$$
T_{1/2} = 4.4 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s}
$$
This single-particle estimate is about 20 times smaller than the experimental value, likely due to collective contributions to the \gamma transition
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the estimated half-life T_{1/2} (in seconds) for the first excited state in 43Ca, based on the Weisskopf single-particle estimate using the provided E_gamma, as a numerical value reported to 2 significant figures.

context: A recent model for collective nuclear states treats them in terms of interacting bosons. Consider states that are fully symmetric superpositions of S bosons and D bosons. Each S boson has spin 0, and each D boson has spin 2. Let N_s denote the number of S bosons and N_d denote the number of D bosons. Let E_s be the single-boson energy of each S boson and E_d be the single-boson energy of each D boson. There is a residual interaction of constant strength alpha between each distinct pair of D bosons, contributing alpha per D–D pair. Let J denote the total spin of a state, and let J_{N_d,k} denote the k-th allowed value of J for a given N_d, ordered from smallest to largest. Determine the allowed total spins for N_d = 0, 1, 2, 3. Then, for all configurations with fixed total boson number N_s + N_d = 3, determine the total energy E of each configuration.
final_answer_instructions: Provide exactly eight lines in the following fixed formats. Lines 1–4 (allowed spins): 'For N_d = 0: J = ...', 'For N_d = 1: J = ...', 'For N_d = 2: J = ...', 'For N_d = 3: J = ...'. On each of these lines, list all allowed J values in ascending order as integers separated by commas. Lines 5–8 (energies for N_s + N_d = 3): 'For N_d = 0, N_s = 3: E = ...', 'For N_d = 1, N_s = 2: E = ...', 'For N_d = 2, N_s = 1: E = ...', 'For N_d = 3, N_s = 0: E = ...'. On lines 5–8, the right-hand side must be an algebraic expression written only in terms of E_s, E_d, and alpha (integer coefficients may be used). Do not include any additional lines or text beyond these labels and expressions.

context:
A simplified model of the complex nuclear interaction is the pairing force in a single j orbit acting in the two-identical-particle space. The two-particle basis states are defined by
$$
\phi_m = (-1)^{j-m} | j m \rangle | j - m \rangle
$$
for the magnetic projections
$$
m = \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}, \dots, j
$$
In this basis the pairing Hamiltonian is
$$
H = - g M
$$
where g > 0 is the pairing strength and M is the matrix with all entries equal to 1. If the basis has dimension n, then
$$
M_{ij} = 1
$$
for i,j = 1,\dots,n, and for a single j orbit the dimension is
$$
n = j + \tfrac{1}{2}
$$
Here H is the two-particle Hamiltonian, j is the single-particle total angular momentum, m is its projection, J is the total spin of a two-particle state, and E denotes an energy eigenvalue. Let \(\Psi^{(N=2)}\) denote a normalized two-particle eigenstate. This interaction has a single outstanding eigenstate. Determine its spin and energy, to be reported as
$$
J_{\mathrm{special}}
$$
$$
E_{\mathrm{special}}
$$
Determine also the spins and energies of the remaining two-particle eigenstates, to be reported as
$$
\{J_{\mathrm{rest}}\}
$$
$$
E_{\mathrm{rest}}
$$
solution:
The Hamiltonian is an n \times n matrix with constant entries in the chosen basis
$$
H_{ij} = - g
$$
with
$$
n = j + \tfrac{1}{2}
$$
A normalized eigenvector with all equal components is
$$
\Psi_i^{(N=2)} = n^{-1/2}
$$
for i = 1,\dots,n. Acting with H gives
$$
H \Psi^{(N=2)} = - g n \Psi^{(N=2)}
$$
Therefore the energy of the outstanding eigenstate is
$$
E_{\mathrm{special}} = - g \bigl(j + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)
$$
The pairing force acts only in the J = 0 channel, so the spin of this eigenstate is
$$
J_{\mathrm{special}} = 0
$$
The trace of H equals the sum of all eigenvalues
$$
\operatorname{tr}(H) = - g \bigl(j + \tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)
$$
Since H is proportional to the all-ones matrix, which has rank 1, all eigenstates orthogonal to \(\Psi^{(N=2)}\) have zero energy
$$
E_{\mathrm{rest}} = 0
$$
The corresponding total spins are the even J values allowed by coupling two identical particles in a single j shell
$$
\{J_{\mathrm{rest}}\} = \{2,4,6,\dots\}
$$

final_answer_instructions.J_special: Your final answer should be written exactly as 'J_special = ...' where '...' is a single integer.
final_answer_instructions.E_special: Your final answer should be written exactly as 'E_special = ...' and should be an algebraic expression using only g and j (and numerical constants). Do not introduce any other variables.
final_answer_instructions.J_rest: Your final answer should be written exactly as '{J_rest} = { ... }' where '...' is a set expression describing all allowed total spins J for the remaining two-particle eigenstates in a single j shell of two identical particles. Express it using only J and j (and numerical constants).

context: Natural gold $^{197}_{79}Au$ is unstable against $\alpha$-decay with $\alpha$-particle kinetic energy $E_{\alpha}=3.3\unit{MeV}$. Use the Geiger–Nuttall law to estimate the half-life $T_{1/2}$ of $^{197}_{79}Au$ and explain why ordinary gold does not noticeably heat itself. Let $\lambda$ be the decay constant in $\unit{1/s}$, $T_{1/2}$ the half-life in $\unit{s}$, $E_{\alpha}$ the $\alpha$-particle energy in $\unit{MeV}$, $Z$ the atomic number, and $C,D$ empirical constants that depend on $Z$. For a rough estimate, use $C\approx52$ and $D\approx140\unit{MeV^{1/2}}$ (values for lead, $Z=82$).
solution:
By the Geiger–Nuttall law

$$
\log_{10}\lambda = C - D E_{\alpha}^{-1/2}
$$

Using $C\approx52$, $D\approx140\unit{MeV^{1/2}}$, and $E_{\alpha}=3.3\unit{MeV}$,

$$
\log_{10}\lambda \approx 52 - 140 (3.3)^{-1/2}
$$

$$
\log_{10}\lambda \approx -25
$$

$$
\lambda \approx 10^{-25}\unit{1/s}
$$

The half-life is

$$
T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
$$

$$
T_{1/2} \approx 6.9\times10^{24}\unit{s}
$$

$$
T_{1/2} \approx 2.2\times10^{17}\unit{yr}
$$

With such an enormous half-life, the number of decays in a human lifetime is negligible.
final_answer_instructions: Provide your final response as two lines: (1) Line 1 must be the numerical estimate of the half-life in the exact format "T_{1/2} = [number] yr", rounded to 2 significant figures and including the unit 'yr'. (2) Line 2 must be a single sentence strictly in the form "It does/does not noticeably heat itself." (choose one of 'does' or 'does not').

context: A sphere of the isotope 239Pu with mass m_Pu = 120.1 g is immersed in liquid nitrogen of sufficient volume to stop all emitted alpha particles. The measured boil-off corresponds to a constant thermal power P = 0.231 W, which equals the energy release rate from radioactive decays. The kinetic energy of each emitted alpha particle is E_alpha = 5.144 MeV. Include the recoil energy of the daughter nucleus 235U in the energy per decay. Assume the decay 239Pu -> 235U + alpha, with mass numbers A_Pu = 239, A_U = 235, and A_alpha = 4. Use the following constants and conversions: 1 MeV = 1.60206 × 10^{-13} J, 1 atomic mass unit u = 1.66 × 10^{-24} g, and 1 year = 3.156 × 10^{7} s. Variables used in the solution: M_alpha and M_U are the masses of the alpha particle and the 235U recoil nucleus; p_alpha and p_U are the magnitudes of their momenta; E_u is the recoil kinetic energy of 235U; E is the total energy deposited per decay in the liquid; E_J is the energy per decay expressed in joules; N is the number of 239Pu nuclei in the sample; dN/dt is the decay rate (activity); lambda is the decay constant; T_{1/2} is the half-life; T_{1/2,round} is the half-life rounded to the nearest hundred years. Approximate nuclear masses by mass numbers where needed, i.e., M_alpha/M_U ≈ A_alpha/A_U.
solution:
By conservation of momentum, the magnitudes of the momenta are equal
$$
p_\alpha = p_U
$$
The recoil kinetic energy of the daughter nucleus is
$$
E_u = \frac{p_U^2}{2 M_U}
$$
The alpha-particle kinetic energy is
$$
E_\alpha = \frac{p_\alpha^2}{2 M_\alpha}
$$
Using p_\alpha = p_U gives
$$
E_u = \frac{M_\alpha}{M_U} E_\alpha
$$
Approximating masses by mass numbers yields
$$
\frac{M_\alpha}{M_U} = \frac{4}{235}
$$
The energy deposited per decay is
$$
E = E_\alpha + E_u
$$
Substituting the recoil relation gives
$$
E = \frac{239}{235} E_\alpha
$$
Numerically,
$$
E = 5.232 \unit{MeV}
$$
The measured power is
$$
P = 0.231 \unit{W}
$$
Convert the energy per decay to joules
$$
E_J = E \times 1.60206 \times 10^{-13} \unit{J/MeV}
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_J = 5.232 \times 1.60206 \times 10^{-13} \unit{J}
$$
The decay rate is
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = \frac{P}{E_J}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = \frac{0.231}{5.232 \times 1.60206 \times 10^{-13}} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
So
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = 2.756 \times 10^{11} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
The number of 239Pu nuclei in the sample is
$$
N = \frac{m_{Pu}}{A_{Pu} u}
$$
Numerically,
$$
N = \frac{120.1 \unit{g}}{239 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-24} \unit{g}}
$$
So
$$
N = 3.002 \times 10^{23}
$$
The half-life is
$$
T_{1/2} = \frac{N \ln 2}{\frac{dN}{dt}}
$$
Numerically,
$$
T_{1/2} = 7.55 \times 10^{11} \unit{s}
$$
Convert to years
$$
T_{1/2} = \frac{7.55 \times 10^{11}}{3.156 \times 10^{7}} \unit{y}
$$
So
$$
T_{1/2} = 2.39 \times 10^{4} \unit{y}
$$
Rounded to the nearest hundred years
$$
T_{1/2,round} = 23900 \unit{y}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the rounded half-life of 239Pu as a numerical value. Provide T_{1/2,round} in years (y), rounded to the nearest hundred years.

context: A neutral atom of ^{34}Cl undergoes positron (β^+) decay to a neutral atom of ^{34}S. Let p denote the magnitude of the positron momentum, and let I(p) dp be the number of decays per unit time that emit a positron with momentum in the interval [p, p+dp]. Using allowed β-decay theory with a constant nuclear matrix element M_{fi} and weak coupling g, neglect the neutrino mass and nuclear recoil. Define E as the total positron energy corresponding to p by E = sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_e^2 c^4}, and let E_m denote the end-point (maximum total) positron energy of the β^+ spectrum. Plot I(p) as a function of p. The difference in the masses of the neutral atoms is ΔM = M(^{34}Cl) − M(^{34}S) = 5.52 \unit{MeV/c^2}. Take the electron mass to be m_e = 0.511 \unit{MeV/c^2}. Define the β^+ Q-value (the maximum positron kinetic energy in the no-recoil, massless-neutrino limit) by Q = (ΔM − 2 m_e) c^2. Use ħ for the reduced Planck constant, c for the speed of light, and ν for the neutrino. Find E_m in \unit{MeV}.
solution:
The decay process is
$$
^{34}Cl \to ^{34}S + e^+ + \nu
$$
The differential spectrum for positrons with momentum in [p, p+dp] is
$$
I(p) dp = \frac{g^2 |M_{fi}|^2}{2 \pi^3 \hbar^7 c^3} (E_m - E)^2 p^2 dp
$$
Thus the momentum spectrum has the shape
$$
I(p) \propto (E_m - E)^2 p^2
$$
The total positron energy as a function of momentum is
$$
E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_e^2 c^4}
$$
The β^+ Q-value in terms of atomic masses is
$$
Q = (\Delta M - 2 m_e) c^2
$$
The end-point total positron energy is
$$
E_m = Q + m_e c^2
$$
Equivalently
$$
E_m = (\Delta M - m_e) c^2
$$
With \(\Delta M = 5.52 \unit{MeV/c^2}\) and \(m_e = 0.511 \unit{MeV/c^2}\), the numerical values are
$$
Q \approx 4.50 \unit{MeV}
$$
$$
E_m \approx 5.01 \unit{MeV}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of I(p) = [g^2 |M_{fi}|^2/(2 \pi^3 \hbar^7 c^3)] (E_m - E)^2 p^2, and your response should use only the symbols p, E, E_m, g, |M_{fi}|, \hbar, and c. Here E is defined by E = sqrt(p^2 c^2 + m_e^2 c^4). Do not introduce any other variables.
Your final answer should express E_m as a numerical value in MeV with three significant figures.

context:
Both ^{161}Ho and ^{163}Ho decay by allowed electron capture to Dy isotopes. The quantity Q_{EC} is defined as the mass difference between the final ground state of the nucleus plus atomic electrons and the initial ground state of the nucleus plus atomic electrons. The Dy orbital electron binding energies are listed in the table below. The capture rate for 3p_{1/2} electrons in ^{161}Ho is about 5% of the 3s capture rate. Using this information, calculate the 3p_{1/2}-to-3s relative capture rate in ^{163}Ho. Then, assuming Q_{EC} remains the same but the neutrino has a mass m_ u = 50 \unit{eV} instead of being massless, determine how much the 3p_{1/2} and 3s capture rates change for both ^{161}Ho and ^{163}Ho. Use the following definitions and symbols consistently in your work: A is a constant prefactor, M_{if} is the transition matrix element, ho(E) is the density of final states, E_ u is the neutrino energy, p_ u is the neutrino momentum, B_s and B_p are the Dy binding energies of the captured 3s and 3p_{1/2} electrons, respectively, and \lambda is the decay constant for a given capture channel. For the neutrino-mass part, define the fractional change as (\lambda_0 - \lambda)/\lambda_0, where \lambda_0 is the decay constant for a massless neutrino. Report the relative rate in ^{163}Ho as R_{163} = \lambda(3p_{1/2})/\lambda(3s), and report the fractional changes for each isotope and orbital as (\lambda_0 - \lambda)/\lambda_0.
OrbitalBinding Energy (keV)
1s54
2s9
2p1/28.6
3s2.0
3p1/21.8
solution:
As ^{161}Ho and ^{163}Ho have the same nuclear charge Z, their orbital electron wave functions are the same, and the 3s and 3p_{1/2} waves differ only in phase. Therefore, the corresponding transition matrix elements for electron capture have the same magnitude.

$$
\lambda = A |M_{if}|^2 \rho(E)
$$

For two-body electron capture, only a neutrino is emitted, so the phase space is proportional to the square of its energy.

$$
\rho(E) \propto E_\nu^2
$$

To leading order the neutrino energy is the decay energy minus the electron binding energy.

$$
E_\nu \approx Q_{EC} - B
$$

Hence the relative 3p_{1/2}-to-3s capture rate is

$$
\frac{\lambda(3p_{1/2})}{\lambda(3s)} = \frac{|M(3p_{1/2})|^2 (Q_{EC} - B_p)^2}{|M(3s)|^2 (Q_{EC} - B_s)^2}
$$

For ^{161}Ho this empirical ratio is

$$
\frac{\lambda(3p_{1/2})}{\lambda(3s)} = 0.05
$$

Therefore the ratio of matrix elements is

$$
\frac{|M(3p_{1/2})|^2}{|M(3s)|^2} = 0.05 \times \left(\frac{850 \unit{keV} - 2.0 \unit{keV}}{850 \unit{keV} - 1.8 \unit{keV}}\right)^2
$$

$$
\frac{|M(3p_{1/2})|^2}{|M(3s)|^2} = 0.04998
$$

For ^{163}Ho the relative 3p_{1/2}-to-3s capture rate is

$$
R_{163} = \frac{\lambda(3p_{1/2})}{\lambda(3s)}
$$

$$
R_{163} = 0.04998 \times \left(\frac{2.5 \unit{keV} - 1.8 \unit{keV}}{2.5 \unit{keV} - 2.0 \unit{keV}}\right)^2
$$

$$
R_{163} \approx 0.098
$$

Now assume the neutrino has mass m_\nu = 50 \unit{eV}. The neutrino energy and momentum satisfy

$$
E_\nu^2 = p_\nu^2 + m_\nu^2
$$

The phase-space factor changes according to

$$
p_\nu^2 \frac{dp_\nu}{dE_\nu} = E_\nu \sqrt{E_\nu^2 - m_\nu^2}
$$

For m_\nu \ll E_\nu this becomes

$$
E_\nu \sqrt{E_\nu^2 - m_\nu^2} \approx E_\nu^2 \left(1 - \frac{m_\nu^2}{2 E_\nu^2}\right)
$$

Thus each channel’s decay constant shifts from \lambda_0 to

$$
\lambda \approx \lambda_0 \left(1 - \frac{1}{2} \frac{m_\nu^2}{E_\nu^2}\right)
$$

Equivalently, the fractional change is

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} \approx \frac{1}{2} \frac{m_\nu^2}{E_\nu^2}
$$

For ^{161}Ho, 3s state with E_\nu = 850 \unit{keV} - 2.0 \unit{keV} = 848 \unit{keV} = 848000 \unit{eV}

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_\0} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{(50 \unit{eV})^2}{(848000 \unit{eV})^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = 1.74 \times 10^{-9}
$$

For ^{161}Ho, 3p_{1/2} state with E_\nu = 850 \unit{keV} - 1.8 \unit{keV} = 848.2 \unit{keV} = 848200 \unit{eV}

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{(50 \unit{eV})^2}{(848200 \unit{eV})^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = 1.74 \times 10^{-9}
$$

For ^{163}Ho, 3s state with E_\nu = 2.5 \unit{keV} - 2.0 \unit{keV} = 0.5 \unit{keV} = 500 \unit{eV}

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{(50 \unit{eV})^2}{(500 \unit{eV})^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = 5 \times 10^{-3}
$$

For ^{163}Ho, 3p_{1/2} state with E_\nu = 2.5 \unit{keV} - 1.8 \unit{keV} = 0.7 \unit{keV} = 700 \unit{eV}

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{(50 \unit{eV})^2}{(700 \unit{eV})^2}
$$

$$
\frac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda_0} = 2.25 \times 10^{-3}
$$

Specifically: (1) Report the relative capture-rate ratio in ^163Ho as a single number R_{163} = λ(3p_{1/2})/λ(3s). (2) Report four separate fractional changes (λ_0 − λ)/λ_0, one for each capture channel: ^161Ho 3s, ^161Ho 3p_{1/2}, ^163Ho 3s, and ^163Ho 3p_{1/2}. Present these quantities as dimensionless numbers (no units).

context: An element of low atomic number Z can undergo an allowed positron beta decay. Let p_0 be the maximum possible momentum of the positron, with p_0 << m_e c, where m_e is the positron mass and c is the speed of light. Let Gamma_{beta} be the total beta-decay rate. An alternative process is K-capture, in which the nucleus captures a K-shell electron and undergoes the same nuclear transition with emission of a neutrino; let Gamma_K be the decay rate for this process. Treat the wave function of the K-shell electron as hydrogenic and ignore the electron binding energy. Define the total available decay energy (Q-value) as E. Let E_0 be the maximum positron kinetic energy and take E_0 approx E under the given nonrelativistic assumption. Let E_e be the positron kinetic energy and E_{nu} the neutrino energy, and let p and p_{nu} be the corresponding momenta. Neglect nuclear recoil throughout. Use u_i and u_f to denote the initial and final nuclear wave functions, respectively. Use psi_i and psi_f for the initial and final total wave functions. The transition is treated in Fermi theory with an interaction Hamiltonian H of constant strength g. The positron and neutrino one-particle wave functions are denoted phi_{beta} and phi_{nu}, respectively, and are taken as plane waves normalized in a volume V. Their wave vectors are k_{beta} and k_{nu}. The spatial coordinate is r and the spatial volume element is d tau. Define the nuclear matrix element M_{fi} by the relation ∫ psi_i u_f^* e^{- i (k_{beta} + k_{nu}) · r} d tau = M_{fi}. Let hbar be the reduced Planck constant and e the elementary charge. The hydrogenic K-shell electron wave function is denoted phi_K. Let d n / d E denote the density of final states per unit energy. Let omega denote the total beta-decay probability per unit time at fixed decay energy E. Define I(p) by omega = ∫ I(p) d p, so that I(p) is the differential spectrum in positron momentum. For convenience define B = g^2 |M_{fi}|^2 / (2 pi^3 hbar^7 c^3). Compute the ratio Gamma_K / Gamma_{beta}.
solution:
The probability per unit time for a beta^+ decay with decay energy E is
$$
\omega = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} \left| \int \psi_f^* H \psi_i d \tau \right|^2 \frac{d n}{d E}
$$
For the three-particle final state one can write
$$
\psi_f = u_f \phi_{\beta} \phi_{\nu}
$$
The outgoing leptons are represented by plane waves
$$
\phi_{\beta}^* = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}} e^{- i k_{\beta} \cdot r}
$$
$$
\phi_{\nu}^* = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}} e^{- i k_{\nu} \cdot r}
$$
Define the nuclear matrix element by
$$
\int \psi_i u_f^* e^{- i (k_{\beta} + k_{\nu}) \cdot r} d \tau = M_{fi}
$$
The number of positron states with momentum between p and p + d p is
$$
 d n_{\beta} = \frac{4 \pi p^2 d p}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} V
$$
The number of neutrino states with momentum between p_{\nu} and p_{\nu} + d p_{\nu} is
$$
 d n_{\nu} = \frac{4 \pi p_{\nu}^2 d p_{\nu}}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} V
$$
Thus the final-state density factor is
$$
\frac{d n}{d E} = \frac{d n_{\beta} d n_{\nu}}{d E}
$$
Using energy conservation and neglecting nuclear recoil
$$
E_e + E_{\nu} = E
$$
For fixed E_e one has
$$
\frac{d E_{\nu}}{d E} = 1
$$
For a massless neutrino
$$
E_{\nu} = c p_{\nu}
$$
Hence
$$
 p_{\nu} = \frac{E - E_e}{c}
$$
And
$$
 d p_{\nu} = \frac{d E}{c}
$$
Substituting, the density of final states becomes
$$
\frac{d n}{d E} = \frac{(E - E_e)^2 p^2 d p}{4 \pi^4 \hbar^6 c^3} V^2
$$
Write the spectrum as
$$
\omega = \int I(p) d p
$$
With
$$
 I(p) d p = \frac{g^2 |M_{fi}|^2}{2 \pi^3 \hbar^7 c^3} (E - E_e)^2 p^2 d p
$$
The total beta^+ decay rate is
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} = \int_0^{p_0} I(p) d p
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} = B \int_0^{p_0} (E - E_e)^2 p^2 d p
$$
Where
$$
 B = \frac{g^2 |M_{fi}|^2}{2 \pi^3 \hbar^7 c^3}
$$
For p_0 << m_e c the positron is nonrelativistic and
$$
E_0 = \frac{p_0^2}{2 m_e}
$$
Also
$$
 E_e = \frac{p^2}{2 m_e}
$$
Thus
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} = B \int_0^{p_0} \frac{1}{(2 m_e)^2} \left( p_0^4 + p^4 - 2 p_0^2 p^2 \right) p^2 d p
$$
Carrying out the integration gives
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} = \frac{B p_0^7}{4 m_e^2} \left( \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{7} - \frac{2}{5} \right)
$$
Therefore
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} = \frac{2}{105} \frac{B p_0^7}{m_e^2}
$$
And numerically
$$
\Gamma_{\beta} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-2} \frac{B p_0^7}{m_e^2}
$$
For K-capture the final state has two particles, so the emitted neutrino is monoenergetic. The rate is
$$
\Gamma_K = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} \left| \int \psi_f^* H \psi_i d \tau \right|^2 \frac{d n}{d E}
$$
The neutrino plane wave is
$$
\phi_{\nu}^* = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}} e^{- i k_{\nu} \cdot r}
$$
The hydrogenic K-shell electron wave function is
$$
\phi_K = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left( \frac{Z m_e e^2}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2} e^{- Z m_e e^2 r / \hbar^2}
$$
Approximating the nuclear matrix element as constant over the nuclear volume yields
$$
\left| \int \psi_f^* H \psi_i d \tau \right| \approx \frac{g}{\sqrt{V \pi}} \left( \frac{Z m_e e^2}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2} |M_{fi}|
$$
The final-state density for the neutrino is
$$
\frac{d n}{d E} = \frac{4 \pi V p_{\nu}^2 d p_{\nu}}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3 d E}
$$
Using E_{\nu} = c p_{\nu} one finds
$$
\frac{d n}{d E} = \frac{4 \pi V}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{E_{\nu}^2}{c^3}
$$
Neglecting nuclear recoil and taking E_{\nu} \approx E one obtains
$$
\Gamma_K = 2 \pi m_e^3 B \left( \frac{Z e^2}{\hbar} \right)^3 E_{\nu}^2
$$
Ignoring the electron binding energy gives
$$
E_{\nu} \approx E_0 + 2 m_e c^2
$$
And hence
$$
E_{\nu} \approx 2 m_e c^2
$$
Therefore the ratio is
$$
\frac{\Gamma_K}{\Gamma_{\beta}} \approx 5.1 \times 10^{-4} Z^3 \left( \frac{m_e c}{p_0} \right)^7
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{\Gamma_K}{\Gamma_{\beta}} \propto \frac{1}{p_0^7}
$$
The ratio increases rapidly as p_0 decreases
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given explicitly as Gamma_K / Gamma_{beta} = ... and expressed solely in terms of Z, m_e, c, and p_0. Do not include any other variables or intermediate parameters.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Gamma_{\beta} = B \int_0^{p_0} \frac{1}{(2 m_e)^2} \left( p_0^4 + p^4 - 2 p_0^2 p^2 \right) p^2 d p$$
$$\phi_K = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} \left( \frac{Z m_e e^2}{\hbar^2} \right)^{3/2} e^{- Z m_e e^2 r / \hbar^2}$$
$$\frac{d n}{d E} = \frac{4 \pi V p_{\nu}^2 d p_{\nu}}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3 d E}$$

context: Suppose a search for solar neutrinos is to be mounted using a large sample of lithium enriched in the isotope 7Li. Detection depends on production, separation, and detection of the electron-capturing isotope 7Be with a half-life of 53 days. The relevant low-lying nuclear levels are shown in Fig. 2.28. Definitions to be used throughout: J_i and J_f are the initial and final nuclear spins, with parities pi_i and pi_f, and changes Delta J and Delta pi. The mirror nuclei 7Li and 7Be have isospin T = 1/2 with projections T_{zi} = +1/2 and T_{zf} = -1/2. The reduced Fermi and Gamow–Teller matrix elements are denoted M_F and M_{GT}. The weak vector and axial couplings are G_V and G_A. The K-shell electron-capture rate is lambda_K. The available neutrino energies for the two electron-capture branches are W_{nu1} and W_{nu2}. The branching ratio for a decay branch is B. The comparative half-life product is ft. The orbital angular momentum quantum number is l. For the detector calibration: I_0 is the neutrino emission rate from a point source at the center, a is the enrichment fraction of 7Li in the target, rho_{Li} is the mass density of the lithium target, n is Avogadro's number, A is the molar mass of 7Li, M is the total mass of the target, R is the target radius, r is the radial coordinate inside the sphere and dr is the shell thickness, phi_nu(r) is the neutrino flux at radius r, sigma is the neutrino-capture cross section on 7Li, Delta N_1 is the production rate of 7Be due to neutrino capture, and R_{dis} is the equilibrium disintegration rate of 7Be. For the two capture branches, take Q = 0.86 \unit{MeV} and the excitation energy of the 7Li 1/2^- state E_x = 0.48 \unit{MeV}, so W_{nu1} = Q and W_{nu2} = Q - E_x. Numerical constants: G_V = 1.42 \times 10^{-49} \unit{erg cm^3}, G_A = 1.60 \times 10^{-49} \unit{erg cm^3}, rho_{Li} = 0.53 \unit{g/cm^3}, n = 6.023 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}, A = 7 \unit{g/mol}, M = 10^6 \unit{g}, a = 0.925, and sigma = 10^{-43} \unit{cm^2}. For part (a), to keep the numerical estimate consistent with the source, use C_{rate} = 5/4 as the effective value of \langle M_{GT} \rangle^2 for the 3/2^- \to 3/2^- branch when evaluating the rate ratio, and use C_{ft} = 5/3 as the single-particle value of \langle M_{GT} \rangle^2 for the same branch when evaluating the ft ratio.

subquestions.subproblem: Discuss the electron-capture modes of the ground state of 7Be by providing estimates for the branching ratios and relative decay probabilities (ft ratios). Use the definitions in the context and assume Fermi (F) and Gamow–Teller (GT) contributions as allowed by selection rules.
subquestions.solution:
Two electron-capture modes are possible from the 7Be ground state to 7Li states.

$$J_i^{\pi_i} = \frac{3}{2}^- \to J_f^{\pi_f} = \frac{3}{2}^-$$

$$\Delta J = 0$$

$$\Delta \pi = +$$

This branch is a mixed Fermi and Gamow–Teller transition.

$$J_i^{\pi_i} = \frac{3}{2}^- \to J_f^{\pi_f} = \frac{1}{2}^-$$

$$\Delta J = 1$$

$$\Delta \pi = +$$

This branch is a pure Gamow–Teller transition.

For the Fermi matrix element between mirror nuclei with T = \frac{1}{2}, T_{zi} = \frac{1}{2}, T_{zf} = -\frac{1}{2}:

$$\langle M_F \rangle^2 = T(T+1) - T_{zi} T_{zf}$$

$$\langle M_F \rangle^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}$$

$$\langle M_F \rangle^2 = 1$$

For the GT matrix element estimate for the \frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{1}{2}^- branch with l = 1 (transition from l + \frac{1}{2} to l - \frac{1}{2}):

$$\langle M_{GT} \rangle^2 = \frac{4 l}{2 l + 1}$$

$$\langle M_{GT} \rangle^2 = \frac{4}{3}$$

For the numerical inputs for the neutrino energies used below:

$$W_{nu1} = 0.86 \unit{MeV}$$

$$W_{nu2} = 0.86 \unit{MeV} - 0.48 \unit{MeV}$$

With the proportionality for K-capture rates

$$\lambda_K \propto |M|^2 W_\nu^2$$

the ratio of K-capture rates is

$$\frac{\lambda_K\big(\frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{3}{2}^-\big)}{\lambda_K\big(\frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{1}{2}^-\big)} = \frac{C_{rate} + \frac{G_V^2}{G_A^2} \langle M_F \rangle^2}{\frac{4}{3}} \cdot \frac{W_{nu1}^2}{W_{nu2}^2}$$

Using the numerical inputs

$$C_{rate} = \frac{5}{4}$$

$$\frac{G_V}{G_A} = \frac{1.42}{1.60}$$

$$W_{nu1} = 0.86 \unit{MeV}$$

$$W_{nu2} = 0.86 \unit{MeV} - 0.48 \unit{MeV}$$

the rate ratio evaluates to

$$\frac{\lambda_K\big(\frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{3}{2}^-\big)}{\lambda_K\big(\frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{1}{2}^-\big)} = 9.43$$

Hence the branching ratios are

$$B\big(\tfrac{3}{2}^- \to \tfrac{3}{2}^-\big) = \frac{9.43}{10.43}$$

$$B\big(\tfrac{3}{2}^- \to \tfrac{1}{2}^-\big) = \frac{1}{10.43}$$

$$B\big(\tfrac{3}{2}^- \to \tfrac{3}{2}^-\big) = 90.4 \unit{\%}$$

$$B\big(\tfrac{3}{2}^- \to \tfrac{1}{2}^-\big) = 9.6 \unit{\%}$$

For the ft ratio of the two branches, using the single-particle value for the \frac{3}{2}^- \to \frac{3}{2}^- branch:

$$C_{ft} = \frac{5}{3}$$

$$\frac{(ft)_{3/2^-}}{(ft)_{1/2^-}} = \frac{\frac{4}{3}}{C_{ft} + \frac{G_V^2}{G_A^2} \langle M_F \rangle^2}$$

$$\frac{(ft)_{3/2^-}}{(ft)_{1/2^-}} = \frac{4}{5 + 3 \times 0.79}$$

$$\frac{(ft)_{3/2^-}}{(ft)_{1/2^-}} = 0.543$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the two branching ratios B(3/2^- -> 3/2^-) and B(3/2^- -> 1/2^-) as percentages, and the relative decay probability as the dimensionless ratio (ft)_{3/2^-}/(ft)_{1/2^-}. Report all three numerical results with 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: To calibrate this detector, a point source emitting 10^{17} monochromatic neutrinos per second with energy 1.5 \unit{MeV} is placed at the center of a one metric ton sphere of 7Li. Estimate the total equilibrium disintegration rate of 7Be. Use the definitions and constants in the context. The final answer should be reported as R_{dis} in units of \unit{s^{-1}}.
subquestions.solution:
Neutrino capture on 7Li produces 7Be, while 7Be decays back to 7Li by electron capture. Let the 7Be production rate be Delta N_1. Consider a spherical shell of radius r and thickness dr inside the target. The number of 7Li nuclei in the shell is

$$dN_{Li} = \frac{4 \pi r^2 \rho_{Li} n a}{A} dr$$

The neutrino flux at radius r is

$$\phi_\nu(r) = \frac{I_0}{4 \pi r^2}$$

The production rate from the shell is

$$d(\Delta N_1) = \phi_\nu(r) \sigma dN_{Li}$$

Integrating from r = 0 to r = R gives

$$\Delta N_1 = \int_0^R \frac{I_0}{4 \pi r^2} \sigma \frac{4 \pi r^2 \rho_{Li} n a}{A} dr$$

$$\Delta N_1 = \frac{I_0 \rho_{Li} n \sigma a R}{A}$$

Given the total target mass M, the target radius is

$$R = \bigg( \frac{3 M}{4 \pi \rho_{Li}} \bigg)^{\frac{1}{3}}$$

Numerically,

$$M = 10^6 \unit{g}$$

$$\rho_{Li} = 0.53 \unit{g/cm^3}$$

$$R = 76.7 \unit{cm}$$

Input values for the rate estimate are

$$a = 0.925$$

$$A = 7 \unit{g/mol}$$

$$n = 6.023 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}$$

$$I_0 = 10^{17} \unit{s^{-1}}$$

$$\sigma = 10^{-43} \unit{cm^2}$$

The production rate is

$$\Delta N_1 = \frac{\big( 10^{17} \unit{s^{-1}} \big) \big( 0.53 \unit{g/cm^3} \big) \big( 6.023 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}} \big) \big( 10^{-43} \unit{cm^2} \big) \big( 0.925 \big) \big( 76.7 \unit{cm} \big)}{7 \unit{g/mol}}$$

$$\Delta N_1 = 3.2 \times 10^{-2} \unit{s^{-1}}$$

At equilibrium, the 7Be disintegration rate equals the production rate

$$R_{dis} = \Delta N_1$$

$$R_{dis} = 3.2 \times 10^{-2} \unit{s^{-1}}$$

The number of 7Li nuclei produced by 7Be decays is negligible compared with the total number present in the target
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express R_{dis} as a numerical value in s^{-1}. Report the result with 2 significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta N_1 = \int_0^R \frac{I_0}{4 \pi r^2} \sigma \frac{4 \pi r^2 \rho_{Li} n a}{A} dr$$

context:
A nucleus of rest mass M is initially at rest in an excited state whose energy is \Delta E above the ground state of the nucleus. The nucleus emits a gamma-ray photon of energy h 
u and makes a transition to its ground state. Explain why the gamma-ray energy h 
u is not equal to the energy-level difference \Delta E and determine the fractional change f. Assume \Delta E < M c^2. Constants and variables: c is the speed of light, h is Planck's constant, 
u is the photon frequency, E is the total relativistic energy of the recoiling nucleus after emission, p is the magnitude of its recoil momentum, E_\gamma is the photon energy, and p_\gamma is the photon momentum. The fractional change is defined as f = (h 
u - \Delta E)/\Delta E.
solution:
The nucleus recoils when it emits a gamma-ray due to conservation of momentum, so part of the excitation energy becomes recoil kinetic energy and the photon energy is less than \Delta E.

$$
p = p_\gamma
$$

$$
E + E_\gamma = M c^2 + \Delta E
$$

$$
E_\gamma = h \nu
$$

$$
E_\gamma = p_\gamma c
$$

$$
E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + M^2 c^4}
$$

Eliminating p and E gives the exact photon energy

$$
E_\gamma = \frac{\Delta E^2 + 2 M c^2 \Delta E}{2 (M c^2 + \Delta E)}
$$

For \Delta E \ll M c^2, this becomes

$$
E_\gamma \approx \Delta E - \frac{(\Delta E)^2}{2 M c^2}
$$

From the definition of the fractional change

$$
f = \frac{h \nu - \Delta E}{\Delta E}
$$

Using E_\gamma = h \nu and the approximation above, we obtain

$$
f = - \frac{\Delta E}{2 M c^2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form f = ... and should be expressed solely in terms of \Delta E, M, and c.

grading_standard.formula: $$E_\gamma = \frac{\Delta E^2 + 2 M c^2 \Delta E}{2 (M c^2 + \Delta E)}$$

context: A hypothetical particle A has a ground-state rest mass m and an excited state A* whose excitation energy is ΔE, so the excited-state rest mass is m + ΔE/c^2. The particle is initially at rest and can be excited by absorbing a single γ-ray photon. Let c denote the speed of light, and let E_γ be the photon energy required to excite A to A*. Assume that ΔE/c^2 is not small compared to m. For intermediate steps one may use p_γ for the photon momentum and p for the recoil momentum of A after absorption. Find the resonant photon energy E_γ.
solution:
The resonant absorption process is
$$
\gamma + A \to A^*
$$
Conservation of energy gives
$$
E_\gamma + m c^2 = \sqrt{\left(m + \frac{\Delta E}{c^2}\right)^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2}
$$
Momentum conservation gives
$$
p = p_\gamma
$$
For a photon
$$
E_\gamma = p_\gamma c
$$
Combining the previous two relations yields
$$
p c = E_\gamma
$$
Substituting into the energy equation gives
$$
E_\gamma + m c^2 = \sqrt{\left(m + \frac{\Delta E}{c^2}\right)^2 c^4 + E_\gamma^2}
$$
Squaring both sides and canceling the common term yields
$$
2 m c^2 E_\gamma = 2 m c^2 \Delta E + (\Delta E)^2
$$
Solving for the resonant photon energy gives
$$
E_\gamma = \Delta E + \frac{(\Delta E)^2}{2 m c^2}
$$
Thus, the required γ-ray energy exceeds the excitation energy ΔE by (ΔE)^2/(2 m c^2), which accounts for the recoil energy of the particle.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_γ = [an expression], and your expression should use only the symbols m, ΔE, and c (no additional variables or numerical values).

grading_standard.formula:
$$
2 m c^2 E_\gamma = 2 m c^2 \Delta E + (\Delta E)^2
$$

context: A gold foil of thickness d = 0.02 \unit{cm} is irradiated by a beam of thermal neutrons with flux I = 10^{12} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}. The nuclide {}^{198}\!Au with a half-life T_{1/2} = 2.7 \unit{day} is produced by the reaction {}^{197}\!Au(n,\gamma){}^{198}\!Au. The density of gold is 19.3 \unit{g/cm^3} and the capture cross section for this reaction is \sigma = 97.8\times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}. {}^{197}\!Au is 100% naturally abundant. Definitions to be used in the solution: N_1(t) and N_2(t) denote the areal number densities (nuclei per unit area) of {}^{197}\!Au and {}^{198}\!Au in the foil at time t, respectively, with N_1(0) the initial value. The decay constant of {}^{198}\!Au is \lambda. The activity per unit area is A(t) = \lambda N_2(t). The saturation (maximum) activity is denoted A_{\max}. Avogadro's constant is N_A = 6.023\times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}

subquestions.subproblem: If the foil is irradiated for 5 minutes, what is the {}^{198}\!Au activity of the foil in decays/cm^2/s?
subquestions.solution:
Initially the number of {}^{197}\!Au nuclei per unit area of foil is
$$N_1(0) = \frac{0.02\times 19.3}{197}\times 6.023\times 10^{23}$$
$$N_1(0) = 1.18\times 10^{21} \unit{cm^{-2}}$$
Let the numbers of {}^{197}\!Au and {}^{198}\!Au nuclei at time t be N_1 and N_2 respectively, \sigma be the cross section of the (n,\gamma) reaction, I be the flux of the incident neutron beam, and \lambda be the decay constant of {}^{198}\!Au. The coupled rate equations are
$$\frac{dN_1}{dt} = -\sigma I N_1$$
$$\frac{dN_2}{dt} = \sigma I N_1 - \lambda N_2$$
Integrating gives
$$N_1(t) = N_1(0) e^{-\sigma I t}$$
$$N_2(t) = \frac{\sigma I}{\lambda - \sigma I} N_1(0) \left(e^{-\sigma I t} - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$$
The decay constant is
$$\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{2.7\times 24\times 3600}$$
$$\lambda = 2.97\times 10^{-6} \unit{s^{-1}}$$
The production rate parameter is
$$\sigma I = \left(9.78\times 10^{-23} \unit{cm^2}\right)\left(10^{12} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}\right)$$
$$\sigma I = 9.78\times 10^{-11} \unit{s^{-1}}$$
Therefore
$$\sigma I \ll \lambda$$
At t = 5 \unit{min} = 300 \unit{s}, the activity is A(t) = \lambda N_2(t), and under \sigma I \ll \lambda the activity simplifies to
$$A(300 \unit{s}) \approx \sigma I N_1(0) \left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$$
Inserting numbers gives
$$A(300 \unit{s}) = 9.78\times 10^{-11} \times 1.18\times 10^{21} \times \left[1 - \exp\left(-2.97\times 10^{-6} \times 300\right)\right] \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$
$$A(300 \unit{s}) = 1.03\times 10^{8} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the 198Au activity after 5 minutes as a numerical value in decays/cm^2/s, to three significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the maximum amount of {}^{198}\!Au/cm^2 that can be produced in the foil?
subquestions.solution:
After equilibrium is attained, the activity of a nuclide, and hence the number of its nuclei, remain constant. At saturation
$$\frac{dN_2}{dt} = 0$$
so
$$\lambda N_2 = \sigma I N_1$$
With negligible depletion of {}^{197}\!Au under these conditions, N_1 \approx N_1(0), giving
$$N_2 = \frac{\sigma I}{\lambda} N_1(0)$$
Numerically
$$N_2 = \frac{9.78\times 10^{-11}}{2.97\times 10^{-6}} \times 1.18\times 10^{21} \unit{cm^{-2}}$$
$$N_2 = 3.89\times 10^{16} \unit{cm^{-2}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the maximum areal number density of 198Au as a numerical value in nuclei/cm^2, to three significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: How long must the foil be irradiated if it is to have 2/3 of its maximum activity?
subquestions.solution:
Using A_{\max} for the saturation activity and the approximation A(t) \approx \sigma I N_1(0) \left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right), set
$$A(t) = \frac{2}{3} A_{\max}$$
Since A_{\max} \approx \sigma I N_1(0), solve for t to get
$$\frac{2}{3} A_{\max} = \sigma I N_1(0) \left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$$
$$t = -\frac{1}{\lambda} \ln\left(1 - \frac{2}{3} \frac{A_{\max}}{\sigma I N_1(0)}\right)$$
$$t = -\frac{1}{\lambda} \ln\left(1 - \frac{2}{3}\right)$$
$$t = 3.70\times 10^{5} \unit{s}$$
$$t = 4.28 \unit{day}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the required irradiation time as a numerical value in days, to three significant figures.

grading_standard.formula: $$N_2(t) = \frac{\sigma I}{\lambda - \sigma I} N_1(0) \left(e^{-\sigma I t} - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$$

context: In the fission of 235U, 4.5% of the fissions produce 133Sb. This isotope is unstable and is the parent of a chain of beta emitters ending in stable 133Cs through 133Te, 133I, and 133Xe. The half-lives are defined as follows. $$T_{1/2,Sb}=10\unit{min}$$ $$T_{1/2,Te}=60\unit{min}$$ $$T_{1/2,I}=22\unit{hours}$$ $$T_{1/2,Xe}=5.3\unit{days}$$ Use the following variable definitions throughout. Let N_1, N_2, N_3 be the numbers of atoms of 133Sb, 133Te, and 133I, respectively. Let \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 be their decay constants. Let f be the neutron flux, \sigma the fission cross section of 235U, N_0 the number of 235U atoms in the sample, C the production rate of 133Sb during irradiation, T the irradiation time, and t the time elapsed after removal from the pile. Use N_A for Avogadro's constant and the barn–centimeter relation given below. $$N_A=6.023\times 10^{23}\unit{mol^{-1}}$$ $$1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}$$ Define the separation efficiency by \eta, where \eta is the fraction of iodine atoms recovered by the chemical separation process, and define N as the number of iodine atoms obtained by that separation. The following approximations are to be used as stated in the solution. Approximation A1 (end of irradiation): $$N_3(T)\approx \frac{C}{\lambda_3}\bigl(1-e^{-\lambda_3 T}\bigr)$$ Approximation A2 (12 hours after removal, with t large compared to the Sb and Te half-lives): $$N_3(t)\approx \Bigl[N_3(T)+\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2-\lambda_3}N_2(T)+\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2 N_1(T)}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)(\lambda_2-\lambda_3)}\Bigr]e^{-\lambda_3 t}$$

subquestions.subproblem: A sample of 1 gram of uranium is irradiated in a pile for 60 minutes. During this time it is exposed to a uniform flux of 10^{11} neutrons/cm^2 sec. Calculate the number of atoms of Sb, Te, and I present upon removal from the pile. Note that uranium consists of 99.3% 238U and 0.7% 235U, and the neutron fission cross section of 235U is 500 barns. (You may neglect the shadowing of one part of the sample by another.)
subquestions.solution: The number of 235U atoms in the 1 gram uranium sample is $$N_0=\frac{1\unit{g}\cdot \frac{7}{1000}}{235\unit{g/mol}}\cdot N_A$$ The neutron flux and cross section are $$f=10^{11}\unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$ $$\sigma=500\unit{barn}$$ The production rate of 133Sb during irradiation is $$C=N_0 f \sigma \cdot \frac{9}{200}$$ The numerical value of the production rate is $$C=4.04\times 10^{7}\unit{s^{-1}}$$ The decay constants are defined by $$\lambda_1=\frac{\ln 2}{10\times 60\unit{s}}$$ $$\lambda_1=1.16\times 10^{-3}\unit{s^{-1}}$$ $$\lambda_2=\frac{\ln 2}{60\times 60\unit{s}}$$ $$\lambda_2=1.93\times 10^{-4}\unit{s^{-1}}$$ $$\lambda_3=\frac{\ln 2}{22\times 3600\unit{s}}$$ $$\lambda_3=8.75\times 10^{-6}\unit{s^{-1}}$$ The irradiation time is $$T=3600\unit{s}$$ For antimony, the rate equation and initial condition are $$\frac{dN_1}{dt}=C-\lambda_1 N_1$$ $$N_1(0)=0$$ The number of Sb atoms at removal is $$N_1(T)=\frac{C}{\lambda_1}(1-e^{-\lambda_1 T})$$ $$N_1(T)=3.43\times 10^{10}$$ For tellurium, the rate equation and initial condition are $$\frac{dN_2}{dt}=\lambda_1 N_1-\lambda_2 N_2$$ $$N_2(0)=0$$ The number of Te atoms at removal is $$N_2(T)=\frac{C}{\lambda_2}\Bigl(1+\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}e^{-\lambda_1 T}-\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}e^{-\lambda_2 T}\Bigr)$$ $$N_2(T)=8.38\times 10^{10}$$ For iodine, the rate equation and initial condition are $$\frac{dN_3}{dt}=\lambda_2 N_2-\lambda_3 N_3$$ $$N_3(0)=0$$ The exact number of I atoms at removal is $$N_3(T)=\frac{C}{\lambda_3}\Bigl[1-\frac{\lambda_2\lambda_3 e^{-\lambda_1 T}}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)}-\frac{\lambda_3\lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_2 T}}{(\lambda_2-\lambda_3)(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)}-\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2 e^{-\lambda_3 T}}{(\lambda_3-\lambda_1)(\lambda_3-\lambda_2)}\Bigr]$$ Using Approximation A1, $$N_3(T)\approx \frac{C}{\lambda_3}(1-e^{-\lambda_3 T})$$ $$N_3(T)=2.77\times 10^{10}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N1(T), N2(T), and N3(T), the numbers of atoms of 133Sb, 133Te, and 133I present upon removal (at time T), as numerical values. Report each value to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Twelve hours after removal from the pile the iodine present is removed by chemical separation. How many atoms of iodine would be obtained if the separation process was 75% efficient?
subquestions.solution: After removal from the pile there is no further production of Sb, but Sb, Te, and I present at t=0 (the removal time) continue to decay with N_1(T), N_2(T), N_3(T) as initial values. For antimony, $$N_1(t)=N_1(T)e^{-\lambda_1 t}$$ For tellurium, $$N_2(t)=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2-\lambda_1}N_1(T)e^{-\lambda_1 t}+\Bigl[N_2(T)+\frac{\lambda_1 N_1(T)}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}\Bigr]e^{-\lambda_2 t}$$ For iodine, $$N_3(t)=\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2 N_1(T)}{(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)(\lambda_3-\lambda_1)}e^{-\lambda_1 t}+\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_3-\lambda_2}\Bigl[N_2(T)+\frac{\lambda_1 N_1(T)}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}\Bigr]e^{-\lambda_2 t}+\Bigl[N_3(T)+\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2-\lambda_3}N_2(T)+\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2 N_1(T)}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)(\lambda_2-\lambda_3)}\Bigr]e^{-\lambda_3 t}$$ Evaluate at twelve hours after removal $$t=12\unit{hours}$$ Using Approximation A2, $$N_3(12\unit{hours})\approx \Bigl[N_3(T)+\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2-\lambda_3}N_2(T)+\frac{\lambda_1\lambda_2 N_1(T)}{(\lambda_1-\lambda_3)(\lambda_2-\lambda_3)}\Bigr]e^{-\lambda_3 t}$$ Numerically, $$N_3(12\unit{hours})=10^{10}[2.77+8.80+3.62]e^{-8.75\times 10^{-6}\times 12\times 3600}$$ $$N_3(12\unit{hours})=1.04\times 10^{11}$$ The separation efficiency is $$\eta=\frac{3}{4}$$ The number of iodine atoms obtained is $$N=\eta\,N_3(12\unit{hours})$$ $$N=7.81\times 10^{10}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N, the number of 133I atoms obtained by the separation (with separation efficiency η = 0.75), as a numerical value. Report the value to 3 significant figures.

context: A foil of 7Li with mass 0.05 \unit{g} is irradiated with thermal neutrons. The 7Li captures neutrons with microscopic capture cross section \sigma = 37 millibarns, with 1 \unit{b} = 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2} and 1 \unit{mb} = 10^{-3} \unit{b}. This forms 8Li, which undergoes \beta^- decay with half-life T_{1/2} = 0.85 \unit{s}. The foil is exposed to a steady neutron flux \phi = 3 \times 10^{12} \unit{s^{-1} cm^{-2}}. Let N_1(t) be the number of 7Li atoms and N_2(t) be the number of 8Li atoms in the foil at time t. Let \lambda be the 8Li decay constant, related to the half-life by \lambda = \ln 2 / T_{1/2}. Let A be the \beta activity, i.e., the number of \beta decays per second. Use Avogadro's number N_A = 6.023 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}. Assume the foil is thin so the flux is uniform and self-shielding is negligible. Find the equilibrium activity A when the foil is exposed to the given flux.
solution:
Define N_1(t) as the 7Li population and N_2(t) as the 8Li population. Initially,

$$
N_1(0) = \frac{1}{140} N_A
$$

$$
N_1(0) \approx 4.3 \times 10^{21}
$$

$$
N_2(0) = 0
$$

During irradiation, the 7Li population obeys

$$
\frac{dN_1}{dt} = - \sigma \phi N_1
$$

so that

$$
N_1(t) = N_1(0) e^{- \sigma \phi t}
$$

The 8Li population obeys

$$
\frac{dN_2}{dt} = - \frac{dN_1}{dt} - \lambda N_2
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dN_2}{dt} = \sigma \phi N_1(0) e^{- \sigma \phi t} - \lambda N_2
$$

Integrating yields

$$
N_2(t) = \frac{\sigma \phi}{\lambda - \sigma \phi} \big( e^{- \sigma \phi t} - e^{- \lambda t} \big) N_1(0)
$$

At the time t when a steady state is reached for N_2(t), set

$$
\frac{dN_2}{dt} = 0
$$

to obtain

$$
t = \frac{1}{\lambda - \sigma \phi} \ln \frac{\lambda}{\sigma \phi}
$$

Compute the parameters

$$
\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{0.85 \unit{s}}
$$

$$
\lambda \approx 0.816 \unit{s^{-1}}
$$

$$
\sigma = 3.7 \times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^2}
$$

$$
\phi = 3 \times 10^{12} \unit{s^{-1} cm^{-2}}
$$

$$
\sigma \phi = 1.11 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$

Thus,

$$
t \approx \frac{1}{\lambda} \ln \frac{\lambda}{\sigma \phi}
$$

$$
 t \approx 3.63 \unit{s}
$$

The equilibrium activity is

$$
A = \lambda N_2
$$

$$
A \approx \frac{\lambda \sigma \phi N_1(0)}{\lambda - \sigma \phi}
$$

$$
A \approx \sigma \phi N_1(0)
$$

$$
A = 4.77 \times 10^8 \unit{Bq}
$$

$$
A = 12.9 \unit{mc}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the equilibrium beta activity A as a numerical value in Bq (s^-1), given to 3 significant figures.

context: In a neutron-activation experiment, a normally incident neutron flux of magnitude φ = 10^8 with units \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}} irradiates a thin foil of area S = 1 with units \unit{cm^{2}}, atomic number density n = 10^{22} with units \unit{atoms/cm^{3}}, and thickness d = 10^{-2} with units \unit{cm}. The total neutron-capture cross section of the target nuclei is σ = 10^{-24} with units \unit{cm^{2}}. The reaction product is beta-unstable with decay constant λ = 10^{-4} with units \unit{s^{-1}}. Define N(t) as the number of untransmuted target nuclei at time t, N_{\beta}(t) as the number of unstable product nuclei at time t, and A(t) as the activity at time t. Assume the foil is sufficiently thin that the incident flux is uniform through the thickness and self-shielding is negligible. The irradiation duration is t = 100 with units \unit{s}. Use N(0) = n S d. Tasks: 1) Derive A(t) during irradiation. 2) Compute the numerical value A(100 \unit{s}).
solution:
Let N(t) be the number of target nuclei and N_{\beta}(t) be the number of unstable nuclei produced by neutron capture. For a thin target the depletion of target nuclei satisfies
$$
\frac{dN(t)}{dt}=-\sigma \phi N(t)
$$
Integrating gives
$$
N(t)=N(0)e^{-\sigma \phi t}
$$
Given
$$
\sigma=10^{-24} \unit{cm^{2}}
$$
$$
\phi=10^{8} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}
$$
Hence
$$
\sigma \phi=10^{-16} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
At the irradiation time
$$
 t=100 \unit{s}
$$
we obtain
$$
\sigma \phi t=10^{-14}
$$
Since
$$
\sigma \phi t \ll 1
$$
we can take
$$
N(t)\approx N(0)
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{dN}{dt}\approx-\sigma \phi N(0)
$$
For the unstable product nuclide the balance during irradiation is
$$
\frac{dN_{\beta}(t)}{dt}\approx\sigma \phi N(0)-\lambda N_{\beta}(t)
$$
Solving gives
$$
N_{\beta}(t)=\frac{\sigma \phi N(0)}{\lambda}(1-e^{-\lambda t})
$$
The activity is
$$
A(t)=\lambda N_{\beta}(t)
$$
Thus
$$
A(t)=\sigma \phi N(0)(1-e^{-\lambda t})
$$
The initial number of target nuclei in the foil is
$$
N(0)=n S d
$$
With the given geometry and number density
$$
 n=10^{22} \unit{atoms/cm^{3}}
$$
$$
 S=1 \unit{cm^{2}}
$$
$$
 d=10^{-2} \unit{cm}
$$
so
$$
N(0)=10^{20}
$$
For the decay constant
$$
\lambda=\frac{1}{10^{4}} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
$$
\lambda=10^{-4} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Evaluating the activity at the irradiation time gives
$$
A(100 \unit{s})=10^{-16}\times10^{22}\times1\times10^{-2}\times(1-e^{-10^{-2}}) \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Hence
$$
A(100 \unit{s})=99.5 \unit{s^{-1}}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form A(t) = ... and must use only the variables σ, φ, N(0), λ, and t.
Your final answer should express A(100 s) as a numerical value with units of s^{-1}. Round to 3 significant figures.

$$10^{-2} \unit{MeV}$$
$$10^{1} \unit{MeV}$$

context: Given the atomic mass excess values ΔM = M − A for neutral atoms (in keV): ΔM(^1n) = 8071 keV, ΔM(^1H) = 7289 keV, ΔM(^7Li) = 14907 keV, ΔM(^7Be) = 15769 keV. The electron rest energy is m_e c^2 = 511 keV. Consider the reaction ^7Li(p,n)^7Be. Notation used below: m_p is the proton rest mass, m_n is the neutron rest mass, m_{Li} is the ^7Li nuclear rest mass, m_{Be} is the ^7Be nuclear rest mass, ΔM(X) is the atomic mass excess of nuclide X, Q is the reaction energy, T is the proton kinetic energy in the laboratory frame, E and P are the proton total energy and momentum in the laboratory frame, V_p is the proton speed in the laboratory frame, and V_c is the center-of-mass speed in the laboratory frame.

subquestions.subproblem: Under what circumstances will the reaction ^7Li(p,n)^7Be occur?
subquestions.solution:
For ^7Li + p -> ^7Be + n + Q, the reaction energy is defined by Q = ΔM(^7Li) + ΔM(^1H) − ΔM(^7Be) − ΔM(^1n). At threshold in the center-of-mass frame, the total kinetic energy of ^7Li and p must equal |Q|. Using the laboratory frame invariant and a nonrelativistic approximation for the incident proton, the threshold kinetic energy can be obtained. We compute Q as follows:
$$Q = \Delta M(^7Li) + \Delta M(^1H) - \Delta M(^7Be) - \Delta M(^1n)$$
$$Q = 14907\unit{keV} + 7289\unit{keV} - 15769\unit{keV} - 8071\unit{keV}$$
$$Q = -1644\unit{keV}$$
The laboratory-frame invariant at threshold is
$$(E + m_{Li} c^2)^2 - P^2 c^2 = (|Q| + m_{Li} c^2 + m_p c^2)^2$$
with
$$E^2 = m_p^2 c^4 + P^2 c^2$$
and, for the incident proton,
$$E \approx T + m_p c^2$$
Using |Q| \ll m_{Li} c^2 and |Q| \ll m_p c^2, one obtains
$$2(E - m_p c^2) m_{Li} c^2 \approx 2|Q|(m_{Li} + m_p) c^2$$
so that
$$T = \frac{m_p + m_{Li}}{m_{Li}} |Q|$$
Numerically,
$$T \approx \frac{8}{7} \times 1644\unit{keV}$$
$$T \approx 1879\unit{keV}$$
Let T_{p,th} denote the threshold proton kinetic energy in the laboratory frame. Then
$$T_{p,th} \approx 1879\unit{keV}$$
and the reaction occurs when
$$T \ge T_{p,th}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should (i) state the condition for occurrence as the sentence 'The reaction occurs when T ≥ T_{p,th}.' and (ii) give the threshold proton kinetic energy in the laboratory frame as a numerical value in keV in the form 'T_{p,th} = ... keV.'

subquestions.subproblem: What will be the laboratory energy of the neutrons at threshold for neutron emission?
subquestions.solution:
At threshold, the neutron is produced at rest in the center-of-mass frame, so in the laboratory frame it moves with the center-of-mass speed V_c. The center-of-mass speed in the laboratory frame is
$$V_c = \frac{m_p}{m_p + m_{Li}} V_p$$
The neutron laboratory kinetic energy at threshold is
$$T_{n,lab} = \frac{1}{2} m_n V_c^2$$
Using the nonrelativistic relation for the proton,
$$T = \frac{1}{2} m_p V_p^2$$
we obtain
$$T_{n,lab} = \frac{m_n m_p}{(m_p + m_{Li})^2} T$$
Approximating m_n \u2248 m_p and m_{Li} \u2248 7 m_p gives
$$T_{n,lab} \approx \frac{T}{64}$$
At threshold, with T \u2248 1879\unit{keV}, this yields
$$T_{n,lab} \approx 29.4\unit{keV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the neutron laboratory kinetic energy at threshold as a numerical value in keV in the form 'T_{n,lab} = ... keV.'

grading_standard.formula: $$2(E - m_p c^2) m_{Li} c^2 \approx 2|Q|(m_{Li} + m_p) c^2$$

context:
A detector is coated with a thin layer of naturally fissioning heavy nuclei. The detector area is 2\unit{cm^2}. The mean life of the fissioning isotope is given by 
$$
\tau = \frac{1}{3} \times 10^9 \unit{yr}
$$
with the conversion 
$$
1\unit{yr} = 3 \times 10^7 \unit{s}
$$
In the absence of an external neutron flux, the number of fissions detected per second is 
$$
R_{\text{nat}} = 20 \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
The detector is then placed in a uniform neutron flux 
$$
\phi = 10^{11} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}
$$
and the total number of fissions detected per second becomes 
$$
R_{\text{tot}} = 120 \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Define the following variables for the solution: N(t) is the number of heavy nuclei at time t, N_0 = N(0) is the initial number of nuclei, \lambda = 1/\tau is the decay constant, \phi is the neutron flux as given above, and \sigma is the neutron-induced fission cross section to be determined. Assume the induced fission rate is 
$$
R_{\text{ind}} = \sigma N \phi
$$
and the natural fission rate is 
$$
R_{\text{nat}} = \lambda N
$$
Find the cross section \sigma.
solution:
The decay of the coated nuclei satisfies 
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N
$$
For the short times considered, the number of nuclei is approximately constant 
$$
N \approx N_0
$$
so the natural fission rate is 
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} \approx -\lambda N_0
$$
From the mean life, 
$$
\tau = \frac{1}{3} \times 10^9 \unit{yr}
$$
Using the time conversion, 
$$
1\unit{yr} = 3 \times 10^7 \unit{s}
$$
we obtain 
$$
\tau = 10^{16} \unit{s}
$$
The decay constant is 
$$
\lambda = \frac{1}{\tau}
$$
Thus 
$$
\lambda = 10^{-16} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
The total fission rate in the flux is the sum of natural and induced contributions 
$$
R_{\text{tot}} = \lambda N_0 + \sigma \phi N_0
$$
Form the ratio using the measured rates 
$$
\frac{R_{\text{tot}}}{R_{\text{nat}}} = \frac{120\unit{s^{-1}}}{20\unit{s^{-1}}}
$$
Hence 
$$
\frac{\lambda N_0 + \sigma \phi N_0}{\lambda N_0} = 6
$$
Therefore 
$$
\frac{\sigma \phi}{\lambda} + 1 = 6
$$
which gives 
$$
\frac{\sigma \phi}{\lambda} = 5
$$
and thus 
$$
\sigma = \frac{5\lambda}{\phi}
$$
Substitute the numerical values 
$$
\phi = 10^{11} \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}
$$
which yields 
$$
\sigma = \frac{5 \times 10^{-16}}{10^{11}} \unit{cm^2}
$$
Therefore 
$$
\sigma = 5 \times 10^{-27} \unit{cm^2}
$$
Using 
$$
1\unit{b} = 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$
and 
$$
1\unit{mb} = 10^{-3} \unit{b}
$$
we finally obtain 
$$
\sigma = 5 \unit{mb}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the neutron-induced fission cross section σ as numerical values in both cm^2 and mb. Report both values to 1 significant figure.

context: Let \sigma denote the total scattering cross-section for low-energy neutron–nucleus scattering, measured in \unit{cm^2}. Let r denote the radius of the sphere of action of nuclear forces, measured in \unit{cm}. Choose the typical value of \sigma from the following options: 10^{-16} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-32} \unit{cm^2}, 10^{-40} \unit{cm^2}.
solution:
For nuclear forces, the range r is of order 10^{-12} to 10^{-13} \unit{cm}, so a typical scattering cross-section is expected to be of the same order as the geometric cross-sectional area of the interaction region
$$\sigma \sim \pi r^2$$
This corresponds to the option 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$\sigma = 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}$$

context: Topic: Particle–antiparticle properties.
