context: Describe the properties of the three pions π+, π0, and π−, and discuss in detail the experiments that determine their spin J, parity P, and isospin I. Conventions and definitions: Use J_X for the spin of particle X, P(X) for its intrinsic parity, I(X) for its isospin, C(X) for the charge-conjugation parity of neutral states, and G(X) for G-parity, defined as charge conjugation followed by a rotation by π about the second isospin axis. Strong interactions conserve isospin and G-parity. Let σ denote a total cross section and dσ/dΩ a differential cross section. The deuteron, proton, and neutron are denoted by d, p, and n, respectively. In center-of-mass kinematics, p_π and p_p are the magnitudes of the center-of-mass momenta of the pion and proton, respectively; J_p and J_d are the proton and deuteron spins. The principle of detailed balance relates forward and inverse reaction cross sections when the transition matrix element is the same. In the decay π0 → 2γ, let ε1 and ε2 be the polarization vectors of the two real photons and k the photon three-momentum in the π0 rest frame; the two-photon final state is exchange symmetric. The symbol γ denotes a real photon. Let l be the orbital angular momentum of the relative motion of two final-state nucleons and J the total angular momentum. Use the isospin basis |I, I3⟩, where I3 is the third component of isospin. The symbols e^+ and e^- denote the positron and electron, respectively. The term s-wave denotes l = 0. Masses should be quoted in \unit{MeV}. Report the final identified quantum numbers as J_{\pi^+}, J_{\pi^-}, J_{\pi^0}, P(\pi^+), P(\pi^-), P(\pi^0), and I(\pi).
solution:
There are three kinds of pion: π+, π0, and π−. The π+ is the antiparticle of π− and π0 is its own antiparticle. They form an isospin triplet with I = 1. The charged pions have mass approximately 139.6 \unit{MeV}, and the neutral pion has mass approximately 135 \unit{MeV}. They are pseudoscalar mesons with negative intrinsic parity as determined below. The pion triplet has G-parity G = −1, and π0 has definite charge-conjugation parity C.

To determine the spin of π+, apply detailed balance to the reversible reaction π+ + d ↔ p + p, for which the forward and inverse processes share the same transition matrix element

$$
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(pp \to d\pi^+) = \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(d\pi^+ \to pp) \times 2 \frac{p_\pi^2 (2J_\pi + 1)(2J_d + 1)}{p_p^2 (2J_p + 1)^2}
$$

Experimental cross sections give

$$
2J_\pi + 1 = 1.00 \pm 0.01
$$

hence

$$
J_\pi = 0
$$

The spin of π− can be determined from the hyperfine structure of π-mesic atoms. By particle–antiparticle symmetry, π+ and π− have the same spin, so

$$
J_{\pi^-} = 0
$$

The spin of π0 can be determined from the decay π0 \to 2\gamma. A spin-1 state cannot decay into two real photons. In the two-photon center-of-mass frame, with photon momenta k and −k and polarization vectors ε1 and ε2, the available vector structures built from k, ε1, and ε2 are

$$
\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2
$$

$$
(\varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2) k
$$

$$
\bigl(k \cdot (\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2)\bigr) k
$$

Each changes sign under exchange of the two photons, but the two-photon system is bosonic and exchange symmetric, so none can represent the final state. Therefore π0 cannot have spin 1. Consider also the low-energy (s-wave) charge-exchange reaction

$$
\pi^- + p \to \pi^0 + n
$$

This reaction is forbidden for

$$
J_{\pi^0} \geq 2
$$

Experimentally the charge-exchange cross section is large, thus

$$
J_{\pi^0} = 0
$$

The parity of π− can be determined from the reaction with low-energy (s-wave) π−

$$
\pi^- + d \to n + n
$$

The deuteron has

$$
J_d^P = 1^+
$$

Thus

$$
P(\pi^-) = P(n)^2 (-1)^l
$$

Because the nn system is a pair of identical fermions, the total two-neutron state must be antisymmetric under exchange, which implies

$$
l = 1
$$

and

$$
J = 1
$$

giving

$$
P(\pi^-) = -1
$$

The parity of π+ can be determined by studying the energy dependence of the cross section for

$$
\pi^+ + d \to p + p
$$

with low-energy (s-wave) π+, yielding

$$
P(\pi^+) = -1
$$

The parity of π0 can be determined from polarization correlations in π0 \to 2\gamma. With J(π0) = 0 and an exchange-symmetric two-photon final state, the possible decay amplitudes are A_+ and A_-, where

$$
A_+ = \varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2
$$

and

$$
A_- = k \cdot (\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2)
$$

The amplitude A_+ corresponds to

$$
P(\pi^0) = +1
$$

and the amplitude A_- corresponds to

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

Observation of e^+e^- pair production by the two photons shows that the planes of the two pairs are predominantly perpendicular, favoring A_-, hence

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

The isospin of the pion can be deduced from strong-interaction processes

$$
n + p \to d + \pi^0
$$

and

$$
p + p \to d + \pi^+
$$

For the latter,

$$
|pp\rangle = |1,1\rangle
$$

and the final state also has

$$
|1,1\rangle
$$

so, with isospin conservation, the transition probability is effectively 100%. For the former,

$$
|np\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|1,0\rangle - |0,0\rangle\bigr)
$$

Only the component

$$
|1,0\rangle
$$

can transition to the final state d + π0 with isospin

$$
|1,0\rangle
$$

Thus the cross sections satisfy

$$
\sigma(pp \to d\pi^+) = 2 \sigma(pn \to d\pi^0)
$$

This agrees with experiment, therefore

$$
I(\pi) = 1
$$

Collecting the results

$$
J_{\pi^+} = 0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^-} = 0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^0} = 0
$$

$$
P(\pi^+) = -1
$$

$$
P(\pi^-) = -1
$$

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

$$
I(\pi) = 1
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the seven quantities J_{\pi^+}, J_{\pi^-}, J_{\pi^0}, P(\pi^+), P(\pi^-), P(\pi^0), and I(\pi) as numerical values. Provide them as a list of explicit equalities, one per line, using exactly these variable names and no additional variables, units, or explanatory text. Present them in the order: J_{\pi^+}, J_{\pi^-}, J_{\pi^0}, P(\pi^+), P(\pi^-), P(\pi^0), I(\pi).

context: The electrically neutral baryon Σ^0(1915) has mass 1915 \unit{MeV/c^2}, isospin I=1, and third component I_3=0. Let Γ_{K^- p}, Γ_{\bar K^0 n}, Γ_{\pi^- p}, and Γ_{\pi^+ \pi^-} denote the partial decay widths for the decays Σ^0(1915) → K^- p, Σ^0(1915) → \bar K^0 n, Σ^0(1915) → \pi^- p, and Σ^0(1915) → \pi^+ \pi^-, respectively. Assume that the masses of the nucleons, K^-, and \pi^- are such that all these decays are kinematically allowed, and disregard the small mass splittings within any isospin multiplet. Use the isospin convention that N=(p,n) is an isospin doublet, (\pi^+,\pi^0,\pi^-) is an isospin triplet, K=(K^+,K^0) is an isospin doublet, and \bar K=(K^-,\bar K^0) is the corresponding antiparticle doublet. The strong-interaction Hamiltonian H is taken to be isospin invariant. States are denoted by |I,I_3\rangle. The change in the third component of isospin between initial and final states is denoted by ΔI_3. The two-particle symbol Ψ(XY) denotes the isospin product state of particles X and Y, and Ψ(Σ^0) denotes the isospin state of the initial Σ^0(1915). Define the target ratios below and determine their values
solution: $$R_{\bar K^0 n} = \frac{\Gamma_{\bar K^0 n}}{\Gamma_{K^- p}}$$ $$R_{\pi^- p} = \frac{\Gamma_{\pi^- p}}{\Gamma_{K^- p}}$$ $$R_{\pi^+ \pi^-} = \frac{\Gamma_{\pi^+ \pi^-}}{\Gamma_{K^- p}}$$ $$|\Sigma^0(1915)\rangle = |1,0\rangle$$ $$|p\rangle = |\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\rangle$$ $$|n\rangle = |\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\rangle$$ $$|\bar K^0\rangle = |\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\rangle$$ $$|K^-\rangle = |\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\rangle$$ $$\Psi(\bar K^0 n) = |\bar K^0\rangle |n\rangle$$ $$\Psi(K^- p) = |K^-\rangle |p\rangle$$ $$\Psi(\bar K^0 n) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} |1,0\rangle + \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} |0,0\rangle$$ $$\Psi(K^- p) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} |1,0\rangle - \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} |0,0\rangle$$ $$\Psi(\Sigma^0) = |1,0\rangle$$ $$a_1 = \langle 1,0|H|1,0\rangle$$ $$\langle 1,0|H|0,0\rangle = 0$$ $$\langle \Psi(\Sigma^0)|H|\Psi(\bar K^0 n)\rangle = \frac{a_1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ $$\langle \Psi(\Sigma^0)|H|\Psi(K^- p)\rangle = \frac{a_1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ $$\Gamma_{\bar K^0 n} \propto \left| \langle \Psi(\Sigma^0)|H|\Psi(\bar K^0 n)\rangle \right|^2$$ $$\Gamma_{\bar K^0 n} \propto \left( \frac{a_1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^2$$ $$\Gamma_{\bar K^0 n} \propto \frac{a_1^2}{2}$$ $$\Gamma_{K^- p} \propto \left| \langle \Psi(\Sigma^0)|H|\Psi(K^- p)\rangle \right|^2$$ $$\Gamma_{K^- p} \propto \left( \frac{a_1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)^2$$ $$\Gamma_{K^- p} \propto \frac{a_1^2}{2}$$ $$R_{\bar K^0 n} = 1$$ $$\Delta I_3 = -\frac{1}{2}$$ $$\Delta I_3 \ne 0$$ $$R_{\pi^- p} \ll 1$$ $$R_{\pi^- p} \sim 10^{-10}$$ $$\Gamma_{\pi^+ \pi^-} = 0$$ $$R_{\pi^+ \pi^-} = 0$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the three ratios R_{\bar K^0 n}, R_{\pi^- p}, and R_{\pi^+ \pi^-} as numerical values. Use scientific notation where appropriate. For any approximate value, report the result to 1 significant figure. Provide your answer in the form: R_{\bar K^0 n} = ..., R_{\pi^- p} = ..., R_{\pi^+ \pi^-} = ....

context: We consider the addition of two angular momenta j_1 and j_2 (for example orbital L and spin S). Individual angular-momentum eigenkets are written |j m⟩ and total-angular-momentum eigenkets are written |J M⟩. The Clebsch–Gordan (CG) coefficients C^{JM}_{j_1 m_1 j_2 m_2} are defined by the expansion |J M⟩ = ∑_{m_1,m_2} C^{JM}_{j_1 m_1 j_2 m_2} |j_1 m_1⟩ |j_2 m_2⟩. The total lowering operator is L_- = J_x - i J_y and acts as L_- |J M⟩ = √(J(J+1) - M(M-1)) |J, M-1⟩. It decomposes as L_- = L_-^{(1)} + L_-^{(2)} with L_-^{(k)} = j_{k x} - i j_{k y} acting on the kth space. In part (b) we work in isospin space with kets |I, I_3⟩. The pion has I_π = 1 with states π^+, π^0, π^- corresponding to I_3 = +1, 0, -1, and the nucleon has I_n = 1/2 with p and n corresponding to I_3 = +1/2 and -1/2. The strong-interaction Hamiltonian Ĥ is assumed to be isospin invariant (charge independent), so its matrix elements within a definite total isospin I are independent of I_3; we denote a_1 = ⟨3/2, m_j| Ĥ |3/2, m_i⟩ and a_2 = ⟨1/2, m_j| Ĥ |1/2, m_i⟩. We denote by σ_1, σ_2, σ_3 the total cross sections for reactions (1), (2), (3) specified below, respectively. At an energy where a single isospin resonance dominates, the contribution from the other isospin channel may be neglected.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for the coupled state with J = j_1 + j_2 and M = m_1 + m_2 for j_1 = 1, j_2 = 1/2, J = 3/2, M = 1/2. Report the nonzero coefficients C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1 m_1; 1/2 m_2} for the allowed pairs (m_1, m_2).
subquestions.solution:
First consider the highest-weight state
$$|\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle = |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
The total lowering operator and its decomposition are
$$L_- = J_x - i J_y$$
$$L_- = (j_{1x} - i j_{1y}) + (j_{2x} - i j_{2y})$$
$$L_- \equiv L_-^{(1)} + L_-^{(2)}$$
Apply L_- to the highest-weight state
$$L_- |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle = L_-^{(1)} |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + L_-^{(2)} |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Using the action of the lowering operator
$$L_- |J, M\rangle = \sqrt{J(J+1) - M(M-1)} |J, M-1\rangle$$
we obtain
$$\sqrt{3}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle = \sqrt{2}\, |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Hence the coupled state is
$$|\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Reading off the CG coefficients
$$C^{\,3/2,\,1/2}_{1,\,0;\,1/2,\,1/2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}$$
$$C^{\,3/2,\,1/2}_{1,\,1;\,1/2,\,-1/2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the numerical values of the nonzero coefficients C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1, 0; 1/2, 1/2} and C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1, 1; 1/2, -1/2}. Report each coefficient explicitly as "C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1, 0; 1/2, 1/2} = ..." and "C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1, 1; 1/2, -1/2} = ...".

subquestions.subproblem: Consider the reactions (1) π^+ p → π^+ p, (2) π^- p → π^- p, (3) π^- p → π^0 n. These reactions conserve isospin and can proceed via total isospin I = 3/2 (Δ resonance) or I = 1/2 (N^* resonance). Calculate the ratio of the cross sections σ_1 : σ_2 : σ_3 at an energy corresponding to a Δ resonance and, separately, at an energy corresponding to an N^* resonance. At a resonance energy you may neglect the contribution from the other isospin channel. The pion has isospin I_π = 1 and the nucleon has isospin I_n = 1/2.
subquestions.solution:
Couple the initial states in isospin space
$$|\pi^+ p\rangle = |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^+ p\rangle = |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^- p\rangle = |1, -1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^- p\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^0 n\rangle = |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^0 n\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle - \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Isospin invariance implies m-independent matrix elements within each I
$$\langle \tfrac{3}{2}, m_j | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2}, m_i \rangle = a_1$$
$$\langle \tfrac{1}{2}, m_j | \hat{H} | \tfrac{1}{2}, m_i \rangle = a_2$$
Orthogonality between different I gives
$$\langle \tfrac{1}{2} | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2} \rangle = 0$$
Thus the transition cross sections are
$$\sigma_1(\pi^+ p \to \pi^+ p) \propto |\langle \tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2} | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2} \rangle|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 \propto |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_2(\pi^- p \to \pi^- p) \propto \left| \tfrac{2}{3} a_2 + \tfrac{1}{3} a_1 \right|^2$$
$$\sigma_3(\pi^- p \to \pi^0 n) \propto \left| -\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a_2 + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a_1 \right|^2$$
At a Δ resonance, |a_1| \gg |a_2|, so we neglect a_2
$$\sigma_1 \propto |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_2 \propto \tfrac{1}{9} |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_3 \propto \tfrac{2}{9} |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 : \sigma_2 : \sigma_3 = 9 : 1 : 2$$
At an N^* resonance, |a_1| \ll |a_2|, so we neglect a_1
$$\sigma_1 \approx 0$$
$$\sigma_2 \propto \tfrac{4}{9} |a_2|^2$$
$$\sigma_3 \propto \tfrac{2}{9} |a_2|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 : \sigma_2 : \sigma_3 = 0 : 2 : 1$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present the ratios at a Δ resonance and at an N^* resonance in the form "σ1 : σ2 : σ3 = ..." for each case, using numerical ratios.

context: Estimate the ratios of decay rates given below, stating clearly the selection rules (fundamental or phenomenological) which are operating. Also state whether each decay (regardless of the ratio) is strong, electromagnetic or weak. If at all possible, express your answer in terms of the fundamental constants G, \alpha, \theta_c, m_K, etc. Assume that the strong interactions have unit strength (i.e., unit dimensionless coupling constant). Conventions and definitions used below: I is total isospin, I_3 its third component, J total angular momentum, and l orbital angular momentum. C(X) and G(X) are the C- and G-parities of state X. CP denotes the combined charge-conjugation and parity transformation. \Delta I, \Delta S, and \Delta Q denote the changes in isospin, strangeness, and hadronic charge. K_s^0 and K_L^0 are the short- and long-lived neutral kaon states. \Gamma(X \to Y) is the partial decay width for X \to Y, and B(X \to Y) its branching ratio. A_0 and A_2 are the nonleptonic K-decay isospin amplitudes with \Delta I = \frac{1}{2} and \frac{3}{2}. For pseudoscalar-to-lepton-neutrino decays, f_\varphi is the meson decay constant, m_\varphi the meson mass, and m_l the charged lepton mass; f_\pi and f_K are the pion and kaon decay constants. m_e and m_\mu are the electron and muon masses. The Cabibbo angle is \theta_c. Charged-current couplings are proportional to G \cos \theta_c for \Delta S = 0 and G \sin \theta_c for \Delta S = 1. Selection rule for semileptonic strangeness-changing decays: \Delta Q = \Delta S for the hadronic current. In the subproblems, a ratio written as X a b c over Y d e f denotes the ratio of partial widths \Gamma(X \to a b c)/\Gamma(Y \to d e f). Units, when used in formulas, are written with \unit{}.

subquestions.solution:
Consider K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0. This is a nonleptonic weak decay with the phenomenological \Delta I = \frac{1}{2} rule dominating. Since I(K) = \frac{1}{2}, and for a spin-0 parent decaying to two pions in an S-wave the two-pion wave function must be symmetric under interchange, the isospin of the two pions must be I = 0 or I = 2. For \pi^+ \pi^0, I_3 = 1, which is incompatible with I = 0, and thus this decay is forbidden by the isospin argument, while K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is allowed and satisfies \Delta I = \frac{1}{2}. Therefore the ratio is strongly suppressed for nonleptonic weak decays.
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \ll 1
$$
The isospin-amplitude relation is
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} = \frac{3}{4} \left( \frac{A_2}{A_0} \right)^2
$$
Numerically,
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-3}
$$
which implies
$$
\frac{A_2}{A_0} \approx 0.045
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide exactly three lines: 1) Ratio: Γ(K^+→π^+π^0)/Γ(K_s^0→π^+π^−) = [algebraic expression written only with A_0 and A_2]. 2) Selection rules: [state the operative selection rules as short phrases]. 3) Interaction types: numerator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak], denominator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak].

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{\rho^0 \pi^0 \pi^0}{\rho^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$
subquestions.solution:
Consider \rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- and \rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0. The mode \rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is an allowed strong decay. For \rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0, C(\rho^0) = -1 while C(\pi^0 \pi^0) = +1, so this strong decay is forbidden by C-parity conservation. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)}{\Gamma(\rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \approx 0
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide exactly three lines: 1) Ratio: express Γ(ρ^0→π^0π^0)/Γ(ρ^0→π^+π^−) as a numerical value to 1 significant figure. 2) Selection rules: [state the operative selection rules as short phrases]. 3) Interaction types: numerator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak], denominator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak].

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-}{K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0}$
subquestions.solution:
Since K_L^0 is not a CP eigenstate, K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0 has a small but nonzero branching ratio
$$
B(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0) \approx 9.4 \times 10^{-4}
$$
The decay K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^- is a second-order weak flavor-changing neutral current process and is more suppressed. Therefore
$$
1 \gg \frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)}
$$
and
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)} \approx 0
$$
Experimentally,
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)} \approx \frac{10^{-8}}{10^{-3}}
$$
which gives
$$
\frac{10^{-8}}{10^{-3}} = 10^{-5}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide exactly three lines: 1) Ratio: express Γ(K_L^0→μ^+μ^−)/Γ(K_L^0→π^0π^0) as a numerical value to 1 significant figure. 2) Selection rules: [state the operative selection rules as short phrases]. 3) Interaction types: numerator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak], denominator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak].

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-}{\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}$ g $\frac{\Lambda^0 K^- \pi^+}{\Lambda^0 p \pi^-}$
subquestions.solution:
Consider \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-. The \eta^0 has J^P = 0^- and decays electromagnetically with total width
$$
\Gamma(\eta^0) = 0.83 \unit{keV}
$$
Since J^P(\pi^{\pm}) = 0^-, a two-pion system from an S-wave has positive parity, and parity is conserved in electromagnetic decays, so \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is forbidden. The decay \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0 is an allowed electromagnetic decay consistent with conservation laws. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)}{\Gamma(\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)} = 0
$$

Block 2 (Λ^0 modes): 4) Ratio 2: express Γ(Λ^0→K^-π^+)/Γ(Λ^0→pπ^-) as a numerical value to 1 significant figure. 5) Selection rules 2: [state the operative selection rules as short phrases]. 6) Interaction types 2: numerator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak], denominator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak].

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{\theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}{\omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}$
subquestions.solution:
Consider \theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0. The \theta^0 has strong decays with total width
$$
\Gamma(\theta^0) = 180 \unit{MeV}
$$
and I^G J^{PC} = 0^+ 2^{++}. For the three-pion final state, G(\pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0) = (-1)^3 = -1, whereas G(\theta^0) = +1, so G-parity is not conserved and the decay is forbidden. For \omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0, with I^G J^{PC}(\omega^0) = 0^- 1^{--}, the decay is allowed. Therefore
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)}{\Gamma(\omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)} = 0
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide exactly three lines: 1) Ratio: express Γ(θ^0→π^+π^-π^0)/Γ(ω^0→π^+π^-π^0) as a numerical value to 1 significant figure. 2) Selection rules: [state the operative selection rules as short phrases]. 3) Interaction types: numerator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak], denominator=[strong/electromagnetic/weak].

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{\Sigma^- \Lambda^0 \pi^-}{\Sigma^- n \pi^-}$
subquestions.solution:
Consider \Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^- and \Sigma^- \to n \pi^-. Since \Delta S = 0 for \Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^-, this decay is forbidden under the nonleptonic weak selection considered here, while \Sigma^- \to n \pi^- is an allowed nonleptonic weak decay. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^-)}{\Gamma(\Sigma^- \to n \pi^-)} = 0
$$

subquestions.subproblem: $\frac{\pi^- e^- \bar{\nu}}{K^+ \mu^+ \nu}$
subquestions.solution:
Consider the semileptonic two-body decays \pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu} and K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu. For \Delta S = 0 the coupling is G \cos \theta_c, and for \Delta S = 1 it is G \sin \theta_c. For a pseudoscalar meson \varphi decaying to a charged lepton l and a neutrino, the width is
$$
\Gamma(\varphi \to l \nu) = \frac{f_{\varphi}^2 m_l^2 (m_{\varphi}^2 - m_l^2)^2}{4 \pi m_{\varphi}^3}
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} = \frac{f_{\pi}^2 m_e^2 (m_{\pi}^2 - m_e^2)^2 m_K^3}{f_K^2 m_{\mu}^2 (m_K^2 - m_{\mu}^2)^2 m_{\pi}^3}
$$
Including the coupling factors gives
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} = \frac{m_K^3 m_e^2 (m_{\pi}^2 - m_e^2)^2}{m_{\pi}^3 m_{\mu}^2 (m_K^2 - m_{\mu}^2)^2} \cot^2 \theta_c
$$
With
$$
\theta_c \approx 13.1 \unit{deg}
$$
we find
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} \approx 1.35 \times 10^{-4}
$$

context: A particle X has two decay modes with partial decay rates gamma_1 (in \unit{s^{-1}}) and gamma_2 (in \unit{s^{-1}}). Let lambda denote the total decay rate of X (in \unit{s^{-1}}), and let tau denote the mean lifetime (in \unit{s}). The inherent uncertainty in the mass of X (also called the decay width) is denoted by Gamma (in energy units), and hbar denotes the reduced Planck constant. In part b, consider the strong-interaction decay X -> pi^+ + pi^+. Assume that isospin is conserved in strong decays. Let I denote the total isospin and I_3 its third component. The charged pion pi^+ has I = 1 and I_3 = +1.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the inherent uncertainty in the mass of X?
subquestions.solution:
The total decay rate is
$$
lambda = gamma_1 + gamma_2
$$
The mean lifetime is
$$
	au = \frac{1}{\lambda}
$$
Using the expression for lambda, the mean lifetime is
$$
\tau = \frac{1}{gamma_1 + gamma_2}
$$
By the uncertainty principle, the mass uncertainty satisfies
$$
\Gamma \tau \sim \hbar
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma \sim \frac{\hbar}{\tau}
$$
Substituting for tau gives
$$
\Gamma \sim \hbar \left(gamma_1 + gamma_2\right)
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of Gamma = ... , and your response should be written with hbar, gamma_1, gamma_2.

subquestions.subproblem: One of the decay modes of X is the strong interaction decay X -> pi^+ + pi^+. What can you conclude about the isotopic spin of X?
subquestions.solution:
Since the decay is strong, isospin is conserved. For the charged pion,
$$
I(\pi^+) = 1
$$
and
$$
I_3(\pi^+) = +1
$$
Therefore, the two-pion final state has
$$
I_3(\text{final}) = +2
$$
The only total isospin that can have I_3 = +2 is
$$
I(\text{final}) = 2
$$
Thus the isospin of X is
$$
I_X = 2
$$

context: A negatively charged pi-meson (a pseudoscalar particle with spin 0 and odd intrinsic parity) is initially bound in the lowest-energy Coulomb wave function around a deuteron. The deuteron is a proton-neutron bound state in the 3S1 channel. It is captured and converted into a pair of neutrons. The reaction is $$\pi^- + d \to n + n$$ The assignments are $$J^P(d)=1^+$$ $$J^P(\pi^-)=0^-$$ $$J^P(n)=\frac{1}{2}^+$$ Let J denote the total angular momentum, L the orbital angular momentum of the relative motion of the two neutrons, and S their total spin. Let J_z, L_z, S_z be the corresponding projections on the quantization axis. The k direction defines the quantization axis. Let Y_\ell^m(\theta,\phi) denote spherical harmonics, and let \chi_{S M_S} denote two-neutron spin states with total spin S and projection M_S. The notation |J,M\rangle denotes a coupled total angular momentum eigenstate with total J and projection M. Let \Psi denote the total two-neutron state vector. The bracket $$\langle L, M_L; S, M_S \mid J, M \rangle$$ denotes a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient. For part (c), let W_{opp} denote the total probability for finding both neutron spins directed opposite to the spin of the initial deuteron. For part (d), let \frac{dW}{d\Omega} denote the differential emission probability per unit solid angle for a neutron whose spin is opposite to that of the initial deuteron

subquestions.subproblem: What is the orbital angular momentum of the neutron pair?
subquestions.solution: $$J=1$$ $$(-1)^L=-1$$ $$(-1)^L(-1)^{S+1}=-1$$ The two neutrons are identical fermions, so the total wave function is antisymmetric, which implies that L+S is even. The allowed total spin values are S equal to 0 or 1. The case S equal to 0 would require L to be even, which contradicts the condition (-1)^L equal to -1, so S must be 1 and L must be odd. If L is at least 3, then J cannot be 1 in the final state. Therefore $$L=1$$

context:
Consider the hyperon nonleptonic weak decays. Assume these ΔS=1 weak decays satisfy the ΔI=1/2 rule. Use Clebsch–Gordan tables to find the values of x, y, z as defined below. Here A denotes the transition amplitude, I is the total isospin, I_3 is its third component, and H_w is the weak Hamiltonian for these nonleptonic transitions. To implement the ΔI=1/2 rule in the isospin-coupling method used in the solution, introduce an auxiliary isodoublet a with isospin I_a=1/2 and third component I_{3,a}=-1/2.

$$\Lambda^0 \to p\,\pi^-$$

$$\Lambda^0 \to n\,\pi^0$$

$$\Sigma^- \to n\,\pi^-$$

$$\Sigma^+ \to p\,\pi^0$$

$$\Sigma^+ \to n\,\pi^+$$

$$\Xi^- \to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-$$

$$\Xi^0 \to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0$$

Define the ratios x, y, z by

$$x=\frac{A(\Lambda^0\to p\,\pi^-)}{A(\Lambda^0\to n\,\pi^0)}$$

$$y=\frac{A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^+ n)-A(\Sigma^-\to \pi^- n)}{A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^0 p)}$$

$$z=\frac{A(\Xi^0\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0)}{A(\Xi^-\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-) }$$
solution:
Impose the ΔI=1/2 rule by introducing an auxiliary isodoublet a with I_a=\tfrac{1}{2} and I_{3,a}=-\tfrac{1}{2}.

$$I_a=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$I_{3,a}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

Initial-state isospin couplings with a are

$$|\Lambda^0, a\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^-, a\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^-, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^+, a\rangle=|1,1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^+, a\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^0, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^0, a\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}|1,0\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}|0,0\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^-, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^-, a\rangle=|1,-1\rangle$$

Final-state isospin decompositions are

$$|\pi^-, p\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, p\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, p\rangle=|1,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, p\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^+, n\rangle=|1,1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^+, n\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, n\rangle=|1,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, n\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, n\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, n\rangle=\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^0\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,|1,0\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^0\rangle=|1,0\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^-\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,|1,-1\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^-\rangle=|1,-1\rangle$$

Define the reduced matrix elements of H_w by

$$M_{1/2}=\big\langle \tfrac{1}{2}\big|H_w\big|\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$M_{3/2}=\big\langle \tfrac{3}{2}\big|H_w\big|\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$M_{1}=\langle 1|H_w|1\rangle$$

For Λ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_1=A(\Lambda^0\to n\,\pi^0)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_2=A(\Lambda^0\to p\,\pi^-)= -\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

Thus

$$x=\frac{A_2}{A_1}$$

$$x=-\sqrt{2}$$

For Σ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_3=A(\Sigma^-\to \pi^- n)=M_{3/2}$$

$$A_4=A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^0 p)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{3/2}-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_4=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\big(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\big)$$

$$A_5=A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^+ n)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{3/2}+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_5=\frac{1}{3}\big(M_{3/2}+2M_{1/2}\big)$$

Hence

$$y=\frac{A_5-A_3}{A_4}$$

$$y=\frac{M_{3/2}+2M_{1/2}-3M_{3/2}}{\sqrt{2}\big(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\big)}$$

$$y=-\sqrt{2}$$

For Ξ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_6=A(\Xi^0\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\,M_1$$

$$A_7=A(\Xi^-\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-)=M_1$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{A_6}{A_7}$$

$$z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express x, y, and z as exact numerical values (you may use radicals). Do not provide decimal approximations.

context:
Consider the leptonic decays μ+ → e+ ν ν̄ and τ+ → e+ ν ν̄, which are both believed to proceed via the same weak interaction. Use the following definitions and data throughout: G_μ and G_τ are the weak-interaction constants governing μ and τ leptonic decays, respectively. λ_μ is the decay probability per unit time (width) for μ+ → e+ ν ν̄. λ_τ(τ+ → e+ ν ν̄) is the partial decay probability per unit time (partial width) for τ+ → e+ ν ν̄. λ is the total decay probability per unit time of τ+. τ_μ is the mean life of the μ+, and τ is the total mean life of the τ+. R is the experimental branching ratio for τ+ → e+ ν ν̄, defined by R = λ_τ(τ+ → e+ ν ν̄)/λ. In part b, E_cm denotes the total center-of-mass energy, E_τ is the τ energy in that frame, γ is the Lorentz factor, β = v/c is the speed in units of c, and L is the mean flight length in the laboratory frame. The speed of light is c = 3 × 10^{10} in units of \unit{cm/s}. Use the following masses:
$$m_\mu = 106 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_\tau = 1784 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_e = \frac{1}{2} \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_\nu = 0 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

subquestions.subproblem: If the μ+ mean life is 2.2 × 10^{-6} \unit{s}, estimate the τ+ mean life given that the experimental branching ratio for τ+ → e+ ν \bar{ν} is 16\%. Use the masses provided above
subquestions.solution:
The weak interaction gives for purely leptonic decays
$$\lambda_\mu = \tau_\mu^{-1}$$
$$\lambda_\mu = \frac{G_\mu^2 m_\mu^5}{192 \pi^3}$$
$$\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu}) = \frac{G_\tau^2 m_\tau^5}{192 \pi^3}$$
As the same weak interaction constant applies,
$$G_\mu = G_\tau$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}{\lambda_\mu} = \frac{m_\tau^5}{m_\mu^5}$$
Let λ be the total decay probability per unit time of τ+. The branching ratio is
$$R = \frac{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}{\lambda}$$
Thus,
$$\tau = \lambda^{-1}$$
$$\tau = \frac{R}{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}$$
Using the ratio with μ decay,
$$\tau = R \left( \frac{m_\mu}{m_\tau} \right)^5 \tau_\mu$$
Numerically,
$$\tau = \frac{4}{25} \left( \frac{106}{1784} \right)^5 2.2 \times 10^{-6} \unit{s}$$
$$\tau = 2.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the τ+ mean life τ as a numerical value in seconds (s), rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: If the τ+ is produced in a colliding-beam accelerator via e+ e− → τ+ τ− at E_cm = 29 \unit{GeV} with e+ and e− having equal and opposite momenta, find the mean distance L (in the laboratory) that the τ+ will travel before decay
subquestions.solution:
In the center-of-mass system, τ+ and τ− have the same energy
$$E_\tau = \frac{E_{cm}}{2}$$
With E_cm = 29 \unit{GeV},
$$E_\tau = \frac{29}{2} \unit{GeV}$$
Converting to MeV for consistency with the masses,
$$E_\tau = 14500 \unit{MeV}$$
Because the beams have equal and opposite momenta, the center-of-mass frame coincides with the laboratory frame. The Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma = \frac{E_\tau}{m_\tau c^2}$$
Numerically,
$$\gamma = \frac{14500}{1784}$$
$$\gamma = 8.13$$
The speed parameter is
$$\beta = \sqrt{1 - \gamma^{-2}}$$
Numerically,
$$\beta = 0.992$$
The mean flight length in the laboratory is
$$L = \beta c \gamma \tau$$
Numerically,
$$L = 0.992 \times 3 \times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s} \times 8.13 \times 2.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s}$$
$$L = 6.29 \times 10^{-2} \unit{cm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the mean flight length L as a numerical value in centimeters (cm), rounded to 3 significant figures.

solution:
Beta-decay theory gives the transition probability per unit time as
$$
W = 2 \pi G^2 |M|^2 \frac{dN}{dE_0}
$$
which implies the total decay rate scales as
$$
\lambda \propto E_0^5
$$
For two processes with the same coupling constant G and the same matrix element M,
$$
\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \left( \frac{E_{01}}{E_{02}} \right)^5
$$
Therefore,
$$
\lambda(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda e^- \bar{\nu}) = \left[ \frac{E_0(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda e^- \bar{\nu})}{E_0(n \to p e^- \bar{\nu})} \right]^5 \lambda_n
$$
Using endpoint energies from mass differences,
$$
\lambda(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda e^- \bar{\nu}) = \left( \frac{m_\Sigma - m_\Lambda - m_e}{m_n - m_p - m_e} \right)^5 \frac{1}{\tau_n}
$$
Inserting the given values,
$$
\lambda(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda e^- \bar{\nu}) = \left( \frac{1197.35 - 1116.058 - 0.51}{939.57 - 938.28 - 0.51} \right)^5 \times 10^{-3} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\lambda(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda e^- \bar{\nu}) = 1.19 \times 10^{7} \unit{s^{-1}}
$$

A high energy neutrino beam traverses a homogeneous detector. The neutrino–nucleon cross section rises linearly with the neutrino energy and is modeled as \(\sigma(E_

u)L\), where \(n\) is the number density of nucleons and \(L\) is the detector length along the beam. Use Avogadro's number \(N_A=6.022	imes 10^{23}\unit{1/mol}\) and the atomic mass unit \(m_u=1\unit{g/mol}\). A beam of neutrinos with energy \(E_

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the required detector length for \(\kappa_a=5.536\times 10^{-40}\unit{cm^2/GeV}\). Give the final answer as \(L_a\).

context:
An experiment in a gold mine in South Dakota has been carried out to detect solar neutrinos using the reaction ν + Cl^{37} → Ar^{37} + e^{-}. The detector contains approximately 4 × 10^5 liters of tetrachloroethylene (CCl4). Estimate how many atoms of Ar^{37} would be produced per day. List your assumptions. How can you improve the experiment?

Definitions and symbols:
- ν is a solar neutrino
- Cl^{37} and Ar^{37} are chlorine-37 and argon-37 nuclei, respectively
- e^{-} is the electron
- M_{Ar} and M_{Cl} are the atomic masses of Ar^{37} and Cl^{37}
- c is the speed of light
- E_{th} is the threshold neutrino energy for the reaction ν + Cl^{37} → Ar^{37} + e^{-}
- E_{ν} is the neutrino energy
- ρ is the density of CCl4
- A is the molecular weight of CCl4
- N_0 is Avogadro's number
- n is the number density of Cl nuclei in CCl4
- V is the detector volume
- \bar{σ} is the average interaction cross section per Cl nucleus
- F is the solar neutrino flux above threshold
- t is the exposure time
- N_{ν} is the expected number of detected neutrino interactions per day (equal to the number of Ar^{37} atoms produced per day)
- N_{Ar,day} is the number of Ar^{37} atoms produced per day
solution:
Threshold energy for the reaction is computed from the atomic mass difference
$$E_{th} = (M_{Ar} - M_{Cl}) c^2$$
Using the given numerical estimate for the mass difference in atomic mass units
$$E_{th} \approx 0.000874 \times 937.9 \unit{MeV}$$
Thus only neutrinos with energy above threshold can be detected
$$E_{th} \approx 0.82 \unit{MeV}$$
$$E_{\nu} > E_{th}$$

Assume the density of CCl4 is close to that of water
$$\rho \approx 1 \unit{g/cm^3}$$
The molecular weight of CCl4 is taken as
$$A = 172$$
Avogadro's number is
$$N_0 = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$$
Each CCl4 molecule contains four Cl atoms, so the number density of Cl nuclei is
$$n = \frac{4 \rho N_0}{A}$$
Numerically
$$n \approx \frac{4}{172} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$
$$n \approx 1.4 \times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$

The detector volume is
$$V = 4 \times 10^5 \unit{L}$$
Unit conversion
$$1 \unit{L} = 10^3 \unit{cm^3}$$
Thus
$$V = 4 \times 10^5 \times 10^3 \unit{cm^3}$$

Assume an average cross section per Cl nucleus
$$\bar{\sigma} \approx 1 \times 10^{-42} \unit{cm^2}$$
Assume the solar neutrino flux above threshold is
$$F = 1 \times 10^9 \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$
One day of running time is
$$t = 24 \times 3600 \unit{s}$$
The expected daily count is
$$N_{\nu} = n V \bar{\sigma} F t$$
Numerically
$$N_{\nu} = 1.4 \times 10^{22} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times 10^3 \times 1 \times 10^{-42} \times 1 \times 10^9 \times 24 \times 3600$$
$$N_{\nu} \approx 4.8 \times 10^2$$
Relating this to produced argon atoms per day
$$N_{Ar,day} = N_{\nu}$$
Thus
$$N_{Ar,day} \approx 4.8 \times 10^2$$

Physical limitation: only neutrinos with energies above threshold are detected, whereas most solar neutrinos from the primary pp process have lower energies. The dominant solar reaction is
$$p + p \to {}^{2}H + e^{+} + \nu_e$$
with a maximum neutrino energy
$$E_{\nu,\max} = 0.42 \unit{MeV}$$
Therefore most solar neutrinos are not detected in this setup.

Assumptions:
- ρ ≈ 1 g/cm^3 (CCl4 density close to water)
- A = 172 for CCl4
- N_0 = 6.02 × 10^{23}
- Average cross section \bar{σ} ≈ 10^{-42} cm^2 per Cl nucleus, weakly dependent on E_{ν} across the contributing spectrum
- Neutrino flux above threshold F ≈ 10^9 cm^{-2} s^{-1}
- All Cl nuclei are equally available as targets and detector efficiency is taken as 100%

Possible improvements:
- Use a target with a lower reaction threshold, such as Ga or In, to detect lower-energy solar neutrinos below 0.82 MeV
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N_{Ar,day} (the number of Ar^{37} atoms produced per day) as a numerical value. Report the value with 2 significant figures. Additionally, include a short bullet list of your assumptions and provide one concise proposal for improving the experiment.

context: Conventions and definitions used throughout. Part (a): We consider the decay Λ0 → p + π−. The Λ0 has spin J = 1/2 with quantization axis along z. The proton emission direction is specified by the solid angle Ω = (θ, φ), where θ is measured from the z-axis. The differential decay rate is dΓ/dΩ. For a fully polarized Λ0 along z, the angular distribution is dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ), where A is a normalization constant and λ is the asymmetry parameter. The proton helicity is λ′ = ±1/2, with helicity amplitudes a+ ≡ aλ′=+1/2 and a− ≡ aλ′=−1/2. The Λ0 spin projection on z is M = ±1/2, and M′ denotes an intermediate spin-projection index appearing in Wigner d-matrix sums. The total decay rate is W. The decay amplitude for a Λ0 of spin projection M decaying at rest into a proton of helicity λ′ emitted along Ω is fλ′M(θ, φ) = (2π)−1/2 D1/2Mλ′(φ, θ, 0) aλ′, where D and d are the Wigner D- and small-d matrices. The proton longitudinal polarization P is the expectation value of the proton helicity h with eigenvalues h = ±1/2, averaged over an unpolarized Λ0 ensemble. We use χ′ = +1/2 for λ′ = +1/2 and χ′ = −1/2 for λ′ = −1/2. Part (b): Isospin conventions are I(K) = 1/2 with I3(K+) = +1/2 and I3(K0) = −1/2, and I(π) = 1 with I3(π+) = +1, I3(π0) = 0, I3(π−) = −1. The short-lived neutral kaon is KS0. For two pions, Bose symmetry requires a symmetric total wavefunction; with spinless pions and orbital angular momentum l = 0, the spatial part is symmetric, so the isospin part must be symmetric, implying Iππ = 0 or 2. The ΔI = 1/2 rule means the weak transition operator transforms as I = 1/2, so from an initial I = 1/2 only Iππ = 0 or 1 is produced; intersecting with Bose symmetry selects Iππ = 0. Decay rates are denoted by Γ, and “relative rates” are ratios of these Γ. In the empirical comparison quoted below, σ(X → Y) denotes the experimentally observed decay rate for X → Y, used only to illustrate a measured hierarchy and not for a theoretical prediction

subquestions.subproblem: As is well known, parity is violated in the decay Λ0 → p + π−. If the Λ0 is fully polarized along the z-axis, then the proton angular distribution obeys dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ). Given the parameter λ, what is the longitudinal polarization P of the proton if the Λ0 is unpolarized? Here P denotes the expectation value of the proton helicity h with eigenvalues h = ±1/2.
subquestions.solution:
Parity is violated in Λ0 decay with s- and p-wave contributions. For a spin-1/2 hyperon at rest emitting a proton of helicity λ′ along Ω = (θ, φ), the decay amplitude is
$$
f_{\lambda' M}(\theta, \phi) = (2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} D^{\frac{1}{2}}_{M \lambda'}(\phi, \theta, 0) a_{\lambda'}
$$
The total decay rate is
$$
W = |a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}
$$
For a Λ0 fully polarized along z with M = +\frac{1}{2}, the angular distribution is
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = W^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} |f_{\lambda', \frac{1}{2}}(\theta, \phi)|^{2}
$$
Using small-d functions, this becomes
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = (2\pi W)^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} |a_{\lambda'}|^{2} \left[d^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\frac{1}{2} \lambda'}(\theta)\right]^{2}
$$
Evaluating the d-matrix elements gives
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = (2\pi W)^{-1} \left( |a_{+}|^{2} \cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2} + |a_{-}|^{2} \sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2} \right)
$$
Comparing with dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ) yields
$$
A = \frac{1}{4\pi}
$$
The asymmetry parameter is
$$
\lambda = \frac{|a_{+}|^{2} - |a_{-}|^{2}}{|a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}}
$$
For an unpolarized Λ0 ensemble, the proton longitudinal polarization is
$$
P = (2W)^{-1} \sum_{M} \int \left( \frac{1}{2} |f_{\frac{1}{2}, M}|^{2} - \frac{1}{2} |f_{-\frac{1}{2}, M}|^{2} \right) d\Omega
$$
Equivalently,
$$
P = (2W)^{-1} \sum_{M} \int \sum_{\lambda'} \chi' |f_{\lambda', M}|^{2} d\Omega
$$
Using the Wigner d-matrix identity with J = \frac{1}{2} and M, M′ = ±\frac{1}{2},
$$
\sum_{M'} \left(d^{J}_{M M'}(\theta)\right)^{2} = \sum_{M'} d^{J}_{M M'}(-\theta) d^{J}_{M' M}(\theta)
$$
and
$$
\sum_{M'} d^{J}_{M M'}(-\theta) d^{J}_{M' M}(\theta) = d^{J}_{M M}(\theta)
$$
one obtains
$$
P = W^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} \chi' |a_{\lambda'}|^{2}
$$
Therefore,
$$
P = \frac{1}{2} \frac{|a_{+}|^{2} - |a_{-}|^{2}}{|a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}}
$$
Substituting the expression for λ gives
$$
P = \frac{1}{2} \lambda
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form P = ... and your response should be written using only the variable λ.

subquestions.subproblem: For strangeness-changing hyperon decays in general, e.g., Λ → p π−, Λ → n π0, Σ+ → n π+, Σ+ → p π0, Σ− → n π−, K+ → π+ π0, KS0 → π+ π−, KS0 → π0 π0, there is ample evidence for the approximate validity of the ΔI = 1/2 rule (the transition Hamiltonian acts like a member of an isotopic spin doublet). What does the ΔI = 1/2 rule predict for the relative rates of K+ → π+ π0, KS0 → π+ π−, KS0 → π0 π0?
subquestions.solution:
With spinless kaons and pions and l = 0, the spatial wavefunction is symmetric, so Bose symmetry requires Iππ = 0 or 2. The ΔI = 1/2 rule from an initial I = 1/2 allows Iππ = 0 or 1, and the intersection implies Iππ = 0. For K+ → π+ π0, the final state has I3 = 1, so I = 0 is impossible and the decay would require I = 2, which violates ΔI = 1/2. The prediction is
$$
\Gamma(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{0}) = 0
$$
Experimentally one finds
$$
\frac{\sigma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{-})}{\sigma(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{0})} \approx 455
$$
For KS0 → π+ π− or π0 π0, the final state has I3 = 0, and the symmetry requirement selects I = 0, I3 = 0. The I = 0, I3 = 0 two-pion state in the isospin-coupled basis is
$$
|I , I_{3}\rangle = |0 , 0\rangle
$$
and
$$
|0 , 0\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \left( |1 , 1 ; 1 , -1\rangle + |1 , -1 ; 1 , 1\rangle - |1 , 0 ; 1 , 0\rangle \right)
$$
In terms of charge states this is
$$
|0 , 0\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \left( |\pi^{+} \pi^{-}\rangle + |\pi^{-} \pi^{+}\rangle - |\pi^{0} \pi^{0}\rangle \right)
$$
Therefore the predicted relative rates are
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{-})}{\Gamma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{0} \pi^{0})} = 2
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the relative rates as numerical values. Specifically, report in the explicit forms: Γ(K+ → π+ π0) = ... and Γ(KS0 → π+ π−)/Γ(KS0 → π0 π0) = ....

context:
Neglect CP violation. Work in natural units with \hbar=1 and c=1, so m_L and m_S denote the rest energies that enter the time evolution phases. The flavor states |K^0> and |\bar K^0> are related to the long- and short-lived eigenstates |K_L> and |K_S> by
$$
|K^0>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K_L>+|K_S>)
$$
$$
|\bar K^0>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K_L>-|K_S>)
$$
The lifetimes are defined by
$$
\tau_L=\frac{1}{\gamma_L}
$$
$$
\tau_S=\frac{1}{\gamma_S}
$$
with distinct rest energies
$$
m_L\neq m_S
$$
At time t=0 a meson is produced in the state
$$
|\psi(0)>=|K^0>
$$
Let H be the effective Hamiltonian that is diagonal in the basis \{|K_L>,|K_S>\} and generates time evolution. The mass eigenstates evolve as
$$
|K_L(t)>=e^{-i m_L t} e^{-\gamma_L t/2} |K_L>
$$
$$
|K_S(t)>=e^{-i m_S t} e^{-\gamma_S t/2} |K_S>
$$
Define the time-evolved state
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|\psi(0)>
$$
Let P_0(t) be the probability to find the system in the state |K^0> at time t and let \bar P_0(t) be the probability to find the system in the state |\bar K^0> at time t. Find P_0(t)-\bar P_0(t) in terms of \gamma_L, \gamma_S, m_L, and m_S
solution:
The time-evolved state is
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|\psi(0)>
$$
Using the initial condition gives
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|K^0>
$$
Time evolution in the mass basis yields
$$
|\Psi(t)>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}|K_L>+e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2}|K_S>\big)
$$
Invert the mixing to the flavor basis
$$
|K_L>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K^0>+|\bar K^0>)
$$
$$
|K_S>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K^0>-|\bar K^0>)
$$
Substituting gives
$$
|\Psi(t)>=\frac{1}{2}\big[(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}+e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2})|K^0>+(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}-e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2})|\bar K^0>\big]
$$
The total survival probability is
$$
<\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)>=P_0(t)+\bar P_0(t)
$$
The individual flavor probabilities are
$$
P_0(t)=\frac{1}{4}\big[e^{-\gamma_L t}+e^{-\gamma_S t}+2 e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)\big]
$$
$$
\bar P_0(t)=\frac{1}{4}\big[e^{-\gamma_L t}+e^{-\gamma_S t}-2 e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)\big]
$$
Therefore
$$
P_0(t)-\bar P_0(t)=e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P_0(t) - \bar P_0(t) = ..., and your response should be written with t, \gamma_L, \gamma_S, m_L, m_S only.

context: Experiments that scatter electrons off protons are used to investigate the proton charge structure, assuming the electromagnetic interaction of the electron is well understood. We consider an analogous process to study the charge structure of the neutral kaon: elastic scattering K^0 + e -> K^0 + e with invariant amplitude A. Neglect CP violation throughout. Define the CP eigenstates K_S^0 and K_L^0 with masses M_S and M_L, respectively, and let ΔM = M_L - M_S. In part (a) we use the equal-mass approximation M_L = M_S for the intermediate step that combines K^0 and \bar K^0 matrix elements, while in part (b) we keep the small mass difference ΔM explicit. Four-momenta are P_e and P_K for the incoming electron and kaon, and P_{e'} and P_{K'} for the outgoing electron and kaon. Three-momentum vectors are denoted by \vec p_e, \vec p_K, \vec p_{e'}, and \vec p_{K'}, with magnitudes p_e = |\vec p_e|, p_K = |\vec p_K|, p_{e'} = |\vec p_{e'}|, and p_{K'} = |\vec p_{K'}|. The corresponding energies are E_e, E_K, E_{e'}, and E_{K'}. The electron mass is m. The electromagnetic current is j_\mu(0). The charge-conjugation operator is C. The invariant matrix element is t_{fi}. The electron spinors are u(P) and \bar u(P) = u(P)^\dagger \gamma^0. The Dirac matrices are \gamma^\mu, and e is the electromagnetic coupling. The neutral-kaon electromagnetic form factor is F_K(q^2) with F_K(q^2) = q^2 g(q^2), where g(q^2) is finite at q^2 = 0. The differential cross section is d\sigma, the initial-state relative speed is v_r, the solid angle of the outgoing kaon is \Omega', and the scattering angle between \vec p_K and \vec p_{K'} is \theta'. Forward scattering means \theta' = 0 with \vec p_{K'} collinear with \vec p_K; for regeneration in the forward direction we have \vec p_{K_L} parallel to \vec p_{K_S}. Define A_s as the amplitude for K_L^0 + e -> K_L^0 + e (scattering) and A_R as the amplitude for K_L^0 + e -> K_S^0 + e (regeneration). Define very high energy for the incident K_L^0 by E_L^2 \gg M_S \Delta M, equivalently E_L \gg \Delta M, where E_L is the K_L^0 energy. For later convenience, define t_{fi}^{(c)} as the spin-conserving component of t_{fi} and t_{fi}^{(f)} as the spin-flip component.

subquestions.subproblem: Neglecting CP violation, express the amplitudes for the following processes in terms of A: K_L^0 + e -> K_L^0 + e (scattering, amplitude A_s) and K_L^0 + e -> K_S^0 + e (regeneration, amplitude A_R).
subquestions.solution: We have $$|K_S^0\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|K^0\rangle+|\bar K^0\rangle\big)$$ $$|K_L^0\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(|K^0\rangle-|\bar K^0\rangle\big)$$ If CP violation is neglected, K_L^0, K_S^0, and K^0 have the same mass. Then $$\langle K_L^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K_L^0 P_K\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\big\{\langle K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K^0 P_K\rangle+\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle\big\}$$ As $$\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle=\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|C^{-1} C j_\mu(0) C^{-1} C|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle$$ $$\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle=-\langle K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K^0 P_K\rangle$$ we obtain $$A_s=0$$ Similarly we have $$A_R=A$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should consist of two equations in the form A_s = ... and A_R = ..., expressed only with the symbols A_s, A_R, and A (no other quantities).

subquestions.subproblem: Consider the regeneration experiment K_L^0 + e -> K_S^0 + e, in which a kaon beam is incident on an electron target. At a very high energy E_K, what is the energy dependence of the differential cross section in the forward direction? Forward means the scattering angle is zero, with \vec p_{K_L} and \vec p_{K_S} collinear. That is, how does (d\sigma/d\Omega')_{\theta'=0} vary with E_K? Also, define very high energy.
subquestions.solution: Averaging over the spins of the initial electrons and summing over the final electrons we get $$d\sigma=\frac{1}{2 v_r}\frac{m^2}{4 E_K E_{K'} E_e E_{e'}}(2\pi)^4\delta(P_e+P_K-P_{e'}-P_{K'})\sum_{spin}|t_{fi}|^2\frac{d^3\vec p_{e'} d^3\vec p_{K'}}{(2\pi)^6}$$ Integration over \vec p_{e'} and E_{K'} gives $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega'}=\frac{m}{32\pi^2}\frac{p_{K'}}{p_K}\frac{\sum_{spin}|t_{fi}|^2}{m+E_K-(p_K E_{K'}/p_{K'})\cos\theta'}$$ where \theta' is the angle between \vec p_{K'} and \vec p_K. Momentum conservation requires $$P_{e'}+P_{K'}-P_e-P_K=0$$ giving $$m+\sqrt{M_L^2+|\vec p_K|^2}=\sqrt{m^2+|\vec p_e|^2}+\sqrt{M_S^2+|\vec p_{K'}|^2}$$ Define $$E_L=\sqrt{M_L^2+|\vec p_K|^2}$$ with $$M_L=M_S+\Delta M$$ so that $$E_L=\sqrt{(M_S+\Delta M)^2+|\vec p_K|^2}$$ If $$E_L^2\gg M_S\Delta M$$ or $$E_L\gg\Delta M$$ K_L^0 is said to have high energy. At this point the momentum equation becomes $$m+\sqrt{M_S^2+|\vec p_K|^2}=\sqrt{m^2+|\vec p_e|^2}+\sqrt{M_S^2+|\vec p_{K'}|^2}$$ which represents an elastic scattering process. For forward scattering, $$p_K=p_{K'}$$ and $$|\vec p_e|=0$$ and hence $$\left.\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega'}\right|_{\theta'=0}=\frac{1}{32\pi}\sum_{spin}|t_{fi}|^2$$ Now $$ (2\pi)^3\sqrt{4 E_K E_{K'}}\langle K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K^0 P_K\rangle=(P_K+P_{K'})_\mu F_K\big((P_{K'}-P_K)^2\big)$$ where the form factor satisfies $$F_K(q^2)=q^2 g(q^2)$$ with g(q^2) not singular at q^2=0. Thus $$t_{fi}=i e^2\bar u(P_{e'})\gamma^\mu u(P_e) g\big((P_{K'}-P_K)^2\big)(P_{K'}+P_K)_\mu$$ In the forward limit with the electron initially and finally at rest, the spin-conserving and spin-flip components are $$t_{fi}^{(c)}=i e^2 2 E_K g(0)$$ $$t_{fi}^{(f)}=0$$ Thus the forward differential cross section has the energy dependence $$\left.\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega'}\right|_{\theta'=0}\propto E_K^2$$ Very high energy here means $$E_L\gg\Delta M$$ equivalently $$E_L^2\gg M_S\Delta M$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two parts: (i) a proportionality statement in the form (dσ/dΩ')|_{θ' = 0} ∝ ... written as a function of E_K only; and (ii) a definition of 'very high energy' expressed as one or more explicit inequality relations of the form E_L ... ΔM (you may also include an equivalent relation involving M_S). Use only the symbols E_K, E_L, ΔM, M_S, (dσ/dΩ'), and θ' in your final expressions.

grading_standard.formula: $$\langle K_L^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K_L^0 P_K\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\big\{\langle K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|K^0 P_K\rangle+\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle\big\}$$
$$\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|j_\mu(0)|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle=\langle \bar K^0 P_{K'}|C^{-1} C j_\mu(0) C^{-1} C|\bar K^0 P_K\rangle$$

context: Conventions and definitions: The Higgs boson field is denoted by φ with mass m_H. A generic elementary fermion is denoted by f with mass m_f and electric charge Q_f in units of the electron charge. The W boson mass is m_W. The electromagnetic coupling is e and the fine-structure constant is α, related by e^2/(ħ c) = α. Four-momenta are k for the Higgs and p, q for the outgoing fermion and antifermion, with k^2 = m_H^2 and p^2 = q^2 = m_f^2. The corresponding energies are k_0, p_0, q_0 in the Higgs rest frame. The decay amplitude is M, the partial width is Γ_f, the total width is Γ, and the lifetime is τ with τ = Γ^{-1}. The color factor is a_f with a_f = 1 for leptons and a_f = 3 for quarks. In e^+ e^- annihilation, the center-of-mass energy squared is S. The magnitude of the final-state three-momentum in the center-of-mass frame is p^*, and the de Broglie wavelength is λ with λ = 1/p^*. The partial width to e^+ e^- is Γ_{ee}. The symbol γ denotes the photon and Z^0 denotes the neutral weak boson. In the phase-space integration in the Higgs rest frame, the symbol q without indices in radial integrals denotes the magnitude |\vec q| of the antifermion three-momentum, while q with indices denotes the antifermion four-momentum; similarly for p. Define σ_γ as the total cross section for e^+ e^- → \bar f f via photon exchange and σ_H as the total cross section for e^+ e^- → φ → \bar f f at resonance. Unless otherwise stated, natural units with ħ = c = 1 are used. For conversion to seconds, use ħ = 6.58 × 10^{-22} \unit{MeV s}. For numerical estimates use m_H ≈ 10\unit{GeV}, m_W ≈ 80\unit{GeV}, m_u = m_d = 0.35\unit{GeV}, m_s = 0.5\unit{GeV}, m_c = 1.5\unit{GeV}, m_b = 4.6\unit{GeV}, m_e = 0.5 × 10^{-3}\unit{GeV}, m_\mu = 0.11\unit{GeV}, m_\tau = 1.8\unit{GeV}, and α ≈ 1/137.

subquestions.subproblem: According to the Weinberg–Salam model, the Higgs boson φ couples to every elementary fermion f (quark or lepton) via the interaction (e m_f / m_W) φ \bar f f, where m_f is the fermion mass, e is the electron charge, and m_W is the mass of the W boson. Assuming that the Higgs boson is much heavier than the known quarks and leptons and that it decays primarily to the known quarks and leptons, calculate its lifetime in terms of its mass m_H. You may assume m_H ≫ m_f. For a numerical estimate, use the masses and constants listed in the context.
subquestions.solution:
Fermi's Golden Rule for the decay into two fermions gives the partial width
$$
\Gamma_f = \int \frac{d^3 p}{(2\pi)^3 2 p_0} \int \frac{d^3 q}{(2\pi)^3 2 q_0} \frac{(2\pi)^4}{2 k_0} \delta^4(k - p - q) |M|^2
$$
The squared matrix element is
$$
|M|^2 = 4 \left( \frac{e m_f}{m_W} \right)^2 (p \cdot q - m_f^2)
$$
Using momentum conservation with p + q = k,
$$
p \cdot q = \frac{k^2 - p^2 - q^2}{2}
$$
Thus,
$$
p \cdot q = \frac{m_H^2 - 2 m_f^2}{2}
$$
Therefore,
$$
|M|^2 = 2 \left( \frac{e m_f}{m_W} \right)^2 m_H^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)
$$
Evaluate the phase-space integral in the Higgs rest frame
$$
\Gamma_f = \int \frac{d^3 p\, d^3 q}{(2\pi)^6 4 p_0 q_0} \frac{(2\pi)^4}{2 m_H} \delta^4(k - p - q) |M|^2
$$
After integrating over angles and using q dq = q_0 dq_0,
$$
\Gamma_f = \frac{1}{8\pi m_H} \int \frac{q^2}{q_0^2} \frac{q_0}{q} dq_0 \delta(m_H - 2 q_0) |M|^2
$$
Carrying out the integral gives
$$
\Gamma_f = \frac{e^2 m_f^2 m_H}{4\pi m_W^2} \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2} \frac{1}{2}
$$
In the limit m_H \gg m_f,
$$
\Gamma_f \approx \frac{e^2 m_f^2 m_H}{8\pi m_W^2}
$$
Summing over all accessible fermions with color factor a_f,
$$
\Gamma = \sum \Gamma_i
$$
Thus,
$$
\Gamma = \frac{e^2 m_H}{8\pi m_W^2} \sum a_f m_f^2
$$
Including the phase-space factor for the b quark in the numerical estimate,
$$
\sum a_f m_f^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2} \approx \sum_{f \ne b} a_f m_f^2 + 3 m_b^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_b^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2}
$$
Using the given masses,
$$
\sum a_f m_f^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2} = 0.005^2 + 0.11^2 + 1.8^2 + 3 \times (0.35^2 + 0.35^2 + 0.5^2 + 1.5^2) + 3 \times 4.6^2 \left[ 1 - 4 \times \left( \frac{4.6}{10} \right)^2 \right]^{3/2}
$$
Hence,
$$
\sum a_f m_f^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2} = 15.3 \unit{GeV^2}
$$
Using e^2/(ħ c) = α,
$$
\Gamma = \frac{1}{8\pi} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right) \hbar c \frac{m_H}{m_W^2} \sum a_f m_f^2 \left( 1 - \frac{4 m_f^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{3/2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Gamma \approx \frac{1}{8\pi \times 137} \times \frac{10}{80^2} \times 15.3
$$
Therefore,
$$
\Gamma \approx 6.9 \times 10^{-6} \unit{GeV}
$$
The lifetime is
$$
\tau = \Gamma^{-1}
$$
In natural units,
$$
\tau = 145 \unit{MeV^{-1}}
$$
For conversion,
$$
\hbar = 6.58 \times 10^{-22} \unit{MeV s}
$$
Thus,
$$
\tau = 6.58 \times 10^{-22} \unit{MeV s} \times 145 \unit{MeV^{-1}}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\tau = 9.5 \times 10^{-20} \unit{s}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the Higgs boson lifetime τ as a numerical value in seconds in the form τ = ... s, rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Some theorists believe that the Higgs boson weighs approximately 10\unit{GeV}. If so, do you believe it would be observed in practice as a resonance in e^+ e^- annihilation (Fig. 3.22)? Roughly how large would the signal-to-background ratio be at resonance? Assume \sqrt{S} = 10\unit{GeV}.
subquestions.solution:
The process e^+ e^- → \bar f f proceeds via photon exchange and via an s-channel Higgs resonance. At \sqrt{S} = 10\unit{GeV}, Z^0 exchange can be neglected. The QED background cross section per fermion species is
$$
\sigma_{\bar f f} = \frac{4\pi \alpha^2}{3 S} Q_f^2
$$
Summing over accessible fermions with color factors a_f gives
$$
\sigma_\gamma = \frac{4\pi \alpha^2}{3 S} \sum Q_f^2 a_f
$$
The charge-weighted sum is
$$
\sum Q_f^2 a_f = \left( \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} \right) \times 3 + 1 + 1 + 1
$$
Thus,
$$
\sum Q_f^2 a_f = \frac{20}{3}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\sigma_\gamma = \frac{4\pi \alpha^2}{3 S} \cdot \frac{20}{3}
$$
Approximately,
$$
\sigma_\gamma \approx \frac{8\pi \alpha^2}{S}
$$
With
$$
S = m_H^2
$$
we have
$$
\sigma_\gamma \approx \frac{8\pi \alpha^2}{m_H^2}
$$
At resonance for the Higgs-mediated process,
$$
\sigma_H = \pi \lambda^2 \frac{\Gamma_{ee}}{\Gamma}
$$
Using λ = 1/p^*,
$$
\sigma_H \approx \pi p^{* -2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee}}{\Gamma}
$$
A rough estimate for the branching ratio is
$$
\frac{\Gamma_{ee}}{\Gamma} \approx \frac{(0.5 \times 10^{-3})^2}{15.3}
$$
Thus,
$$
\frac{\Gamma_{ee}}{\Gamma} \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-8}
$$
With
$$
(p^*)^2 = \frac{m_H^2}{4}
$$
Define the signal-to-background ratio
$$
R = \frac{\sigma_H}{\sigma_\gamma}
$$
Hence,
$$
R = \left( \frac{4\pi}{m_H^2} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-8} \right) \left( \frac{8\pi \alpha^2}{m_H^2} \right)^{-1}
$$
Therefore,
$$
R \approx \frac{0.8 \times 10^{-8}}{\alpha^2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
R \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}
$$
In e^+ e^- annihilation near 10\unit{GeV}, the background from photon exchange is thus roughly 10^4 times larger than the Higgs-resonance signal, making practical detection of the resonance extremely difficult.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the signal-to-background ratio at resonance as a numerical value in the form R = ..., where R denotes the signal-to-background ratio, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: It is generally recognized that there are at least three different kinds of neutrino. They can be distinguished by the reactions in which the neutrinos are created or absorbed. Let these three flavor eigenstates be denoted by ν_e, ν_μ, and ν_τ. It has been speculated that each of the neutrinos has a small but finite rest mass, possibly different for each type. For this question, suppose there is a small perturbing interaction between these neutrino types, in the absence of which all three types have the same nonzero rest mass M_0. Let the off-diagonal matrix element of this perturbation have the same real value ℏ ω_1 between each pair of neutrino types, and let the diagonal elements vanish in the flavor basis. Here ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. In parts (a) and the repeated entry later, the neutrino state is expanded as |ψ⟩ = a_1(t)|ν_e⟩ + a_2(t)|ν_μ⟩ + a_3(t)|ν_τ⟩, where a_1(t), a_2(t), a_3(t) are complex amplitudes and t is time. The probabilities to find the neutrino in ν_μ and ν_τ at time t are denoted by P_μ(t) and P_τ(t), with P_μ(t) = |a_2(t)|^2 and P_τ(t) = |a_3(t)|^2. The symbols A, A_1, A_2 denote integration constants determined by initial conditions. In part (b) we also consider a two-flavor approximation with flavor states ν_1 and ν_2, mixing angle θ, energy eigenvalues E_1 and E_2, flight path l, neutrino energy E, and mass-squared difference Δm^2, where l is in \unit{m}, E is in \unit{MeV}, and Δm^2 is in \unit{eV^2}. The second subquestion (b) can be answered independently of (a).

context: Calculate the ratio R for e^+ e^- -> hadrons at leading order (ignoring QCD and quark-mass effects). Define R = sigma(e^+ e^- -> hadrons) / sigma(e^+ e^- -> mu^+ mu^-). Let N_c = 3 be the number of QCD colors. Let Q_i be the electric charge (in units of e) of the quark flavor i that is kinematically accessible at the given center-of-mass energy. Use the leading-order expression R = N_c * sum_i Q_i^2. Compute R in the specified energy ranges.

subquestions.subproblem: just below the threshold for “charm” production,
subquestions.solution:
At this energy, the accessible quark flavors are u, d, and s, with charges Q_u = 2/3 and Q_d = Q_s = -1/3.
$$R = 3 \sum_{i} Q_i^2$$
For these flavors:
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s} Q_i^2 = \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9}$$
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s} Q_i^2 = \frac{2}{3}$$
$$R = 2$$

subquestions.subproblem: above that threshold but below the $b$ quark production threshold.
subquestions.solution:
At this energy, the accessible quark flavors are u, d, s, and c, with Q_c = 2/3.
$$R = 3 \sum_{i} Q_i^2$$
For these flavors:
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s,c} Q_i^2 = \frac{4}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{4}{9}$$
$$\sum_{i=u,d,s,c} Q_i^2 = \frac{10}{9}$$
$$R = \frac{10}{3}$$

context:
The bag model of hadron structure has colored quarks moving as independent spin-half Dirac particles within a spherical cavity of radius R. To obtain wave functions for particular hadron states, the individual quark orbitals must be combined to produce states of zero total color and the appropriate values of the spin and flavor (isospin, charge, strangeness) quantum numbers. In the approximation that the up and down quarks are massless, the lowest energy s-wave bag orbitals are given by the Dirac spinor
$$
\psi = N \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi \end{pmatrix}
$$
where N is a normalization constant, j_l is the spherical Bessel function, σ denotes the Pauli matrices, χ is a 2-component Pauli spinor, s is the position vector, r is the radial coordinate r = |s|, and \hat s = s / r is the radial unit vector. The wave number k is fixed by the bag boundary condition
$$
k = \frac{2.04}{R}
$$
Color labels are denoted by R, G, B. The single-quark electric charge eigenvalues (in units of the proton charge e) are defined by
$$
Q_u = \frac{2}{3}
$$
$$
Q_d = -\frac{1}{3}
$$
The total magnetic moment operator is defined by
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
where J_{EM} is the usual Dirac electromagnetic current for a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q in {\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3}}

subquestions.subproblem: The lowest-lying baryons (proton and neutron) are obtained by putting three quarks in this orbital. How would you construct the wave function for the proton and for the neutron, i.e., which quarks would be combined and what is the structure of the spin wave function consistent with the quantum numbers of proton and neutron and Pauli’s principle?
subquestions.solution:
Neglecting color, the lowest states of a baryon are symmetric under exchange of any two quarks. The third component of isospin for the proton is I_3 = \frac{1}{2}, while u has I_3 = \frac{1}{2} and d has I_3 = -\frac{1}{2}, so the proton’s quark content is uud. Since the total isospin is \frac{1}{2}, the flavor part cannot be completely symmetric under u \leftrightarrow d exchange; thus it must contain components of the form uud − udu. To maintain overall symmetry, multiply this by a spin wave function antisymmetric under exchange of the corresponding quarks. A convenient spin-up building block under exchange of quarks 2 and 3 is
$$
\nu_1 = u\uparrow(1)\, u\uparrow(2)\, d\downarrow(3) - u\uparrow(1)\, d\uparrow(2)\, u\downarrow(3)
$$
Exchanging the first and second quarks gives
$$
\nu_2 = u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow + d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Exchanging the first and third quarks gives
$$
\nu_3 = d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow + u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Combining and normalizing, the totally symmetric spin-flavor wave function for a spin-up proton is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}\big( 2\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow + 2\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow + 2\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, d\uparrow - u\uparrow\, d\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow \big)
$$
The totally antisymmetric color wave function is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big)
$$
Introduce the s-wave spinor orbitals
$$
\psi_{\uparrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\uparrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\uparrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\uparrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\psi_{\downarrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\downarrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\downarrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\downarrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Promote each spin arrow to the corresponding orbital spinor to obtain the spin-up proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
The spin-up neutron state is obtained by the isospin flip u \leftrightarrow d acting on the proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
For spin-down nucleons, interchange \uparrow and \downarrow in the above spin-up wave functions
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as explicit, normalized algebraic expressions for the spin-up proton and spin-up neutron three-quark states. Write each in the form (normalization) × (RGB − RBG + GBR − GRB + BRG − BGR) × [linear combination of uψ_↑, uψ_↓, dψ_↑, dψ_↓]. Use only the symbols R, G, B, u, d, ψ_↑, ψ_↓ and numerical constants in the final expressions. Do not introduce any additional variables, and provide both proton and neutron spin-up expressions explicitly.

subquestions.subproblem: The magnetic moment operator is defined as μ = ∫_{|s|<R} (1/2) s × J_EM d^3 s, where J_EM is the usual Dirac electric current operator. Find an expression for this operator in terms of the spin operators of the constituent quarks. You may leave integrals over Bessel functions undone.
subquestions.solution:
For a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q, the Dirac current is
$$
J_{EM} = Q \psi^{\dagger} \alpha \psi
$$
with
$$
\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma \\ \sigma & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Inserting the s-wave spinor gives
$$
J_{EM} = 2 Q |N|^2 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) \chi^{\dagger} ( \sigma \times \hat s ) \chi
$$
The magnetic moment operator is
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
Using the vector triple product and integrating over angles, the second term vanishes and we obtain
$$
\mu = 4 \pi Q |N|^2 \Big[ \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr \Big] \chi^{\dagger} \sigma \chi
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form μ = (scalar coefficient) × χ^† σ χ, written only with the symbols Q, N, k, R, r, j_0, j_1, π, χ, σ, and standard integral notation. You may leave the radial integral unevaluated and should not introduce any additional variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that μ_n / μ_p = -2/3. You may need the following Clebsch–Gordon coefficients:
subquestions.solution:
The Clebsch–Gordon coefficients are
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 1; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
$$
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 0; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = - \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}
$$
Let the common positive factor be
$$
C = 4 \pi |N|^2 \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr
$$
The expectation value of the proton magnetic moment for the spin-up state is
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = C
$$
Similarly, for the spin-up neutron
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 3 \times 4 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) + 6 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = - \frac{2}{3} C
$$
Therefore the ratio is
$$
\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = - \frac{2}{3}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be in the form μ_n/μ_p = (numerical value).

context:
In e^+ e^- annihilation experiments, a narrow resonance (with width smaller than the intrinsic energy spread of the two beams) has been observed at the center-of-mass energy E_{CM} = 9.5 \unit{GeV} for both channels. The reactions are
$$
e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^-
$$
$$
e^+ e^- \to \text{hadrons}
$$
Let E denote the center-of-mass energy variable that appears in the cross sections \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) and \sigma_h(E). Let M be the mass of the resonance and J its spin; for this resonance we take
$$
M = E_{CM}
$$
$$
E_{CM} = 9.5 \unit{GeV}
$$
$$
J = 1
$$
Let \Gamma be the total width, and \Gamma_{ee}, \Gamma_{\mu\mu}, \Gamma_h, \Gamma_{\tau\tau} be the partial widths for decays into e^+ e^-, \mu^+ \mu^-, hadrons, and \tau^+ \tau^- respectively. Assume lepton universality and neglect small phase-space differences so that
$$
\Gamma_{ee} = \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = \Gamma_{\tau\tau}
$$
The experimentally measured integrated cross sections are
$$
\int \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) dE = 8.5\times 10^{-33} \unit{cm^2 MeV}
$$
$$
\int \sigma_h(E) dE = 3.3\times 10^{-31} \unit{cm^2 MeV}
$$
Use the Breit–Wigner resonance formula to determine the partial widths \Gamma_{\mu\mu} and \Gamma_h for the \mu\mu and hadronic decays of the resonance. Report the final answers for \Gamma_{\mu\mu} and \Gamma_h in \unit{MeV}. You may use the conversion constant
$$
\hbar c = 197\times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV\,cm}
$$
solution:
The Breit–Wigner cross section for e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^- is
$$
\sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) = \frac{\pi (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_{\mu\mu}}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4}
$$
For e^+ e^- \to hadrons it is
$$
\sigma_h(E) = \frac{\pi (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_h}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4}
$$
The total width is
$$
\Gamma = \Gamma_{ee} + \Gamma_{\tau\tau} + \Gamma_{\mu\mu} + \Gamma_h
$$
By lepton universality
$$
\Gamma_{ee} = \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = \Gamma_{\tau\tau}
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma = 3 \Gamma_{\mu\mu} + \Gamma_h
$$
For this resonance
$$
M = 9.5 \unit{GeV}
$$
$$
J = 1
$$
The Breit–Wigner integral is
$$
\int \frac{dE}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4} = \frac{2\pi}{\Gamma}
$$
Therefore
$$
\int \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) dE = \frac{2\pi^2 (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_{\mu\mu}}{\Gamma}
$$
With J = 1 and \Gamma_{ee} = \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\int \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) dE = \frac{6 \pi^2}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{\mu\mu}^2}{\Gamma}
$$
Similarly
$$
\int \sigma_h(E) dE = \frac{6 \pi^2}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{\mu\mu} \Gamma_h}{\Gamma}
$$
Taking the ratio gives
$$
\Gamma_h = 38.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma = 41.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
Using the hadronic integral to solve for \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = \frac{M^2}{6 \pi^2} \frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma_h} \times 3.3\times 10^{-31} \unit{MeV^3\,cm^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = 5.42\times 10^{-26} \unit{MeV^3\,cm^2}
$$
To convert to usual units we use
$$
\hbar c = 197\times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV\,cm}
$$
and
$$
1 \unit{cm} = \frac{1}{197\times 10^{-13}} \unit{MeV^{-1}}
$$
Thus
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = 1.40\times 10^{-3} \unit{MeV}
$$
Using \Gamma_h = 38.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\Gamma_h = 5.42\times 10^{-2} \unit{MeV}
$$
For the total width
$$
\Gamma = 5.84\times 10^{-2} \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the partial widths as numerical values in MeV. Provide both values explicitly, labeled as Γ_μμ = ... MeV and Γ_h = ... MeV. Report each value to three significant figures and include units.

context: An accelerator under study at SLAC has as output bunches of electrons and positrons which are made to collide head-on. The laboratory frame is denoted by Σ, and the comoving frame of one bunch is denoted by Σ_0 with the x axis along the motion. Each particle has total energy E = 50 \unit{GeV} in Σ. Each bunch contains N = 10^{10} particles and is approximated in Σ as a cylinder of uniform charge density with laboratory radius R_b = 1 \unit{\mu m} and laboratory length L = 2 \unit{mm}. Let e be the elementary charge, m the electron rest mass, c the speed of light, and \mu_0 the vacuum permeability. Define v as the particle speed in Σ, \beta = v/c, and \gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}} = E/(m c^{2}). In Σ_0, let L_0 be the proper length and R_{b,0} the transverse radius of the comoving bunch. For the opposite bunch as seen in Σ_0, let \beta' be its dimensionless velocity (negative sign indicates opposite direction), with magnitude |\beta'| = 2\beta/(1+\beta^{2}), and let \gamma' = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta'^{2}} be the corresponding Lorentz factor. Let L' be the length of the opposite bunch in Σ_0. In part (b), t' is the total overlap time in Σ_0. For the field calculation in Σ, let \rho be the charge density magnitude, J the current density magnitude, B(s) the azimuthal magnetic field magnitude at cylindrical radius s from the bunch axis, l the laboratory bunch length (so l = L), C the circular Amperian contour of radius s, and I the total current enclosed by C. In part (d), let p be the particle momentum magnitude in Σ, p_{\perp} the acquired transverse momentum, \theta the deflection angle in Σ, and \Delta t the encounter duration with the opposite bunch. We also use pc = m \gamma v c and, in the ultrarelativistic limit relevant here, pc \approx E.

subquestions.subproblem: To an observer traveling with a bunch, what are the radius and length of its bunch and also the one of opposite sign?
subquestions.solution:
The Lorentz factor in Σ is
$$
\gamma = \frac{E}{m c^{2}}
$$
$$
