\gamma = \frac{50\times 10^{9}}{\frac{1}{2}\times 10^{6}}
$$
$$
\gamma = 1\times 10^{5}
$$
The laboratory length L and the proper length L_0 satisfy
$$
L = \frac{1}{\gamma} L_0
$$
Hence
$$
L_0 = \gamma L
$$
$$
L_0 = 1\times 10^{5} \times 2\times 10^{-3}
$$
$$
L_0 = 200 \unit{m}
$$
There is no transverse contraction, so
$$
R_{b,0} = R_b = 1 \unit{\mu m}
$$
The speed parameter satisfies
$$
\gamma^{2} = \frac{1}{1 - \beta^{2}}
$$
The opposite bunch has, in Σ_0,
$$
\beta' = -\frac{2\beta}{1+\beta^{2}}
$$
Its length in Σ_0 is
$$
L' = \frac{1}{\gamma'} L_0
$$
Using \gamma'^{-1} = \sqrt{1-\beta'^{2}},
$$
L' = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \beta'^{2}}
$$
$$
L' = L_0 \sqrt{1 - \left( \frac{2\beta}{1+\beta^{2}} \right)^{2}}
$$
$$
L' = L_0 \left( \frac{1 - \beta^{2}}{1 + \beta^{2}} \right)
$$
$$
L' = \frac{L_0}{2\gamma^{2} - 1}
$$
$$
L' = \frac{200}{2\times 10^{10} - 1} \unit{m}
$$
$$
L' \approx 10^{-8} \unit{m}
$$
$$
L' \approx 0.01 \unit{\mu m}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express R_{b,0}, L_0, and L' as numerical values with appropriate units.

subquestions.subproblem: How long will it take the two bunches to pass completely through each other as seen by an observer traveling with a bunch?
subquestions.solution:
The total overlap time in Σ_0 is
$$
 t' = \frac{L_0 + L'}{|\beta'| c}
$$
With
$$
\beta = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}}
$$
and
$$
|\beta'| = \frac{2\beta}{1+\beta^{2}}
$$
we have |\beta'| \approx 1 for \gamma \gg 1, so
$$
 t' \approx \frac{200 + 10^{-8}}{c}
$$
$$
 t' \approx \frac{200}{3\times 10^{8}} \unit{s}
$$
$$
 t' \approx 6.67\times 10^{-7} \unit{s}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express t' as a numerical value with appropriate units.

subquestions.subproblem: Draw a sketch of the radial dependence of the magnetic field as measured in the laboratory when the two bunches overlap. What is the value of B in gauss at a radius of 1 micron?
subquestions.solution:
The charge density magnitude in Σ is
$$
\rho = \frac{e N}{\pi R_b^{2} l}
$$
The current density magnitude (two opposite charges moving oppositely) is
$$
J = 2 \rho \beta c
$$
The Lorentz factor is
$$
\gamma = \frac{E}{m c^{2}}
$$
which implies
$$
\gamma = (1 - \beta^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$
Ampere's law around a circular contour C of radius s gives
$$
\oint_{C} B dl = \mu_{0} I
$$
For s > R_b,
$$
2\pi s B = \mu_{0} J \pi R_b^{2}
$$
$$
B = \frac{\mu_{0} e N}{\pi l} \frac{\beta c}{s}
$$
For s < R_b,
$$
2\pi s B = \mu_{0} J \pi s^{2}
$$
$$
B = \frac{\mu_{0} e N}{\pi l} \frac{\beta c s}{R_b^{2}}
$$
Thus B(s) grows linearly with s inside the bunch and falls as 1/s outside. At s = R_b = 1 \unit{\mu m} with \beta \approx 1,
$$
B = \frac{4\pi\times 10^{-7} \times 1.6\times 10^{-19} \times 10^{10}}{\pi \times 2\times 10^{-3} \times 10^{-6}} \times 3\times 10^{8}
$$
$$
B = 96 \unit{T}
$$
$$
B = 9.6\times 10^{5} \unit{G}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express B(s = 1 μm) in gauss as a numerical value.

subquestions.subproblem: Estimate in the impulse approximation the angle in the laboratory by which an electron at the surface of the bunch will be deflected in passing through the other bunch. (Ignore particle-particle interaction.)
subquestions.solution:
The transverse impulse gives, with encounter duration \Delta t,
$$
 p_{\perp} = e v B \Delta t
$$
The deflection angle is
$$
 \theta \approx \frac{p_{\perp}}{p}
$$
With
$$
 \Delta t = \frac{l}{v}
$$
we obtain
$$
 \theta = \frac{e v B \Delta t}{m \gamma v}
$$
$$
 \theta = \frac{e B l}{m \gamma v}
$$
Using pc = m \gamma v c,
$$
 \theta = \frac{e B c l}{p c}
$$
Numerically,
$$
 \theta = \frac{1.6\times 10^{-19} \times 96 \times 3\times 10^{8} \times 2\times 10^{-3}}{50\times 10^{9} \times 1.6\times 10^{-19}}
$$
$$
 \theta = 1.15\times 10^{-3} \unit{rad}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express θ (in radians) as a numerical value.

context: A certain elementary process is observed to produce a relativistic meson with electric charge magnitude e moving in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B. The trajectory has radius of curvature ρ, so the product (ρB) is measured. Initially, (ρB)1 = 2.7 \unit{T m}. After passing through matter and losing energy, the same meson is found to have (ρB)2 = 0.34 \unit{T m}, while a time-of-flight measurement yields a speed v2 = 1.8 \times 10^8 \unit{m/s} for this slow meson. Use c = 3 \times 10^8 \unit{m/s}. Define β = v/c and γ = 1/\sqrt{1-β^2}. The momentum is p = γ m v with rest mass m, and the kinetic energy is T = γ m c^2 - m c^2. In a uniform magnetic field, the relation p = e B ρ applies for this meson. When ρ is in \unit{m} and B in \unit{T}, use p c in \unit{GeV} via p c = 0.3 (ρB) \unit{GeV}. For decay, let N be the number of surviving mesons after time t and distance l in the laboratory from an initial number N0. Define the laboratory half-life τ by N/N0 = \exp(-t/τ) = \exp(-l/(β c τ)). The intrinsic (rest-frame) half-life is τ0 = τ/γ. Let l2 = 4 \unit{m} denote the path length at which the slow meson has 50% survival probability. For the initial full-energy mesons, define β1 and γ1 as their velocity and Lorentz factor, and let l1 be the corresponding laboratory distance at which 50% survive. Report energies to two significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the rest mass and the kinetic energies of the meson (in MeV) before and after slowing down (2-figure accuracy).
subquestions.solution: Using p = e B ρ and p = γ m v, we have $$\frac{(\rho B)_1}{(\rho B)_2} = \frac{\gamma_1 \beta_1}{\gamma_2 \beta_2}$$ For the slow meson, $$\beta_2 = \frac{v_2}{c}$$ $$\beta_2 = \frac{3}{5}$$ $$\gamma_2 \beta_2 = \frac{\beta_2}{\sqrt{1-\beta_2^2}}$$ $$\gamma_2 \beta_2 = \frac{3}{4}$$ The momentum of the slow meson in energy units is $$p_2 c = 0.3 (\rho B)_2 \unit{GeV}$$ $$p_2 c = 0.102 \unit{GeV}$$ The rest mass is $$m = \frac{p_2 c}{\gamma_2 \beta_2 c^2}$$ $$m = 0.14 \unit{GeV/c^2}$$ Before slowing down, the momentum is $$p_1 c = 0.3 (\rho B)_1 \unit{GeV}$$ $$p_1 c = 0.81 \unit{GeV}$$ The kinetic energy before slowing down is $$T_1 = \sqrt{(p_1 c)^2 + (m c^2)^2} - m c^2$$ $$T_1 = 0.68 \unit{GeV}$$ The kinetic energy after slowing down is $$T_2 = \sqrt{(p_2 c)^2 + (m c^2)^2} - m c^2$$ $$T_2 = 0.033 \unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the rest mass m (in MeV/c^2) and the kinetic energies T1 and T2 (in MeV) as numerical values. Provide each to two significant figures. Give your results in the order: m, T1, T2.

subquestions.subproblem: If this ‘slow’ meson is seen to have a 50% probability of decaying in a distance of 4 meters, compute the intrinsic half life of this particle in its own rest frame, as well as the distance that 50% of the initial full-energy mesons would travel in the laboratory frame.
subquestions.solution: The survival probability satisfies $$\exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{l}{\beta c \tau}\right)$$ At 50% survival, $$\exp\left(-\frac{t}{\tau}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$$ Solving for the laboratory half-life gives $$\tau = \frac{l}{\beta c \ln 2}$$ The intrinsic half-life is $$\tau_0 = \frac{\tau}{\gamma_2}$$ For l2 = 4 \unit{m} this gives $$\tau_0 = \frac{l_2}{\gamma_2 \beta_2 c \ln 2}$$ $$\tau_0 = 2.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{s}$$ For the full-energy mesons, $$\gamma_1 \beta_1 = \frac{p_1 c}{m c^2}$$ $$\gamma_1 \beta_1 = 5.8$$ The 50% decay distance in the laboratory is $$l_1 = \tau_0 \gamma_1 \beta_1 c \ln 2$$ $$l_1 = 31 \unit{m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the intrinsic half-life tau_0 (in seconds) and the 50% decay distance l1 (in meters) as numerical values. Provide each to two significant figures. Give your results in the order: tau_0, l1.

context: The Princeton synchrotron (PPA) has recently been used to accelerate highly charged nitrogen ions. The ring has fixed bending radius rho and a maximum magnetic field B_m. For a particle of charge magnitude |q| moving in the same ring, the magnetic rigidity limit gives the maximum attainable momentum p_m through p_m = |q| rho B_m. The PPA can produce protons of nominal total energy E_p = 3\unit{GeV}. Use the proton rest energy m_p c^2 = 0.938\unit{GeV}. Work in natural units with c = 1 for energy–momentum relations, and report momenta in \unit{GeV/c} and energies in \unit{GeV}. A fully stripped nitrogen-14 ion has charge magnitude |q|_N = 6 e, where e is the elementary charge, and rest mass m_N = 14 m_p. Define p_p as the proton momentum at the magnetic limit, p_N as the nitrogen momentum at the same limit, E_N as the nitrogen total energy at that limit, and T_max as the maximum kinetic energy of the ^{14}N^{6+} ions. Find T_max.
solution:
For fixed rho and B_m in the same synchrotron, the magnetic rigidity limit gives
$$
p_m = |q| rho B_m
$$
Comparing a proton and a fully stripped nitrogen-14 ion in the same ring gives
$$
\frac{p_p}{p_N} = \frac{|q|_p}{|q|_N}
$$
With |q|_p = e and |q|_N = 6 e, it follows that
$$
p_N = 6 p_p
$$
The proton total energy is
$$
E_p = 3\unit{GeV}
$$
The proton energy–momentum relation is
$$
E_p^2 = p_p^2 + m_p^2
$$
The proton rest energy is
$$
m_p c^2 = 0.938\unit{GeV}
$$
Hence
$$
p_p = \sqrt{E_p^2 - m_p^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
p_p \approx 2.85\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Thus
$$
p_N = 6 p_p
$$
Numerically
$$
p_N \approx 17.1\unit{GeV/c}
$$
The nitrogen-14 rest mass is
$$
m_N = 14 m_p
$$
The nitrogen total energy at the field limit is
$$
E_N = \sqrt{p_N^2 + m_N^2}
$$
The maximum kinetic energy is
$$
T_{max} = E_N - m_N
$$
Numerically
$$
T_{max} \approx 8.43\unit{GeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T_max as a numerical value in GeV. Report the value with 3 significant figures.

context: Conventions and definitions used throughout: c is the speed of light with c=3×10^8\unit{m/s}. For muons, τ_0 is the proper (rest-frame) lifetime and τ is the laboratory-frame lifetime. The speed is v and β=v/c. The Lorentz factor is γ. The muon rest mass is m_μ, its rest energy is E_0=m_μ c^2, and its laboratory-frame total energy is E=γ E_0. The path length from production altitude to the Earth's surface is l, with l=10^4\unit{m}. The Earth's magnetic field magnitude at the equator is B=1\unit{gauss}=10^{-4}\unit{T}. The elementary charge is e=1.6×10^{-19}\unit{C}. Use 1\unit{GeV}=1.6×10^{-10}\unit{J} when converting to SI. In the magnetic deflection problem, p is the muon relativistic momentum, R is the curvature radius of the muon trajectory, and a is the horizontal deflection from the undeflected path at the surface. For the threshold reaction in part (c), T=3\unit{K} is the cosmic background temperature, k=8.6×10^{-5}\unit{eV/K} is Boltzmann’s constant, E_γ is the photon energy, m_p=0.938\unit{GeV} is the proton mass, m_π=0.140\unit{GeV} is the pion mass, E_p is the proton total energy, and p_p is the proton momentum. In part (c) natural units with c=1 are used in the threshold kinematics. All numerical results are approximate unless explicitly stated otherwise.

subquestions.subproblem: A muon at rest has lifetime τ_0=10^{-6}\unit{s} and rest mass m_μ such that m_μ c^2=100\unit{MeV}. How energetic must a muon be to reach the Earth’s surface if it is produced high in the atmosphere, at l≈10^4\unit{m} above the surface? Let E denote the muon's laboratory-frame total energy.
subquestions.solution: The time dilation relation is $$\tau=\tau_0\gamma$$ The travel distance before decay in the lab is $$l=\tau\beta c$$ Substituting gives $$l=\tau_0\gamma\beta c$$ The rest energy is $$E_0=m_\mu c^2$$ The laboratory energy is $$E=\gamma E_0$$ Eliminating γ yields $$E=\frac{l E_0}{\beta\tau_0 c}$$ For highly relativistic muons, β≈1, so $$E\approx\frac{l E_0}{\tau_0 c}$$ Using the numerical values $$l=10^4\unit{m}$$ $$E_0=100\unit{MeV}$$ $$E_0=\frac{1}{10}\unit{GeV}$$ $$\tau_0=10^{-6}\unit{s}$$ $$c=3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}$$ we find $$E\approx\frac{10^4\times \frac{1}{10}}{10^{-6}\times 3\times 10^8}\unit{GeV}$$ $$E\approx 3.3\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the muon's laboratory-frame total energy E as a numerical value in GeV, rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose, to a zeroth approximation, that the Earth has a 1-gauss magnetic field pointing in the direction of its axis, extending out to l≈10^4\unit{m}. How much, and in what direction, is a muon of energy E, normally incident at the equator, deflected by the field? Let R be the trajectory curvature radius and a the horizontal deflection at the surface.
subquestions.solution: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force for a μ^+ $$e v B=\frac{m_\mu\gamma v^2}{R}$$ Using the relativistic momentum definition $$p=m_\mu\gamma v$$ this gives $$R=\frac{p}{e B}$$ For highly relativistic motion, $$p c\approx E$$ so $$R\approx\frac{E}{e c B}$$ With E in GeV and R in meters, using 1\unit{GeV}=1.6\times 10^{-10}\unit{J}, e=1.6\times 10^{-19}\unit{C}, c=3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}, and B=10^{-4}\unit{T}, $$R\approx\frac{1.6\times 10^{-10} E}{1.6\times 10^{-19}\times 3\times 10^8\times 10^{-4}}\unit{m}$$ $$R\approx\frac{10^5}{3} E\unit{m}$$ From the geometry of a circular arc and its tangent, $$\frac{a}{\sqrt{l^2+a^2}}=\frac{\sqrt{l^2+a^2}}{2 R}$$ which leads to $$a^2-2 a R+l^2=0$$ Solving the quadratic gives $$a=\frac{2 R\pm\sqrt{4 R^2-4 l^2}}{2}$$ For a\ll l\ll R, $$a\approx\frac{l^2}{2 R}$$ With l=10^4\unit{m} and the above R, $$a\approx\frac{3\times 10^8}{2\times 10^5 E}\unit{m}$$ $$a\approx\frac{1.5\times 10^3}{E}\unit{m}$$ For example, with $$E=3.3\unit{GeV}$$ one finds $$a\approx 455\unit{m}$$ and with $$E=20\unit{GeV}$$ one finds $$a\approx 75\unit{m}$$ As the Earth's magnetic field points north at the equator, a μ^+ moving vertically downward is deflected eastward, while a μ^- is deflected westward.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be two formulas in the forms R = ... and a = ... . The right-hand side of the first formula must use only E, e, c, and B. The right-hand side of the second formula must use only l and R. In addition, specify the sign of a for μ+ and for μ−, taking the eastward horizontal direction as positive.

subquestions.subproblem: Very high-energy protons in cosmic rays can lose energy through collisions with 3-K cosmological background radiation via p+γ→p+π. How energetic must a proton be to be above threshold for this reaction? Use m_p=0.938\unit{GeV}, m_π=0.140\unit{GeV}, and k=8.6×10^{-5}\unit{eV/K}. Let E_p denote the proton total energy and p_p its momentum.
subquestions.solution: Take a characteristic photon energy at temperature T to be $$E_\gamma=\frac{3 k T}{2}$$ Numerically, with T=3\unit{K}, $$E_\gamma=3.87\times 10^{-4}\unit{eV}$$ Converting to GeV, $$E_\gamma=3.87\times 10^{-13}\unit{GeV}$$ For a head-on collision at threshold in natural units c=1, $$\big(E_p+E_\gamma\big)^2-\big(p_p-E_\gamma\big)^2=(m_p+m_\pi)^2$$ Using the mass-shell condition, $$E_p^2-p_p^2=m_p^2$$ and taking p_p\approx E_p at very high energy, $$E_p\approx\frac{m_\pi^2+2 m_p m_\pi}{4 E_\gamma}$$ With the given masses and E_\gamma, $$m_p=0.938\unit{GeV}$$ $$m_\pi=0.140\unit{GeV}$$ $$E_\gamma=3.87\times 10^{-13}\unit{GeV}$$ Hence $$E_p\approx\frac{0.14^2+2\times 0.938\times 0.14}{4\times 3.87\times 10^{-13}}\unit{GeV}$$ $$E_p\approx 1.82\times 10^{11}\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the proton total energy E_p at threshold as a numerical value in GeV, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: A muon has rest mass m such that m c^2 ≈ 100 \unit{MeV} and proper lifetime at rest \tau_0 ≈ 2 \unit{\mu s}. Assume the Earth’s magnetic field could, in principle, bend the muon into a circular path around the Earth of radius R ≈ 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m}. Use the speed of light c ≈ 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}, the elementary charge e ≈ 1.6\times 10^{-19} \unit{C}, and the conversion 1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J}. Also use 1 \unit{G} = 10^{-4} \unit{T}. Let v be the muon speed, define \beta = v/c and \gamma = (1 - \beta^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}. Let p denote the relativistic momentum magnitude, E the total energy, and B the magnetic flux density. Define E_{min} as the minimum total energy such that the time-dilated lifetime is at least the travel time for one circumnavigation, p_{min} as the corresponding minimum momentum, and B_{min} as the minimum magnetic field needed to keep the muon in a circular orbit of radius R. A "fair chance" means the time-dilated lifetime \gamma \tau_0 is at least the travel time 2\pi R/v. Compute E_{min} and B_{min}, and decide whether the Earth’s surface field (about 0.25 to 0.65 \unit{G}) is sufficient to keep the muon in orbit.
solution:
Requiring the time-dilated lifetime to be at least the travel time gives
$$
\gamma \tau_0 \geq \frac{2\pi R}{\beta c}
$$
The relativistic momentum is
$$
p = \gamma m \beta c
$$
Combining the two relations yields
$$
p \tau_0 \geq 2\pi R m
$$
Therefore the minimum momentum is
$$
p_{min} = \frac{2\pi R m}{\tau_0}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
p_{min} c = \frac{2\pi R m c}{\tau_0}
$$
The total energy is
$$
E = \sqrt{m^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2}
$$
Thus the minimum total energy is
$$
E_{min} = m c^2 \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{2\pi R}{\tau_0 c} \right)^2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_{min} = 100 \unit{MeV} \times \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{2\pi \times 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m}}{2\times 10^{-6} \unit{s} \times 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}} \right)^2}
$$
$$
E_{min} \approx 6.7\times 10^6 \unit{MeV}
$$
For a circular orbit of radius R in a transverse magnetic field,
$$
p = e B R
$$
Hence the minimum field is
$$
B_{min} = \frac{p_{min}}{e R}
$$
For an ultrarelativistic muon,
$$
E \approx p c
$$
Therefore,
$$
B_{min} \approx \frac{E_{min}}{e R c}
$$
Using the conversion,
$$
1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J}
$$
We obtain
$$
B_{min} \approx \frac{6.7\times 10^6 \unit{MeV} \times 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J/MeV}}{1.6\times 10^{-19} \unit{C} \times 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m} \times 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}}
$$
$$
B_{min} \approx 3.49\times 10^{-3} \unit{T}
$$
Using the conversion,
$$
1 \unit{G} = 10^{-4} \unit{T}
$$
$$
B_{min} \approx 35 \unit{G}
$$
Since the Earth’s typical surface field is about 0.25 to 0.65 \unit{G}, which is much less than B_{min}, it is not strong enough to keep the muon in this orbit while it survives long enough to circumnavigate the Earth.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_min (minimum total energy) and B_min (minimum magnetic field) as numerical values, rounded to 2 significant figures. Report E_min in MeV and B_min in gauss (G). Additionally, include a final sentence exactly in one of the following forms: "The Earth’s surface field is sufficient to keep the muon in orbit." or "The Earth’s surface field is not sufficient to keep the muon in orbit."

context: Relativistic kinematics is used throughout. Symbols and conventions: c is the speed of light. Beta is the dimensionless speed fraction beta=v/c, and the Lorentz factor is gamma=(1-beta^2)^{-1/2}. The neutron's rest mass-energy is denoted m_0, its total energy is E, its momentum magnitude is p, and its rest-frame half-life is tau_{1/2}. For part (b), m_mu is the muon rest mass-energy, E_mu is the muon total energy, E_nu is the neutrino energy, and m_pi is the pion rest mass-energy. We use natural units (c=1) for energy-momentum relations, so masses, energies, and momenta are in MeV; when converting light-years to time, recall 1 ly = c × 1 yr, with 1 yr = 365 days, 1 day = 24 h, and 1 h = 60 min.

subquestions.subproblem: A neutron 5000 light-years from Earth has rest mass 940 MeV and a half-life of 13 minutes. How much energy must it have to reach the Earth at the end of one half-life?
subquestions.solution:
Let the neutron have total energy E, dimensionless speed beta, and rest-frame half-life tau_{1/2}. The dilated half-life in Earth's frame is gamma tau_{1/2}, where gamma=(1-beta^2)^{-1/2}. To arrive at Earth exactly at the end of one dilated half-life, its travel distance must equal 5000 light-years. Using 1 ly = c × 1 yr and converting years to minutes gives
$$
\gamma \beta c \, \tau_{1/2} = 5000 \times 365 \times 24 \times 60 \; c
$$
Canceling c and inserting tau_{1/2}=13 \unit{min} yields
$$
\gamma \beta = 2.02 \times 10^{8}
$$
Using E^2 = m_0^2 + p^2 with p = \gamma m_0 \beta (natural units) gives
$$
E = \sqrt{m_0^2 + p^2}
$$
$$
E = m_0 \sqrt{1 + (\gamma \beta)^2}
$$
With m_0 = 940 \unit{MeV} and \gamma \beta = 2.02 \times 10^{8}, the required energy is
$$
E = 1.9 \times 10^{11} \unit{MeV}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E (the neutron's total energy) as a numerical value in MeV, reported to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: In the spontaneous decay of pi^+ mesons at rest, pi^+ -> mu^+ + nu_mu, the mu^+ mesons are observed to have a kinetic energy of 4.0 MeV. The rest mass of the mu^+ is 106 MeV. The rest mass of the neutrino is zero. What is the rest mass of pi^+?
subquestions.solution:
For the two-body decay at rest, the momenta of the muon and neutrino are equal and opposite with common magnitude p. Their energies are
$$
E_{\mu} = \sqrt{m_{\mu}^2 + p^2}
$$
$$
E_{\nu} = p
$$
Given m_{\mu} = 106 \unit{MeV} and muon kinetic energy 4.0 \unit{MeV}, the muon total energy is
$$
E_{\mu} = m_{\mu} + 4.0 \unit{MeV}
$$
$$
E_{\mu} = 110 \unit{MeV}
$$
Hence the common momentum magnitude is
$$
p = \sqrt{E_{\mu}^2 - m_{\mu}^2}
$$
$$
p = 29.4 \unit{MeV}
$$
Energy conservation for the parent at rest gives the pion rest mass-energy
$$
m_{\pi} = E_{\mu} + E_{\nu}
$$
$$
m_{\pi} = 110 \unit{MeV} + 29.4 \unit{MeV}
$$
$$
m_{\pi} = 139.4 \unit{MeV}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express m_pi (the pion's rest mass-energy) as a numerical value in MeV, reported to 4 significant figures.

context: An electron-positron pair in a cloud chamber produces circular tracks of radius of curvature rho = 3 cm in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B = 0.11 T (Fig. 4.3). Assume both leptons have the same momentum magnitude p and neglect energy loss and nuclear recoil. Use the following definitions and constants: e is the elementary charge, v is the particle speed, m is the electron rest mass, gamma is the Lorentz factor, rho is the radius of curvature, B is the magnetic field magnitude, p is the relativistic momentum magnitude, c is the speed of light, m_e is the electron rest mass energy with m_e = 0.51 MeV in natural units where c = 1, E is the total energy of each lepton, and E_gamma is the incident gamma-ray energy. Use the magnetic rigidity relation derived from motion in a uniform magnetic field to find p, then compute E and E_gamma. Report p in MeV/c, E in MeV, and E_gamma in MeV.
solution:
From uniform circular motion in a magnetic field for charge magnitude e

$$
e v B = \frac{m \gamma v^2}{\rho}
$$

Using the definition of relativistic momentum

$$
p = m \gamma v
$$

Eliminating m \gamma v gives

$$
p = e B \rho
$$

Multiplying by c yields

$$
p c = e c B \rho
$$

Using e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \unit{C}, c = 3 \times 10^{8} \unit{m/s}, and 1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{J}, we obtain

$$
p c = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \unit{C} \times 3 \times 10^{8} \unit{m/s}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{J/MeV}} B \rho
$$

Therefore, with B in \unit{T} and \rho in \unit{m}

$$
p c = 300 B \rho \unit{MeV}
$$

For B = 0.11 \unit{T} and \rho = 0.03 \unit{m}

$$
p c = 300 \times 0.11 \times 0.03 \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
p c = 0.99 \unit{MeV}
$$

Thus the momentum magnitude is

$$
p = 0.99 \unit{MeV/c}
$$

In natural units c = 1, taking p = 0.99 \unit{MeV} and m_e = 0.51 \unit{MeV}, the lepton energy is

$$
E = \sqrt{p^2 + m_e^2}
$$

$$
E = \sqrt{0.99^2 + 0.51^2} \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
E = 1.1 \unit{MeV}
$$

Neglecting recoil, the gamma-ray energy is

$$
E_\gamma = 2 E
$$

$$
E_\gamma = 2.2 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express p, E, and E_gamma as numerical values. Report p in MeV/c, E in MeV, and E_gamma in MeV. Round each to 2 significant figures.

context: In a high-energy collision analyzed in natural units where c=1, an incident proton collides with a proton at rest to produce, in addition to the two protons, a new particle of rest mass M. Let m_p denote the proton rest mass. In the fixed-target case, let E_p and p_p denote the total energy and the magnitude of the three-momentum of the incident (moving) proton in the laboratory frame. Let S denote the invariant mass squared of the initial two-proton system. At threshold (minimum incident energy for the process to occur), all final-state particles are produced at rest in the center-of-momentum frame. Find the minimum E_p required in the fixed-target case. Then consider a collider configuration in which two protons approach one another with equal speeds, each with energy E_p and momentum magnitude p_p, and find the corresponding threshold energy per proton.
solution:
At threshold, consider the reaction
$$
p+p \to M+p+p
$$
In the fixed-target case, the invariant mass squared of the initial state at threshold is
$$
S = (E_p + m_p)^2 - p_p^2
$$
At threshold, the total rest mass of the final state is
$$
S = (2 m_p + M)^2
$$
The incident proton satisfies
$$
E_p^2 = m_p^2 + p_p^2
$$
Combining these relations gives
$$
E_p = \frac{(2 m_p + M)^2 - 2 m_p^2}{2 m_p}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
E_p = m_p + 2 M + \frac{M^2}{2 m_p}
$$
For the collider case with equal and opposite momenta, the invariant mass squared is
$$
S = (E_p + E_p)^2 - (p_p - p_p)^2
$$
At threshold,
$$
S = (2 m_p + M)^2
$$
Thus,
$$
E_p = m_p + \frac{M}{2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions for the threshold energy per proton. Fixed-target case: Your final answer should be written as 'E_p = ...' using only m_p and M. Collider case (equal and opposite momenta): Your final answer should be written as 'E_p = ...' using only m_p and M.

context: A relativistic particle of rest mass m_0 and kinetic energy 2 m_0 c^2 strikes and sticks to a stationary particle of rest mass 2 m_0. Let c denote the speed of light. Let p denote the magnitude of the three-momentum. Let S denote the invariant mass squared of the two-particle system. Let M denote the rest mass of the composite particle. Let \beta=v/c and \gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}. In intermediate steps, adopt natural units with c=1; reinstate c when reporting the velocity.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the rest mass of the composite.
subquestions.solution:
The moving particle has total energy 3 m_0 in natural units.

$$p=\sqrt{(3 m_0)^2-m_0^2}$$

$$p=\sqrt{8}\,m_0$$

$$S=(3 m_0+2 m_0)^2-p^2$$

$$S=17 m_0^2$$

Let the rest mass of the composite particle be M. Its momentum equals p by momentum conservation.

$$S=(\sqrt{M^2+p^2})^2-p^2$$

$$S=M^2$$

$$M=\sqrt{S}$$

$$M=\sqrt{17}\,m_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form M = ... , and the right-hand side should be written only in terms of m_0.

subquestions.subproblem: Find its velocity.
subquestions.solution:
For the composite particle, using p and M from part (a):

$$\gamma\beta=\frac{p}{M}$$

$$\gamma\beta=\sqrt{\frac{8}{17}}$$

$$\gamma=\sqrt{\gamma^2\beta^2+1}$$

$$\gamma=\sqrt{\frac{8}{17}+1}$$

$$\gamma=\frac{5}{\sqrt{17}}$$

$$\beta=\frac{\gamma\beta}{\gamma}$$

$$\beta=\frac{\sqrt{8}}{5}$$

$$v=\beta c$$

$$v\approx 1.7\times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the velocity v as a numerical value in cm/s with 2 significant figures.

context: Determine the threshold kinetic energy T_p of a proton beam needed to produce the reaction p + p -> p + p + \pi^0 on a stationary proton target in the laboratory frame. Use natural units with c=1 so that rest masses are expressed as energies. Let m_p denote the proton rest energy and m_\pi the neutral pion rest energy. Use m_p = 938 \unit{MeV} and m_\pi = 135 \unit{MeV}. Let E_p denote the total energy of the incident proton at threshold.
solution:
Using the threshold condition for p + p -> p + p + \pi^0 with a stationary target, the incident proton's total energy is

$$
E_p = m_p + 2 m_\pi + \frac{m_\pi^2}{2 m_p}
$$

Given

$$
m_p = 938 \unit{MeV}
$$

and

$$
m_\pi = 135 \unit{MeV}
$$

we evaluate

$$
E_p = 938 \unit{MeV} + 2 \times 135 \unit{MeV} + \frac{135^2}{2 \times 938} \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
E_p = 1218 \unit{MeV}
$$

The threshold kinetic energy is

$$
T_p = E_p - m_p
$$

$$
T_p = 1218 \unit{MeV} - 938 \unit{MeV}
$$

$$
T_p = 280 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T_p as a numerical value in MeV. Present it in the format 'T_p = ... MeV' using 3 significant figures.

context:
In high-energy proton-proton collisions, one or both protons may diffractively dissociate into a system consisting of a proton and several charged pions. Consider the reactions:
- Reaction (1): p + p -> p + (p + nπ)
- Reaction (2): p + p -> (p + nπ) + (p + mπ)
Here n and m are nonnegative integers that count the number of produced pions. In the laboratory frame, an incident proton (the projectile) of total energy E strikes a proton (the target) at rest. Define m_p as the proton mass, m_π as the charged pion mass, s as the Mandelstam invariant, M_f as the total final-state rest mass at threshold, and E_min as the minimum incident laboratory energy (threshold). At threshold for this fixed-target setup, the invariant is
$$s = 2 m_p^2 + 2 m_p E$$
The threshold condition on the final state is
$$s = M_f^2$$
Combining these gives the incident threshold energy
$$E_{min} = \frac{M_f^2 - 2 m_p^2}{2 m_p}$$
Use m_π = 0.140 \unit{GeV} and m_p = 0.938 \unit{GeV}.

subquestions.subproblem: the minimum energy for reaction 1 to take place when the target dissociates into a proton and 4 pions,
subquestions.solution:
At threshold the total final-state rest mass is
$$M_f = 2 m_p + 4 m_\pi$$
Using the threshold formula,
$$E_{min} = \frac{M_f^2 - 2 m_p^2}{2 m_p}$$
Numerically,
$$E_{min} = 2.225 \unit{GeV}$$

subquestions.subproblem: the minimum energy for reaction 1 to take place when the projectile dissociates into a proton and 4 pions,
subquestions.solution:
Because the two protons are identical, the threshold is the same as in part (a)
$$E_{min} = 2.225 \unit{GeV}$$

subquestions.subproblem: the minimum energy for reaction 2 to take place when both protons dissociate into a proton and 4 pions. (m_π = 0.140 \unit{GeV}, m_p = 0.938 \unit{GeV})
subquestions.solution:
Here the total final-state rest mass is
$$M_f = 2 m_p + 8 m_\pi$$
Using the threshold formula,
$$E_{min} = \frac{M_f^2 - 2 m_p^2}{2 m_p}$$
Numerically,
$$E_{min} = 3.847 \unit{GeV}$$

final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_min as a numerical value in the form E_min = ... with units of GeV, rounded to 4 significant figures.

context: Determine the threshold energy E_{\gamma,\mathrm{th}} for a gamma ray to create an electron–positron pair in an interaction with an electron at rest. Consider the reaction gamma + e^- -> e^- + e^+ + e^-. Use natural units with c=1, so energies and masses are measured in MeV. Let m_e denote the electron rest mass energy, E_\gamma the incident gamma-ray energy, p_\gamma its momentum magnitude, and S the invariant mass squared of the system. Use m_e=0.511 MeV.
solution:
From lepton number conservation, the reaction is
$$
\gamma + e^- \to e^- + e^+ + e^-
$$
At threshold, the invariant mass squared is
$$
S = (E_\gamma + m_e)^2 - p_\gamma^2
$$
and it equals the square of the total final rest mass
$$
S = (3 m_e)^2
$$
For a photon,
$$
E_\gamma = p_\gamma
$$
Combining these at threshold gives
$$
m_e^2 + 2 m_e E_\gamma = 9 m_e^2
$$
Solving for the threshold gamma-ray energy yields
$$
E_{\gamma,\mathrm{th}} = 4 m_e
$$
With m_e specified as
$$
m_e = 0.511 \unit{MeV}
$$
the numerical value is
$$
E_{\gamma,\mathrm{th}} \approx 2.044 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_{\gamma,\mathrm{th}} as a numerical value in MeV, rounded to 4 significant figures. Present it in the form 'E_{\gamma,\mathrm{th}} = ... MeV'.

context: Consider a beam of negative pions impinging on a fixed proton target at rest in the laboratory frame. Determine the threshold pion energy required for K^- production. Use natural units with c=1 so that energies, masses, and momenta are all in GeV. Define the following quantities: m_p for the proton mass, m_n for the neutron mass, m_K for the kaon mass, m_pi for the pion mass, E_pi for the pion energy at threshold in the lab frame, p_pi for the corresponding pion momentum in the lab frame, and S for the invariant mass squared of the total four-momentum, defined by S=(ΣE)^2-(Σp)^2, where ΣE is the total energy and Σp is the magnitude of the total three-momentum. The third component of isospin is denoted by I_z, and strangeness is conserved. The final answer should be reported as E_pi.
solution:
Conservation of strangeness requires that a K^+ be produced together with K^-. Conservation of I_z requires p -> n because the incoming pi^- has I_z = -1. Thus the threshold reaction is
$$
\pi^- + p \to K^- + K^+ + n
$$
Let E_pi and p_pi be the pion energy and momentum at threshold in the lab. The invariant mass squared of the initial state is
$$
S = (E_\pi + m_p)^2 - p_\pi^2
$$
At threshold the final-state hadrons are at rest in the center-of-mass frame, so
$$
S = (2 m_K + m_n)^2
$$
Using the on-shell relation for the pion,
$$
E_\pi^2 - p_\pi^2 = m_\pi^2
$$
we solve for the threshold pion energy in the lab frame
$$
E_\pi = \frac{(2 m_K + m_n)^2 - m_p^2 - m_\pi^2}{2 m_p}
$$
With numerical values in GeV,
$$
E_\pi = \frac{(2 \times 0.494\unit{GeV} + 0.94\unit{GeV})^2 - (0.938\unit{GeV})^2 - (0.14\unit{GeV})^2}{2 \times 0.938\unit{GeV}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_pi = ..., and your response should be written with m_K, m_n, m_p, m_pi.

context: A particle of rest mass m has kinetic energy T' equal to twice its rest energy. It collides with a particle of equal rest mass m that is at rest. The two combine into a single new particle of rest mass M. Use natural units with c=1 so that the rest energy of a particle of rest mass m equals m. Let E denote the total energy of the incident particle, p its momentum magnitude, and S the invariant mass squared of the two-particle system. Compute M in terms of m.
solution:
Let the mass of the new particle be M and that of each initial particle be m. The kinetic energy is twice the rest energy, so
$$
T' = 2 m
$$
The total energy of the incident particle is
$$
E = m + T'
$$
Thus
$$
E = 3 m
$$
The invariant mass squared of the two-particle system is
$$
S = (E + m)^2 - p^2
$$
At production, the final state is a single particle, so
$$
S = M^2
$$
Using the dispersion relation for the incident particle,
$$
E^2 - p^2 = m^2
$$
Substituting gives
$$
M^2 = 2 E m + 2 m^2
$$
With E = 3 m,
$$
M^2 = 8 m^2
$$
Therefore
$$
M = 2 \sqrt{2} m
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of M = ..., and your response should be written using only the variable m.

context: In the CERN colliding-beam storage ring, two protons, each of total energy E_b = 30\unit{GeV}, collide head-on. Consider instead a fixed-target collision in which a proton of laboratory total energy E and momentum magnitude P strikes a stationary proton. Let m_p denote the proton rest mass energy and let s denote the invariant mass squared of the two-proton system. Find E such that the fixed-target collision has the same s as the collider case. Use m_p \approx 0.938\unit{GeV}. Report the required E in \unit{GeV}.
solution:
For the collider case, the invariant mass squared is
$$
s=(2E_b)^2
$$
For the fixed-target case,
$$
s=(E+m_p)^2-P^2
$$
Using the on-shell relation for the incident proton,
$$
E^2-P^2=m_p^2
$$
Hence,
$$
s=2 m_p E+2 m_p^2
$$
Equating the two expressions for s,
$$
4 E_b^2=2 m_p E+2 m_p^2
$$
Solving for E,
$$
E=\frac{4 E_b^2-2 m_p^2}{2 m_p}
$$
Substituting E_b=30\unit{GeV} and m_p=0.938\unit{GeV},
$$
E=\frac{4 (30\unit{GeV})^2-2 (0.938\unit{GeV})^2}{2 (0.938\unit{GeV})}
$$
Numerical result,
$$
E\approx 1.92\times 10^3\unit{GeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E as a numerical value in GeV, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: Calculate the fractional change in the kinetic energy of an \alpha-particle when it is scattered through 180^\circ by an O^{16} nucleus initially at rest. Assume nonrelativistic, elastic scattering. Use E for the initial kinetic energy of the \alpha-particle, p for its initial momentum magnitude, m_{\alpha} for its mass, E' and p' for the kinetic energy and momentum magnitude after scattering, M for the mass of the O^{16} nucleus, and P_0 for the magnitude of the recoil momentum of the O^{16} nucleus. Take M \approx 4 m_{\alpha}. Define the fractional change to be \chi = (E' - E)/E.
solution:
In the nonrelativistic approximation, the momentum-energy relations are
$$
p = \sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E}
$$
$$
p' = \sqrt{2 m_{\alpha} E'}
$$
For 180^\circ backscattering, the recoil momentum magnitude of the O^{16} nucleus is
$$
P_0 = p + p'
$$
Conservation of energy gives
$$
E = E' + \frac{P_0^2}{2M}
$$
Substituting P_0 = p + p' yields
$$
E = E' + \frac{(p + p')^2}{2M}
$$
Using p^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E, p'^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E', and p p' = 2 m_{\alpha} \sqrt{E E'} gives
$$
(p + p')^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E + 2 m_{\alpha} E' + 4 m_{\alpha} \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Hence
$$
E = E' + \frac{m_{\alpha}}{M} \left(E + E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}\right)
$$
With M \approx 4 m_{\alpha}
$$
E = E' + \frac{1}{4} \left(E + E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}\right)
$$
Rearranging
$$
\frac{3}{4} E = \frac{5}{4} E' + \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Multiplying by 4
$$
3 E = 5 E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Let u = \sqrt{E'} and v = \sqrt{E}
$$
5 u^2 + 2 u v - 3 v^2 = 0
$$
Factoring
$$
(5 u - 3 v)(u + v) = 0
$$
Physical considerations give 5 \sqrt{E'} - 3 \sqrt{E} = 0, so
$$
E' = \frac{9}{25} E
$$
Therefore, the fractional change \chi = (E' - E)/E is
$$
\chi = -\frac{16}{25}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the fractional change as a numerical value in the form 'chi = ...'.

grading_standard.formula: $$(p + p')^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E + 2 m_{\alpha} E' + 4 m_{\alpha} \sqrt{E E'}$$

context: A beam of positively charged pions pi^+ with laboratory-frame kinetic energy T produces some positively charged muons mu^+ that travel backward in the laboratory frame. The mu^+ are produced via the two-body decay reaction pi^+ -> mu^+ + nu, where nu is a (massless) neutrino. Use natural units with c=1 so that all masses are expressed in energy units. Let T be the laboratory-frame kinetic energy T_pi of the incident pion, and let E_pi be its total laboratory-frame energy. Denote quantities evaluated in the center-of-mass frame of the decay (which is the rest frame of the parent pion) by an overbar. Let beta denote speed in units of c, so beta_pi is the laboratory-frame speed of the pion and bar beta_mu is the center-of-mass speed of the muon. The rest energies are given by the following numerical values: $$m_{\pi} c^2 = 139.57 \unit{MeV}$$ $$m_{\mu} c^2 = 105.66 \unit{MeV}$$ $$m_{\nu} c^2 = 0.0 \unit{MeV}$$ For what range of T is backward emission of some mu^+ in the laboratory frame possible?
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the allowed range of the laboratory-frame kinetic energy T for which backward emission occurs as a single numerical inequality in the form 0 <= T <= [threshold] MeV. Report the threshold to 3 significant figures.

context: Two accelerator facilities are under construction which will produce the neutral intermediate vector boson Z^0 via the process $$e^+ + e^- \to Z^0$$ The mass of the Z^0 is given by $$M_Z=92\unit{GeV}$$ Conventions and symbols: Natural units with c=1 are used unless a velocity is written explicitly with c. The electron mass is m_e and the muon mass is m_\mu. In the colliding-beam case, E denotes the beam energy per lepton in the laboratory, which coincides with the center-of-mass frame. In the fixed-target case, E_{e^+} and p_{e^+} are the laboratory energy and momentum of the incident positron, and the target electron is at rest. An overbar denotes a quantity in the center-of-mass (Z^0 rest) frame, for example \bar{E} and \bar{E}_\mu. The invariant mass squared of the initial state is S. The symbols \gamma_0 and \beta_0 are the Lorentz factor and speed (in units of c) of the center-of-mass frame relative to the laboratory. The symbols \gamma_\mu, \bar{\gamma}_\mu, and \bar{\beta}_\mu denote, respectively, the laboratory Lorentz factor of a decay muon and its Lorentz factor and speed in the Z^0 rest frame. The laboratory energy and speed of the produced Z^0 are E_Z and v_Z, and \beta_Z=v_Z/c.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the energy of the electron beam needed for the colliding beam facility under construction. Assume that a fixed target facility is to be built, such that a beam of e^+ will strike a target of e^- at rest.
subquestions.solution: For the colliding-beam machine, the laboratory and center-of-mass frames coincide, so the threshold beam energy per lepton is $$E=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ Using M_Z=92\unit{GeV}, this gives $$E=46\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E as a numerical value.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the required e^+ beam energy for this case?
subquestions.solution: For the fixed-target facility, conservation of the invariant mass gives $$\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2=M_Z^2$$ Using the dispersion relation for the incident positron, $$E_{e^+}^2-p_{e^+}^2=m_e^2$$ we find the threshold energy $$E_{e^+}=\frac{M_Z^2-2 m_e^2}{2 m_e}$$ Neglecting the small term in m_e^2, $$E_{e^+}\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ Numerically, $$E_{e^+}\approx 8.30\times 10^6\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_{e^+} as a numerical value.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the energy and velocity of the Z^0 (in the laboratory) after production?
subquestions.solution: Invariance of S gives $$S=\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2$$ and also $$S=\left(2\bar{E}\right)^2$$ Therefore, $$\bar{E}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_e E_{e^+}+2 m_e^2}}{2}$$ At high energy, $$\bar{E}\approx\sqrt{\frac{m_e E_{e^+}}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\bar{E}=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ The Lorentz factor of the center-of-mass frame relative to the lab is $$\gamma_0=\frac{\bar{E}}{m_e}$$ Expressed in terms of laboratory quantities, $$\gamma_0=\sqrt{\frac{E_{e^+}}{2 m_e}+\frac{1}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\gamma_0\approx\frac{M_Z}{2 m_e}$$ Since the Z^0 is produced at rest in the center-of-mass frame, its laboratory energy is $$E_Z=\gamma_0 M_Z$$ Hence, at threshold, $$E_Z\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and numerically $$E_Z\approx E_{e^+}$$ The corresponding speed parameter is $$\beta_Z=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\gamma_0^2}}$$ and the laboratory speed is $$v_Z=\beta_Z c$$ Using the threshold approximation, $$v_Z\approx\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2 m_e}{M_Z}\right)^2} c$$ To first order, $$v_Z\approx\left(1-\frac{2 m_e^2}{M_Z^2}\right) c$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answers should be given in the forms E_Z = ... and v_Z = ..., and your response should be written with M_Z, m_e, and c only.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the maximum energy in the laboratory frame of muons from the subsequent decay Z^0 \to \mu^+ + \mu^-.
subquestions.solution: In the Z^0 rest frame, the decay is isotropic. Muons emitted in the direction of the incident e^+ have the maximum laboratory energy. In the center-of-mass frame, the Z^0 decays at rest into two muons, so $$\bar{E}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ and the corresponding Lorentz factor is $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{\bar{E}_\mu}{m_\mu}$$ hence $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2 m_\mu}$$ For a muon moving along the boost direction, the inverse Lorentz transformation gives $$\gamma_\mu=\gamma_0\left(\bar{\gamma}_\mu+\beta_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu\bar{\beta}_\mu\right)$$ With \beta_0\approx\bar{\beta}_\mu\approx 1, $$\gamma_\mu\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu$$ The maximum laboratory energy is $$E_{\mu,\max}=\gamma_\mu m_\mu$$ Hence, $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu m_\mu$$ which evaluates to $$E_{\mu,\max}=\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and therefore $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx E_{e^+}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E_{\mu,\max} = ..., and your response should be written with M_Z and m_e only.

context: Reaction on a stationary proton target in the laboratory frame: K^- + p -> π^0 + Λ^0. The proton target is at rest initially. Use natural units with c = 1 so that energies, momenta, and masses share the same units. Let m_{π^0}, m_{K^-}, m_p, and m_{Λ^0} denote the rest masses of the π^0, K^-, proton, and Λ^0, respectively. Let E_K be the total energy of the incident K^- in the lab frame, and p_K its momentum magnitude. Let E_π and p_π be the total energy and momentum magnitude of the outgoing π^0 in the lab frame. The Λ^0 is produced at rest in the lab, so its momentum magnitude is p_{Λ^0} = 0. Find the special value of E_K such that Λ^0 is produced at rest, and express your answer in terms of m_{π^0}, m_{K^-}, m_p, and m_{Λ^0}.
solution:
Conservation of the invariant mass squared between initial and final states gives
$$(E_K + m_p)^2 - p_K^2 = (E_π + m_{Λ^0})^2 - p_π^2$$
The Λ^0 is produced at rest, so
$$p_{Λ^0} = 0$$
By momentum conservation, the pion carries the initial momentum
$$p_π = p_K$$
With p_π = p_K, the energy balance reduces to
$$E_K + m_p = E_π + m_{Λ^0}$$
The on-shell relations are
$$E_π^2 = p_π^2 + m_{π^0}^2$$
$$E_K^2 = p_K^2 + m_{K^-}^2$$
Hence
$$p_K^2 = E_K^2 - m_{K^-}^2$$
From the energy balance,
$$E_π = E_K + m_p - m_{Λ^0}$$
Therefore
$$E_π^2 = E_K^2 + (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)^2 - 2 E_K (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)$$
Equating the two expressions for E_π^2 gives
$$p_K^2 + m_{π^0}^2 = E_K^2 + (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)^2 - 2 E_K (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)$$
Substituting p_K^2 = E_K^2 - m_{K^-}^2 yields
$$E_K^2 - m_{K^-}^2 + m_{π^0}^2 = E_K^2 + (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)^2 - 2 E_K (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)$$
Rearranging gives
$$2 E_K (m_{Λ^0} - m_p) = m_{K^-}^2 - m_{π^0}^2 + (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)^2$$
Thus the required incident K^- energy is
$$E_K = \frac{m_{K^-}^2 - m_{π^0}^2 + (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)^2}{2 (m_{Λ^0} - m_p)}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_K = ... , and your response should be written only with m_{π^0}, m_{K^-}, m_p, and m_{Λ^0}.

context: K^+ mesons can be photoproduced in the reaction gamma + p -> K^+ + Lambda^0. Work in natural units with c = 1 for intermediate steps; report energies in \unit{MeV}, momenta in \unit{MeV/c}, and masses in \unit{MeV/c^2}. Let P_\gamma and P_p denote the four-momenta of the incident photon and the target proton, respectively. Let p_\gamma and p_p denote their three-momenta, and E_\gamma and E_p their energies in the laboratory. Let S denote the invariant mass squared of the initial state. Overbars indicate quantities evaluated in the Lambda^0 rest frame. Let \beta_0 and \gamma_0 denote the velocity (in units of c) and Lorentz factor of the Lambda^0 in the laboratory. Let p_\pi^{max} denote the maximum laboratory momentum of the pi^- and p_{\pi,\perp}^{max} the maximum laboratory momentum component perpendicular to the Lambda^0 direction. Use the particle masses m_p = 938 \unit{MeV/c^2}, m_{K^+} = 494 \unit{MeV/c^2}, m_{\Lambda^0} = 1116 \unit{MeV/c^2}, and m_{\pi^-} = 140 \unit{MeV/c^2}.

subquestions.subproblem: Give the minimum gamma-ray energy in the laboratory, where p is at rest, that can cause this reaction to take place.
subquestions.solution:
Define the invariant mass squared of the initial state
$$S = - (P_\gamma + P_p)^2$$
With the proton at rest in the laboratory,
$$S = m_p^2 + 2 E_\gamma m_p$$
At threshold for gamma + p -> K^+ + Lambda^0,
$$S = (m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2$$
Solving for the threshold photon energy,
$$E_\gamma = \frac{(m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2 - m_p^2}{2 m_p}$$
Numerically,
$$E_\gamma \approx 913 \unit{MeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the threshold photon energy in the laboratory (with the proton at rest) as a numerical value with 3 significant figures, reported as E_gamma = ... MeV.

subquestions.subproblem: If the target proton is not free but is bound in a nucleus, then the motion of the proton in the nucleus (Fermi motion) allows the reaction to proceed with a lower incident photon energy. Assume a reasonable value for the Fermi momentum and compute the minimum photon energy.
subquestions.solution:
Assume the bound proton has Fermi momentum
$$p_p = 200 \unit{MeV/c}$$
The invariant mass squared is
$$S = - (P_\gamma + P_p)^2$$
In terms of energies and three-momenta,
$$S = (E_\gamma + E_p)^2 - (p_\gamma + p_p)^2$$
At threshold,
$$S = (m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2$$
For the photon,
$$E_\gamma = p_\gamma$$
For the proton,
$$E_p^2 - p_p^2 = m_p^2$$
Solving for the incident photon energy,
$$E_\gamma = \frac{(m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2 - m_p^2 + 2 p_\gamma \cdot p_p}{2 E_p}$$
The minimum threshold occurs when the proton moves opposite to the photon, giving
$$E_\gamma = \frac{(m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2 - m_p^2}{2 (E_p + p_p)}$$
With
$$E_p = \sqrt{p_p^2 + m_p^2}$$
Numerically,
$$E_\gamma \approx 739 \unit{MeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the minimum photon energy in the laboratory as a numerical value with 3 significant figures, reported as E_gamma = ... MeV, assuming a bound proton with Fermi momentum p_p = 200 MeV/c.

subquestions.subproblem: This entry corresponds to the same physical question as part (b) (Fermi motion lowering the threshold). Restate and compute the minimum photon energy using a reasonable Fermi momentum.
subquestions.solution:
Using the same assumptions and steps as in part (b), the minimum photon energy with Fermi momentum p_p = 200 \unit{MeV/c} is
$$E_\gamma = \frac{(m_{K^+} + m_{\Lambda^0})^2 - m_p^2}{2 (E_p + p_p)}$$
with
$$E_p = \sqrt{p_p^2 + m_p^2}$$
Numerically,
$$E_\gamma \approx 739 \unit{MeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the minimum photon energy in the laboratory as a numerical value with 3 significant figures, reported as E_gamma = ... MeV, assuming a bound proton with Fermi momentum p_p = 200 MeV/c.

subquestions.subproblem: The Lambda^0 decays in flight into a proton and a pi^- meson. If the Lambda^0 has a velocity of 0.8c, what is the maximum momentum that the pi^- can have in the laboratory, and what is the maximum component of the laboratory momentum perpendicular to the Lambda^0 direction?
subquestions.solution:
In the Lambda^0 rest frame, energy conservation gives
$$\bar E_\pi + \bar E_p = m_{\Lambda^0}$$
Momentum conservation gives
$$\bar p_\pi + \bar p_p = 0$$
Using the on-shell relations and eliminating \bar p_p,
$$(m_{\Lambda^0} - \bar E_\pi)^2 = \bar p_p^2 + m_p^2$$
$$\bar p_\pi^2 + m_{\pi^-}^2 = \bar p_p^2 + m_p^2$$
Solving for the pion energy in the Lambda^0 rest frame,
$$\bar E_\pi = \frac{m_{\Lambda^0}^2 + m_{\pi^-}^2 - m_p^2}{2 m_{\Lambda^0}}$$
Numerically,
$$\bar E_\pi \approx 173 \unit{MeV}$$
The pion momentum in that frame is
$$\bar p_\pi = \sqrt{\bar E_\pi^2 - m_{\pi^-}^2}$$
Numerically,
$$\bar p_\pi \approx 101 \unit{MeV/c}$$
For the moving Lambda^0,
$$\beta_0 = \frac{4}{5}$$
The Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma_0 = \frac{5}{3}$$
The maximum laboratory momentum occurs for emission along the Lambda^0 direction,
$$p_\pi^{max} = \gamma_0 (\bar p_\pi + \beta_0 \bar E_\pi)$$
Numerically,
$$p_\pi^{max} \approx 399 \unit{MeV/c}$$
The transverse component is invariant under boosts along the flight direction,
$$p_{\pi,\perp}^{max} = \bar p_\pi$$
Numerically,
$$p_{\pi,\perp}^{max} \approx 101 \unit{MeV/c}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express (i) the maximum laboratory momentum of the pion and (ii) the maximum component of its laboratory momentum perpendicular to the Lambda^0 direction as numerical values, each with 3 significant figures, reported as p_pi^{max} = ... MeV/c and p_{pi,perp}^{max} = ... MeV/c, for a Lambda^0 speed beta_0 = 0.8.

subquestions.subproblem: Using the masses m_{K^+} = 494 \unit{MeV/c^2}, m_{\Lambda^0} = 1116 \unit{MeV/c^2}, and m_{\pi^-} = 140 \unit{MeV/c^2}, report (i) the maximum momentum that the pi^- can have in the laboratory, and (ii) the maximum component of laboratory momentum perpendicular to the Lambda^0 direction.
subquestions.solution:
From part (c),
$$p_\pi^{max} \approx 399 \unit{MeV/c}$$
$$p_{\pi,\perp}^{max} \approx 101 \unit{MeV/c}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express (i) the maximum laboratory momentum of the pion and (ii) the maximum component of its laboratory momentum perpendicular to the Lambda^0 direction as numerical values, each with 3 significant figures, reported as p_pi^{max} = ... MeV/c and p_{pi,perp}^{max} = ... MeV/c, using the same Lambda^0 speed beta_0 = 0.8 as in part (c).

context: The rho meson resonance of interest is the neutral rho, denoted rho^0, with rest mass m_rho = 769 MeV and decay width Gamma = 154 MeV. It can be produced experimentally by bombarding a hydrogen target with a pi^- meson beam via the reaction $$ \pi^- + p \to \rho^0 + n $$. Use the following conventions and constants throughout: m_pi = 140 MeV for the charged pion mass, m_p = 938 MeV for the proton mass, m_n = 940 MeV for the neutron mass, c = 3\times10^{10} \unit{cm/s} for the speed of light, and \hbar = 6.58\times10^{-22} \unit{MeV s} for the reduced Planck constant. The Lorentz factor of a particle with energy E and mass m is \gamma = E/m, and its speed parameter is \beta = \sqrt{1 - 1/\gamma^2}. In what follows, E_\rho denotes the laboratory energy of the produced rho^0, \tau_0 its proper lifetime, \tau its laboratory lifetime, and d its mean decay distance in the laboratory. The symbol S denotes the invariant mass squared of the system, E_\pi and p_\pi denote the energy and momentum of the incident pion, respectively, and \sigma, l, \rho, N_0, A denote the production cross section, target length, target density, Avogadro's number, and the target mass number, respectively. In part (d), quantities evaluated in the rho^0 rest frame \Sigma are denoted with an overbar, and \theta_{min} denotes the minimum opening angle between the outgoing pions in the laboratory frame.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the lifetime \tau and mean decay distance d for a rho^0 with laboratory energy E_\rho = 5 \unit{GeV}?
subquestions.solution: The Lorentz factor of the rho^0 is $$ \gamma_0 = \frac{E_\rho}{m_\rho} $$ $$ \gamma_0 = \frac{5 \unit{GeV}}{0.769 \unit{GeV}} $$ $$ \gamma_0 = 6.50 $$ The proper lifetime is $$ \tau_0 = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma} $$ $$ \tau_0 = \frac{6.58\times10^{-22} \unit{MeV s}}{154 \unit{MeV}} $$ $$ \tau_0 = 4.27\times10^{-24} \unit{s} $$ The laboratory lifetime is $$ \tau = \gamma_0 \tau_0 $$ $$ \tau = 2.78\times10^{-23} \unit{s} $$ The mean decay distance is $$ d = \tau_0 c \sqrt{\gamma_0^2 - 1} $$ $$ d = 4.27\times10^{-24} \unit{s} \times 3\times10^{10} \unit{cm/s} \times \sqrt{6.50^2 - 1} $$ $$ d = 8.23\times10^{-13} \unit{cm} $$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form 'τ = ..., d = ...', with both values expressed as numerical values with units using \unit{}. Use three significant figures for each value.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the pi^- threshold energy E_\pi for producing rho^0 mesons on a stationary proton target?
subquestions.solution: At threshold the invariant mass squared is $$ S = (E_\pi + m_p)^2 - p_\pi^2 $$ $$ S = (m_\rho + m_n)^2 $$ Using the on-shell condition for the incident pion, $$ E_\pi^2 = m_\pi^2 + p_\pi^2 $$ one obtains the threshold pion energy $$ E_\pi = \frac{(m_\rho + m_n)^2 - m_\pi^2 - m_p^2}{2 m_p} $$ Substituting numerical values gives $$ E_\pi = \frac{(769 \unit{MeV} + 940 \unit{MeV})^2 - (140 \unit{MeV})^2 - (938 \unit{MeV})^2}{2 \times 938 \unit{MeV}} $$ $$ E_\pi = 1077 \unit{MeV} $$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be written in the form 'E_\pi = ...' as a numerical value with units using \unit{}. Use four significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: If the production cross section is \sigma = 1 \unit{mb} \equiv 10^{-27} \unit{cm^2} and the liquid hydrogen target is l = 30 \unit{cm} long, how many rho^0 are produced on average per incident pi^-? The density of liquid hydrogen is \rho = 0.07 \unit{g/cm^3}. Use N_0 = 6.02\times10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}} and A = 1 for hydrogen.
subquestions.solution: The average number of rho^0 events per incident pi^- is $$ N = \frac{\rho l \sigma N_0}{A} $$ Substituting the given values, $$ N = 0.07 \unit{g/cm^3} \times 30 \unit{cm} \times 10^{-27} \unit{cm^2} \times 6.02\times10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}} $$ $$ N = 1.3\times10^{-3} $$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form 'N = ...' as a numerical value (unitless). Use two significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: rho^0 mesons decay almost instantaneously into pi^+ + pi^-. Given that the rho^0 is produced in the forward direction in the laboratory frame with energy E_\rho = 5 \unit{GeV}, what is the minimum opening angle \theta_{min} between the outgoing pi^+ and pi^- in the laboratory frame?
subquestions.solution: In the rho^0 rest frame \Sigma, the two pions are back to back with equal energies $$ \bar E_\pi = \frac{m_\rho}{2} $$ The corresponding Lorentz factor for each pion in \Sigma is $$ \bar \gamma_\pi = \frac{\bar E_\pi}{m_\pi} $$ $$ \bar \gamma_\pi = \frac{m_\rho}{2 m_\pi} $$ The corresponding speed parameter is $$ \bar \beta_\pi = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\bar \gamma_\pi^2}} $$ $$ \bar \beta_\pi = \frac{1}{m_\rho} \sqrt{m_\rho^2 - 4 m_\pi^2} $$ $$ \bar \beta_\pi = 0.93 $$ The rho^0 moves forward in the laboratory with $$ \gamma_0 = 6.50 $$ $$ \beta_0 = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{6.50^2}} $$ $$ \beta_0 = 0.99 $$ For pions emitted parallel and antiparallel to the rho^0 flight direction in \Sigma, both pions move forward in the laboratory because \beta_0 > \bar \beta_\pi, so the minimum opening angle is $$ \theta_{min} = 0 $$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be written exactly as 'θ_min = ...' as a numerical value in radians. This value is exact; no rounding specification applies.

context: Notation and definitions used throughout: m_p is the proton mass, m_K is the common kaon mass (for K^+, K^0, K^-), m_\Omega is the mass of the \Omega^- baryon, and m_\pi is the neutral pion mass. In part (a), the initial proton is at rest in the laboratory frame. The incident K^- has laboratory-frame total energy E_K, momentum magnitude p_K, and threshold kinetic energy T_K. The invariant mass squared of the initial state is denoted by S. In part (b), the speed of light is c, and the K^0 moves in the laboratory frame with speed v_0 = (4/5) c, so \beta_0 = v_0/c = 4/5 and \gamma_0 = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta_0^2}. The rest frame of the K^0 is denoted by \Sigma, and an overbar indicates a quantity measured in \Sigma (for example, \bar E_1, \bar p_1, \bar \theta_1). Unbarred quantities (for example, E_1, p_1, \theta_1) are measured in the laboratory frame. The pions produced in K^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0 are labeled 1 and 2. Angles \theta_1 (laboratory) and \bar \theta_1 (frame \Sigma) are measured with respect to the K^0 line of flight. The pion speed in \Sigma is \bar \beta = \bar p_1/\bar E_1. Define \theta_{1,\max} as the maximum laboratory-frame angle one of the pions can make with the K^0 line of flight.

subquestions.subproblem: The \Omega^- was discovered in the reaction K^- + p \to \Omega^- + K^+ + K^0. In terms of the masses of the various particles, what is the threshold kinetic energy for the reaction to occur if the proton is at rest?
subquestions.solution:
At threshold the invariant mass squared satisfies
$$S = (E_K + m_p)^2 - p_K^2$$
$$S = (m_\Omega + 2 m_K)^2$$
Using the on-shell relation for the incident kaon
$$E_K^2 = p_K^2 + m_K^2$$
Solving for the incident kaon energy gives
$$E_K = \frac{(m_\Omega + 2 m_K)^2 - m_p^2 - m_K^2}{2 m_p}$$
Hence the threshold kinetic energy is
$$T_K = E_K - m_K$$
$$T_K = \frac{(m_\Omega + 2 m_K)^2 - (m_p + m_K)^2}{2 m_p}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of T_K = ... , and your response should be written with m_p, m_K, m_\Omega only.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose the K^0 travels at a speed of (4/5) c. It decays in flight into two neutral pions. Find the maximum angle (in the laboratory frame) that the pions can make with the K^0 line of flight.
subquestions.solution:
Work in the K^0 rest frame \Sigma and label the pions by 1 and 2. In \Sigma,
$$\bar p_1 = \bar p_2$$
$$\bar E_1 + \bar E_2 = m_K$$
$$\bar E_1 = \bar E_2$$
$$\bar E_1 = \frac{m_K}{2}$$
$$\bar p_1 = \sqrt{\bar E_1^2 - m_\pi^2}$$
$$\bar p_1 = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{m_K^2 - 4 m_\pi^2}$$
Lorentz transforming to the laboratory frame for pion 1 gives
$$p_1 \cos \theta_1 = \gamma_0 (\bar p_1 \cos \bar \theta_1 + \beta_0 \bar E_1)$$
$$p_1 \sin \theta_1 = \bar p_1 \sin \bar \theta_1$$
Therefore
$$\tan \theta_1 = \frac{\sin \bar \theta_1}{\gamma_0 \left(\cos \bar \theta_1 + \beta_0/\bar \beta\right)}$$
with
$$\bar \beta = \frac{\bar p_1}{\bar E_1}$$
Maximization yields
$$\cos \bar \theta_1 = - \frac{\bar \beta}{\beta_0}$$
The condition for an interior extremum is
$$|\cos \bar \theta_1| \le 1$$
which requires
$$\bar \beta \le \beta_0$$
Here
$$\beta_0 = \frac{4}{5}$$
and
$$\bar \beta = \frac{1}{m_K} \sqrt{m_K^2 - 4 m_\pi^2}$$
Equivalently, an interior extremum would require
$$3 m_K \le 10 m_\pi$$
For the physical masses one has
$$3 m_K > 10 m_\pi$$
so no interior extremum occurs and the maximum is attained at the boundary. Therefore
$$\theta_{1,\max} = \pi$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \theta_{1,\max} as a numerical value in radians.

context: The Q-value (energy released) of the reaction He-3(n,p) that produces tritium is given as Q=0.770 MeV. The maximum kinetic energy of the beta particle (electron) emitted in tritium beta decay is E_max=0.018 MeV. Using the conversion 1 amu = 931 MeV, calculate the mass difference between a neutron and a hydrogen atom (protium), defined as M(n) - M(^1H), and report it in amu. Definitions: M(X) denotes the atomic mass-energy equivalent of species X expressed in MeV via mc^2, n is the neutron, p is the proton, ^1H is the hydrogen atom (protium), Q is the Q-value of the reaction ^3He(n,p)^3H, and E_max is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron in the decay ^3H -> ^3He + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express M(n) − M(^1H) as a numerical value in amu, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: Suppose that a slowly moving antiproton is annihilated in a collision with a proton, leading to 2 negative pions and 2 positive pions. Assume the four pions share the available energy equally in the center-of-mass frame. Use natural units with c=1 in intermediate formulas, and write final numeric results with units using \unit{}. Define m_p as the proton mass with rest energy m_p c^2 = 938 \unit{MeV}. The charged-pion mass is m_\pi with rest energy m_\pi c^2 = 140 \unit{MeV}. Let E_\pi denote the total energy of one pion. Let E denote the same pion energy where it appears in the solution. Let p be the magnitude of a pion momentum and \beta=v/c its speed in units of c. For the two-photon final state, let E_\gamma be the energy of each photon, \lambda its wavelength, and \nu its frequency. Use h for Planck’s constant and \hbar for the reduced Planck constant with 2\pi\hbar=h and \hbar c = 197 \times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV cm}.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the average kinetic energy per pion? (MeV)
What is the magnitude of the momentum of a pion with such an energy? (MeV/ $c$ )
subquestions.solution:
The momentum of each pion is
$$p=\sqrt{E_{\pi}^2-m_{\pi}^2}$$
Using equal sharing of the available energy among four pions gives
$$p\approx\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{m_p^2-4m_{\pi}^2}$$
Numerically,
$$p=448\unit{MeV/c}$$

subquestions.subproblem: What is the magnitude of the velocity? (In units of $c$ )
subquestions.solution:
Its velocity is
$$\beta=\frac{p}{E}$$
Using equal sharing,
$$\beta\approx\frac{2p}{m_p}$$
Numerically,
$$\beta=0.955$$

subquestions.subproblem: If the annihilation led instead to 2 photons, what would be the wavelength of each? (cm)
subquestions.solution:
If the annihilation had led to two photons, the energy of each photon would be
$$E_{\gamma}=\frac{2m_p}{2}$$
Thus,
$$E_{\gamma}=m_p$$
Numerically,
$$E_{\gamma}=938\unit{MeV}$$
The wavelength of each photon is
$$\lambda=\frac{c}{\nu}$$
Using h=2\pi\hbar,
$$\lambda=\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{h\nu}$$
With E_{\gamma}=h\nu,
$$\lambda=\frac{2\pi\hbar c}{E_{\gamma}}$$
Using the constant,
$$2\pi\hbar c=2\pi\times 197\times 10^{-13}\unit{MeV cm}$$
Substituting numerically,
$$\lambda=\frac{2\pi\times 197\times 10^{-13}\unit{MeV cm}}{938\unit{MeV}}$$
Therefore,
$$\lambda=1.32\times 10^{-13}\unit{cm}$$

final_answer_instructions: For each subproblem, your final answer should express the requested quantity as a numerical value with the units indicated at the end of the question. Use 3 significant figures.

context: Consider the process of Compton scattering. A photon of initial wavelength λ is scattered by a free electron initially at rest. The scattered photon emerges at polar angle θ relative to the incident direction with wavelength λ'. Use m for the electron rest mass, c for the speed of light, h for Planck's constant, p for the incident photon momentum, p' for the scattered photon momentum, p_e for the electron momentum after the collision, and T for the kinetic energy of the recoiled electron. The relations p=h/λ and p'=h/λ' are to be used for the photon momenta.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute λ' in terms of λ, θ and universal parameters.
subquestions.solution:
First, from energy-momentum conservation for Compton scattering we have
$$p' c=\frac{m c^{2}}{1-\cos\theta+\frac{m c}{p}}$$
Using the photon momentum-wavelength relations
$$p=\frac{h}{\lambda}$$
$$p'=\frac{h}{\lambda'}$$
Solving for the scattered wavelength gives
$$\lambda'=\lambda+\frac{h}{m c}(1-\cos\theta)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of λ' = ..., and your response should be written with λ, θ, h, m, c.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the kinetic energy of the recoiled electron.
subquestions.solution:
The kinetic energy of the recoiled electron is
$$T=\sqrt{p_{e}^{2} c^{2}+m^{2} c^{4}}-m c^{2}$$
From energy conservation for the photons we have
$$T=p c-p' c$$
Expressing T in terms of p and the scattering angle θ yields
$$T=\frac{p c(1-\cos\theta)}{1-\cos\theta+\frac{m c}{p}}$$
Using p=h/\lambda gives
$$T=\frac{(1-\cos\theta)\frac{h c}{\lambda}}{1-\cos\theta+\frac{m c\lambda}{h}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of T = ..., and your response should be written with λ, θ, h, m, c.

context: An X-ray photon with initial frequency nu_0 collides with an electron at rest and is scattered through an angle theta. The electron Compton wavelength is lambda_c. Use c for the speed of light, h for Planck's constant, m for the electron rest mass, lambda_0 for the incident wavelength, lambda' for the scattered wavelength, and nu' for the scattered frequency. Given nu_0=3×10^{19} Hz, theta=90°, lambda_c=2.4×10^{-12} m, and c=3×10^8 m/s. Find nu'.
solution:
Suppose that the target electron is free. The Compton shift relation is
$$
\lambda'=\lambda_0+\frac{h}{mc}(1-\cos\theta)
$$
Using the definition of the electron Compton wavelength
$$
\lambda_c=\frac{h}{mc}
$$
At theta=90^\circ, the scattered wavelength is
$$
\lambda'=\lambda_0+\lambda_c
$$
The incident wavelength is
$$
\lambda_0=\frac{c}{\nu_0}
$$
Substituting the given values
$$
\nu_0=3\times 10^{19}\unit{Hz}
$$
$$
\lambda_c=2.4\times 10^{-12}\unit{m}
$$
$$
 c=3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}
$$
Compute the incident wavelength
$$
\lambda_0=\frac{3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}}{3\times 10^{19}\unit{Hz}}
$$
$$
\lambda_0=1\times 10^{-11}\unit{m}
$$
Then the scattered wavelength is
$$
\lambda'=1.24\times 10^{-11}\unit{m}
$$
Finally, the new frequency is
$$
\nu'=\frac{c}{\lambda'}
$$
$$
\nu'=\frac{3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}}{1.24\times 10^{-11}\unit{m}}
$$
$$
\nu'=2.42\times 10^{19}\unit{Hz}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express nu' (the scattered frequency) as a numerical value in Hz. Report your answer to 3 significant figures.

context: Consider Compton scattering of photons that collide head-on with moving electrons, and observe back-scattered photons at scattering angle θ=180°. Let the incident photon energy be E_γ=hν=2\unit{eV}, where h is Planck's constant and ν is the photon frequency. The incident electron has kinetic energy T_e=1\unit{GeV}. Work in natural units with c=1, so the photon energy equals its momentum magnitude. Define the electron rest mass energy m_e=0.511\unit{MeV}. Denote the total energy and momentum magnitude of the incident electron by E_e and p_e, and those of the incident photon by E_γ and p_γ. After the collision, denote the corresponding quantities by E_e', p_e', E_γ', p_γ'. For photons E_γ=p_γ and E_γ'=p_γ'. Find the energy of the back-scattered photons, E_γ'.
solution:
Conservation of energy gives
$$
E_\gamma+E_e=E_\gamma'+E_e'
$$
For photons
$$
E_\gamma=p_\gamma
$$
$$
E_\gamma'=p_\gamma'
$$
Conservation of momentum along the collision axis for a head-on collision with back-scattering gives
$$
-p_\gamma+p_e=p_\gamma'+p_e'
$$
Adding the previous two conservation equations gives
$$
E_e'+p_e'=-2p_\gamma'+E_e+p_e
$$
Subtracting the momentum equation from the energy equation gives
$$
E_e'-p_e'=2p_\gamma+E_e-p_e
$$
Multiplying the last two equations yields
$$
E_e'^2-p_e'^2=E_e^2-p_e^2+2p_\gamma(E_e+p_e)-2p_\gamma'(E_e-p_e+2p_\gamma)
$$
Using the on-shell conditions for the electron
$$
E_e'^2-p_e'^2=m_e^2
$$
$$
E_e^2-p_e^2=m_e^2
$$
Solving for the scattered photon momentum gives
$$
 p_\gamma'=\frac{p_\gamma(E_e+p_e)}{E_e-p_e+2p_\gamma}
$$
For an ultrarelativistic electron we use the approximations
$$
E_e-p_e=E_e-\sqrt{E_e^2-m_e^2}
$$
$$
\sqrt{E_e^2-m_e^2}\approx E_e\Big(1-\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e^2}\Big)
$$
$$
E_e-p_e\approx\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e}
$$
$$
E_e+p_e\approx 2E_e
$$
$$
E_e\approx T_e
$$
Substituting these into the expression for p_\gamma' gives
$$
 p_\gamma'\approx\frac{2p_\gamma E_e}{\frac{m_e^2}{2E_e}+2p_\gamma}
$$
Use the numerical values
$$
T_e=1\unit{GeV}
$$
$$
T_e=10^3\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
m_e=0.511\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
E_\gamma=2\unit{eV}
$$
$$
E_\gamma=2\times10^{-6}\unit{MeV}
$$
$$
p_\gamma=E_\gamma
$$
Substituting the numbers yields
$$
 p_\gamma'\approx\frac{2\times2\times10^{-6}\times10^{3}}{\frac{0.511^{2}}{2\times10^{3}}+2\times2\times10^{-6}}\unit{MeV/c}
$$
Evaluating the expression gives
$$
 p_\gamma'\approx29.7\unit{MeV/c}
$$
Since for photons E_\gamma'=p_\gamma', the back-scattered photon energy is
$$
E_\gamma'\approx29.7\unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_γ' as a numerical value with units of energy. Report the value to 3 significant figures.

context: Assume natural units with c=1. Two photons with energies ε and E (take E ≥ ε) collide head-on along a line. Let P and p denote their three-momentum vectors, which are antiparallel, with magnitudes |P| = E and |p| = ε. Let β denote the speed (in units of c) of the inertial frame in which the total three-momentum of the two-photon system is zero. Let S denote the squared invariant mass of the two-photon system. Let m_e be the electron rest mass, expressed in energy units via c=1. In part (b), take ε = 1\unit{eV}.

subquestions.subproblem: Two photons with energies ε and E collide head-on. Show that the speed β of the frame in which the total three-momentum is zero is given by $$\beta=\frac{E-\varepsilon}{E+\varepsilon}$$
subquestions.solution: Let P and p be the three-momenta of the photons, antiparallel, with magnitudes $$|P|=E$$ $$|p|=\varepsilon$$ The total momentum magnitude is $$|P+p|=E-\varepsilon$$ The total energy is $$E+\varepsilon$$ Hence the speed of the zero-momentum frame is $$\beta=\frac{|P+p|}{E+\varepsilon}$$ which gives $$\beta=\frac{E-\varepsilon}{E+\varepsilon}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of β = ..., and it should be expressed solely in terms of E and ε.

subquestions.subproblem: If the colliding photons are to produce an electron-positron pair and \varepsilon is 1\unit{eV}, what must be the minimum value of the energy E?
subquestions.solution: At threshold the squared invariant mass of the two-photon system equals the squared mass of the produced pair $$S=(E+\varepsilon)^2-|P+p|^2$$ $$S=(2m_e)^2$$ For head-on photons $$|P+p|^2=(E-\varepsilon)^2$$ Combining these gives $$(E+\varepsilon)^2-(E-\varepsilon)^2=(2m_e)^2$$ which yields $$4E\varepsilon=4m_e^2$$ Thus the minimum required energy is $$E=\frac{m_e^2}{\varepsilon}$$ For \varepsilon=1\unit{eV} and m_e=0.511\unit{MeV} one finds $$E=261\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the minimum energy E as a numerical value in GeV, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: The J/psi particle has rest mass m_J = 3.097 \unit{GeV/c^2} and total decay width Gamma = 63 \unit{keV}. A specific J/psi is produced with laboratory momentum p_J = 100 \unit{GeV/c} and subsequently decays as J/psi -> e^+ + e^-. Use c for the speed of light, \hbar for the reduced Planck constant, tau_0 for the proper lifetime, tau for the laboratory lifetime, beta = v/c, and gamma for the Lorentz factor. Let l denote the mean decay length in the laboratory. Use E_J for the laboratory energy of the J/psi, E_e and p_e for the laboratory energy and momentum magnitude of the decay electron, and theta for the electron’s laboratory angle with respect to the J/psi flight direction. The electron mass is m_e = 0.511 \unit{MeV/c^2}. When evaluating square roots of energy–momentum relations, use E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2 with consistent units.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the mean distance traveled by the J/psi in the laboratory before decaying.
subquestions.solution:
The proper lifetime is
$$
\tau_0 = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma}
$$
Using \hbar = 6.58\times 10^{-16} \unit{eV s} and \Gamma = 63\times 10^3 \unit{eV},
$$
\tau_0 = \frac{6.58\times 10^{-16} \unit{eV s}}{63\times 10^3 \unit{eV}}
$$
$$
\tau_0 = 1.045\times 10^{-20} \unit{s}
$$
The mean decay length is
$$
l = \tau \beta c
$$
with
$$
\tau = \gamma \tau_0
$$
and
$$
\gamma \beta = \frac{p_J c}{m_J c^2}
$$
Hence
$$
l = \tau_0 \frac{p_J c}{m_J c^2} c
$$
Numerically,
$$
l = 1.045\times 10^{-20} \unit{s} \times \frac{100}{3.097} \times 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}
$$
$$
l = 1.012\times 10^{-10} \unit{m}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the mean decay length l as a numerical value in meters (m), rounded to 4 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: For a symmetric decay (i.e., e^+ and e^- have the same laboratory momenta), find the energy of the decay electron in the laboratory.
subquestions.solution:
Energy conservation gives
$$
E_J = 2 E_e
$$
The J/psi energy is
$$
E_J = \sqrt{(p_J c)^2 + (m_J c^2)^2}
$$
Thus
$$
E_e = \frac{1}{2} E_J
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_e = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{100^2 + 3.097^2} \unit{GeV}
$$
$$
E_e = 50.024 \unit{GeV}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the laboratory energy E_e of the decay electron as a numerical value in GeV, rounded to 5 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the laboratory angle of the electron with respect to the direction of the J/psi.
subquestions.solution:
For a symmetric decay, momentum conservation along the J/psi direction gives p_J = 2 p_e \cos \theta and energy conservation gives E_J = 2 E_e. Using E_e^2 = (p_e c)^2 + (m_e c^2)^2, one finds
$$
\cos \theta = \frac{p_J c}{\sqrt{(p_J c)^2 + (m_J c^2)^2 - 4 (m_e c^2)^2}}
$$
With p_J in \unit{GeV/c} and masses in \unit{GeV/c^2},
$$
\cos \theta = \frac{100}{\sqrt{100^2 + 3.097^2 - 4\times (0.511\times 10^{-3})^2}}
$$
$$
\cos \theta = 0.9995
$$
$$
\theta = 1.77 \unit{deg}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the laboratory angle \theta in degrees (deg) as a numerical value, rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: A negative Xi^- particle decays into a Lambda^0 and a pi^- as follows: $$\Xi^- \to \Lambda^0 + \pi^-$$ The Xi^- moves in the laboratory frame along the positive x direction with momentum defined as $$p_\Xi=2\unit{GeV/c}$$ In the Xi^- rest frame (denoted by an overbar on any quantity), the Lambda^0 is emitted at a polar angle of 30^\circ relative to the initial Xi^- direction. Using natural units with c=1, so that energies and rest masses are given in GeV and momenta in GeV/c, find the laboratory-frame momenta and angles of the Lambda^0 and the pi^- with respect to the positive x axis after the decay. Use the following rest energies: $$M_\Xi c^2=1.3\unit{GeV}$$ $$M_\Lambda c^2=1.1\unit{GeV}$$ $$M_\pi c^2=0.14\unit{GeV}$$ Definitions and notation to be used in the solution: m_\Xi, m_\Lambda, and m_\pi denote the rest masses expressed in GeV via m=M c^2. E denotes total energy in GeV and p denotes the magnitude of the three-momentum in GeV/c. The Lorentz factors for the initial Xi^- in the lab are beta_\Xi=v_\Xi/c and gamma_\Xi=1/\sqrt{1-\beta_\Xi^2}. A bar over a symbol indicates the Xi^- rest frame. The unknowns to determine are p_\Lambda, \theta_\Lambda, p_\pi, and \theta_\pi in the laboratory frame.
solution: Compute the Xi^- lab energy, speed parameter, and Lorentz factor: $$E_\Xi=\sqrt{p_\Xi^2+m_\Xi^2}$$ $$E_\Xi=2.385\unit{GeV}$$ $$\beta_\Xi=\frac{p_\Xi}{E_\Xi}$$ $$\beta_\Xi=0.839$$ $$\gamma_\Xi=\frac{E_\Xi}{m_\Xi}$$ $$\gamma_\Xi=1.835$$ Work in the Xi^- rest frame (barred quantities). Conservation of momentum and energy give: $$\bar{\mathbf p}_\pi+\bar{\mathbf p}_\Lambda=\mathbf 0$$ $$\bar E_\pi+\bar E_\Lambda=m_\Xi$$ Therefore, the magnitudes satisfy: $$\bar p_\Lambda=\bar p_\pi$$ On-shell relations: $$\bar E_\pi^2-\bar p_\pi^2=m_\pi^2$$ $$\bar E_\Lambda^2-\bar p_\Lambda^2=m_\Lambda^2$$ Solve for the Xi^- rest-frame energies and momenta: $$\bar E_\pi=\frac{m_\Xi^2+m_\pi^2-m_\Lambda^2}{2m_\Xi}$$ $$\bar E_\pi=0.192\unit{GeV}$$ $$\bar E_\Lambda=m_\Xi-\bar E_\pi$$ $$\bar E_\Lambda=1.108\unit{GeV}$$ $$\bar p_\Lambda=\bar p_\pi$$ $$\bar p_\Lambda=\sqrt{\bar E_\pi^2-m_\pi^2}$$ $$\bar p_\Lambda=0.132\unit{GeV/c}$$ The emission angles in the Xi^- rest frame are: $$\bar{\theta}_\Lambda=30^\circ$$ $$\bar{\theta}_\pi=210^\circ$$ Transform to the laboratory frame.
