Transverse momentum is invariant: $$p\sin\theta=\bar p\sin\bar\theta$$ Longitudinal momentum transforms as: $$p\cos\theta=\gamma_\Xi\left(\bar p\cos\bar\theta+\beta_\Xi\bar E\right)$$ For the pion: $$p_\pi\sin\theta_\pi=\bar p_\pi\sin\bar\theta_\pi$$ $$p_\pi\sin\theta_\pi=-0.066\unit{GeV/c}$$ $$p_\pi\cos\theta_\pi=\gamma_\Xi\left(\bar p_\pi\cos\bar\theta_\pi+\beta_\Xi\bar E_\pi\right)$$ $$p_\pi\cos\theta_\pi=0.086\unit{GeV/c}$$ $$\tan\theta_\pi=\frac{p_\pi\sin\theta_\pi}{p_\pi\cos\theta_\pi}$$ $$\tan\theta_\pi=-0.767$$ $$\theta_\pi=-37.5^\circ$$ $$p_\pi=\sqrt{\left(p_\pi\cos\theta_\pi\right)^2+\left(p_\pi\sin\theta_\pi\right)^2}$$ $$p_\pi=0.11\unit{GeV/c}$$ For the Lambda: $$p_\Lambda\sin\theta_\Lambda=\bar p_\Lambda\sin\bar\theta_\Lambda$$ $$p_\Lambda\sin\theta_\Lambda=0.066\unit{GeV/c}$$ $$p_\Lambda\cos\theta_\Lambda=\gamma_\Xi\left(\bar p_\Lambda\cos\bar\theta_\Lambda+\beta_\Xi\bar E_\Lambda\right)$$ $$p_\Lambda\cos\theta_\Lambda=1.92\unit{GeV/c}$$ $$\tan\theta_\Lambda=\frac{p_\Lambda\sin\theta_\Lambda}{p_\Lambda\cos\theta_\Lambda}$$ $$\tan\theta_\Lambda=0.034$$ $$\theta_\Lambda=1.9^\circ$$ $$p_\Lambda=\sqrt{\left(p_\Lambda\cos\theta_\Lambda\right)^2+\left(p_\Lambda\sin\theta_\Lambda\right)^2}$$ $$p_\Lambda=1.92\unit{GeV/c}$$ The angle between the Lambda and the pion directions in the laboratory is: $$\theta=\theta_\Lambda-\theta_\pi$$ $$\theta=39.4^\circ$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express p_\Lambda (in GeV/c), \theta_\Lambda (in degrees), p_\pi (in GeV/c), and \theta_\pi (in degrees) as numerical values. Report them in the format: p_\Lambda = ..., \theta_\Lambda = ..., p_\pi = ..., \theta_\pi = .... Angles must be measured with respect to the positive x axis. Use 3 significant figures for all reported values.

context: A K-meson (denoted K) of rest energy 494 MeV decays at rest into a muon (denoted mu) of rest energy 106 MeV and a neutrino of zero rest energy. Work in natural units with c=1. Define m_K=494 MeV and m_mu=106 MeV as the rest energies of K and mu, respectively. Let E_mu and E_nu denote the total energies of the muon and neutrino. Let p_mu and p_nu denote the magnitudes of their three-momenta. Let T_mu and T_nu denote their kinetic energies, with T=E-m for massive particles and T=E for massless particles. Find T_mu and T_nu in the K rest frame.
solution:
In the K rest frame, momentum conservation implies

$$
p_mu=p_nu
$$

Energy conservation gives

$$
E_mu+E_nu=m_K
$$

For the neutrino,

$$
E_nu=p_nu
$$

For the muon,

$$
E_mu^2=p_mu^2+m_mu^2
$$

From energy conservation,

$$
E_mu^2=(m_K-E_nu)^2
$$

Expanding,

$$
E_mu^2=m_K^2+E_nu^2-2 m_K E_nu
$$

Using E_nu=p_nu and p_mu=p_nu together with E_mu^2=p_mu^2+m_mu^2, we obtain

$$
p_mu=\frac{m_K^2-m_mu^2}{2 m_K}
$$

Numerically,

$$
p_mu=236 \unit{MeV/c}
$$

For the neutrino kinetic energy,

$$
T_nu=E_nu
$$

Also,

$$
E_nu=p_nu
$$

Thus,

$$
T_nu=236 \unit{MeV}
$$

For the muon kinetic energy,

$$
T_mu=\sqrt{p_mu^2+m_mu^2}-m_mu
$$

Therefore,

$$
T_mu=152 \unit{MeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T_mu and T_nu as numerical values in MeV (natural units with c=1), each reported to 3 significant figures, in the form: T_mu = ..., T_nu = ....

context: The η′ meson, with mass M, can decay into a ρ0 meson, with mass m, and a photon with zero mass via the process η′ → ρ0 + γ. The decay is isotropic in the rest frame of the parent η′ meson. Consider a monoenergetic beam of η′ mesons traveling with speed v in the laboratory along a fixed beam direction. Let θ be the angle between the photon momentum and the beam direction in the laboratory frame. Define P(θ) d(cos θ) as the normalized probability that cos θ lies in the interval (cos θ, cos θ + d cos θ). Work in natural units with c = 1. Define β = v/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β^2). An overbar denotes quantities measured in the rest frame of the parent η′. Let E and p be the photon energy and momentum magnitude in the laboratory frame, and let \bar{E} and \bar{p} be the corresponding quantities in the rest frame of the η′. Let E_η and p_η be the laboratory energy and momentum magnitude of the parent η′ meson.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute P(θ).
subquestions.solution:
Lorentz transformation of the photon 4-momentum components gives
$$\bar p \cos \bar \theta = \gamma \left( p \cos \theta - \beta E \right)$$
$$\bar E = \gamma \left( E - \beta p \cos \theta \right)$$
For a photon in natural units, E = p in any frame and \bar E = \bar p
$$p = E$$
$$\bar p = \bar E$$
Hence the aberration formula is
$$\cos \bar \theta = \frac{\cos \theta - \beta}{1 - \beta \cos \theta}$$
Differentiating with respect to cos θ yields
$$\frac{d \cos \bar \theta}{d \cos \theta} = \frac{1 - \beta^2}{\left( 1 - \beta \cos \theta \right)^2}$$
Isotropy in the η′ rest frame implies a constant probability per unit solid angle
$$d \bar \Omega = 2 \pi \sin \bar \theta d \bar \theta$$
$$d \bar \Omega = 2 \pi d \cos \bar \theta$$
$$dP = \frac{d \bar \Omega}{4 \pi}$$
Thus
$$dP = \frac{1}{2} d \cos \bar \theta$$
Relating to the laboratory variable gives
$$dP = P(\theta) d \cos \theta$$
Therefore
$$P(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{d \cos \bar \theta}{d \cos \theta}$$
Finally
$$P(\theta) = \frac{1 - \beta^2}{2 \left( 1 - \beta \cos \theta \right)^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P(θ) = ..., and your response should be written with β and θ only.

subquestions.subproblem: Let E(θ) be the laboratory energy of the photon emitted at angle θ. Compute E(θ).
subquestions.solution:
In the η′ rest frame, energy-momentum conservation for the decay η′ → ρ0 + γ gives
$$\bar E_\rho = M - \bar E$$
$$\bar p_\rho = \bar p$$
The ρ0 is on its mass shell
$$\bar E_\rho^2 - \bar p_\rho^2 = m^2$$
Using \bar p = \bar E for the photon, this implies
$$m^2 = M^2 - 2 M \bar E$$
Hence the photon energy in the η′ rest frame is
$$\bar E = \frac{M^2 - m^2}{2 M}$$
Transforming to the laboratory frame using the photon energy transformation
$$\bar E = \gamma E \left( 1 - \beta \cos \theta \right)$$
Solving for E gives
$$E = \frac{\bar E}{\gamma \left( 1 - \beta \cos \theta \right)}$$
Expressing γ and β in terms of the laboratory energy and momentum of the parent η′
$$\gamma = \frac{E_\eta}{M}$$
$$\beta = \frac{p_\eta}{E_\eta}$$
Substituting yields
$$E(\theta) = \frac{M^2 - m^2}{2 \left( E_\eta - p_\eta \cos \theta \right)}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E(θ) = ..., and your response should be written with M, m, E_η, p_η, and θ only.

context: A neutral long-lived kaon K_L^0 with rest mass M decays in flight into two charged pions pi^+ and pi^- with rest mass m. The rest energies are M c^2 = 498 \unit{MeV} and m c^2 = 140 \unit{MeV}. The kaon's laboratory momentum magnitude p satisfies p/(M c) = 1. Use natural units c = 1 in intermediate formulas; numerical answers must be reported with units. Definitions: E_K is the kaon laboratory-frame energy, beta_c = v_K/c is the kaon speed parameter, and gamma_c = 1/sqrt(1 - beta_c^2) is the corresponding Lorentz factor. In the kaon rest frame, \bar{E} and \bar{p} are respectively the energy and momentum magnitude of a decay pion, and \bar{\theta} is its emission angle relative to the kaon's laboratory flight direction. In the laboratory, p_t and p_l are respectively the transverse and longitudinal components of a decay pion's momentum. Determine p_{t,max}, the maximum possible transverse momentum, and p_{l,max}, the maximum possible longitudinal momentum, of a decay pion in the laboratory.
solution:
In the laboratory frame, the kaon speed parameter is
$$
\beta_c = \frac{p}{E_K}
$$
The kaon laboratory-frame energy is
$$
E_K = \sqrt{p^2 + M^2}
$$
Using p/(M c) = 1 with c = 1 gives
$$
\beta_c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
$$
The Lorentz factor is
$$
\gamma_c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_c^2}}
$$
Hence
$$
\gamma_c = \sqrt{2}
$$
In the kaon rest frame, energy conservation gives
$$
2 \bar{E} = M
$$
Thus
$$
\bar{E} = \frac{M}{2}
$$
The pion momentum magnitude in that frame is
$$
\bar{p} = \sqrt{\bar{E}^2 - m^2}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\bar{p} = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{M^2 - 4 m^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
\bar{p} \approx 206 \unit{MeV/c}
$$
A boost along the kaon flight direction does not change the transverse component, so
$$
p_{t,\max} = \bar{p}
$$
Hence
$$
 p_{t,\max} \approx 206 \unit{MeV/c}
$$
The longitudinal component of a pion's momentum in the laboratory is
$$
 p_l = \gamma_c ( \bar{p} \cos \bar{\theta} + \beta_c \bar{E} )
$$
Thus the maximum occurs at \cos \bar{\theta} = 1, giving
$$
 p_{l,\max} = \gamma_c ( \bar{p} + \beta_c \bar{E} )
$$
Using \bar{E} = M/2 gives
$$
 p_{l,\max} = \gamma_c \left( \bar{p} + \beta_c \frac{M}{2} \right)
$$
Numerically
$$
 p_{l,\max} \approx 540 \unit{MeV/c}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express p_{t,max} and p_{l,max} as numerical values with units of MeV/c. Report both values to 3 significant figures, in the form: p_{t,max} = [value] MeV/c and p_{l,max} = [value] MeV/c.

context: The proper (rest-frame) mean lifetime of a charged pion is tau_0=2.6\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}. A monoenergetic beam of charged pions travels a distance l=10\unit{m} in the laboratory frame, during which 10\% of the pions decay, so N(l)=\frac{9}{10}N_0, where N_0 is the initial number of pions and N(l) is the number remaining after distance l. Let v be the pion speed, define \beta=\frac{v}{c} with 0<\beta<1, and let c=3\times 10^8\unit{m/s} be the speed of light. Define the Lorentz factor \gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}. Let t be the flight time over distance l, \tau the mean lifetime in the lab frame, and \lambda=\frac{1}{\tau} the decay constant in the lab frame. Let m be the charged pion rest mass with numerical value m=0.14\unit{GeV/c^2}. Use p for the pion momentum and T for the pion kinetic energy, to be reported in \unit{GeV/c} and \unit{GeV}, respectively.
solution:
The flight time is
$$
t=\frac{l}{\beta c}
$$
The number of undecayed pions after traveling distance l is
$$
N(l)=N_0\exp\Big(-\frac{t}{\tau}\Big)
$$
The decay constant in the lab frame is
$$
\lambda=\frac{1}{\tau}
$$
Time dilation gives
$$
\tau=\gamma\tau_0
$$
Hence the survival ratio is
$$
\frac{N(l)}{N_0}=\exp\Big(-\frac{l}{\gamma\beta c\tau_0}\Big)
$$
Solving for \gamma\beta,
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{l}{\tau_0 c\ln\Big(\frac{N_0}{N(l)}\Big)}
$$
Using l=10\unit{m}, \tau_0=2.6\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}, c=3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}, and \frac{N(l)}{N_0}=\frac{9}{10},
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{10\unit{m}}{\big(2.6\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}\big)\big(3\times 10^8\unit{m/s}\big)\ln\Big(\frac{10}{9}\Big)}
$$
$$
\gamma\beta=12.2
$$
The momentum is
$$
p=\gamma\beta\,m c
$$
$$
p=1.71\unit{GeV/c}
$$
The kinetic energy is
$$
T=\sqrt{p^2 c^2+m^2 c^4}-m c^2
$$
Substituting p=1.71\unit{GeV/c} and m=0.14\unit{GeV/c^2},
$$
T=\sqrt{\big(1.71\unit{GeV}\big)^2+\big(0.14\unit{GeV}\big)^2}-0.14\unit{GeV}
$$
$$
T=1.58\unit{GeV}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the pion momentum p and kinetic energy T as numerical values. Report p in GeV/c and T in GeV. Present them in the format: p = ... and T = .... Include units. Report both values to 3 significant figures.

context: Neutral mesons are produced by a proton beam striking a thin target. Each meson decays into two gamma rays. The photon emitted in the forward direction (along the beam) has energy 96 MeV, and the photon emitted in the backward direction (opposite the beam) has energy 48 MeV. Treat the neutral meson as a neutral pion pi^0. Define E as the meson total energy in the laboratory frame, p as the magnitude of the meson momentum along the beam, v as the meson speed, c as the speed of light, and beta = v/c. Let E_1 and p_1 be the energy and momentum magnitude of the forward photon, and E_2 and p_2 be those of the backward photon. For photons, p_i = E_i/c. Define gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - beta^2). Let m be the meson rest mass, with rest energy m c^2.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine beta = v / c for the mesons.
subquestions.solution:
Given
$$E_1 = 96 \unit{MeV}$$
$$E_2 = 48 \unit{MeV}$$
Conservation of energy gives
$$E = E_1 + E_2$$
$$E = 144 \unit{MeV}$$
For the photon momenta
$$p_1 = \frac{E_1}{c}$$
$$p_2 = \frac{E_2}{c}$$
Conservation of momentum along the beam gives
$$p = p_1 - p_2$$
$$p = \frac{E_1 - E_2}{c}$$
$$p = 48 \unit{MeV/c}$$
The meson speed parameter is
$$\beta = \frac{pc}{E}$$
$$\beta = \frac{1}{3}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as beta = [number], expressed as a numerical value.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the (approximate) rest energy of the mesons.
subquestions.solution:
Using m = E/\gamma
$$m = \frac{E}{\gamma}$$
With
$$\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}}$$
We have
$$m = E \sqrt{1 - \beta^2}$$
Numerically
$$m = 144 \unit{MeV} \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{9}}$$
$$m = 48 \sqrt{8} \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m \approx 136 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as m c^2 = [number] MeV, expressed as a numerical value.

context: A particle of mass M=3\unit{GeV/c^2} moves along the x-axis in the laboratory with momentum p=4\unit{GeV/c}. It decays into two photons. In the parent-particle rest frame (denoted by overbars), the emission is isotropic: for the photon polar angle \theta^* measured from the x-axis in that frame, we have $$\frac{dP}{d\cos\theta^*}=\frac{1}{2}$$ Overbars, as in \bar E_i and \bar p_i for i=1,2, denote the energy and three-momentum of photon i in the parent-particle rest frame. Let p_x denote the x-component of a photon's momentum in the laboratory frame. Let \gamma be the Lorentz factor of the parent particle in the laboratory and \beta its speed in units of c in the laboratory. Define (p_x)_{max} and (p_x)_{min} as the maximum and minimum possible values of p_x, respectively. Determine (p_x)_{max} and (p_x)_{min}. Then find the probability density dP/dp_x as a function of p_x, and specify the domain on which it is valid.
solution:
In the rest frame of the parent particle, conservation of energy and momentum gives
$$
\bar E_1+\bar E_2=M
$$
$$
\bar p_1+\bar p_2=0
$$
The photon momentum magnitudes are equal and opposite, and the photon energies are equal, so
$$
\bar p_1=\bar p
$$
$$
\bar p_2=\bar p
$$
$$
\bar E_1=\bar E
$$
$$
\bar E_2=\bar E
$$
Energy conservation then implies
$$
\bar E=\frac{M}{2}
$$
For photons in these units
$$
\bar p=\bar E
$$
With M=3\unit{GeV/c^2}
$$
\bar E=\frac{3}{2}\unit{GeV}
$$
$$
\bar p=\frac{3}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
For the parent particle in the laboratory
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{p}{M}
$$
$$
\gamma\beta=\frac{4}{3}
$$
$$
\gamma=\sqrt{(\gamma\beta)^2+1}
$$
$$
\gamma=\frac{5}{3}
$$
$$
\beta=\frac{\gamma\beta}{\gamma}
$$
$$
\beta=\frac{4}{5}
$$
The Lorentz transformation for the x component of a photon momentum gives
$$
 p_x=\gamma(\bar p\cos\theta^*+\beta\bar E)
$$
Using \bar p=\bar E
$$
 p_x=\gamma\bar p(\cos\theta^*+\beta)
$$
The maximum occurs at \theta^*=0, hence
$$
(p_x)_{max}=\gamma\bar p(1+\beta)
$$
$$
(p_x)_{max}=\frac{9}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
The minimum occurs at \theta^*=\pi, hence
$$
(p_x)_{min}=\gamma\bar p(-1+\beta)
$$
$$
(p_x)_{min}=-\frac{1}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Differentiating the transformation relation gives
$$
 dp_x=\gamma\bar p\,d\cos\theta^*
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{dP}{d\cos\theta^*}\frac{d\cos\theta^*}{dp_x}
$$
With isotropy in the rest frame
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\gamma\bar p}
$$
Compute the factor
$$
\gamma\bar p=\frac{5}{2}\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{dP}{dp_x}=\frac{1}{5}\unit{c/GeV}
$$
This result holds on the support given by
$$
 p_x\ge (p_x)_{min}
$$
$$
 p_x\le (p_x)_{max}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express (p_x)_{max} and (p_x)_{min} as numerical values in GeV/c. Then give the probability density explicitly in the form dP/dp_x = ... as a numerical value with units c/GeV, and state its valid domain as numerical inequalities for p_x: (p_x)_{min} <= p_x <= (p_x)_{max}, with both endpoints given numerically in GeV/c. Use exact values if convenient; otherwise round to 3 significant figures.

context: A neutral pion (pi^0) decays into two gamma rays. Work in natural units with c=1. Let m_{pi} be the rest mass of the pion, E its total energy in the lab frame, and p_{pi} its momentum. Let the two photons have energies E_{gamma_1} and E_{gamma_2} and momenta p_{gamma_1} and p_{gamma_2}. When the two photons are emitted symmetrically about the pion’s original direction, let their common energy and momentum be E_{gamma} and p_{gamma}, respectively. Let theta be the angle each photon makes with the pion’s initial direction, and let theta_{2gamma} be the angle between the two photons. In part (c), take m_{pi}=135\unit{MeV} and E=1\unit{GeV}.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the energies of the gamma-rays if the decay process causes them to be emitted in opposite directions along the pion’s original line of motion?
subquestions.solution: Conservation of energy gives $$E=E_{\gamma_1}+E_{\gamma_2}$$ Conservation of momentum gives $$p_{\pi}=p_{\gamma_1}-p_{\gamma_2}$$ The pion energy-momentum relation is $$E^2=p_{\pi}^2+m_{\pi}^2$$ For each photon, $$E_{\gamma_1}=p_{\gamma_1}$$ For each photon, $$E_{\gamma_2}=p_{\gamma_2}$$ Combining these results gives $$m_{\pi}^2=4E_{\gamma_1}E_{\gamma_2}$$ Using E_{\gamma_2}=E-E_{\gamma_1} gives $$m_{\pi}^2=4E_{\gamma_1}(E-E_{\gamma_1})$$ Solving the quadratic for the photon energies gives $$E_{\gamma_1}=\frac{E+\sqrt{E^2-m_{\pi}^2}}{2}$$ $$E_{\gamma_2}=\frac{E-\sqrt{E^2-m_{\pi}^2}}{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_{gamma_1} = ... and E_{gamma_2} = ... , and your response should be written only with E and m_{pi}.

subquestions.subproblem: What angle is formed between the two gamma rays if they are emitted at equal angles to the direction of the pion’s motion?
subquestions.solution: By symmetry, the two photons have equal energies and momenta, denoted E_{\gamma} and p_{\gamma}, and make angles +\theta and -\theta with the pion’s original direction. Conservation of energy gives $$E=2E_{\gamma}$$ Conservation of momentum along the initial direction gives $$p_{\pi}=2p_{\gamma}\cos\theta$$ The photon dispersion relation gives $$E_{\gamma}=p_{\gamma}$$ The pion satisfies $$E^2=p_{\pi}^2+m_{\pi}^2$$ Hence $$m_{\pi}^2=E^2-p_{\pi}^2$$ Substituting p_{\pi}=2p_{\gamma}\cos\theta gives $$m_{\pi}^2=E^2-4p_{\gamma}^2\cos^2\theta$$ Using E=2E_{\gamma} gives $$m_{\pi}^2=4E_{\gamma}^2-4p_{\gamma}^2\cos^2\theta$$ Using E_{\gamma}=p_{\gamma} gives $$m_{\pi}^2=4E_{\gamma}^2-4E_{\gamma}^2\cos^2\theta$$ Re-expressing in terms of E gives $$m_{\pi}^2=E^2-E^2\cos^2\theta$$ Therefore $$m_{\pi}^2=E^2\sin^2\theta$$ Solving for the emission angle gives $$\theta=\pm\arcsin\frac{m_{\pi}}{E}$$ The angle between the two photons is $$\theta_{2\gamma}=2\theta$$ Hence $$\theta_{2\gamma}=2\arcsin\frac{m_{\pi}}{E}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of theta_{2gamma} = ... , and your response should be written only with E and m_{pi}.

subquestions.subproblem: Taking m_{\pi}=135\unit{MeV} and E=1\unit{GeV}, give approximate numerical values for your above answers.
subquestions.solution: Using E=1000\unit{MeV} and m_{\pi}=135\unit{MeV} gives $$E_{\gamma_1}=\frac{10^3+\sqrt{10^6-135^2}}{2}$$ $$E_{\gamma_1}=995.4\unit{MeV}$$ $$E_{\gamma_2}=\frac{10^3-\sqrt{10^6-135^2}}{2}$$ $$E_{\gamma_2}=4.6\unit{MeV}$$ $$\theta_{2\gamma}=2\arcsin\frac{135}{1000}$$ $$\theta_{2\gamma}=15.5\unit{deg}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_{gamma_1}, E_{gamma_2}, and theta_{2gamma} as numerical values using m_{pi} = 135 MeV and E = 1 GeV. Report energies in MeV and the angle in degrees. Report each value to 3 significant figures.

context: A pi^0 meson decays isotropically into two photons in its rest frame. Consider a laboratory where a pi^0 moves along the z axis with momentum magnitude p_pi=280\unit{MeV/c}. The pion rest energy is m_pi c^2=140\unit{MeV}. Let theta be the laboratory polar angle of an emitted photon measured with respect to the pi^0 flight direction, and let phi be the corresponding laboratory azimuthal angle. Let theta^* and phi^* be the corresponding photon angles in the pion rest frame. Define w^*(cos theta^*,phi^*) as the rest-frame probability density per unit solid angle d\Omega^*=d(cos theta^*) d phi^* for photons produced in a single pi^0 decay, counting both photons, normalized by \int w^* d\Omega^*=2. Define the azimuth-integrated rest-frame distribution W^*(cos theta^*) by W^*(cos theta^*)=\int_0^{2\pi} w^*(cos theta^*,phi^*) d phi^*. Define the laboratory azimuth-integrated distribution W(cos theta) by \int_{-1}^{1} W(cos theta) d\cos\theta=2, so that W(cos theta) d\cos\theta is the probability to find a photon between cos theta and cos theta+d\cos\theta in the laboratory. Let k and E be the laboratory photon momentum magnitude and energy, and let k^* and E^* be their values in the pion rest frame. Let gamma_0 and beta_0 be the Lorentz factor and speed (in units of c) of the moving pi^0. Work in natural units c=1 in the derivation, while using \unit{} for the given input values. Find the explicit expression for W(cos theta) and give the final answer as W(cos theta)=...
solution:
In the pion rest frame the two-photon emission is isotropic, so w^*(cos theta^*,phi^*) is constant and satisfies the normalization
$$
\int w^*(cos theta^*,phi^*) d\Omega^*=2
$$
Because of isotropy,
$$
4\pi w^*=2
$$
Thus
$$
w^*=\frac{1}{2\pi}
$$
Define the azimuth-integrated rest-frame distribution
$$
W^*(\cos\theta^*)=\int_0^{2\pi} w^*(\cos\theta^*,\phi^*) d\phi^*
$$
Hence
$$
W^*(\cos\theta^*)=1
$$
The laboratory and rest-frame azimuth-integrated distributions are related by the Jacobian
$$
W(\cos\theta) d\cos\theta=W^*(\cos\theta^*) d\cos\theta^*
$$
For a photon, the longitudinal momentum component transforms as
$$
k\cos\theta=\gamma_0\big(k^*\cos\theta^*+\beta_0 E^*\big)
$$
The energy transforms as
$$
E=\gamma_0\big(E^*+\beta_0 k^*\cos\theta^*\big)
$$
For photons,
$$
E=k
$$
Differentiate the longitudinal component transformation with respect to \cos\theta^* to obtain
$$
\cos\theta\frac{dk}{d\cos\theta^*}+k\frac{d\cos\theta}{d\cos\theta^*}=\gamma_0 k^*
$$
Differentiate the energy transformation to obtain
$$
\frac{dk}{d\cos\theta^*}=\gamma_0\beta_0 k^*
$$
Eliminating \frac{dk}{d\cos\theta^*} gives
$$
\frac{d\cos\theta^*}{d\cos\theta}=\frac{k}{\gamma_0 k^*\big(1-\beta_0\cos\theta\big)}
$$
Use the inverse energy transformation
$$
E^*=\gamma_0\big(E-\beta_0 k\cos\theta\big)
$$
Since E^*=k^* and E=k,
$$
k^*=\gamma_0 k\big(1-\beta_0\cos\theta\big)
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{d\cos\theta^*}{d\cos\theta}=\frac{1}{\gamma_0^2\big(1-\beta_0\cos\theta\big)^2}
$$
With W^*(\cos\theta^*)=1,
$$
W(\cos\theta)=\frac{1}{\gamma_0^2\big(1-\beta_0\cos\theta\big)^2}
$$
For the given pion,
$$
p_\pi=280\unit{MeV/c}
$$
And
$$
m_\pi c^2=140\unit{MeV}
$$
Using p_\pi=\gamma_0\beta_0 m_\pi c,
$$
\gamma_0\beta_0=\frac{p_\pi c}{m_\pi c^2}
$$
Thus
$$
\gamma_0\beta_0=\frac{280}{140}
$$
Hence
$$
\gamma_0\beta_0=2
$$
Using \gamma_0^2=1+(\gamma_0\beta_0)^2,
$$
\gamma_0^2=5
$$
Therefore
$$
\gamma_0=\sqrt{5}
$$
And
$$
\beta_0=\frac{\gamma_0\beta_0}{\gamma_0}
$$
Hence
$$
\beta_0=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}
$$
Substitute into the distribution
$$
W(\cos\theta)=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{5})^2\big(1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\cos\theta\big)^2}
$$
Finally
$$
W(\cos\theta)=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{5}-2\cos\theta)^2}
$$

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the mean distance traveled by the pions before they decay.
subquestions.solution: The pions have Lorentz factor $$\gamma=\frac{E_\pi}{m_\pi}$$ For ultrarelativistic pions $$\gamma\approx\frac{p_\pi}{m_\pi}$$ The beam momentum is $$p_\pi=200\times 10^3 \unit{MeV/c}$$ Thus $$\gamma=\frac{200000}{139.6}$$ Hence $$\gamma\approx 1433$$ The laboratory lifetime is $$\tau=\gamma\tau_0$$ With \tau_0=2.60\times 10^{-8} \unit{s} $$\tau=3.72\times 10^{-5} \unit{s}$$ Using the speed of light $$c=3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}$$ the mean decay distance is $$l=c\tau$$ Therefore $$l=1.12\times 10^4 \unit{m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the mean decay distance l in meters (m) as a numerical value, rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the maximum angle of the muon (relative to the pion direction) in the laboratory.
subquestions.solution: In \Sigma^*, conservation of energy gives $$E_\nu^*+E_\mu^*=m_\pi$$ Back-to-back emission implies equal magnitudes $$p_\nu^*=p_\mu^*$$ The muon energy in \Sigma^* is $$E_\mu^*=\frac{m_\pi^2+m_\mu^2}{2m_\pi}$$ Numerically $$E_\mu^*=109.8 \unit{MeV}$$ The Lorentz transformation to \Sigma for the muon components yields $$p_\mu\sin\theta=p_\mu^*\sin\theta^*$$ and $$p_\mu\cos\theta=\gamma(p_\mu^*\cos\theta^*+\beta E_\mu^*)$$ Therefore $$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta^*}{\gamma\left(\cos\theta^*+\frac{E_\mu^*}{p_\mu^*}\right)}$$ Define $$\beta_\mu^*=\frac{p_\mu^*}{E_\mu^*}$$ Hence $$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta^*}{\gamma\left(\cos\theta^*+\frac{1}{\beta_\mu^*}\right)}$$ To maximize \theta, set $$\frac{d\tan\theta}{d\theta^*}=0$$ which gives $$\cos\theta^*=-\beta_\mu^*$$ and $$\sin\theta^*=\frac{1}{\gamma_\mu^*}$$ where $$\gamma_\mu^*=\frac{E_\mu^*}{m_\mu}$$ Numerically $$\gamma_\mu^*=\frac{109.8}{105.7}$$ so $$\gamma_\mu^*=1.039$$ Therefore $$\left(\tan\theta\right)_{\max}=\frac{\sqrt{\gamma_\mu^{*2}-1}}{\gamma}$$ The maximum angle is $$\theta_{\max}=\arctan\left((\tan\theta)_{\max}\right)$$ For \gamma=1433 $$\theta_{\max}\approx\frac{\sqrt{\gamma_\mu^{*2}-1}}{\gamma}$$ Hence $$\theta_{\max}=1.97\times 10^{-4} \unit{rad}$$ and in degrees $$\theta_{\max}=0.011 \unit{deg}$$

context: A beam of pions of laboratory energy E_0 travels along the z-axis and can decay via the two-body process π → μ + ν. The neutrino is massless and emerges in the lab at polar angle θ_ν relative to the z-axis. Work in natural units with c=1. Definitions: m_π is the pion rest mass, m_μ is the muon rest mass, E_μ and E_ν are the lab-frame energies of the muon and neutrino, and p_μ and p_ν are their lab-frame momentum magnitudes. The muon lab polar angle is θ, and the neutrino lab polar angle is θ_ν. In part (b), γ is the Lorentz factor of the parent pion, β is its speed in units of c, and an overbar denotes quantities measured in the pion rest frame. Define θ_m as the lab polar angle such that half of the neutrinos have θ_ν < θ_m.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the neutrino energy as a function of θ_ν. Show that if E_0 ≫ m_π and θ_ν ≪ 1, then E_ν ≈ E_0 [1 − (m_μ/m_π)^2] / [1 + (E_0/m_π)^2 θ_ν^2].
subquestions.solution: Conservation of energy gives $$E_0=E_μ+E_ν$$ Conservation of momentum along z gives $$\sqrt{E_0^2-m_π^2}=p_μ\cos\theta+p_ν\cos\theta_ν$$ Conservation of momentum transverse to z gives $$0=p_μ\sin\theta+p_ν\sin\theta_ν$$ For a massless neutrino, $$p_ν=E_ν$$ From the momentum components, $$p_μ^2=E_0^2-m_π^2+p_ν^2-2\sqrt{E_0^2-m_π^2}E_ν\cos\theta_ν$$ From the energy relation, $$p_μ^2=E_0^2-m_μ^2+p_ν^2-2E_0E_ν$$ Subtracting the last two results, $$E_ν=\frac{m_π^2-m_μ^2}{2\bigl(E_0-\sqrt{E_0^2-m_π^2}\cos\theta_ν\bigr)}$$ Equivalently, $$E_ν=\frac{m_π^2}{2E_0}\frac{1-(m_μ/m_π)^2}{1-\sqrt{1-(m_π/E_0)^2}\cos\theta_ν}$$ In the limit E_0 \gg m_π and θ_ν \ll 1, use $$\sqrt{1-(m_π/E_0)^2}\approx 1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{m_π}{E_0}\right)^2$$ and $$\cos\theta_ν\approx 1-\frac{1}{2}\theta_ν^2$$ so that $$\sqrt{1-(m_π/E_0)^2}\cos\theta_ν\approx\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{m_π}{E_0}\right)^2\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\theta_ν^2\right)$$ and $$\sqrt{1-(m_π/E_0)^2}\cos\theta_ν\approx 1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{m_π}{E_0}\right)^2-\frac{1}{2}\theta_ν^2$$ which gives $$E_ν\approx\frac{m_π^2}{E_0}\frac{1-(m_μ/m_π)^2}{(m_π/E_0)^2+\theta_ν^2}$$ and hence $$E_ν\approx E_0\frac{1-(m_μ/m_π)^2}{1+(E_0/m_π)^2\theta_ν^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide two expressions: (i) an exact expression for the neutrino lab energy in the form of E_ν = ..., written only in terms of E_0, m_π, m_μ, and θ_ν; and (ii) the high-energy, small-angle approximation in the form of E_ν ≈ ..., using the same variables.

subquestions.subproblem: The decay is isotropic in the pion rest frame. Determine the angle θ_m such that half the neutrinos will have θ_ν < θ_m.
subquestions.solution: The pion Lorentz factor is $$\gamma=\frac{E_0}{m_π}$$ and its speed is $$\beta=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\gamma^2}}$$ The transverse component transforms as $$p_ν\sin\theta_ν=\bar p_ν\sin\bar\theta_ν$$ The longitudinal component transforms as $$p_ν\cos\theta_ν=\gamma\bigl(\bar p_ν\cos\bar\theta_ν+\beta\bar E_ν\bigr)$$ For a massless neutrino in the rest frame, $$\bar E_ν=\bar p_ν$$ Hence, $$p_ν\cos\theta_ν=\gamma\bar p_ν\bigl(\cos\bar\theta_ν+\beta\bigr)$$ Therefore, $$\tan\theta_ν=\frac{\sin\bar\theta_ν}{\gamma\bigl(\beta+\cos\bar\theta_ν\bigr)}$$ Isotropy in the rest frame implies the median rest-frame polar angle is $$\bar\theta_ν=\frac{\pi}{2}$$ Evaluating the transform at \bar\theta_ν=\pi/2 gives $$\tan\theta_m=\frac{1}{\gamma\beta}$$ Also, $$\tan\theta_m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma^2-1}}$$ and $$\tan\theta_m=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(E_0/m_π)^2-1}}$$ and $$\tan\theta_m=\frac{m_π}{\sqrt{E_0^2-m_π^2}}$$ so $$\theta_m=\arctan\left(\frac{m_π}{\sqrt{E_0^2-m_π^2}}\right)$$ Monotonicity follows since $$\frac{d\theta_ν}{d\bar\theta_ν}=\frac{\cos^2\theta_ν}{\gamma}\frac{1+\beta\cos\bar\theta_ν}{\bigl(\beta+\cos\bar\theta_ν\bigr)^2}$$ and $$\frac{d\theta_ν}{d\bar\theta_ν}\ge 0$$ so the mapping preserves order, and half of the neutrinos satisfy θ_ν < θ_m
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form θ_m = ..., expressed only in terms of E_0 and m_π.

context: High-energy protons with momentum p_p strike a fixed target and produce secondary pions. Use c for the speed of light, v for particle speed, beta = v/c, and gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - beta^2). The proton rest mass is m_p = 0.94\unit{GeV/c^2} and the charged pion rest mass is m_pi = 0.14\unit{GeV/c^2}. The laboratory decay pipe has length l = 400\unit{m}. The detector is located at distance d = 1200\unit{m} from the decay point. Let p_p denote the proton momentum in the lab and p_pi the pion momentum in the lab. Let E_0 denote the pion total energy in the lab and L denote the detector diameter required to intercept neutrinos emitted within a lab half-angle theta_{1/2}. In part (c), the length of the pipe measured in the pion rest frame is denoted by \bar l. In part (d), consider the two-body decay pi -> mu + nu_mu in the pion rest frame, where the neutrino rest mass is zero. Use E_mu, E_nu for the muon and neutrino energies, and p_mu, p_nu for the magnitudes of their momenta. Let M = m_pi be the pion rest mass and m = m_mu be the muon rest mass. subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the pion momentum p_pi when the pion has the same velocity as a proton whose laboratory momentum is p_p = 400\unit{GeV/c}. Use m_p = 0.94\unit{GeV/c^2} and m_pi = 0.14\unit{GeV/c^2}.
subquestions.solution:
For the same velocity, the proton and the pion have the same beta and gamma.
$$p_\pi = m_\pi \gamma \beta$$
$$p_p = m_p \gamma \beta$$
$$p_\pi = \frac{m_\pi}{m_p} p_p$$
$$p_\pi = \frac{0.14}{0.94} \times 400\unit{GeV/c}$$
$$p_\pi = 59.6\unit{GeV/c}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express p_pi as a numerical value in GeV/c.

subquestions.subproblem: Assuming the produced pions are highly relativistic, estimate the neutrino emission half-angle theta_{1/2} of the forward cone in the lab and the minimum detector diameter L at distance d = 1200\unit{m} needed to intercept neutrinos emitted within that cone. Express theta_{1/2} in terms of the pion lab energy E_0 or the Lorentz factor gamma.
subquestions.solution:
Using p_\pi from part (a), the pion energy is computed with c = 1 and then gamma is obtained.
$$E_0 = \sqrt{p_\pi^2 + m_\pi^2}$$
$$E_0 \approx 59.6\unit{GeV}$$
$$\gamma = \frac{E_0}{m_\pi}$$
$$\gamma \approx 426$$
The neutrino emission half-angle and the detector diameter follow.
$$\theta_{1/2} = \arctan \frac{m_\pi}{\sqrt{E_0^2 - m_\pi^2}}$$
$$\theta_{1/2} = \arctan \frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma^2 - 1}}$$
$$\theta_{1/2} \approx \frac{1}{\gamma}$$
$$L = 2 d \tan \theta_{1/2}$$
$$L \approx \frac{2 d}{\gamma}$$
$$L = \frac{2 \times 1200}{426}\unit{m}$$
$$L = 5.63\unit{m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two algebraic expressions: (1) provide theta_{1/2} as an explicit function of either E_0 and m_pi or of gamma; and (2) provide L in terms of d and theta_{1/2}, or directly in terms of d and gamma. Write your expressions using only the variables theta_{1/2}, E_0, m_pi, gamma, and d.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the length of the decay pipe as measured in the pion rest frame?
subquestions.solution:
Length contraction gives
$$\bar l = \frac{l}{\gamma}$$
$$\bar l = \frac{400\unit{m}}{426}$$
$$\bar l = 0.94\unit{m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \bar l as a numerical value in meters.

subquestions.subproblem: The pion decays into a muon and a neutrino, pi -> mu + nu_mu, where the neutrino has zero rest mass. Using the relation between total relativistic energy and momentum, show in the pion rest frame that the common magnitude p of the decay momenta satisfies p = (M^2 - m^2)/(2M), where M is the pion rest mass and m is the muon rest mass. Use natural units c = 1.
subquestions.solution:
Energy and momentum conservation in the pion rest frame give
$$E_\mu + E_\nu = m_\pi$$
$$p_\mu + p_\nu = 0$$
$$p_\mu = p_\nu$$
The energy-momentum relation is
$$E^2 = p^2 + m^2$$
For the massless neutrino we have
$$E_\nu = p_\nu$$
Using E_\mu = m_\pi - E_\nu and p_\mu = p_\nu, we obtain
$$p_\mu^2 + m_\mu^2 = m_\pi^2 - 2 p_\nu m_\pi + p_\nu^2$$
Solving for p_\nu yields
$$p_\nu = \frac{m_\pi^2 - m_\mu^2}{2 m_\pi}$$
Identifying M = m_\pi and m = m_\mu gives
$$p = \frac{M^2 - m^2}{2M}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form p = (M^2 - m^2)/(2M), written only with the variables p, M, and m.

subquestions.subproblem: The neutrino detectors are, on the average, approximately 1.2\unit{km} from the point where the pions decay. How large should the transverse dimension (radius) of the detector be in order to have a chance of detecting all neutrinos that are produced in the forward hemisphere in the pion rest frame?
subquestions.solution: The decay pi mu nu is isotropic in the rest frame of the pion. Problem 4057

context: Consider the two-body decay K^0 -> pi^+ + pi^-. The transition matrix element is specified as T_{if} = [G / sqrt(8 E_K E_+ E_-)] [P_K (P_+ + P_-)] / m_K. Here E_K, E_+, and E_- are the relativistic energies of K^0, pi^+, and pi^- respectively, and P_K, P_+, and P_- are the corresponding four-momenta. The symbol P_A P_B denotes the Lorentz-invariant scalar product. The constants are: m_K for the K-meson mass, mu for the pion mass, G for the coupling constant, hbar for the reduced Planck constant, and c for the speed of light. In the rest frame of the decaying K^0, let p_1 and p_2 be the magnitudes of the three-momenta of pi^+ and pi^- respectively, E_1 and E_2 their energies (with E_1 = E_+ and E_2 = E_-), and Omega the solid angle. Let E denote the total final-state energy E = E_1 + E_2. The total transition probability per unit time is W, the density of final states is rho(E), and the lifetime measured in the K^0 rest frame is tau, with tau = 1/W. Assume the decay is isotropic. Show that the lifetime of the K^0 meson in its rest frame is tau = [ G^2 / (8 pi hbar^4 c) sqrt(m_K^2/4 - mu^2) ]^{-1}.
solution:
The transition probability per unit time is
$$
W = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} |T_{if}|^2 \rho(E)
$$
In the K^0 rest frame,
$$
E_K = m_K c^2
$$
For a two-body decay into equal-mass pions,
$$
E_+ = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
$$
E_- = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
Four-momentum conservation gives
$$
P_K = P_+ + P_-
$$
Hence
$$
P_K^2 = m_K^2 c^2
$$
and
$$
(P_+ + P_-)^2 = P_K^2
$$
Therefore
$$
P_K (P_+ + P_-) = P_K^2
$$
The squared matrix element is
$$
|T_{if}|^2 = \frac{G^2}{8 E_K E_+ E_-} \frac{[P_K (P_+ + P_-)]^2}{m_K^2}
$$
Substituting the rest-frame relations yields
$$
|T_{if}|^2 = \frac{G^2}{2 m_K c^2}
$$
For a two-body decay in the parent rest frame, the density of final states is
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{d}{dE} \int p_1^2 dp_1 d\Omega
$$
Assuming isotropy,
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{4 \pi}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right)
$$
Momentum magnitudes satisfy
$$
p_1 dp_1 = p_2 dp_2
$$
The total energy differential is
$$
dE = dE_1 + dE_2
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right) = \frac{p_1^2 dp_1}{dE_1 + dE_2}
$$
Using the relativistic relation for each pion
$$
E_i^2 = p_i^2 c^2 + \mu^2 c^4
$$
we have
$$
\frac{dE_i}{p_i dp_i} = \frac{c^2}{E_i}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{d}{dE} \left( \frac{1}{3} p_1^3 \right) = \frac{E_1 E_2 p_1}{c^2 (E_1 + E_2)}
$$
Therefore
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{4 \pi}{(2 \pi \hbar)^3} \frac{E_1 E_2 p_1}{c^2 (E_1 + E_2)}
$$
In the K^0 rest frame,
$$
E_1 = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
$$
E_2 = \frac{1}{2} m_K c^2
$$
The pion three-momentum magnitude is
$$
 p_1 = c \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Thus
$$
\rho(E) = \frac{m_K c}{8 \pi^2 \hbar^3} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Putting everything together,
$$
W = \frac{2 \pi}{\hbar} \frac{G^2}{2 m_K c^2} \frac{m_K c}{8 \pi^2 \hbar^3} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
Hence
$$
W = \frac{G^2}{8 \pi \hbar^4 c} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2}
$$
The lifetime in the K^0 rest frame is
$$
\tau = W^{-1}
$$
Therefore
$$
\tau = \left[ \frac{G^2}{8 \pi \hbar^4 c} \sqrt{\frac{m_K^2}{4} - \mu^2} \right]^{-1}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of tau = ..., and your response should be written with the variables G, hbar, c, m_K, mu only.

context: The possible radioactive decay of the proton is a topic of much current interest. A typical experiment to detect proton decay is to construct a very large reservoir of water and instrument it to detect Cherenkov radiation produced by the products of proton decay. Let N_A denote Avogadro's number. Unless otherwise stated, energies and momenta are evaluated in the proton rest frame.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that you have built a reservoir with 10,000 metric tons of water, with 1 ton = 1000 \unit{kg}. Assume that the proton mean life is \tau_p = 10^{32} \unit{year}, that your detector is 100% efficient, and that protons bound in nuclei and free protons decay at the same rate. Use N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}, and the facts that each H2O molecule contains 10 protons and has molar mass 18 \unit{g/mol}. Let N_p denote the total number of protons in the reservoir, and let \Delta N denote the expected number of proton decays per year. Compute \Delta N.
subquestions.solution:
The number of protons is
$$
N_p = \frac{10}{18} \times 10^{10} \times N_A
$$
With N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}} this gives
$$
N_p = 3.34 \times 10^{33}
$$
The expected number of decays per year is
$$
\Delta N = \frac{N_p}{\tau_p}
$$
With \tau_p = 10^{32} \unit{year} this yields
$$
\Delta N = 33.4 \unit{year^{-1}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express \Delta N as a numerical value in units of year^{-1}, reported to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: A possible proton decay mode is p \to \pi^0 + e^+. The neutral pion \pi^0 promptly decays (in 10^{-16} \unit{s}) to two photons, \pi^0 \to \gamma + \gamma. Calculate the maximum and minimum photon energies expected from a proton decaying at rest. Use the masses m_p = 938 \unit{MeV}, m_{e^+} = 0.51 \unit{MeV}, m_{\pi^0} = 135 \unit{MeV}. Let E_\pi and p_\pi be the energy and momentum magnitude of the \pi^0, and E_{e^+} and p_{e^+} those of the positron. Primes denote quantities in the \pi^0 rest frame. Let \theta' be the angle between the photon momentum and the boost direction in the \pi^0 rest frame. Let \gamma_\pi and \beta_\pi be the Lorentz factor and speed (in units of c) of the \pi^0 in the proton rest frame. Let E_{\gamma,\max} and E_{\gamma,\min} denote, respectively, the maximum and minimum photon energies in the proton rest frame.
subquestions.solution:
Energy conservation gives
$$
m_p = E_\pi + E_{e^+}
$$
Momentum conservation gives
$$
p_\pi = p_{e^+}
$$
The dispersion relation is
$$
E^2 = m^2 + p^2
$$
Solving for the \pi^0 energy yields
$$
E_\pi = \frac{m_p^2 + m_{\pi^0}^2 - m_{e^+}^2}{2 m_p}
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_\pi = \frac{938^2 + 135^2 - 0.51^2}{2 \times 938} \unit{MeV}
$$
Thus,
$$
E_\pi = 479 \unit{MeV}
$$
In the \pi^0 rest frame, each photon has energy
$$
E' = \frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2}
$$
and momentum magnitude
$$
p' = \frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2}
$$
The \pi^0 Lorentz factor is
$$
\gamma_\pi = \frac{E_\pi}{m_{\pi^0}}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\gamma_\pi = \frac{479}{135}
$$
Thus,
$$
\gamma_\pi = 3.548
$$
The \pi^0 speed is
$$
\beta_\pi = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\gamma_\pi^2}}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\beta_\pi = 0.9595
$$
The photon energy in the proton rest frame is
$$
E_\gamma = \gamma_\pi E' + \gamma_\pi \beta_\pi p' \cos \theta'
$$
Equivalently,
$$
E_\gamma = \frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2} \gamma_\pi \bigl(1 + \beta_\pi \cos \theta'\bigr)
$$
Or,
$$
E_\gamma = \frac{E_\pi}{2} \bigl(1 + \beta_\pi \cos \theta'\bigr)
$$
The maximum occurs at \theta' = 0, so
$$
E_{\gamma,\max} = \frac{E_\pi}{2} (1 + \beta_\pi)
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_{\gamma,\max} = \frac{479}{2} (1 + 0.9595) \unit{MeV}
$$
Thus,
$$
E_{\gamma,\max} = 469.3 \unit{MeV}
$$
The minimum occurs at \theta' = \pi, so
$$
E_{\gamma,\min} = \frac{E_\pi}{2} (1 - \beta_\pi)
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_{\gamma,\min} = \frac{479}{2} (1 - 0.9595) \unit{MeV}
$$
Thus,
$$
E_{\gamma,\min} = 9.7 \unit{MeV}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_{\gamma,\max} and E_{\gamma,\min} as numerical values in MeV. Report E_{\gamma,\max} to 4 significant figures and E_{\gamma,\min} to 2 significant figures.

context: Consider the decay in flight of a charged pion into a muon and a muon neutrino, π → μ + ν_μ. Work in units with c = 1. Let Σ denote the laboratory frame and Σ_π denote the pion rest frame. For any particle with 3-velocity β in a given frame, define the Lorentz factor γ = (1 - β^2)^{-1/2}. In Σ the pion has 3-velocity β_π and Lorentz factor γ_π. In Σ_π the muon has 3-velocity β_μ and Lorentz factor γ_μ. In Σ the same muon has 3-velocity β and Lorentz factor γ. Let m_π and m_μ be the pion and muon masses, respectively. Define the muon helicity in any frame by h = (S · β)/(s β), where S is the muon spin 3-vector and s = |S| is its magnitude. We also use the spin 4-vector S_α = (S, i S_0); in the muon rest frame S_0 = 0. In Σ_π assume the muon is produced with helicity h_μ = 1, so its spin is parallel to its velocity in that frame. Let p_μ and p_ν denote the magnitudes of the muon and neutrino 3-momenta in Σ_π, and let E_μ and E_ν denote the muon and neutrino energies in Σ_π. Let θ denote the angle between β_π and β_μ. For a given laboratory pion energy E_π, there exists a unique laboratory muon energy E_μ^{(0)} at which the average muon helicity in the laboratory vanishes.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the relation between the laboratory pion energy E_π and the unique laboratory muon energy E_μ^{(0)} at which the average muon helicity in the laboratory vanishes.
subquestions.solution:
Consider the muon spin 4-vector in the muon rest frame
$$S_\alpha = (S, i S_0)$$
$$S_0 = 0$$
In the pion rest frame Σ_π, the muon has speed β_μ and Lorentz factor γ_μ, and its spin 4-vector is
$$S'_\alpha = (S', i S'_0)$$
The spatial and time components transform as
$$S' = S + (\gamma_\mu - 1) \frac{S \cdot \beta_\mu}{\beta_\mu^2} \beta_\mu$$
$$S'_0 = \gamma_\mu (S_0 + S \cdot \beta_\mu)$$
Using S_0 = 0 and h_\mu = 1 in Σ_π gives
$$S \cdot \beta_\mu = s \beta_\mu$$
so that
$$S'_0 = \gamma_\mu s \beta_\mu$$
and
$$S' = S + (\gamma_\mu - 1) s \beta_\mu^{-1} \beta_\mu$$
Transform from Σ_π to the laboratory frame Σ, where the pion has β_π and γ_π, and the muon has β and γ. The muon spin 4-vector becomes S^Lab_α = (S'', i S''_0) with
$$S''_0 = \gamma_\pi (S'_0 + \beta_\pi \cdot S')$$
Substituting S'_0 and S' yields
$$S''_0 = \gamma_\pi \gamma_\mu s \beta_\mu + \gamma_\pi \beta_\pi \cdot S + \gamma_\pi (\gamma_\mu - 1) (\beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu) s \beta_\mu^{-1}$$
Since S is parallel to β_μ in Σ_π, we have
$$\beta_\pi \cdot S = (\beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu) s \beta_\mu^{-1}$$
Hence
$$S''_0 = \gamma_\pi \gamma_\mu s (\beta_\mu^2 + \beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu) \beta_\mu^{-1}$$
By definition of the laboratory helicity h,
$$S''_0 = \gamma \beta s h$$
Thus
$$h = \gamma_\pi \gamma_\mu \gamma^{-1} \beta^{-1} (\beta_\mu^2 + \beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu) \beta_\mu^{-1}$$
At the special laboratory muon energy E_μ^{(0)}, the average helicity vanishes and h = 0, so
$$\beta_\mu^2 = - \beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu$$
The Lorentz transformation for the muon energy gives
$$\gamma = \gamma_\pi \gamma_\mu (1 + \beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu)$$
Using the h = 0 condition gives
$$\gamma = \gamma_\pi \gamma_\mu (1 - \beta_\mu^2)$$
Thus
$$\gamma = \frac{\gamma_\pi}{\gamma_\mu}$$
Therefore
$$E_\mu^{(0)} = m_\mu \gamma$$
and hence
$$E_\mu^{(0)} = \frac{m_\mu}{m_\pi} \frac{E_\pi}{\gamma_\mu}$$
To evaluate γ_μ, consider the decay in Σ_π. Momentum conservation implies
$$p_\nu = p_\mu$$
Energy conservation implies
$$E_\nu + E_\mu = m_\pi$$
Combining these for a massless neutrino gives
$$E_\mu = \frac{m_\pi^2 + m_\mu^2}{2 m_\pi}$$
Hence
$$\gamma_\mu = \frac{E_\mu}{m_\mu}$$
so that
$$\gamma_\mu = \frac{m_\pi^2 + m_\mu^2}{2 m_\pi m_\mu}$$
Substituting this into E_μ^{(0)} yields
$$E_\mu^{(0)} = \frac{2 m_\mu^2}{m_\pi^2 + m_\mu^2} E_\pi$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_μ^{(0)} = ..., and your response should be written with E_π, m_π, m_μ only.

subquestions.subproblem: In the nonrelativistic limit, find the minimum value of the laboratory pion energy E_π for which it is possible to have zero-helicity muons in the laboratory.
subquestions.solution:
For the average muon helicity to vanish in the laboratory, we require
$$\beta_\pi \cdot \beta_\mu = - \beta_\mu^2$$
Let θ be the angle between β_π and β_μ. Then
$$\beta_\pi \cos \theta = - \beta_\mu$$
This implies
$$\beta_\pi \ge \beta_\mu$$
and hence
$$\gamma_\pi \ge \gamma_\mu$$
Therefore, the minimum laboratory pion energy needed is
$$(E_\pi)_{\min} = \gamma_\mu m_\pi$$
Using the value of γ_μ from part (a) gives
$$(E_\pi)_{\min} = \frac{m_\pi^2 + m_\mu^2}{2 m_\mu}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of (E_π)_min = ..., and your response should be written with m_π, m_μ only.

context: Consider a plastic scintillator of thickness 2\unit{cm} directly coupled to the surface of a photomultiplier tube (PMT) with gain 10^6. A 10\unit{GeV} particle beam is incident on the scintillator as shown in Fig. 4.8. Let Q(E) denote the PMT anode charge produced by an energy deposit E in the scintillator. The calibration is Q(4\unit{MeV})=\frac{16}{5}\times 10^{-10}\unit{C}, and the PMT detection threshold is Q_{th}=1\times 10^{-12}\unit{C}. In Part b, a neutron scatters elastically in the scintillator by a small laboratory angle \theta, transferring transverse momentum p\theta to a recoil nucleus of mass m and imparting it recoil kinetic energy E_r. Let p be the incident neutron momentum, and m_p the proton mass. For numerical substitution use natural units with c=1 so that momenta and masses are expressed in \unit{eV}, take p_n=10^{10}\unit{eV} for the neutron momentum and 2m_p=2\times 10^9\unit{eV}. Define \theta_{\min} as the minimum detectable scattering angle.

subquestions.subproblem: Same as Part
, but it scatters elastically from a carbon nucleus.
subquestions.solution:
For a small laboratory scattering angle \theta, the recoil kinetic energy is
$$E_r=\frac{p^2\theta^2}{2m}$$
The calibration point is
$$Q(4\unit{MeV})=\frac{16}{5}\times 10^{-10}\unit{C}$$
The detection threshold is
$$Q_{th}=1\times 10^{-12}\unit{C}$$
Thus the minimum detectable recoil energy is
$$E_{r,\min}=4\unit{MeV}\times \frac{Q_{th}}{Q(4\unit{MeV})}$$
With the given values
$$E_{r,\min}=4\unit{MeV}\times \frac{1\times 10^{-12}}{\frac{16}{5}\times 10^{-10}}$$
Which gives
$$E_{r,\min}=\frac{5}{4}\times 10^{-2}\unit{MeV}$$
Equivalently
$$E_{r,\min}=\frac{25}{2}\unit{keV}$$
Assuming the recoiling nucleus is a proton and using p=p_n and m=m_p, the smallest detectable angle satisfies
$$\theta_{\min}^2=\frac{2m_p}{p_n^2}E_{r,\min}$$
Substituting the numerical values
$$\theta_{\min}^2=\frac{2\times 10^9\unit{eV}}{(10^{10}\unit{eV})^2}\times \frac{25}{2}\times 10^3\unit{eV}$$
Which yields
$$\theta_{\min}^2=\frac{5}{2}\times 10^{-7}\unit{rad^2}$$
Therefore
$$\theta_{\min}=5\times 10^{-4}\unit{rad}$$
assuming the recoiling nucleus is a proton

final_answer_instructions: For each subquestion, your final answer should express \theta_{\min} (the minimum detectable scattering angle) as a numerical value in radians. Give your answer to 1 significant figure.

context: Estimate the attenuation of a monoenergetic beam of 50\unit{keV} X-rays passing through a 1\unit{cm}-thick layer of human soft tissue. Assume the tissue density equals that of water and use the mass attenuation coefficient at 50\unit{keV}. Define I_0 as the incident intensity, I as the transmitted intensity after thickness x, ρ as the tissue mass density, μ_m as the mass attenuation coefficient, A as the areal density A=ρx, and f_att as the attenuation fraction f_att=1-I/I_0. Use ρ≈1\unit{g/cm^3} and μ_m≈0.221\unit{cm^2/g}. Compute f_att for x=1\unit{cm}.
solution:
Assume the tissue density equals that of water

$$
\rho \approx 1\unit{g/cm^3}
$$

Use the mass attenuation coefficient at 50\unit{keV}

$$
\mu_m \approx 0.221\unit{cm^2/g}
$$

Set the thickness

$$
x=1\unit{cm}
$$

Define the areal density

$$
A=\rho x
$$

Compute the areal density for the given values

$$
A=1\unit{g/cm^2}
$$

The transmitted intensity fraction is

$$
\frac{I}{I_0}=\exp(-\mu_m A)
$$

Define the attenuation fraction

$$
f_{att}=1-\frac{I}{I_0}
$$

Evaluate numerically

$$
f_{att}=1-\exp(-0.221\times 1)
$$

Final numerical result

$$
f_{att}\approx 0.20
$$

Thus, the attenuation is approximately 20\%.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express f_att as a numerical value with no units, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: Fast neutrons can be detected by observing scintillations caused by recoil protons in certain optically transparent hydrocarbons. Consider a slab of scintillator of thickness d=5\unit{cm} containing equal number densities n_H=n_C=4\times 10^{22}\unit{cm^{-3}} of hydrogen (H) and carbon (C) nuclei. A beam of neutrons of energy E_n\approx 5\unit{MeV} is incident normal to the slab. Let \sigma_H and \sigma_C denote the total interaction cross sections for neutrons on H and C, respectively, with 1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}. Let N_0 be the number of neutrons incident on the entrance face, N(x) the number that have not interacted after traversing a depth x, and \eta=N(d)/N_0 the transmission fraction through the full thickness d. For part (b), define \eta'=1-\eta as the fraction that undergo at least one interaction in the slab, and let \eta'' be the fraction of incident neutrons that produce at least one recoil proton, assuming only interactions with H produce recoil protons.

subquestions.subproblem: What fraction of approximately 5\unit{MeV} neutrons incident normal to the slab will pass through the slab without interacting with either C or H nuclei?
subquestions.solution:
The attenuation satisfies
$$\Delta N=-N(\sigma_H n_H+\sigma_C n_C)\Delta x$$
After integration over depth x,
$$N(x)=N_0\exp(-(\sigma_H n_H+\sigma_C n_C)x)$$
The transmission fraction is
$$\eta=\frac{N(d)}{N_0}$$
Therefore
$$\eta=\exp(-\tau)$$
with optical depth
$$\tau=(\sigma_H n_H+\sigma_C n_C)d$$
Using \sigma_H=\frac{3}{2}\unit{barn}, \sigma_C=1\unit{barn}, n_H=n_C=4\times 10^{22}\unit{cm^{-3}}, d=5\unit{cm}, and 1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2},
$$\tau=\left(\frac{3}{2}+1\right)\times 10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}\times 4\times 10^{22}\unit{cm^{-3}}\times 5\unit{cm}$$
Thus
$$\tau=\frac{1}{2}$$
Hence
$$\eta=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)$$
Numerically,
$$\eta\approx 0.606$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the transmission fraction η as a numerical value. Report η to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: What fraction of the incident neutrons will produce a recoil proton? Assume \sigma_H=\frac{3}{2}\unit{barn}, \sigma_C=1\unit{barn}, and 1\unit{barn}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}.
subquestions.solution:
The fraction that undergo at least one interaction is
$$\eta'=1-\eta$$
Only interactions on hydrogen produce recoil protons, so the conditional fraction is
$$\frac{\sigma_H}{\sigma_H+\sigma_C}$$
Thus the fraction producing recoil protons is
$$\eta''=\eta'\frac{\sigma_H}{\sigma_H+\sigma_C}$$
With \sigma_H=\frac{3}{2} and \sigma_C=1,
$$\frac{\sigma_H}{\sigma_H+\sigma_C}=\frac{3}{5}$$
Therefore
$$\eta''=\frac{3}{5}\eta'$$
Numerically, using \eta\approx 0.606,
$$\eta'\approx 0.394$$
Hence
$$\eta''\approx 0.236$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the fraction of incident neutrons that produce at least one recoil proton, η'', as a numerical value. Report η'' to 3 significant figures.

context: Given: The mean free path l of fast neutrons in lead (Pb) is l=5\unit{cm}. Lead has density \rho=10\unit{g/cm^3} and molar mass approximated by A=200\unit{g/mol} (atomic mass number ~200). Let N_0=6.022\times 10^{23}\unit{mol^{-1}} be Avogadro's constant. Let n denote the number density of Pb atoms and \sigma the total neutron–Pb interaction cross section. Express the final answer for \sigma both in \unit{cm^2} and in barns b, where 1\unit{b}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}.
solution:
The number density n of Pb atoms is
$$
n=\frac{\rho}{A}N_0
$$
Substituting values gives
$$
n=\frac{10}{200}\times 6.022\times 10^{23}
$$
Thus
$$
n=3.01\times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}
$$
The mean free path relation is
$$
l=\frac{1}{n\sigma}
$$
So the cross section is
$$
\sigma=\frac{1}{nl}
$$
Substituting values gives
$$
\sigma=\frac{1}{3.01\times 10^{22}\times 5\unit{cm}}
$$
Hence
$$
\sigma=6.64\times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}
$$
Using the barn conversion
$$
1\unit{b}=10^{-24}\unit{cm^2}
$$
we obtain
$$
\sigma=6.64\unit{b}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the neutron–Pb total interaction cross section σ as numerical values in both cm^2 and barns (b). Present it in the form: 'σ = [value] cm^2, [value] b'. Use three significant figures.

context: A sheet of cadmium (Cd) is placed in a beam of slow neutrons to reduce the transmitted intensity to one twentieth of its original value. Let t be the Cd sheet thickness, I_0 the initial beam intensity, and I(t) the transmitted intensity after passing through thickness t. Let n be the number density of Cd atoms, given by n=ρN_A/A, where ρ is the mass density of Cd, A is the atomic weight of Cd, and N_A is Avogadro's constant. Let σ be the microscopic absorption cross section of Cd. Use the unit conversion 1 barn = 10^{-24} cm^2. Given data are A=112 g/mol, ρ=8.7×10^3 kg/m^3, σ=2500 barn, and N_A=6.022×10^{23} mol^{-1}. Find t such that the transmitted intensity condition holds
solution:
Target transmission condition

$$I(t)=
\frac{1}{20} I_0$$

Beer–Lambert law for attenuation

$$I(t)=I_0 e^{-n\sigma t}$$

Solve for thickness

$$t=\frac{1}{n\sigma} \ln \frac{I_0}{I(t)}$$

Substitute the target transmission

$$t=\frac{1}{n\sigma} \ln 20$$

Convert density to convenient units

$$\rho=8.7\times 10^3 \unit{kg/m^3}$$

$$\rho=8.7 \unit{g/cm^3}$$

Material constants

$$A=112 \unit{g/mol}$$

$$N_A=6.022\times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}$$

Number density

$$n=\frac{\rho N_A}{A}$$

$$n\approx 4.7\times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$

Cross section and unit conversion

$$\sigma=2500 \unit{barn}$$

$$1 \unit{barn}=10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}$$

$$\sigma=2500\times 10^{-24} \unit{cm^2}$$

Required thickness

$$t=\frac{1}{n\sigma} \ln 20$$

$$t\approx 0.025 \unit{cm}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the required cadmium sheet thickness t as a single numerical value in centimeters (cm), rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A beam of neutrons passes through a hydrogen target and is detected in a counter C as shown in Fig. 4.10. The atomic number density of the hydrogen target is n=4×10^{22} atom/cm^3, and the target thickness is t=100 cm. The detector C has neutron-detection efficiency η that is independent of the presence of the target. The number of neutrons recorded without the target is N'=5×10^{5}, and with the target in place is N''=4.6×10^{5}. Assume attenuation in the target follows N_{out}=N_{in} e^{-n σ t}, where σ is the total neutron–proton cross section. Counting statistics are Poisson with ΔN=√N. Determine σ and its statistical uncertainty. Report σ in both cm^2 and millibarns, using 1 mb=10^{-27} cm^2.
solution:
Let σ be the total n–p cross section, n the atomic concentration, t the target thickness, N_0 the number of neutrons incident on the detector region in the absence of the target, η the detection efficiency, N' the counts without the target, and N'' the counts with the target in place.

After passing through the target, the transmitted neutrons are
$$
N_0 e^{-n \sigma t}
$$

The detected counts without and with the target are
$$
N'=\eta N_0
$$
$$
N''=\eta N_0 e^{-n \sigma t}
$$

Hence,
$$
\frac{N''}{N'}=e^{-n \sigma t}
$$

Solving for σ gives
$$
\sigma=\frac{1}{n t} \ln \frac{N'}{N''}
$$

With n and t specified as
$$
\nn=4\times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}
$$
$$
 t=100 \unit{cm}
$$

and with the measured counts
$$
N'=5\times 10^{5}
$$
$$
N''=4.6\times 10^{5}
$$

the cross section is
$$
\sigma=\frac{1}{4\times 10^{22} \times 100} \ln \frac{5\times 10^{5}}{4.6\times 10^{5}} \unit{cm^{2}}
$$
$$
\sigma=2.08\times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^{2}}
$$

For the statistical uncertainty, use error propagation with
$$
\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial N'}=\frac{1}{n t N'}
$$
$$
\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial N''}=-\frac{1}{n t N''}
$$

and Poisson counting uncertainties
$$
\Delta N'=\sqrt{N'}
$$
$$
\Delta N''=\sqrt{N''}
$$

Thus,
$$
(\Delta \sigma)^2=\left(\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial N'}\right)^2 (\Delta N')^2+\left(\frac{\partial \sigma}{\partial N''}\right)^2 (\Delta N'')^2
$$
$$
(\Delta \sigma)^2=\frac{1}{(n t)^2} \left( \frac{1}{N'}+\frac{1}{N''} \right)
$$
$$
\Delta \sigma=\frac{1}{n t} \sqrt{ \frac{1}{N'}+\frac{1}{N''} }
$$

Substituting the numbers,
$$
\Delta \sigma=\frac{1}{4\times 10^{22} \times 100} \sqrt{ \frac{1}{5\times 10^{5}}+\frac{1}{4.6\times 10^{5}} } \unit{cm^{2}}
$$
$$
\Delta \sigma\approx 5\times 10^{-28} \unit{cm^{2}}
$$

Therefore,
$$
\sigma=(2.08\pm 0.05)\times 10^{-26} \unit{cm^{2}}
$$
$$
\sigma=(20.8\pm 0.5) \unit{mb}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the total neutron–proton cross section σ and its statistical uncertainty as numerical values in both cm^2 and millibarns (1 mb = 10^{-27} cm^2). Report the central value with 3 significant figures and the uncertainty with 1 significant figure in each unit.

context: A beam of energetic neutrons with a broad energy spectrum is incident down the axis of a very long rod of crystalline graphite as shown in Fig. 4.11. The graphite is effectively a cold-neutron filter. Use the following definitions: n is the Bragg order, d is the lattice spacing of the microcrystals, θ is the Bragg diffraction angle, λ is the neutron de Broglie wavelength, h is Planck’s constant, ħ is the reduced Planck’s constant, c is the speed of light, m_n is the neutron mass, and v_max is the maximum speed of neutrons that can traverse the rod without significant deflection. Assume the graphite is polycrystalline with random microcrystal orientations and that its neutron absorption cross section is small.
solution:
Crystalline graphite acts as a cold neutron filter. High-energy neutrons undergo elastic scattering from nuclei and, due to multiple deflections, leave the rod through the sides. When neutron wavelengths are comparable to the lattice spacing, coherent interference leads to Bragg scattering characterized by Bragg’s law

$$n \lambda = 2 d \sin \theta$$

$$n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$

For wavelengths exceeding the Bragg cutoff, coherent scattering occurs only in the forward direction, so neutrons pass without deflection

$$\lambda > 2 d$$

Because the neutron absorption cross section of graphite is small, attenuation for these long-wavelength neutrons is weak. In a polycrystalline sample, high-energy and hot neutrons are deflected by elastic and Bragg scattering from microcrystals of various orientations and exit laterally, while only cold neutrons with wavelengths above the cutoff traverse the rod. For graphite, the Bragg cutoff is

$$2 d = 6.69 \times 10^{-10} \unit{m}$$

The maximum velocity of neutrons that still pass unimpeded corresponds to the shortest wavelength that satisfies the pass condition, namely \(\lambda_{\min} = 2d\)

$$\lambda_{\min} = 2 d$$

Using the de Broglie relation, the maximum speed is

$$v_{\max} = \frac{h}{m_n \lambda_{\min}}$$

Numerically, this gives

$$v_{\max} \approx 5.9 \times 10^{2} \unit{m/s}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the maximum neutron speed v_max as a numerical value in m/s. Round your result to 2 significant figures.

context: Cerenkov radiation is emitted by a high-energy charged particle moving through a medium with speed exceeding the phase speed of electromagnetic waves in that medium. Notation used throughout: v = beta c is the particle speed, c is the speed of light in vacuum, n is the index of refraction of the medium, and theta is the emission angle of Cerenkov light relative to the particle trajectory. The Lorentz factor is gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - beta^2). The particle rest mass is m_0, momentum is p, and the kinetic energy is T = (gamma - 1) m c^2 where m is the particle mass. In part (c), intermediate algebra is performed using natural units with c = 1; numerical values are reported with explicit units. See Fig. 4.12 for a typical Cerenkov wavefront geometry.

subquestions.subproblem: Derive the relationship among the particle velocity v = beta c, the index of refraction n of the medium, and the angle theta at which the Cerenkov radiation is emitted relative to the line of flight of the particle.
subquestions.solution:
Let the particle move from O to A in time t. Radiation emitted when the particle is at O forms a spherical wavefront of radius R in the medium. The wavefront speed in the medium is c/n, so
$$R = \frac{c t}{n}$$
The particle displacement in time t is OA, with
$$\mathrm{OA} = v t$$
Using v = beta c gives
$$\mathrm{OA} = \beta c t$$
From the right triangle geometry, the cone half-angle satisfies
$$\cos \theta = \frac{R}{\mathrm{OA}}$$
Substituting the expressions for R and OA gives
$$\cos \theta = \frac{1}{n \beta}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form cos(theta) = ... and should use only the variables theta, n, and beta.

subquestions.subproblem: Hydrogen gas at one atmosphere and 20^\circ C has an index of refraction n = 1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4}. What is the minimum kinetic energy in MeV that an electron of mass 0.5\,\unit{MeV/c^2} must have to emit Cerenkov radiation while traversing hydrogen gas at 20^\circ C and one atmosphere? Define T as the minimum kinetic energy.
subquestions.solution:
From part (a), emission requires a real angle, so
$$\cos \theta = \frac{1}{n \beta}$$
Thus the threshold condition is
$$\beta \geq \frac{1}{n}$$
The minimum speed is
$$\beta_{\min} = \frac{1}{n}$$
With n = 1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4},
$$\beta_{\min} = \frac{1}{1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4}}$$
Using the first-order expansion 1/(1 + \epsilon) \approx 1 - \epsilon,
$$\beta_{\min} \approx 1 - 1.35 \times 10^{-4}$$
The corresponding Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma_{\min} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta_{\min}^2}}$$
Using 1 - \beta_{\min}^2 = (1 - \beta_{\min})(1 + \beta_{\min}) and 1 + \beta_{\min} \approx 2,
$$1 - \beta_{\min}^2 \approx 2 \times 1.35 \times 10^{-4}$$
Therefore
$$\gamma_{\min} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \times 1.35 \times 10^{-4}}}$$
Numerically,
$$\gamma_{\min} \approx 60.86$$
The threshold kinetic energy is
$$T = (\gamma_{\min} - 1) m c^2$$
With m = 0.5\,\unit{MeV/c^2},
$$T \approx 29.9 \unit{MeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express T (the minimum kinetic energy) as a numerical value in MeV, to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: A Cerenkov-radiation particle detector is made by fitting a long pipe of one-atmosphere, 20^\circ C hydrogen gas with an optical system capable of detecting the emitted light and measuring the emission angle theta with accuracy delta theta = 10^{-3}\,\unit{rad}. A beam of charged particles with momentum p = 100\,\unit{GeV/c} passes through the counter. Since p is known, measuring the Cerenkov angle effectively measures the rest mass m_0. For a particle with m_0 near 1\,\unit{GeV/c^2}, and to first order in small quantities, find the fractional error delta m_0 / m_0 in determining m_0 with this Cerenkov counter. Use natural units c = 1 for intermediate steps.
subquestions.solution:
Starting from
$$m_0^2 = \frac{p^2}{(\gamma \beta)^2}$$
and using 1 - \beta^2 = 1/\gamma^2,
$$m_0^2 = \frac{p^2 (1 - \beta^2)}{\beta^2}$$
Rewriting,
$$m_0^2 = \frac{p^2}{\beta^2} - p^2$$
From part (a),
$$\cos \theta = \frac{1}{n \beta}$$
Thus
$$m_0^2 = p^2 n^2 \cos^2 \theta - p^2$$
Differentiating with respect to \theta gives
$$2 m_0 \mathrm{d} m_0 = -2 p^2 n^2 \cos \theta \sin \theta \mathrm{d} \theta$$
Therefore, to first order,
$$\delta m_0 = \frac{p^2 n^2}{2 m_0} \sin 2 \theta \delta \theta$$
With m_0 \approx 1\,\unit{GeV/c^2} and p = 100\,\unit{GeV/c}, the Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma = \frac{\sqrt{p^2 + m_0^2}}{m_0}$$
Numerically,
$$\gamma = \sqrt{10^4 + 1}$$
Using
$$\cos \theta = \frac{\gamma}{n \sqrt{\gamma^2 - 1}}$$
with n = 1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4},
$$\cos \theta \approx \frac{\sqrt{10^4 + 1}}{(1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4}) \times 10^2}$$
Expanding to first order,
$$\cos \theta \approx \frac{1 + 0.5 \times 10^{-4}}{1 + 1.35 \times 10^{-4}}$$
Hence
$$\cos \theta \approx 1 - 0.85 \times 10^{-4}$$
For small \theta,
$$\cos \theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}$$
Thus
$$\theta^2 \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-4}$$
and
$$\theta \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-2} \unit{rad}$$
With \sin 2\theta \approx 2\theta and \delta \theta = 10^{-3}\,\unit{rad}, the fractional error is
$$\frac{\delta m_0}{m_0} = \frac{p^2 n^2 \theta}{m_0^2} \delta \theta$$
Using p/m_0 = 100 and n \approx 1,
$$\frac{\delta m_0}{m_0} \approx 10^4 \times 1.3 \times 10^{-2} \times 10^{-3}$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{\delta m_0}{m_0} \approx 0.13$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the fractional error delta m_0 / m_0 as a numerical value, to 2 significant figures.

context: Charmed hadrons produced in high-energy proton–iron interactions may decay promptly to muons, while charged pions may produce muons only if they decay before hadronic interaction in the iron beam dump. Consider 400\unit{GeV} protons incident on a thick iron target and compare the number of muons from charm decays to those from pion decays at a fixed detected muon energy. Definitions and symbols used throughout: E_p is the incident proton energy with E_p=400\unit{GeV}. E_0 is the maximum secondary energy with E_0=400\unit{GeV}. E_\mu is the detected muon energy. R(E_\mu) is the ratio of the differential muon yield from charm decays to that from pion decays at muon energy E_\mu, defined by R(E_\mu)=(d\sigma_{\mu,c}/dE_\mu)/(d\sigma_{\mu,\pi}/dE_\mu). m_\pi c^2=0.140\unit{GeV} and m_\mu c^2=0.106\unit{GeV}. r is the mass ratio r=m_\mu/m_\pi. The charged-pion proper lifetime is \tau_\pi=2.60\times10^{-8}\unit{s}. The speed of light is c=3.00\times10^8\unit{m/s}. The nuclear interaction length in iron for high-energy pions is \lambda_I=0.17\unit{m} as an additional assumption. The inelastic proton–proton cross section is \sigma_{\text{inel}}^{pp}=30\unit{mb}. The iron mass number is A=56, and the inelastic proton–iron cross section is approximated by \sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}}=A\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{pp} as an additional assumption. The mean charged-pion multiplicity per inelastic interaction is N_\pi=8. The inclusive production cross section for a single charmed hadron per Fe nucleus is \sigma_c=10\unit{\mu b}. The branching fraction for c\to\mu\nu is B=0.10. Parent-energy variables: E_\pi is the charged-pion energy and E_c is the charmed-hadron energy, both in the lab frame. P_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi) is the probability that a pion of energy E_\pi decays before its first hadronic interaction in iron. l_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi) is the pion decay length in the lab frame. \gamma_\pi is the pion Lorentz factor. dN_\pi/dE_\pi is the pion energy spectrum per inelastic interaction. d\sigma_c/dE_c is the charmed-hadron energy spectrum per Fe nucleus. f(E_\mu|E_\pi) is the conditional probability density of muon energy in pion decay given E_\pi. f(E_\mu|E_c) is the conditional probability density of muon energy in charm decay given E_c. dN_{\mu,\pi}/dE_\mu is the differential number of muons from pions per inelastic interaction. d\sigma_{\mu,\pi}/dE_\mu is the differential cross section for muons from pions per Fe nucleus. d\sigma_{\mu,c}/dE_\mu is the differential cross section for muons from charm per Fe nucleus. All muon-energy distributions and parent spectra are assumed flat where stated below.

subquestions.subproblem: Assume that any charged pion which undergoes a hadronic interaction in the iron dump is completely removed from the beam.
Assume the lab-frame energy spectra of both charged pions and charmed hadrons are flat from their kinematic minimum up to the maximum possible secondary energy E_0.
Assume the charmed hadron has mass m_c c^2=2\unit{GeV} and lifetime \ll10^{-10}\unit{s}, so that it decays promptly in the dump without prior hadronic interaction.
Ignore muon energy loss in iron.
Ignore any complications due to the geometry or acceptance of the muon detector.

Given \sigma_{\text{inel}}^{pp}=30\unit{mb} and mean charged-pion multiplicity N_\pi=8 in inelastic interactions, compute the ratio R(E_\mu) of muons from charm decays to those from pion decays. Give a numerical value at E_\mu=100\unit{GeV}, assuming \sigma_c=10\unit{\mu b} per Fe nucleus and B=0.10. State any additional assumptions you use.
subquestions.solution:
Flat parent spectra and decay kinematics. The flat pion spectrum per inelastic interaction is
$$
\frac{dN_\pi}{dE_\pi}=\frac{N_\pi}{E_0}
$$
For charged-pion decay \pi\to\mu\nu at high energy, the muon energy is taken to be uniformly distributed in the interval E_\mu\in[r^2E_\pi,E_\pi], where r=m_\mu/m_\pi. The conditional density is
$$
f(E_\mu|E_\pi)=\frac{1}{(1-r^2)E_\pi}
$$
The pion decay probability before interaction in a thick dump is approximated by
$$
P_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi)=\frac{\lambda_I}{l_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi)}
$$
The lab-frame decay length is
$$
l_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi)=\gamma_\pi c \tau_\pi
$$
The pion Lorentz factor is
$$
\gamma_\pi=\frac{E_\pi}{m_\pi c^2}
$$
Hence the decay probability is
$$
P_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi)=\frac{\lambda_I m_\pi c^2}{E_\pi c \tau_\pi}
$$
The differential muon yield per inelastic interaction from pion decays is
$$
\frac{dN_{\mu,\pi}}{dE_\mu}=\int_{E_\mu}^{E_\mu/r^2}\frac{dN_\pi}{dE_\pi} P_{\text{dec}}(E_\pi) f(E_\mu|E_\pi) dE_\pi
$$
Carrying out the integral gives
$$
\frac{dN_{\mu,\pi}}{dE_\mu}=\frac{N_\pi}{E_0} \frac{\lambda_I m_\pi c^2}{c \tau_\pi} \frac{1}{E_\mu}
$$
The corresponding differential cross section per Fe nucleus is
$$
\frac{d\sigma_{\mu,\pi}}{dE_\mu}=\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}} \frac{dN_{\mu,\pi}}{dE_\mu}
$$
For charm, the flat energy spectrum per Fe nucleus is
$$
\frac{d\sigma_c}{dE_c}=\frac{\sigma_c}{E_0}
$$
For the two-body decay c\to\mu\nu at high energy, the muon energy is taken to be uniformly distributed in the interval E_\mu\in[0,E_c] with conditional density
$$
f(E_\mu|E_c)=\frac{1}{E_c}
$$
The differential muon cross section from charm decays is
$$
\frac{d\sigma_{\mu,c}}{dE_\mu}=\int_{E_\mu}^{E_0}\frac{\sigma_c}{E_0} B \frac{1}{E_c} dE_c
$$
The result is
$$
\frac{d\sigma_{\mu,c}}{dE_\mu}=\frac{\sigma_c B}{E_0} \ln\left(\frac{E_0}{E_\mu}\right)
$$
The desired ratio is
$$
R(E_\mu)=\frac{\frac{d\sigma_{\mu,c}}{dE_\mu}}{\frac{d\sigma_{\mu,\pi}}{dE_\mu}}
$$
Substituting the above expressions yields
$$
R(E_\mu)=\frac{\sigma_c B \ln\left(\frac{E_0}{E_\mu}\right)}{\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}} N_\pi} \frac{c \tau_\pi}{\lambda_I m_\pi c^2} E_\mu
$$
Numerical inputs. The maximum secondary energy is
$$
E_0=400\unit{GeV}
$$
The evaluation point is
$$
E_\mu=100\unit{GeV}
$$
The branching fraction is
$$
B=0.10
$$
The pion multiplicity is
$$
N_\pi=8
$$
The charm cross section is
$$
\sigma_c=10\unit{\mu b}
$$
The inelastic proton–proton cross section is
$$
\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{pp}=30\unit{mb}
$$
The proton–iron inelastic cross section is
$$
\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}}=A \sigma_{\text{inel}}^{pp}
$$
The iron mass number is
$$
A=56
$$
Therefore
$$
\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}}=1680\unit{mb}
$$
Convert \sigma_c to millibarns
$$
\sigma_c=0.01\unit{mb}
$$
The speed of light and pion lifetime give
$$
c \tau_\pi=7.80\unit{m}
$$
The nuclear interaction length in iron is
$$
\lambda_I=0.17\unit{m}
$$
The pion mass parameter is
$$
m_\pi c^2=0.140\unit{GeV}
$$
The logarithmic factor at E_\mu=100\unit{GeV} is
$$
\ln\left(\frac{E_0}{E_\mu}\right)=\ln(4)
$$
Assemble the ratio using dimensionless intermediate factors. The cross-section ratio is
$$
\frac{\sigma_c}{\sigma_{\text{inel}}^{p\text{Fe}}}=\frac{0.01\unit{mb}}{1680\unit{mb}}
$$
The kinematic-length factor is
$$
\frac{c \tau_\pi}{\lambda_I}=\frac{7.80\unit{m}}{0.17\unit{m}}
$$
The energy-mass factor is
$$
\frac{E_\mu}{N_\pi m_\pi c^2}=\frac{100\unit{GeV}}{8\times0.140\unit{GeV}}
$$
Hence the numerical value at E_\mu=100\unit{GeV} is
$$
R(100\unit{GeV})\approx3.4\times10^{-3}
$$
This result follows from the stated flat-spectrum and prompt-decay assumptions, the thick-dump decay–interaction competition for pions, and the given cross sections and branching fraction.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express R(100 GeV) as a numerical value rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: In a cloud chamber filled with air at atmospheric pressure, 5 \unit{MeV} alpha particles make tracks about L = 4 \unit{cm} long. Using the nuclear radius model R = r_0 A^{1/3} with r_0 = 1.2 \unit{fm} and A = 14.7 for the average air nucleus, and taking the density of air to be \rho = 1.293 \unit{kg/m^3} and Avogadro's number N_A = 6.023 \times 10^{23} \unit{mol^{-1}}, estimate how many tracks must be observed to have a good chance of finding one with a distinct sharp bend resulting from a nuclear encounter. Let \sigma denote the nuclear geometric cross section, n the number density of nuclei, and \lambda the mean free path for such encounters. Define N_{obs} as the required number of observed tracks such that the expected number of encounters in N_{obs} tracks of length L is of order one. Assume that a distinct sharp bend corresponds to a single large-angle scattering event with probability per unit path length equal to n \sigma.
solution:
Using the nuclear radius model, the radius of an average air nucleus is
$$
R = r_0 A^{1/3}
$$
The corresponding geometric cross section is
$$
\sigma \approx \pi R^2
$$
Substituting the given values,
$$
R = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 14.7^{1/3} \unit{m}
$$
Using 14.7^{1/3} \approx 2.45, we have
$$
R \approx 2.94 \times 10^{-15} \unit{m}
$$
Thus,
$$
\sigma \approx \pi \times \left(2.94 \times 10^{-15}\right)^2 \unit{m^2}
$$
and hence
$$
\sigma \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-29} \unit{m^2}
$$
The number density of nuclei in air is
$$
 n = \frac{\rho N_A}{A}
$$
Substituting numerical values in SI units,
$$
 n = \frac{1.293 \times 6.023 \times 10^{23}}{0.0147} \unit{m^{-3}}
$$
which gives
$$
 n \approx 5.3 \times 10^{25} \unit{m^{-3}}
$$
The mean free path for a nuclear encounter is
$$
\lambda = \frac{1}{n \sigma}
$$
Numerically,
$$
\lambda \approx \frac{1}{5.3 \times 10^{25} \times 2.7 \times 10^{-29}} \unit{m}
$$
so that
$$
\lambda \approx 7.0 \times 10^{2} \unit{m}
$$
The given track length is
$$
L = 4 \unit{cm}
$$
which is
$$
L = 4 \times 10^{-2} \unit{m}
$$
For a good chance of observing one large-angle scattering, the required number of tracks is
$$
N_{obs} \approx \frac{\lambda}{L}
$$
Substituting the values,
$$
N_{obs} \approx \frac{7.0 \times 10^{2}}{4 \times 10^{-2}}
$$
which yields
$$
N_{obs} \approx 1.75 \times 10^{4}
$$
Rounding to one significant figure for an order-of-magnitude estimate,
$$
N_{obs} \approx 2 \times 10^{4}
$$
