context:
The positive muon decays into a positron and two neutrinos with the process described by
$$
\mu^+ \to e^+ + \nu_e + \bar \nu_\mu
$$
The mean lifetime of the muon is approximately 2\unit{\mu s}. Consider muons at rest polarized along the z-axis with degree of polarization P. We confine observations to the highest-energy positrons from muon decays. The angular distribution for these positrons is
$$
I(\cos \theta) d \Omega = \frac{1 + P \cos \theta}{4 \pi} d \Omega
$$
where \theta is the angle between the positron direction and the z-axis, and d \Omega is the solid angle element. The forward hemisphere is defined by \cos \theta > 0 and the backward hemisphere by \cos \theta < 0. Let P_f denote the probability that a positron is emitted into the forward hemisphere and P_b the probability for the backward hemisphere. Let N be the total number of observed positrons, with N = N_f + N_b, where N_f and N_b are the observed counts in the forward and backward hemispheres, respectively. Let W be the binomial probability of observing a specific pair (N_f, N_b) given P_f and P_b. In statistical estimates, \Delta denotes the one-standard-deviation uncertainty. In part (b), let N_{min} denote the minimum total number N required to achieve the target accuracy.

subquestions.subproblem: Assume P = +1. What is the probability that for the first six positrons observed, three are in the forward hemisphere (\cos \theta > 0) and three are in the backward hemisphere (\cos \theta < 0)?
subquestions.solution:
Using azimuthal symmetry, the element of solid angle can be written as
$$
d \Omega = 2 \pi d \cos \theta
$$
The probability of a forward decay is
$$
P_f = 2 \pi \int_0^1 \frac{1 + P \cos \theta}{4 \pi} d \cos \theta
$$
Thus
$$
P_f = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + \frac{P}{2} \right)
$$
The probability of a backward decay is
$$
P_b = 2 \pi \int_{-1}^0 \frac{1 + P \cos \theta}{4 \pi} d \cos \theta
$$
Thus
$$
P_b = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 - \frac{P}{2} \right)
$$
For N observed positrons, the probability of finding N_f forward and N_b backward positrons is
$$
W = \frac{N!}{N_f! N_b!} P_f^{N_f} P_b^{N_b}
$$
For P = 1
$$
P_f = \frac{3}{4}
$$
$$
P_b = \frac{1}{4}
$$
With N = 6 and N_f = N_b = 3
$$
W = \frac{6!}{3! 3!} \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^3 \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)^3
$$
Hence
$$
W = \frac{135}{1024}
$$
Numerically, W \approx 0.132
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the probability W as a numerical value rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Assume that P is in the neighborhood of 1, but not accurately known. You wish to determine P by comparing the numbers of observed forward (N_f) and backward (N_b) decay positrons. How many muon decays, N (N = N_f + N_b), must you observe to determine P to an accuracy of \pm 1\%?
subquestions.solution:
From the angular distribution
$$
P_f - P_b = \frac{P}{2}
$$
Therefore
$$
P = 2 \left( P_f - P_b \right)
$$
Equivalently
$$
P = 2 \left( 2 P_f - 1 \right)
$$
The experimental estimators are
$$
P_f = \frac{N_f}{N}
$$
$$
P_b = \frac{N_b}{N}
$$
With N events observed, the standard deviation of N_f is
$$
\Delta N_f = \sqrt{N P_f \left( 1 - P_f \right)}
$$
Hence
$$
\Delta P_f = \frac{\Delta N_f}{N}
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta P_f = \sqrt{\frac{P_f \left( 1 - P_f \right)}{N}}
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta P = 4 \Delta P_f
$$
Solving for N gives
$$
N = \frac{16 P_f \left( 1 - P_f \right)}{\left( \Delta P \right)^2}
$$
With P \approx 1
$$
P \approx 1
$$
Target accuracy
$$
\Delta P \approx 0.01 P
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta P \approx 0.01
$$
And for P near 1
$$
P_f \approx \frac{3}{4}
$$
The required minimum number of events is
$$
N_{min} = \frac{16 \cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{4}}{\left( 10^{-2} \right)^2}
$$
Therefore
$$
N_{min} = 30000
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N_min as a numerical value (an integer count).

context: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere contains a nearly steady-state concentration of radioactive ^{14}C produced by secondary cosmic rays interacting with atmospheric nitrogen. When a living organism dies, its carbon contains ^{14}C at the atmospheric concentration, but as time passes the fraction of ^{14}C decreases due to radioactive decay. This is the basis for radiocarbon dating. Assume the atmospheric ratio ^{14}C/^{12}C equals 10^{-12} and the half-life of ^{14}C beta decay is 5730\unit{yr}. Variable definitions used throughout: N(t) is the number of ^{14}C atoms at time t after death, N_0 is N(0), T_{1/2} is the half-life, \lambda is the decay constant, A is the expected number of sample counts observed in a counting time of 1\unit{h} with a 100% efficient detector and no dead time, \Delta A is the standard deviation of A from Poisson statistics in the 1\unit{h} counting interval, \Delta t is the desired standard deviation of the inferred age, N_A is Avogadro's number, x is the required carbon sample mass in grams, t is the actual sample age, and A_B is the known average background counts observed in the same 1\unit{h} counting interval

subquestions.subproblem: It is desired to use radiocarbon dating to determine the age of a carbon sample. How many grams of a sample are needed to measure the age to a precision of ±50 years (standard deviation of 50 years)? Assume that the sample is actually 5000 years old, that the radioactivity is counted for one hour with a 100% efficient detector, and that there is no background
subquestions.solution:
Radioactive decay gives
$$
N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}
$$
The counting rate satisfies
$$
A = -\frac{dN}{dt}
$$
and
$$
A = \lambda N_0 e^{-\lambda t}
$$
Thus
$$
A = \lambda N
$$
Differentiating yields
$$
\frac{dA}{dt} = -\lambda A
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\Delta A}{A} = \lambda \Delta t
$$
The decay constant is
$$
\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}
$$
with
$$
T_{1/2} = 5730\unit{yr}
$$
so
$$
\lambda = 1.21\times 10^{-4}\unit{yr^{-1}}
$$
For a 1\unit{h} Poisson count,
$$
\Delta A = \sqrt{A}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{\Delta A}{A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}
$$
Imposing \(\Delta t = 50\unit{yr}\) gives
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{A}} = 50\lambda
$$
Therefore
$$
A = \left(\frac{1}{50\times 1.21\times 10^{-4}}\right)^2
$$
so
$$
A = 2.73\times 10^{4}\unit{h^{-1}}
$$
The expected sample counts in 1\unit{h} from mass x of carbon at age t are
$$
A = \frac{\lambda \left(\frac{x N_A}{12}\right) 10^{-12} e^{-\lambda t}}{365\times 24}
$$
Solving for x at \(t = 5000\unit{yr}\) gives
$$
x = \frac{12 A (365\times 24) e^{\lambda t} 10^{12}}{N_A \lambda}
$$
Numerically,
$$
x = \frac{12 \times 2.73\times 10^{4} \times 365 \times 24}{6.023\times 10^{23} \times 1.21\times 10^{-4}} \times 10^{12} \times e^{5000\times 1.21\times 10^{-4}}
$$
Therefore
$$
x = 72.1\unit{g}
$$

subquestions.subproblem: Repeat part (a), but now assume that there is a background counting rate in the detector (due to radioactivity in the detector itself, cosmic rays, etc.) whose average value is accurately known to be 4000 counts per hour
subquestions.solution:
With known background A_B, the total 1\unit{h} counts have mean A + A_B and Poisson standard deviation
$$
\Delta A = \sqrt{A + A_B}
$$
Hence
$$
\frac{\Delta A}{A} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{A} + \frac{A_B}{A^2}}
$$
Define
$$
C = \lambda \Delta t
$$
Imposing \(\Delta A/A = C\) yields
$$
C^2 A^2 - A - A_B = 0
$$
Therefore
$$
A = \frac{1}{2 C^2} \left(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4 C^2 A_B}\right)
$$
With
$$
\lambda = 1.21\times 10^{-4}\unit{yr^{-1}}
$$
and
$$
\Delta t = 50\unit{yr}
$$
we have
$$
C = 1.21\times 10^{-4} \times 50
$$
and
$$
A_B = 4000\unit{h^{-1}}
$$
which gives
$$
A = 3.09\times 10^{4}\unit{h^{-1}}
$$
The required mass is
$$
x = \frac{12 A (365\times 24) e^{\lambda t} 10^{12}}{N_A \lambda}
$$
Substituting values with \(t = 5000\unit{yr}\) gives
$$
x = \frac{12 \times 3.09\times 10^{4} \times 365 \times 24}{6.023\times 10^{23} \times 1.21\times 10^{-4}} \times 10^{12} \times e^{5000\times 1.21\times 10^{-4}}
$$
Therefore
$$
x = 81.6\unit{g}
$$

context: A radioactive source emits two types of radiation, A and B. A counter distinguishes between them. In a given counting interval, the number of detected A-type events is N_A=1000 and the number of detected B-type events is N_B=2000. Assume the two counting processes are independent and follow Poisson statistics. Let r denote the measured ratio r=N_A/N_B. Let Δr denote the standard (1σ) statistical uncertainty of r, and let ΔN_A and ΔN_B denote the standard deviations of N_A and N_B, respectively. Compute Δr.
solution:
Using logarithmic error propagation, write
$$
\ln r = \ln N_A - \ln N_B
$$
Differentiating gives
$$
\frac{dr}{r} = \frac{dN_A}{N_A} - \frac{dN_B}{N_B}
$$
Since N_A and N_B are independent, the variances add in quadrature
$$
\left(\frac{\Delta r}{r}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\Delta N_A}{N_A}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta N_B}{N_B}\right)^2
$$
For Poisson statistics
$$
\Delta N_A = \sqrt{N_A}
$$
$$
\Delta N_B = \sqrt{N_B}
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_A} + \frac{1}{N_B}}
$$
With the given values
$$
r = \frac{N_A}{N_B}
$$
$$
r = \frac{1000}{2000}
$$
$$
r = \frac{1}{2}
$$
$$
\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{1000} + \frac{1}{2000}}
$$
Numerically
$$
\frac{\Delta r}{r} \approx 0.039
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta r = r \frac{\Delta r}{r}
$$
$$
\Delta r = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.039
$$
$$
\Delta r \approx 0.020
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express Δr as a numerical value, rounded to 2 significant figures.

context: A sample of $\beta$-radioactive isotope is studied with the aid of a scintillation counter that detects decay electrons and timestamps individual detected decays. Let $\tau$ denote the mean decay lifetime, $N$ the number of atoms present during the measurement, $\varepsilon$ the detection probability per decay (detection efficiency), and $R$ the average detected counting rate (counts per unit time). In time-integrated measurements over an interval of duration $T$, let $n$ be the total number of detected counts and let $\Delta$ denote a standard deviation. In part (b), define $P(t)$ as the probability density such that, given a detected count at a reference time, the probability that the next detected count occurs between times $t$ and $t+dt$ equals $P(t) dt$. For the Poisson-process reasoning used in part (b), define $m=Rt$ as the expected mean number of detected counts in an interval of duration $t$, $m'=R dt$ as the expected mean number of detected counts in an infinitesimal interval of duration $dt$, $P_0(t)$ as the probability of zero counts in an interval of duration $t$, and $P_1(dt)$ as the probability of exactly one count in an interval of duration $dt$.

subquestions.subproblem: Let $\tau$ denote the mean decay lifetime. The sample contains a large number $N$ of atoms, and the detection probability per decay is $\varepsilon$. Calculate the average counting rate in the scintillator. You may assume $\tau$ to be much longer than any period of time over which measurements are made. In a measurement of $\tau$, 10,000 counts are collected over a period of precisely one hour. The detection efficiency of the scintillator is independently determined to be 0.4 and $N$ is determined to be $10^{23}$. What is the measured value of $\tau$? What is the statistical error in this determination of $\tau$ (standard deviation)?
subquestions.solution:
Because $\tau$ is much longer than the measurement time, $N$ can be taken as constant and the average counting rate is
$$R=\frac{\varepsilon N}{\tau}$$
For the one-hour run, the total number of counts and the duration are
$$n=10^{4}$$
$$T=1\unit{h}$$
so the measured counting rate is
$$R=\frac{n}{T}$$
The lifetime inferred from the rate is
$$\tau=\frac{\varepsilon N}{R}$$
Using $\varepsilon=\frac{2}{5}$ and $N=10^{23}$ gives
$$\tau=\frac{2}{5}\times 10^{19}\unit{h}$$
Converting to years,
$$\tau\approx 4.6\times 10^{14}\unit{yr}$$
Counting statistics are Poissonian, so the standard deviation of the number of counts is
$$\Delta n=\sqrt{n}$$
and the standard deviation of the rate is
$$\Delta R=\frac{\Delta n}{T}$$
Thus the fractional uncertainty in $\tau$ is
$$\frac{\Delta \tau}{\tau}=\frac{\Delta R}{R}$$
Using $n=10^{4}$ and $T=1\unit{h}$,
$$\frac{\Delta \tau}{\tau}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$$
$$\frac{\Delta \tau}{\tau}=\frac{1}{100}$$
so the absolute uncertainty is
$$\Delta \tau\approx 4.6\times 10^{12}\unit{yr}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the measured mean lifetime τ and its statistical standard deviation Δτ as numerical values in years. Use 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: Let $P(t) dt$ be the probability that two successive counts in the scintillator are at $t$ and $t+dt$. Compute $P(t)$ in terms of $t$, $\varepsilon$, $N$, $\tau$.
subquestions.solution:
The expected mean number of detected counts in an interval of duration $t$ is
$$m=Rt$$
The probability that no count occurs in that interval is
$$P_0(t)=e^{-m}$$
For the subsequent infinitesimal interval $dt$, the expected mean is
$$m'=R dt$$
The probability of exactly one count in $dt$ is
$$P_1(dt)=e^{-m'} m'$$
For infinitesimal $dt$,
$$P_1(dt)\approx R dt$$
Therefore,
$$P(t) dt=P_0(t) P_1(dt)$$
which gives
$$P(t) dt=R e^{-Rt} dt$$
Using $R=\frac{\varepsilon N}{\tau}$ yields
$$P(t)=\frac{\varepsilon N}{\tau} e^{-\frac{\varepsilon N t}{\tau}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form P(t) = ... and written only in terms of t, ε, N, τ.

context:
A proton synchrotron at Batavia accelerates protons to total energy E = 500 GeV. Let R be the bending radius in a uniform dipole magnetic field B. The proton has rest mass m, charge magnitude e, speed v, and moves relativistically with the following definitions. Use c for the speed of light. Assume a typical guide field B = 1 T and that at this energy the motion is ultrarelativistic with beta approximately 1. Choose the closest order of magnitude for R from {10^2 m, 10^3 m, 10^4 m, 10^5 m}. Report the selected option as R_ans = ...

$$
\beta = \frac{v}{c}
$$

$$
\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}
$$

$$
p = m \gamma \beta c
$$

$$
R = \frac{p}{e B}
$$

$$
E = m \gamma c^2
$$

$$
B = 1 \unit{T}
$$
solution:
From the magnetic rigidity relation and the definition of relativistic momentum, we have

$$
R = \frac{p}{e B}
$$

$$
p = m \gamma \beta c
$$

Using the total energy of the proton,

$$
E = m \gamma c^2
$$

At 500 GeV, the motion is ultrarelativistic, so

$$
\beta \approx 1
$$

Eliminating p and m \gamma gives

$$
R = \frac{E}{e B c}
$$

Numerically, with E = 500 \unit{GeV}, B = 1 \unit{T}, and

$$
c \approx 3 \times 10^8 \unit{m/s}
$$

the elementary charge cancels when E is expressed in \unit{eV}, yielding

$$
R = \frac{500 \times 10^9}{1 \times 3 \times 10^8} \unit{m}
$$

$$
R = \frac{5}{3} \times 10^3 \unit{m}
$$

Thus the closest order-of-magnitude choice is

$$
R_{ans} = 10^3 \unit{m}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the selected order-of-magnitude bending radius as a numerical value in the exact form R_ans = 10^2 m, R_ans = 10^3 m, R_ans = 10^4 m, or R_ans = 10^5 m. Provide only one of these four options and no additional text.

context: A modern accelerator produces two counter-rotating proton beams which collide head-on. Each beam has per-proton energy E_b = 30 GeV. Let m_p = 0.938 GeV be the proton rest energy. subquestions.subproblem: What would be the required energy of a conventional proton accelerator in which protons strike a stationary hydrogen target to give the same center-of-mass energy?
subquestions.solution: For a fixed-target collision with incident proton energy E_inc, momentum p_inc, and a stationary target proton, the invariant mass squared is $$S = (E_{inc} + m_p)^2 - p_{inc}^2$$ Using the on-shell relation for the incident proton, $$E_{inc}^2 - p_{inc}^2 = m_p^2$$ Expanding S and substituting gives $$S = E_{inc}^2 - p_{inc}^2 + 2 E_{inc} m_p + m_p^2$$ $$S = 2 E_{inc} m_p + 2 m_p^2$$ For the collider, the same invariant is set by the center-of-mass energy, $$E_{cm} = 60\unit{GeV}$$ $$S = E_{cm}^2$$ $$S = 60^2\unit{GeV^2}$$ $$S = 3600\unit{GeV^2}$$ Equating invariants, $$2 E_{inc} m_p + 2 m_p^2 = 3600\unit{GeV^2}$$ Solving for E_inc, $$E_{inc} = \frac{1800 - m_p^2}{m_p}$$ $$m_p = 0.938\unit{GeV}$$ $$E_{inc} = \frac{1800 - 0.938^2}{0.938}\unit{GeV}$$ $$E_{inc} = 1918\unit{GeV}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express E_inc as a numerical value in GeV.

subquestions.subproblem: If the proton-proton collision rate in this new machine is 10^4/sec, estimate the required vacuum in the system such that the collision rate of protons with residual gas be of this same order of magnitude in 5 m of pipe. Take 1000 m as the accelerator circumference, sigma_{p-air} = 10^{-25} cm^2, and the area of the beam as 1 mm^2.
subquestions.solution: Let N_p be the number of protons per beam in one orbit and N the number of proton-proton collisions per time interval Delta t = L/c. $$N_p = n s L$$ $$r = \frac{N}{\Delta t}$$ $$\Delta t = \frac{L}{c}$$ $$r = \frac{N_p^2 \sigma_{pp}}{L/c}$$ $$r = \frac{(n s L)^2 c \sigma_{pp}}{L}$$ $$r = n^2 s^2 L c \sigma_{pp}$$ For collisions with residual gas over length l, let N_a be the number of target air molecules in the beam tube segment of volume s l. $$N_a = \frac{\rho s l N_A}{A}$$ Let N' be the number of proton–air collisions in time interval Delta t' and r' the corresponding rate. $$r' = \frac{N'}{\Delta t'}$$ $$\Delta t' = \frac{L + l}{c}$$ Approximating the revolution time by L/c gives $$r' \approx \frac{N_p N_a \sigma_{pa}}{L/c}$$ Equating r' = r gives $$\rho = \frac{A}{N_A} \frac{L}{l} \frac{\sigma_{pp}}{\sigma_{pa}} n$$ From r we first solve for n, $$n = \left( \frac{r}{s^2 L c \sigma_{pp}} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$ Using the given values, $$r = 10^4\unit{s^{-1}}$$ $$s = 1\unit{mm^2}$$ $$s = 10^{-2}\unit{cm^2}$$ $$L = 1000\unit{m}$$ $$L = 10^5\unit{cm}$$ $$c = 3 \times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s}$$ $$\sigma_{pp} = 30\unit{mb}$$ $$\sigma_{pp} = 3 \times 10^{-26}\unit{cm^2}$$ $$n = \left( \frac{10^4}{10^{-4} \times 10^5 \times 3 \times 10^{10} \times 3 \times 10^{-26}} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$ $$n = 1.8 \times 10^9\unit{cm^{-3}}$$ Then, with sigma_pa = 10^{-25}\unit{cm^2}, $$A = 29\unit{g/mol}$$ $$N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\unit{mol^{-1}}$$ $$l = 5\unit{m}$$ $$\rho = \frac{29}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \left( \frac{1000}{5} \right) \left( \frac{3 \times 10^{-26}}{10^{-25}} \right) \times 1.8 \times 10^9$$ $$\rho = 5.3 \times 10^{-12}\unit{g/cm^3}$$ Using rho/rho_0 = P/(1 atm), $$\rho_0 = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\unit{g/cm^3}$$ $$\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \frac{P}{1\unit{atm}}$$ $$\frac{5.3 \times 10^{-12}}{1.3 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{P}{1\unit{atm}}$$ $$P = 4 \times 10^{-9}\unit{atm}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express both rho (mass density of the residual gas, in g/cm^3) and P (pressure, in atm) as numerical values.

context: An electron with mass m and charge e moves in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B. If radiative energy loss is neglected, the trajectory is a circle of radius R. Let E be the total electron energy, allowing for relativistic kinematics with E much greater than m c^2. Define: c as the speed of light, v as the velocity vector of the electron, p as its relativistic momentum vector, a as its acceleration vector, P as the radiated power, ε0 as the vacuum permittivity, r0 = e^2/(4 π ε0 m c^2) as the classical electron radius, γ = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) as the Lorentz factor, β = v/c, and ΔE as the energy lost by radiation per revolution. The magnetic field vector is B, and the vector cross product is denoted by ×. When no confusion arises, we also use the same symbols for magnitudes. For unit conversions, 1\unit{T} = 10^4\unit{G}.

subquestions.subproblem: Explain the needed field strength B analytically in terms of the above parameters. Compute B numerically, in gauss, for the case where R = 30 meters, E = 2.5 × 10^9 electron volts. For this part of the problem you will have to recall some universal constants.
subquestions.solution:
The momentum is
$$p = m \gamma v$$
The Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma = \left(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$$
Newton's second law with the Lorentz force gives
$$\frac{d p}{d t} = m \gamma \frac{d v}{d t}$$
The magnetic force is
$$\frac{d p}{d t} = e v \times B$$
Define the acceleration as
$$a = \frac{d v}{d t}$$
Since v is perpendicular to B, the speed and γ are constant, so
$$a = \frac{e v B}{m \gamma}$$
For circular motion of radius R,
$$a = \frac{v^2}{R}$$
Eliminating a gives the required field magnitude
$$B = \frac{m \gamma v}{e R}$$
Using the energy-momentum relation,
$$E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4$$
and the identity p = m γ v, we obtain
$$B = \frac{\sqrt{E^2 - m^2 c^4}}{e R c}$$
In the ultrarelativistic limit E much greater than m c^2,
$$B \approx \frac{E}{e R c}$$
Numerically, with R = 30\unit{m}, E = 2.5 \times 10^9\unit{eV}, e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\unit{C}, and c = 3 \times 10^8\unit{m/s},
$$B = \frac{2.5 \times 10^9 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 30 \times 3 \times 10^8} \unit{T}$$
$$B = 2.8 \times 10^{-1} \unit{T}$$
$$B = 2.8 \times 10^{3} \unit{G}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the magnetic field strength B as a numerical value in gauss (G), rounded to 2 significant figures. Only the numerical value is required as the final answer.

subquestions.subproblem: Actually, the electron radiates electromagnetic energy because it is being accelerated by the B field. However, suppose that the energy loss per revolution ΔE is small compared to E. Explain the ratio ΔE / E analytically in terms of the parameters. Then evaluate this ratio numerically for the particular value of R given above.
subquestions.solution:
The relativistic Lienard power is
$$P = \frac{e^2}{6 \pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} \gamma^6 \left[a^2 - \left(\frac{v \times a}{c}\right)^2\right]$$
For uniform circular motion v is perpendicular to a, so
$$P = \frac{e^2}{6 \pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} \gamma^4 a^2$$
For circular motion,
$$a = \frac{v^2}{R}$$
Therefore,
$$P = \frac{e^2 v^4}{6 \pi \varepsilon_0 c^3} \frac{\gamma^4}{R^2}$$
The energy loss per revolution is
$$\Delta E = \frac{2 \pi R P}{v}$$
Using r_0 = \frac{e^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 m c^2} and β = \frac{v}{c},
$$\Delta E = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \left(\frac{r_0}{R}\right) (\gamma \beta)^3 \gamma m c^2$$
Thus,
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \left(\frac{r_0}{R}\right) (\gamma \beta)^3$$
Equivalently,
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \left(\frac{r_0}{R}\right) \left(\gamma^2 - 1\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}$$
For r_0 = 2.8 \times 10^{-15}\unit{m}, R = 30\unit{m}, and using m c^2 = 0.511 \times 10^{6}\unit{eV},
$$\gamma = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{9}}{0.511 \times 10^{6}}$$
$$\gamma = 4.9 \times 10^{3}$$
Hence,
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} \approx \frac{4 \pi}{3} \times \frac{2.8 \times 10^{-15}}{30} \times \left(4.9 \times 10^{3}\right)^{3}$$
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = 4.6 \times 10^{-5}$$
Using convenient high energy relations with p in \unit{GeV/c}, B in \unit{T}, R in \unit{m},
$$p = 0.3 B R$$
Thus,
$$B = \frac{p}{0.3 R}$$
With p \u2248 E/c and E = 2.5\unit{GeV},
$$B = \frac{2.5}{0.3 \times 30} \unit{T}$$
$$B \approx 0.28 \unit{T}$$
For the energy loss per turn in \unit{keV} (E in \unit{GeV}, R in \unit{m}),
$$\Delta E \approx 88 \frac{E^4}{R} \unit{keV}$$
Thus,
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = 88 \frac{E^3}{R} \times 10^{-6}$$
For E = 2.5\unit{GeV} and R = 30\unit{m},
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{88 \times 2.5^3 \times 10^{-6}}{30}$$
$$\frac{\Delta E}{E} = 4.6 \times 10^{-5}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the ratio ΔE/E as a numerical value (dimensionless), rounded to 2 significant figures. Only the numerical value is required as the final answer.

context: Draw a simple, functional cyclotron magnet in cross section, showing pole pieces of diameter D = 1 \unit{m}, the yoke, and the windings. The spacing between the pole pieces is d = 10 \unit{cm}, and the required magnetic induction in the gap is B = 2 \unit{T} (= 20 \unit{kgauss}). Take the vacuum permeability as \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \unit{N/A^2}. Let N be the number of turns of the coil, I the current through the windings, and N I the required ampere-turns. Let S be the area of each pole piece, R the magnetic reluctance of the gap, and \phi the magnetic flux crossing the gap. Compute N I.
solution:
Figure 4.14 shows the cross section of a cyclotron magnet. The magnetic flux \phi crossing the gap between the pole pieces satisfies

$$
\phi = \frac{N I}{R}
$$

The reluctance of the gap of spacing d and pole area S is

$$
R = \frac{d}{\mu_0 S}
$$

The magnetic induction in the gap is

$$
B = \frac{\phi}{S}
$$

Thus the required ampere-turns are

$$
N I = \phi R
$$

Combining the relations gives

$$
N I = \frac{B d}{\mu_0}
$$

With the given data

$$
B = 2\unit{T}
$$

$$
d = \frac{1}{10}\unit{m}
$$

$$
\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\unit{N/A^2}
$$

the numerical result is

$$
N I = \frac{2 \times \frac{1}{10}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}\unit{A.turn}
$$

$$
N I \approx 1.59 \times 10^5\unit{A.turn}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N I as a numerical value in A.turn (ampere-turns), rounded to 3 significant figures.

context: Space charge in a charged particle beam produces a potential difference between the beam axis and its surface. A 10\unit{mA} beam of 50\unit{keV} protons travels along the axis of an evacuated beam pipe with speed v = 3 \times 10^{6}\unit{m/s}. The beam has a circular cross section of diameter 1\unit{cm}. Assume the current density is uniform over the beam diameter. Let I be the beam current, v the particle speed, R the beam radius, r the radial coordinate within the beam, j the uniform current density, \rho the charge density, E the electric field magnitude at radius r, V the electric potential, \varepsilon_0 the vacuum permittivity, S the beam cross-sectional disk, dS the outward differential area vector on S, and l the length of a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface. Define the desired potential difference as \Delta V = V(0) - V(R). Compute \Delta V.
solution:
Given data
$$I = 10 \times 10^{-3}\unit{A}$$
$$v = 3 \times 10^{6}\unit{m/s}$$
$$R = \frac{1}{2}\unit{cm}$$
$$R = 5 \times 10^{-3}\unit{m}$$
Definition of the quantity to be found
$$\Delta V = V(0) - V(R)$$
Beam current through the cross section
$$I = \int_S j \cdot dS$$
For a circular cross section with uniform j
$$I = \int_0^R j 2 \pi r dr$$
Area form
$$I = \pi R^2 j$$
Relation between current and charge densities
$$j = \rho v$$
Beam charge density
$$\rho = \frac{I}{\pi R^2 v}$$
Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface of radius r and length l
$$2 \pi r l E = \pi r^2 l \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$$
Electric field inside the uniformly charged beam
$$E(r) = \frac{r \rho}{2 \varepsilon_0}$$
Express E(r) in terms of I, v, and R
$$E(r) = \frac{r}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{I}{v R^2}$$
Field-potential relation
$$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$$
Potential difference from axis to surface
$$\Delta V = \int_0^R E(r) dr$$
Substitute E(r)
$$\Delta V = \frac{I}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 v R^2} \int_0^R r dr$$
Evaluate the integral
$$\int_0^R r dr = \frac{R^2}{2}$$
Resulting expression
$$\Delta V = \frac{I}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 v}$$
Numerical constant
$$\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\unit{N\,m^2/C^2}$$
Final numerical result
$$\Delta V = 30\unit{V}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express ΔV as a numerical value in volts (V). Report your result to 1 significant figure.

context: Estimate the ground-level differential cosmic-ray flux per unit area, per unit time, and per unit solid angle. Let Φ_total denote the total flux, Φ_hard the hard component, and Φ_soft the soft component, all measured in counts per unit area per unit time per unit solid angle. Among the following approximate rates per unit area and solid angle, select the closest to the true value at ground level: 1/\unit{year}, 1/\unit{min}, 1/\unit{ms}, 1/\unit{\mu s}, per \unit{cm^{2} sr}.
